title: MULTIPLE TOPICS COMBINED
subject: English Language
rawText:
GOVERNMENT SECONDARY SCHOOL, GWARINPA SS 1 ENGLISH NOTES Word Stress In English, we do not say each syllable with the same force or strength. In one word, we accentuate one syllable. We say one syllable very loudly (big, strong, important) and all the other syllables very quietly. Let's take 3 words: photograph , photographer and photographic . Do they sound the same when spoken? No. Because we accentuate (stress) one syllable in each word. And it is not always the same syllable. So the ‘ shape ’ of each word is different. Listen to these words. Do you hear the stressed syllable in each word? 3 syllables, stressed on #1 PHO - to - graph 4 syllables, stressed on #2 pho - TO - graph - er 4 syllables, stressed on #3 pho - to - GRAPH - ic Some more examples are: 2 syllables, stressed on #1 and #2 Noun Verb 1 Object obJECT 2 Import imPORT 3 TRANSport transPORT Adjective Verb 1 PREsent preSENT

If you use word stress in your speech, you will instantly and automatically improve your pronunciation and your comprehension. There are two very important rules about word stress: 1. One word, one stress. (One word cannot have two stresses. So if you hear two stresses, you have heard two words, not one word.) 2. The stress is always on a vowel. Why is Word Stress Important? Word stress is not an optional extra that you can add to the English language if you want. It is part of the language! example, you do not hear a word clearly, you can still understand the word because of the position of the stress. Think again about the two words photograph and photographer . If you keep a vocabulary book, make a note to show which syllable is stressed. If you do not know, you can look in a dictionary. All dictionaries give the phonetic spelling of a word. This is where they show which syllable is stressed, usually with an apostrophe ( ' ) just before or just after the stressed syllable. (The notes in the dictionary will explain the system used.) Phrase A phrase is a group or combination of two or more words . It is a unit of a complete sentence . By itself, a phrase is not a complete sentence, as it does not

relay a complete thought. It does not contain the subject and the predicate both, so it is not a clause either. The length of the phrase may differ from two words to many more words. This does not have any connection to whether it is a phrase or a sentence. For example “old dog” is a phrase. So is “the old, smelly, shivering dog” is also a phrase. Types of Phrase 1] Noun Phrases These are the phrases contains a noun - name, place or things and at least one modifier associated to the noun. The modifier can prefix or suffix the noun. The entire phrase will act as a noun for that particular sentence. Here are some examples;  He was wearing a black linen shirt .  They lived in a small, tidy cottage .  Alex rode her old bicycle to their shiny new school .  The black car got towed. 2] Verb Phrases Every sentence will generally contain a verb. But somet imes the action being described requires a more nuanced multi - words verb phrase. The phrase consists of the main verb/verbs and then auxiliary verbs , i.e. helping verbs. Some such verb phrases are as follows;  The teacher is writing the answer  They have been playing since the last two hours  You must call your friend at once  He has taken the dog along

3] Prepositional Phrases Any phrase that consists of a preposition and the object of the preposition which will be a noun or a pronoun is what we call a prepositional phrase. Such a phrase also at times consists of other modifiers describing the object of the prepositional phrase. Let us look at some examples;  Students are advised to be on time  Please turn t owards the right at the intersection 4] Infinitive Phrases A phrase that includes an infinitive along with a simple verb is an infinitive phrase. There may also be modifiers attached to the object in the phrase, it contains a verb, so it plays the role of expressing an action in the sentence. Infinitive phrases can act as a noun, adjective or adverb in a complete sentence.  Alex likes to read comics (functions as a noun here)  To attend the morning lecture, I set my alarm for 6 am. (noun form)  To keep his dogs calm, Alex turned on the radio. (functions as an adverb here) 5] Participle Phrases A participle phrase will begin with a participle, which can be a present participle (ending with - ing) or a past participle (ending with - ed). There may be a few modifiers and associated words included in the phrase. One thing to remember is that a participle phrase always takes the form of an adjective in a sentence. Some examples of the participle phrase are;  We got a call from my aunt today telling us the good news .  The house was severely damaged by the flood .  Please sit down without making a sound

6] Gerund Phrases Now a gerund is a word that invariably ends with “ - ing”, without exception. So a gerund phrase is a phrase that contains an ‘ing” word, with some modifiers in some cases. But participle phrases also have a similar pattern ( - ing words), so how do you tell the difference between t he two? Well while participle phrases function as adjectives, Gerund Phrases exclusively function as nouns. Let us look at some examples,  She is currently writing her memoir .  Washing the dishes is Alex’s chore  Waking up before sunrise had become his habit. 7] Absolute Phrases An absolute phrase will contain a noun or a pronoun with a participle. Again it may also contain additional associative words and modifiers. An absolute participle will modify a whole clause, or even a whole sentence, not only one word . However, it does not constitute a complete sentence or a clause. Generally, an absolute phrase is separated by commas. Let us take a look at a few examples;  He looked towards the beggar, his face expressing pity  We were glued to the match, our eyes alway s following the ball .  He sat on the bed, his clothes neatly folded by his side. Vocabulary Development: Islamic Religion 1. ALLAH: The name of the Creator of the universe. 2. AL-HAMDU LILLAH: Means all praise be to Allah. 3. AAYAH: Means verse of the Holy Qur’aan (also a ‘sign’ of Allah) 4. BISMILLAH: ‘In the name of Allah’, this statement is usually made by Muslims who are about to indulge in a task. 5. DAJJAL: Anti-Christ

6. DIIN: Usually translated as ‘religion’. Diin is a comprehensive word which means a total way of life, following the commandments of Allah. 7. DU’A: Supplication: invoking Allah for whatever one desires. 8. EID-AL-FITR: Three day festival marking the end of Ramadaan – the 9th month (the month of fasting). 9. EID-AL-ADHA: The feast of Sacrifice. A four-day festival that completes the rites of pilgrimage and takes place on the 10th-13th of Dhul Hijjah (the last Islamic month). 10. FAATIHA: The opening chapter of the Qur’aan. 11. HADIITH: Sayings and traditions of the Prophet Muhammad 12. HAJJ: Pilgrimage to the Holy city of Makkah. 13. HIJAAB: Veil worn by Muslim women for reasons of modesty and protection. 14. IMAAM: A person who leads the prayer. 15. IMAN: Truthfulness, faithfulness and acceptance. 16. ISLAAM: Literally means ‘submission to the will of Allah’. 17. JAHANNAM: Hell 18. JANNAH: Paradise. 19. JIBRIIL: Angel Gabriel. 20. JINN: A race of created beings that are made out of smokeless fire. 21. KA’BA: Holiest and first house of worship constructed for the worship of Allah. 22. KHUTBA: Sermon. 23. MALAA’IKAH: Angels. 24. MASJID: Mosque (place of worship for the Muslims). 25. MUHAMMAD: The name of the final Messenger and Prophet of Allah to humanity. 26. MUSLIM: Literally means ‘submitter to the will of Allah’. 27. QIBLA: Direction in which all Muslims face when praying, which is the Ka’ba, in Makkah, Saudi Arabia. 28. QUR’AAN: The last revelation of Allah given to humanity, through his last Prophet and Messenger, Muhammad - peace be upon him. 29. RAMADAAN: The month of Fasting, the 9th month of the Islamic Calendar. 30. SAHAABI: Companion of Prophet Muhammad – peace be upon him.

31. SAJDA: Prostration 32. SALAAM: peace 33. SALAAT: Prayer 34. SALLALLAHU ALAIHE WA SALLAM: Means ‘may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him’. This phrase is recited whenever the name of the Prophet Muhammad - peace be upon him is mentioned. 35. SAUM: Fasting 36. SHAHAADA: The creed of Islam; ‘I bear witness that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the final Messenger of Allah. 37. SHAYDAAN: Satan. 38. SHIRK: Associating partners with Allah. The grave sin of Shirk is not forgiven if a person dies in that state. 39. SUBHAN ALLAH: Means ‘Glory be to Allah’. 40. SUURAH: Chapters of the Qur’aan. UMRA: A lesser-pilgrimage to Makkah. 43. WUDU: Purifying with water before performing prayers. 44. ZAKAAT: Obligatory Charity 45. FAJR: Early morning prayer 46. Vocabulary Development: Medicine 1. Anaesthetic : a drug that causes temporary loss of bodily sensations. 2. Blunt : not sharp (used of a knife or other blade). 3. Brace : a support that steadies or strengthens something else. 4. Cast : put or send forth. 5. Casualty : someone injured or died in an accident. 6. Ease : freedom from difficulty or hardship. 7. Filling : any material that fills a space or container.

8. Fracture : breaking of hard tissue such as bone. 9. Indigestion : a stomach disorder characterized by discomfort or pain. 10. Knee Brace : a brace worn to strengthen the knee. 11. Lotion : any of various cosmetic preparations that are applied to the skin. 12. Operating Room : a room in a hospital equipped for the performance of surgical operations. 13. Optician : a worker who makes glasses for remedying defects of vision. 14. Painkiller : a medicine used to relieve pain. 15. Surgery : science treating disease or injury by operative procedures. 25. Syringe : a medical instrument used to inject or withdraw fluids. 26. Syrup : a thick sweet sticky liquid. 27. Tickle : touch (a body part) lightly so as to excite the surface nerves and cause uneasiness, laughter, or spasmodic movements. 28. Tonsil : either of two masses of lymphatic tissue one on each side of the oral pharynx. 29. Tonsillitis : inflammation of the tonsils. 30. Tooth Decay : soft damaged area in a tooth. 31. Walking Stick : a stick carried in the hand for support in walking. 32. Wheelchair : a movable chair mounted on large wheels. 33. Prescribe : issue commands or orders for patient. 34. Reimburse : pay back for some expense incurred. 35. Reimbursement : compensation paid for damages or money already spent. 36. Slippery : causing or tending to cause things to slip or slide. 37. Shoehorn : a device used for easing the foot into a shoe.

38. Velvet : a silky densely piled fabric with a plain back. Creative Writing Creative writing is defined as using words to convey emotion to the reader through imagination and invention. Elements of Creative Writing:  Action  Character  Conflict  Dialogue  Genre  Narration  Plot  Point of view  Scene  Setting  Style  Suspense  Theme  Tone  Voice Pronoun (possessive, Demonstrative) Pronoun is basically a word used in place of noun or noun phrase. Pronoun can be viewed as a replacer of nouns in a sentence. In short, the word ‘ Pronoun ’ means “ on behalf of a noun ”, meaning that it stands for a noun. Possessive Pronoun is used to show that someone owns a particular thing or to show that someone or something is related to another thing. Possessive Pronouns are: yours, hers, mine, theirs, etc. The functions of Possessive pronoun are: (a) Subject of verb (b) Object of verb (c) Complement Demonstrative Pronoun is a kind of pronoun that is usually pointing-out or identifying specific things or people in a sentence. Demonstrative Pronouns are: this ( these ) and that ( those ). The functions of Demonstrative Pronoun are: (a) Singular form, near reference

(b) Singular form, distant reference (c) Plural form, near reference (d) Plural form, distant reference (e) Combination with nouns to form noun phrase The positions in examples: =>This bicycle is his. =>That bicycle is his. =>These tables are too dirty. =>Those tables are too dirty. =>That school has been closed down. Verbs (Regular and Irregular) A lexical verb is said to be regular if its past and past participle are formed by merely adding –d or –ed to the base or root form, while a lexical verb is said to be irregular if its past or past participle are formed in different ways. Examples: Regular verbs: arrive = arrived, achieve = achieved, attend = attended, call = called, carry = carried, etc. Irregular verbs: shake = shook, bite = bit, choose = chosen, begin = began, eat = ate, tear = tore, drive = drove, etc. Adjuncts (Types) Adjuncts are adverbs which answer the questions – how, where, when, why, under what condition, to what degree, how often, for how long, etc. In other words, they are adverbs of time, place/direction, reason/cause, result, purpose, duration, frequency, comparison, condition and concession. Examples: They went to his house yesterday . (time) The food is on the table . (place) She was sacked since she refused to apologise . (reason) He moves proudly . (degree/manner) She stole the money so that she would pay her fees. (result)

He locked the door in order to shut-off air. (purpose) He spent two years in this city. (duration) Children usually cry. (frequency) Michael is wiser than his brother. (comparison) He will relay your message if he sees him. (condition) They laughed whereas I told them not to . (concession) Concord The word ‘concord’ simply means agreement or harmony, it is the agreement which must exist between the subject of a sentence; whether noun, pronoun or its phrase, and the verb or its phrase. The simple and basic rule is singular subject must carry singular verb, while plural subject must carry plural verb. Examples: The boy jumps/the boys jump She likes eating/they like eating Article Writing Articles are written documents that focus on a massive audience to view and conventionally are published in newspapers, journals, books, magazines, etc. Hence, they are considerably shorter than other types of writing like essays or books. Types of Article Every type of article has its objective, writing style, and purpose. Some are published to consider public opinion, while others are used to inform people about certain topics. According to the purpose, article writing is categorised into four major parts. 1. Expository Article Expository article writing focuses on explaining concepts and ideas precisely. It informs the public about the questions raised through information about the topic. The sole purpose of this article is to define the complex part of the information in a simple format.

Examples: “How to guide...” 2. Descriptive Article Descriptive article elaborates and describes a specific topic, information, or event. This article's writing method demands the writer to explain it thoroughly with every minute detail. The article intends to offer the audience an accurate and reliable event picture. Examples: Event descriptions, product reviews, etc. 3. Narrative Article In this type of article writing, writer narrates a story of a topic, information, or an event. Here, the style of writing words should be highly engaging and creative. The key emphasis of the narrative article writing is to drive attention to the article and to offer an engaging experience to the readers. Examples: Biography of famous people, fictional stories, historical events, etc. 4. Persuasive Article Persuasive article is a style that can pursue the views of the user reading or against any information, topic, or event. Creating a hook with a catchy introduction and conclusion is also a part of this writing style. Persuasive writing methods include a convincing representation of an article. It also includes presenting facts and evidence with the topic, offering readers an argumentative opportunity. Examples: Call To Action (CTA), Sales Pitch, etc. How to Write an Article? 1. Choose Topic for Article Writing A good article should discuss a core topic around which everything else revolves. The stronger the topic is, the less likely to move on a tangent while the writing process happens. For example, writing an article to promote a new product, like, ‘sleeping bag’. Without a clear focus, the article can be a collection of vague thoughts that can’t offer anything specific to the reader’s understanding. However, when article talks about ‘how sleeping bags can change the sleeping habits of infants’, it showcases the particular benefits or impacts the product makes for the specific target audience. 2. Understand the Audience

It is important to understand what and why before you write an article. Who is the target audience, what age group do they belong to, what respective professional backgrounds, or which industry do they fall under? All these questionable factors pave the way to making a perfectly planned article. These types of questions should be kept in mind before you get started. You should have a detailed understanding of your audience while you plan the article. With the audience and their behavioural patterns in mind, writer can gather a broad understanding of how the article should head. 3. Conduct Research A well-laid topic research lets you dive deeper, explore valuable insights, and offer the audience reliable and accurate information. To build authority on your articles, ensure you select reliable sources — government reports, academic journals, or publications. Get into the minute details of your topic, understand different viewpoints, and decide on how valuable the article should be. Make a fact check, and give credit to the sources you cite in the article to increase reliability and trust. Also, conduct interviews with the subject matter experts for firsthand knowledge. 4. Create an Outline An outline is an essential part that helps you focus clearly on writing and make the outcome clearer to the audience. The outline can be as simple as a set of subheadings/subtopics, or a long paragraph summary of the article. Another outlining technique is using mind mapping. Structuring an article works best when writer can classify it into similar sections. An article should have a clear introduction and a conclusion. If your introduction focuses on answering a particular query, the conclusion should list the summary points or broad ideas of the answers to that typical question. 5. Write the Draft If one is writing a long article, delve section by section. Take breaks to refresh his/her mind and review the content written. Keep in mind what the article is about and stick close to the outline. If the writer needs to make any significant changes while writing, he/she get back to the outline, make the necessary changes there, and get an overview of how the differences reflect in the final article. After being caught up in the writing process, ensure one does not deviate from the article’s core idea or forget who he/she writes for. Begin every section by tying back to the earlier section. Or begin each section by

referring back to the main topic or idea in the article. Mention sources while including statistics, facts, and figures from an external source. If one is writing an academic article, add citations. 6. Get the Visual Elements Ready An article might not necessarily have visual elements. However, the visual elements, such as images, photographs, embedded videos, illustrations, and info-graphics, can improve an article. In the case of a long article, the visual elements can break the long sections of text, making it highly readable. Also, they can focus on the points made in the article. The decision on whether to accommodate visual elements or not in the article and the number of elements to include in the article depends on capability to create or source the visuals. 7. Revise and Edit The work doesn’t stop after writing the conclusion paragraph. Once the writer finishes his/her first draft, it is time to give article the space for a detailed review. Check the article for grammatical errors. Also, ensure the article is well-structured and every section seamlessly flows into the next. Put yourself in the audience’s shoes while reviewing the article. Also, think back to your article's core topic and idea, and check whether you have stayed on track with the content. You may also get the article reviewed by another person, probably the team member or the proofreading expert for genuine feedback. Format of a Good Article Writing 1. Title A title grabs the attention in the beginning and persuades the reader to go through the article further. With a comp elling title, writer can engage the audience and convey the significance of the article to the reader. For instance, “10 Untold Facts About Artificial Intelligence that Leave You Shocked” grabs attention quickly, which forces the readers to go through the article and explore these hidden facts. 2. Byline The next part is a byline, which appears beneath the title and beholds the author’s name. It helps the author to earn credit for the content he/she has created.

3. Introduction The introduction is as import ant as it offers a clear preview of the content, which makes the audience choose whether to read the article further. This is a gateway to the entire article. 4. Body The part of the content that holds the entire soul of an article is its body. Here, the w riter explains his/her views. It includes paragraphs, and sections that explain the matter. It usually includes the following elements: Sections and headings: Dividing the main content into headings and sections improves the structure and readability of th e article. It classifies the information, which makes the article more accessible and engaging. Heading 1: Heading 1 is also called the H1 tag, it gets reserved specifically for the article’s main title. This is the most important heading, which should pro vide a detailed overview of the content and include the target keyword. It is usually at the top in terms of hierarchy. A page usually contains only one <H1> tag. Heading 2: Also called the H2 tag, it classifies your content into key topics or sections. Th ese give the audience an idea of all the major points you will incorporate in the article. Use them as the outline’s skeleton and to convey the search intent. H2 tags are seen as the next level down in the hierarchy. Heading 3: Also called the H3 tag, thes e subheadings divide main sections into smaller subheadings. They offer specific information to support the H2 heading and make a logical flow. Writer may also subdivide content with H4, H5, and H6 tags. However, writers don’t need to emphasise these tags. Conclusion: The conclusion holds everything together and reminds readers about the key ideas, leaving a deep impression while making the article’s true intent stick in their minds. Speaking to Persuade Persuasion is the process of creating, reinforcing, or changing people’s beliefs or actions.

1. Speeches on Questions of Fact 2. Speeches on Questions of Value 3. Speeches on Questions of Policy 1. Speeches on Questions of Fact: In some ways, a persuasive speech on a question of fact is similar to an informative speech. However, the situation for an informative speech is nonpartisan. The aim is to give information as impartially as possible. The situation for a persuasive speech on a question of fact is partisan. The speaker’s aim is to present one view of the facts as persuasively as possible. There are 3 basic types of questions of fact: historical controversy, questions of current existence and predictions. 2. Speeches on Questions of Value: Persuasive speeches of value depend on a judgement that something is right or wrong, moral or immoral, or better or worse than another thing. The speech should include an appeal, criteria for judgement, and facts that support the appeal using the judgement criteria. 3. Speeches on Questions of Policy: the speaker’s goal is to convince the audience that a given policy is desirable without encouraging the audience to take action in support of the policy. Record Keeping It is the maintenance of a history of one's activities, as personal, educational or financial dealings, by entering data in ledgers or journals, putting documents in files, etc. What is the Importance of Record Keeping? Good recordkeeping can be your proof that you have made considered decisions and taken appropriate actions. Records become your protection if you are questioned or challenged. Without them, you are at risk. Good recordkeeping can not only protect you but can support your organisation in legal or other challenges. Businesses should also keep current and past employee names and addresses, time sheets, and paystubs. Generally, records should also include bank statements, insurance documents, contracts, loans and mortgages, purchase receipts , customer bills, profit and loss statements, and balance sheets.

Some examples of the participle phrase are;  We got a call from my aunt today telling us the good news .  The house was severely damaged by the flood .  Please sit down without making a sound

6] Gerund Phrases Now a gerund is a word that invariably ends with “ - ing”, without exception. So a gerund phrase is a phrase that contains an ‘ing” word, with some modifiers in some cases. But participle phrases also have a similar pattern ( - ing words), so how do you tell the difference between t he two? Well while participle phrases function as adjectives, Gerund Phrases exclusively function as nouns. Let us look at some examples,  She is currently writing her memoir .  Washing the dishes is Alex’s chore  Waking up before sunrise had become his habit. 7] Absolute Phrases An absolute phrase will contain a noun or a pronoun with a participle. Again it may also contain additional associative words and modifiers. An absolute participle will modify a whole clause, or even a whole sentence, not only one word . However, it does not constitute a complete sentence or a clause. Generally, an absolute phrase is separated by commas. Let us take a look at a few examples;  He looked towards the beggar, his face expressing pity  We were glued to the match, our eyes alway s following the ball .  He sat on the bed, his clothes neatly folded by his side. Vocabulary Development: Islamic Religion 1. ALLAH: The name of the Creator of the universe. 2. AL-HAMDU LILLAH: Means all praise be to Allah. 3. AAYAH: Means verse of the Holy Qur’aan (also a ‘sign’ of Allah) 4. BISMILLAH: ‘In the name of Allah’, this statement is usually made by Muslims who are about to indulge in a task. 5. DAJJAL: Anti-Christ

6. DIIN: Usually translated as ‘religion’. Diin is a comprehensive word which means a total way of life, following the commandments of Allah. 7. DU’A: Supplication: invoking Allah for whatever one desires. 8. EID-AL-FITR: Three day festival marking the end of Ramadaan – the 9th month (the month of fasting). 9. EID-AL-ADHA: The feast of Sacrifice. A four-day festival that completes the rites of pilgrimage and takes place on the 10th-13th of Dhul Hijjah (the last Islamic month). 10. FAATIHA: The opening chapter of the Qur’aan. 11. HADIITH: Sayings and traditions of the Prophet Muhammad 12. HAJJ: Pilgrimage to the Holy city of Makkah. 13. HIJAAB: Veil worn by Muslim women for reasons of modesty and protection. 14. IMAAM: A person who leads the prayer. 15. IMAN: Truthfulness, faithfulness and acceptance. 16. ISLAAM: Literally means ‘submission to the will of Allah’. 17. JAHANNAM: Hell 18. JANNAH: Paradise. 19. JIBRIIL: Angel Gabriel. 20. JINN: A race of created beings that are made out of smokeless fire. 21. KA’BA: Holiest and first house of worship constructed for the worship of Allah. 22. KHUTBA: Sermon. 23. MALAA’IKAH: Angels. 24. MASJID: Mosque (place of worship for the Muslims). 25. MUHAMMAD: The name of the final Messenger and Prophet of Allah to humanity. 26. MUSLIM: Literally means ‘submitter to the will of Allah’. 27. QIBLA: Direction in which all Muslims face when praying, which is the Ka’ba, in Makkah, Saudi Arabia. 28. QUR’AAN: The last revelation of Allah given to humanity, through his last Prophet and Messenger, Muhammad - peace be upon him. 29. RAMADAAN: The month of Fasting, the 9th month of the Islamic Calendar. 30. SAHAABI: Companion of Prophet Muhammad – peace be upon him.

31. SAJDA: Prostration 32. SALAAM: peace 33. SALAAT: Prayer 34. SALLALLAHU ALAIHE WA SALLAM: Means ‘may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him’. This phrase is recited whenever the name of the Prophet Muhammad - peace be upon him is mentioned. 35. SAUM: Fasting 36. SHAHAADA: The creed of Islam; ‘I bear witness that there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the final Messenger of Allah. 37. SHAYDAAN: Satan. 38. SHIRK: Associating partners with Allah. The grave sin of Shirk is not forgiven if a person dies in that state. 39. SUBHAN ALLAH: Means ‘Glory be to Allah’. 40. SUURAH: Chapters of the Qur’aan. Qur’aan has 114 Suurah or chapters. 41. TAWHEED: The Divine Unity, in its most profound sense. Allah is One in His Essence and His Attributes and His Acts. 42. UMRA: A lesser-pilgrimage to Makkah. 43. WUDU: Purifying with water before performing prayers. 44. ZAKAAT: Obligatory Charity 45. FAJR: Early morning prayer 46. ZUHR: Noon prayer (early afternoon prayer) 47. ASR: Late afternoon prayer 48. MAGHRIB: Sunset prayer 49. ISHA: Night prayer 50. JUMU’A: ‘Friday’, the Muslim’s day of gathering on Friday noon prayers. Vocabulary Development: Medicine 1. Anaesthetic : a drug that causes temporary loss of bodily sensations. 2. Blunt : not sharp (used of a knife or other blade). 3. Brace : a support that steadies or strengthens something else. 4. Cast : put or send forth. 5. Casualty : someone injured or died in an accident. 6. Ease : freedom from difficulty or hardship. 7. Filling : any material that fills a space or container.

8. Fracture : breaking of hard tissue such as bone. 9. Indigestion : a stomach disorder characterized by discomfort or pain. 10. Knee Brace : a brace worn to strengthen the knee. 11. Lotion : any of various cosmetic preparations that are applied to the skin. 12. Operating Room : a room in a hospital equipped for the performance of surgical operations. 13. Optician : a worker who makes glasses for remedying defects of vision. 14. Painkiller : a medicine used to relieve pain. 15. Prescription : the action of issuing authoritative rules or directions. 16. Prevent : keep from happening or arising; make impossible. 17. Recuperate : restore to good health or strength. 18. Sprain : twist suddenly so as to wrench. 19. Stiff : incapable of or resistant to bending. 20. Stitch : a link or loop made by sewing, knitting, or needlework. 21. Stitchery : needlework on which you are working with needle and thread. 22. Strain : exert much effort or energy. 23. Surgeon : a physician who specializes in surgery. 24. Surgery : science treating disease or injury by operative procedures. 25. Syringe : a medical instrument used to inject or withdraw fluids. 26. Syrup : a thick sweet sticky liquid. 27. Tickle : touch (a body part) lightly so as to excite the surface nerves and cause uneasiness, laughter, or spasmodic movements. 28. Tonsil : either of two masses of lymphatic tissue one on each side of the oral pharynx. 29. Tonsillitis : inflammation of the tonsils. 30. Tooth Decay : soft damaged area in a tooth. 31. Walking Stick : a stick carried in the hand for support in walking. 32. Wheelchair : a movable chair mounted on large wheels. 33. Prescribe : issue commands or orders for patient. 34. Reimburse : pay back for some expense incurred. 35. Reimbursement : compensation paid for damages or money already spent. 36. Slippery : causing or tending to cause things to slip or slide. 37. Shoehorn : a device used for easing the foot into a shoe.

38. Velvet : a silky densely piled fabric with a plain back. Creative Writing Creative writing is defined as using words to convey emotion to the reader through imagination and invention. Elements of Creative Writing:  Action  Character  Conflict  Dialogue  Genre  Narration  Plot  Point of view  Scene  Setting  Style  Suspense  Theme  Tone  Voice Pronoun (possessive, Demonstrative) Pronoun is basically a word used in place of noun or noun phrase. Pronoun can be viewed as a replacer of nouns in a sentence. In short, the word ‘ Pronoun ’ means “ on behalf of a noun ”, meaning that it stands for a noun. Possessive Pronoun is used to show that someone owns a particular thing or to show that someone or something is related to another thing. Possessive Pronouns are: yours, hers, mine, theirs, etc. The functions of Possessive pronoun are: (a) Subject of verb (b) Object of verb (c) Complement Demonstrative Pronoun is a kind of pronoun that is usually pointing-out or identifying specific things or people in a sentence. Demonstrative Pronouns are: this ( these ) and that ( those ). The functions of Demonstrative Pronoun are: (a) Singular form, near reference

(b) Singular form, distant reference (c) Plural form, near reference (d) Plural form, distant reference (e) Combination with nouns to form noun phrase The positions in examples: =>This bicycle is his. =>That bicycle is his. =>These tables are too dirty. =>Those tables are too dirty. =>That school has been closed down. Verbs (Regular and Irregular) A lexical verb is said to be regular if its past and past participle are formed by merely adding –d or –ed to the base or root form, while a lexical verb is said to be irregular if its past or past participle are formed in different ways. Examples: Regular verbs: arrive = arrived, achieve = achieved, attend = attended, call = called, carry = carried, etc. Irregular verbs: shake = shook, bite = bit, choose = chosen, begin = began, eat = ate, tear = tore, drive = drove, etc. Adjuncts (Types) Adjuncts are adverbs which answer the questions – how, where, when, why, under what condition, to what degree, how often, for how long, etc. In other words, they are adverbs of time, place/direction, reason/cause, result, purpose, duration, frequency, comparison, condition and concession. Examples: They went to his house yesterday . (time) The food is on the table . (place) She was sacked since she refused to apologise . (reason) He moves proudly . (degree/manner) She stole the money so that she would pay her fees. (result)

He locked the door in order to shut-off air. (purpose) He spent two years in this city. (duration) Children usually cry. (frequency) Michael is wiser than his brother. (comparison) He will relay your message if he sees him. (condition) They laughed whereas I told them not to . (concession) Concord The word ‘concord’ simply means agreement or harmony, it is the agreement which must exist between the subject of a sentence; whether noun, pronoun or its phrase, and the verb or its phrase. The simple and basic rule is singular subject must carry singular verb, while plural subject must carry plural verb. Examples: The boy jumps/the boys jump She likes eating/they like eating Article Writing Articles are written documents that focus on a massive audience to view and conventionally are published in newspapers, journals, books, magazines, etc. Hence, they are considerably shorter than other types of writing like essays or books. Types of Article Every type of article has its objective, writing style, and purpose. Some are published to consider public opinion, while others are used to inform people about certain topics. According to the purpose, article writing is categorised into four major parts. 1. Expository Article Expository article writing focuses on explaining concepts and ideas precisely. It informs the public about the questions raised through information about the topic. The sole purpose of this article is to define the complex part of the information in a simple format.

Examples: “How to guide...” 2. Descriptive Article Descriptive article elaborates and describes a specific topic, information, or event. This article's writing method demands the writer to explain it thoroughly with every minute detail. The article intends to offer the audience an accurate and reliable event picture. Examples: Event descriptions, product reviews, etc. 3. Narrative Article In this type of article writing, writer narrates a story of a topic, information, or an event. Here, the style of writing words should be highly engaging and creative. The key emphasis of the narrative article writing is to drive attention to the article and to offer an engaging experience to the readers. Examples: Biography of famous people, fictional stories, historical events, etc. 4. Persuasive Article Persuasive article is a style that can pursue the views of the user reading or against any information, topic, or event. Creating a hook with a catchy introduction and conclusion is also a part of this writing style. Persuasive writing methods include a convincing representation of an article. It also includes presenting facts and evidence with the topic, offering readers an argumentative opportunity. Examples: Call To Action (CTA), Sales Pitch, etc. How to Write an Article? 1. Choose Topic for Article Writing A good article should discuss a core topic around which everything else revolves. The stronger the topic is, the less likely to move on a tangent while the writing process happens. For example, writing an article to promote a new product, like, ‘sleeping bag’. Without a clear focus, the article can be a collection of vague thoughts that can’t offer anything specific to the reader’s understanding. However, when article talks about ‘how sleeping bags can change the sleeping habits of infants’, it showcases the particular benefits or impacts the product makes for the specific target audience. 2. Understand the Audience

It is important to understand what and why before you write an article. Who is the target audience, what age group do they belong to, what respective professional backgrounds, or which industry do they fall under? All these questionable factors pave the way to making a perfectly planned article. These types of questions should be kept in mind before you get started. You should have a detailed understanding of your audience while you plan the article. With the audience and their behavioural patterns in mind, writer can gather a broad understanding of how the article should head. 3. Conduct Research A well-laid topic research lets you dive deeper, explore valuable insights, and offer the audience reliable and accurate information. To build authority on your articles, ensure you select reliable sources — government reports, academic journals, or publications. Get into the minute details of your topic, understand different viewpoints, and decide on how valuable the article should be. Make a fact check, and give credit to the sources you cite in the article to increase reliability and trust. Also, conduct interviews with the subject matter experts for firsthand knowledge. 4. Create an Outline An outline is an essential part that helps you focus clearly on writing and make the outcome clearer to the audience. The outline can be as simple as a set of subheadings/subtopics, or a long paragraph summary of the article. Another outlining technique is using mind mapping. Structuring an article works best when writer can classify it into similar sections. An article should have a clear introduction and a conclusion. If your introduction focuses on answering a particular query, the conclusion should list the summary points or broad ideas of the answers to that typical question. 5. Write the Draft If one is writing a long article, delve section by section. Take breaks to refresh his/her mind and review the content written. Keep in mind what the article is about and stick close to the outline. If the writer needs to make any significant changes while writing, he/she get back to the outline, make the necessary changes there, and get an overview of how the differences reflect in the final article. After being caught up in the writing process, ensure one does not deviate from the article’s core idea or forget who he/she writes for. Begin every section by tying back to the earlier section. Or begin each section by

referring back to the main topic or idea in the article. Mention sources while including statistics, facts, and figures from an external source. If one is writing an academic article, add citations. 6. Get the Visual Elements Ready An article might not necessarily have visual elements. However, the visual elements, such as images, photographs, embedded videos, illustrations, and info-graphics, can improve an article. In the case of a long article, the visual elements can break the long sections of text, making it highly readable. Also, they can focus on the points made in the article. The decision on whether to accommodate visual elements or not in the article and the number of elements to include in the article depends on capability to create or source the visuals. 7. Revise and Edit The work doesn’t stop after writing the conclusion paragraph. Once the writer finishes his/her first draft, it is time to give article the space for a detailed review. Check the article for grammatical errors. Also, ensure the article is well-structured and every section seamlessly flows into the next. Put yourself in the audience’s shoes while reviewing the article. Also, think back to your article's core topic and idea, and check whether you have stayed on track with the content. You may also get the article reviewed by another person, probably the team member or the proofreading expert for genuine feedback. Format of a Good Article Writing 1. Title A title grabs the attention in the beginning and persuades the reader to go through the article further. With a comp elling title, writer can engage the audience and convey the significance of the article to the reader. For instance, “10 Untold Facts About Artificial Intelligence that Leave You Shocked” grabs attention quickly, which forces the readers to go through the article and explore these hidden facts. 2. Byline The next part is a byline, which appears beneath the title and beholds the author’s name. It helps the author to earn credit for the content he/she has created.

3. Introduction The introduction is as import ant as it offers a clear preview of the content, which makes the audience choose whether to read the article further. This is a gateway to the entire article. 4. Body The part of the content that holds the entire soul of an article is its body. Here, the w riter explains his/her views. It includes paragraphs, and sections that explain the matter. It usually includes the following elements: Sections and headings: Dividing the main content into headings and sections improves the structure and readability of th e article. It classifies the information, which makes the article more accessible and engaging. Heading 1: Heading 1 is also called the H1 tag, it gets reserved specifically for the article’s main title. This is the most important heading, which should pro vide a detailed overview of the content and include the target keyword. It is usually at the top in terms of hierarchy. A page usually contains only one <H1> tag. Heading 2: Also called the H2 tag, it classifies your content into key topics or sections. Th ese give the audience an idea of all the major points you will incorporate in the article. Use them as the outline’s skeleton and to convey the search intent. H2 tags are seen as the next level down in the hierarchy. Heading 3: Also called the H3 tag, thes e subheadings divide main sections into smaller subheadings. They offer specific information to support the H2 heading and make a logical flow. Writer may also subdivide content with H4, H5, and H6 tags. However, writers don’t need to emphasise these tags. Conclusion: The conclusion holds everything together and reminds readers about the key ideas, leaving a deep impression while making the article’s true intent stick in their minds. Speaking to Persuade Persuasion is the process of creating, reinforcing, or changing people’s beliefs or actions.

1. Speeches on Questions of Fact 2. Speeches on Questions of Value 3. Speeches on Questions of Policy 1. Speeches on Questions of Fact: In some ways, a persuasive speech on a question of fact is similar to an informative speech. However, the situation for an informative speech is nonpartisan. The aim is to give information as impartially as possible. The situation for a persuasive speech on a question of fact is partisan. The speaker’s aim is to present one view of the facts as persuasively as possible. There are 3 basic types of questions of fact: historical controversy, questions of current existence and predictions. 2. Speeches on Questions of Value: Persuasive speeches of value depend on a judgement that something is right or wrong, moral or immoral, or better or worse than another thing. The speech should include an appeal, criteria for judgement, and facts that support the appeal using the judgement criteria. 3. Speeches on Questions of Policy: the speaker’s goal is to convince the audience that a given policy is desirable without encouraging the audience to take action in support of the policy. Record Keeping It is the maintenance of a history of one's activities, as personal, educational or financial dealings, by entering data in ledgers or journals, putting documents in files, etc. What is the Importance of Record Keeping? Good recordkeeping can be your proof that you have made considered decisions and taken appropriate actions. Records become your protection if you are questioned or challenged. Without them, you are at risk. Good recordkeeping can not only protect you but can support your organisation in legal or other challenges. Businesses should also keep current and past employee names and addresses, time sheets, and paystubs. Generally, records should also include bank statements, insurance documents, contracts, loans and mortgages, purchase receipts , customer bills, profit and loss statements, and balance sheets.

title: PHRASE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Phrase A phrase is a group of related words standing together as a unit within the syntax of a sentence. Phrases function as parts of speech within a sentence thus; a sentence is made up of phrases. How to Identify a Phrase  If the verb in the sentence starts with ‘to’ then it is a non-finite verb thus, a phrase. Example. He is always ready to fight anybody To pass examination is hard work  If the verb functions as an adjective, it is a non-finite verb and therefore a phrase. Example I have boiled yam in my pot The flying horse is bad  If the verb in the sentence is in the ‘ing form’ then it is a phrase. Example Eating late is what I hate I saw the boy going to school Types of Phrases  The Noun phrase.  The Adjectival phrase.  The Verb phrase  The Adverbial phrase and  The prepositional phrase. The Noun Phrase A noun phrase is a phrase that has the noun or pronoun as its head word. It can be a single noun, a noun + a pronoun, a noun + determiner, a noun + a preposition, a noun + a post modifier. Eg. A single Noun = boy Noun + a determiner/article = the boy, a cap, an umbrella Noun + a pronoun = my brother, your umbrella, her car Noun + a post modifier = Noun + preposition = behind the door A noun phrase has the noun or pronoun as its head word and can be pre-modified by an article/determiner, an adjective, a pronoun and preposition. The pronoun can be possessive or demonstrative. Eg. Your umbrella That umbrella. The noun phrase can also be post modified by adjective, prepositional phrase, or adjectival/relative clause. In example (1) the noun phrase is pre-modified by the definite article ‘ the ’.

In example (2) the noun phrase is pre-modified by the possessive pronoun ‘ your ’. In example (3) the noun phrase is pre-modified by the demonstrative pronoun ‘ that ’. Eg. Something terrible has happened. Here, ‘ terrible ’ is an adjective and a post modifier of the noun phrase ‘ something ’. Thus in this case, we have a pronoun ‘ something ’ as the head word of the noun phrase. Eg. The boy in the room is my nephew. Here, the noun phrase, ‘ the boy ’ is post modified by the prepositional phrase ‘ in the room ’. Eg. The boy who came in is my uncle’s son. Here, we have an adjective or a relative clause ‘ who came in ’ functioning as a post modifier of the noun phrase ‘ the boy ’. Grammatical Functions of the Noun Phrase 1. A noun phrase functions as the subject of the verb in a sentence. A subject is a word or phrase which performs the action or acts upon the verb in a sentence. The following are examples of noun phrase functioning as the subject of the verb in a sentence. - The armed robbers have invaded the city. - The boy in the room is my friend. 2. A noun phrase functions as object of the verb in a sentence. -I met the new English teacher = here, ‘ the new English teacher’ is the noun phrase functioning as the object of the verb ‘ met ’. -His dad suspended the programme. -The man bought a T-shirt. 3. A noun phrase functions as object complement of preposition. When a noun phrase functions as object complement of preposition, it comes immediately after the preposition. -The boy behind the door is a thief. Here, you have ‘ the door ’ functioning as the complement of the preposition ‘ behind ’. -The little girl gave her pen to her brother . Here, ‘ her brother ’ is the noun phrase complementing the preposition ’ to ’. 4. The noun phrase functions as object complement. An object complement is a word, phrase or clause that directly follows and describes the direct object of a sentence. -We made him our class representative . Here, ‘ our class representative ’ is the noun phrase functioning as the complement of the object ’ him ’ in the sentence. 5. A noun phrase also functions as subject complement. -The brilliant girl is my friend . Here, ‘ my friend ’ which is a noun phrase functions as the complement of the subject, the brilliant girl . -John is a student . Here, ‘ a student ’ is the complement of the entire sentence.

6. The noun phrase functions as an appositive. An appositive is a word, phrase or clause that modifies or gives more information about the subject in a sentence. -Mr. Tammy, our new English teacher is a good teacher. Here, ‘ our new English teacher ’ which is a noun phrase is in apposition to the noun phrase ‘ Mr. Tammy ’. -2baba, the musician is very rich. Here, ‘ the musician ’ is in apposition to the noun phrase ‘ 2baba ’. Adjectival Phrase An adjectival phrase is a word or group of words that act as an adjective in a sentence to give more information about a noun or pronoun. Adjective phrase usually starts with an adjective, adverb or preposition. Example: My dog was extremely tired after going on a hike with me. The car covered in mud is mine. She wore very expensive shoes. Grammatical Functions of the Adjectival Phrase 1. It functions as attributive adjectives. Attributive adjective phrase typically sits before te noun it modifies. Example: fat men seldom run fast. The slim lady is my wife. 2. Adjectival phrase functions as predicative. A predicative adjective comes after the noun it modifies using linking verb. Example: those questions are tough The man looks stupid. 3. Adjectival phrase functions as post modifiers. Example: the boy with a brown cap is my class mate. The fund available will not be enough for the project. 4. Adjectival phrase functions as nouns. Example: The rich are usually unmindful of the poor. The government should cater for the needy. 5. Adjectival phrase functions as the complement to a finite or non-finite clause. Example: To speak in class is very difficult for some students. Here, ‘ very difficult ’ is an adjectival phrase functioning as complement to the non-finite clause ‘ to speak in class ’ -What he did is totally unacceptable . Here, ‘ totally unacceptable ’ is an adjectival phrase which complements the finite clause ‘ what he did ’. 6. Adjectival phrases pre-modify nouns, Example: Extremely loud sound. Very intelligent young man.

7. Adjectival phrases functions as subject complement and object complement. Example: The singer is exceptionally good. Here, ‘ exceptionally good ’ is an adjectival phrase complementing ‘ the singer ’ which is the subject of the sentence. He made his children very useful. Here, ‘ very useful ’ is an adjectival phrase complementing ‘ his children ’ which is the object of the sentence. Adverbial Phrase Adverbial phrase is a phrase that has the adverb as its head word. An adverb phrase consists of one or more words. The adverb is the head of the phrase and can appear alone or it can be modified by a fellow adverb or even an entire sentence. Grammatical Functions of the Adverb phrase 1. It functions as a modifier in an adjectival phrase. In the instances below. - Your piercingly loud scream has broken the silence. Here, ‘ piercingly ’ is an adverbial phrase pre-modifying the adjectival phase, ‘ loud ’ in the sentence. - Employees who are regularly absent will be disciplined. 2. It functions as a head in adverbial phrase. Eg. Quite separately. Here, ‘separately’ which is also an adverb is functioning as the head in the adverbial phrase ‘ quite separately ’. Other examples are; Incredibly quickly Quickly enough 3. It functions as modifier in adverbial phrase. Eg. Quite separately (we kept the money quite separately ) Really carefully (he drives really carefully ) 4. It functions as a modifier of verb. Eg. He sings very well . Here, ‘ very well’ is an adverbial phrase modifying the verb ‘ sings ’ I eat quite healthy . Here, ‘ quite healthy ’ is an adverbial phrase modifying the verb ‘ eat ’. 5. It functions as adverbial. Adverbial is a word, phrase or clause that modifies a verb, an adjective or an entire clause by providing information such as time, place, manner, reason, condition, frequency and concession. Eg. Husbands should speak for their wives adoringly (manner) Ade drove the car outside (place) They almost never invite people to their house these days.(degree) Verb Phrase

A verb phrase is headed by a verb. It functions primarily as predicate in the structure of a clause/sentence. The verb phrase like other phrases has a modifier and a head word. The modifier is an optional element while the head word is an obligatory element. Lexical verbs functions as head word in the structure of a verb phrase whereas auxiliary verbs functions as modifiers in the structure of a verb phrase. In the examples below, the heads are emboldened while the modifiers are not.

A noun phrase functions as object complement of preposition. When a noun phrase functions as object complement of preposition, it comes immediately after the preposition. -The boy behind the door is a thief. Here, you have ‘ the door ’ functioning as the complement of the preposition ‘ behind ’. -The little girl gave her pen to her brother . Here, ‘ her brother ’ is the noun phrase complementing the preposition ’ to ’. 4. The noun phrase functions as object complement. An object complement is a word, phrase or clause that directly follows and describes the direct object of a sentence. -We made him our class representative . Here, ‘ our class representative ’ is the noun phrase functioning as the complement of the object ’ him ’ in the sentence. 5. A noun phrase also functions as subject complement. -The brilliant girl is my friend . Here, ‘ my friend ’ which is a noun phrase functions as the complement of the subject, the brilliant girl . -John is a student . Here, ‘ a student ’ is the complement of the entire sentence.

6. The noun phrase functions as an appositive. An appositive is a word, phrase or clause that modifies or gives more information about the subject in a sentence. -Mr. Tammy, our new English teacher is a good teacher. Here, ‘ our new English teacher ’ which is a noun phrase is in apposition to the noun phrase ‘ Mr. Tammy ’. -2baba, the musician is very rich. Here, ‘ the musician ’ is in apposition to the noun phrase ‘ 2baba ’. Adjectival Phrase An adjectival phrase is a word or group of words that act as an adjective in a sentence to give more information about a noun or pronoun. Adjective phrase usually starts with an adjective, adverb or preposition. Example: My dog was extremely tired after going on a hike with me. The car covered in mud is mine. She wore very expensive shoes. Grammatical Functions of the Adjectival Phrase 1. It functions as attributive adjectives. Attributive adjective phrase typically sits before te noun it modifies. Example: fat men seldom run fast. The slim lady is my wife. 2. Adjectival phrase functions as predicative. A predicative adjective comes after the noun it modifies using linking verb. Example: those questions are tough The man looks stupid. 3. Adjectival phrase functions as post modifiers. Example: the boy with a brown cap is my class mate. The fund available will not be enough for the project. 4. Adjectival phrase functions as nouns. Example: The rich are usually unmindful of the poor. The government should cater for the needy. 5. Adjectival phrase functions as the complement to a finite or non-finite clause. Example: To speak in class is very difficult for some students. Here, ‘ very difficult ’ is an adjectival phrase functioning as complement to the non-finite clause ‘ to speak in class ’ -What he did is totally unacceptable . Here, ‘ totally unacceptable ’ is an adjectival phrase which complements the finite clause ‘ what he did ’. 6. Adjectival phrases pre-modify nouns, Example: Extremely loud sound. Very intelligent young man.

7. Adjectival phrases functions as subject complement and object complement. Example: The singer is exceptionally good. Here, ‘ exceptionally good ’ is an adjectival phrase complementing ‘ the singer ’ which is the subject of the sentence. He made his children very useful. Here, ‘ very useful ’ is an adjectival phrase complementing ‘ his children ’ which is the object of the sentence. Adverbial Phrase Adverbial phrase is a phrase that has the adverb as its head word. An adverb phrase consists of one or more words. The adverb is the head of the phrase and can appear alone or it can be modified by a fellow adverb or even an entire sentence. Grammatical Functions of the Adverb phrase 1. It functions as a modifier in an adjectival phrase. In the instances below. - Your piercingly loud scream has broken the silence. Here, ‘ piercingly ’ is an adverbial phrase pre-modifying the adjectival phase, ‘ loud ’ in the sentence. - Employees who are regularly absent will be disciplined. 2. It functions as a head in adverbial phrase. Eg. Quite separately. Here, ‘separately’ which is also an adverb is functioning as the head in the adverbial phrase ‘ quite separately ’. Other examples are; Incredibly quickly Quickly enough 3. It functions as modifier in adverbial phrase. Eg. Quite separately (we kept the money quite separately ) Really carefully (he drives really carefully ) 4. It functions as a modifier of verb. Eg. He sings very well . Here, ‘ very well’ is an adverbial phrase modifying the verb ‘ sings ’ I eat quite healthy . Here, ‘ quite healthy ’ is an adverbial phrase modifying the verb ‘ eat ’. 5. It functions as adverbial. Adverbial is a word, phrase or clause that modifies a verb, an adjective or an entire clause by providing information such as time, place, manner, reason, condition, frequency and concession. Eg. Husbands should speak for their wives adoringly (manner) Ade drove the car outside (place) They almost never invite people to their house these days.(degree) Verb Phrase

A verb phrase is headed by a verb. It functions primarily as predicate in the structure of a clause/sentence. The verb phrase like other phrases has a modifier and a head word. The modifier is an optional element while the head word is an obligatory element. Lexical verbs functions as head word in the structure of a verb phrase whereas auxiliary verbs functions as modifiers in the structure of a verb phrase. In the examples below, the heads are emboldened while the modifiers are not.

title: ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText:
Argumentative Essay Argument is the process of organizing and stating objectively and dispassionately the facts and reasons surrounding a particular stand or point of view. In many cases, the argumentative essay attempts to influence and persuade the reader/listener to the author’s opinions on a particular issue and even to effect a change in the behavior of others. For an argument to be effective, it must be relatively objective, well organized and logical. Similar principles apply in informal argument as in the different forms of daily arguments between classmates, brothers, sisters or market people. They each require that u list your reasons why or why not. Marshalling out your reasons ahead of time helps clarify your thinking, lends force and conviction to what you have to say as well as provide unity and coherence to your thought. Reasons for Argument 1. One may have a need to justify one’s opinions ad ideas o a particular issue or topic 2. A individual may hope to effect certain changes I a situation that one feels very strongly about. Eg electing a particular candidate, exposing injustice I a system, changing certain rules in an institution etc. 3. Most of the positive changes we see around us are as a result of someone’s argument for such changes to e made. Strategies for Effective Argument 1. Effective argument must be grounded on facts, verifiable and accurate statistics as arguments is weighed by reasons and not by verbosity. 2. Effective argument should be presented in a well organized form (introduction with a thesis, paragraphs that develops topic sentences of the thesis ad a conclusion that summarizes the argument ad restates the thesis). 3. An effective argument must be presented objectively without passion or vehemence. 4. An argument must be based on sound logic ie it must avoid any emotive language, personal attacks, over simplification and generalizations. Its conclusion must be valid and true. 5. An effective argument must anticipates the possible points of the opposition in order to conquer them by over whelming them with greater facts and figures. How to Organize an Argumentative Essay 1. Arrange your reasons in either a chronological or a logical order (according to relative importance, usually with the strongest point at the end for climatic effect). 2. Your introductory paragraph should include background information on the topic, a definition of ay important term. It must also include a thesis statement, stating clearly what you intend to argue, followed by a summary of the major points you are going to advance in the order in which they will be treated. 3. In the body of the essay, each major point should e developed I one or a number of paragraph to the ext

4. The conclusion should contain a summary of your position as well as final rounding off argument. At this point, the thesis statement should be restated in new terms. Suggested Topics for Argumentative Essay 1. Young me are the most reckless drivers 2. The Nigeria oil boom is not blessing 3. All men are equal 4. Teachers are more essential in a community than doctors 5. Students should take active part in politics. Debate/Argumentative Essay A debate is an interactive and positive presentation in which two or more present their argument or persuade others to accept their point of view. It shows skill and ability in argument. Criteria for Debate 1. Timing: the debate must be made within the specified time frame allocated. Thus the need for a time keeper 2. Presentation: the manner adopted in communicating ones ideas/views, there should be;  Content: sufficient information relevant to the topic  Organization: give a definite statement of facts supported by, experience, history or literature neatly presented on paragraphs. Let each paragraph end with a conclusion drawn from the fact. As usual, the normal debate greeting should be observed accordingly. While the introductory paragraph should be interesting and captivating enough to arrest the attention of the reader/audience.  Human elements used as examples  Expressing your argument should be as clear as possible. Figures of speech could be of great advantage if properly used. 3. Accuracy of points: your points must be generally acceptable with facts to support your views. 4. Elocution: oral delivery which involves adequate voice control, correct pronunciation. Your voice should be clear without fear. 5. Comportment: confidence to deliver with body movement without tension. 6. Appearance: your outlook, neatness and proper dressing Guidelines for Debate 1. The Greetings eg. Mr Chairman, Panel of Judges, Moderator, Accurate time keeper, Fellow students, Distinguished guests, Ladies and Gentlemen.

2. State your vocatives 3. Define content 4. Make sure you are convinced about the side you support if not, you will run out of points. 5. Do not draw conclusion from one example 6. Oppose or counter your opponents points 7. Use polite language 8. Use rhetorical questions 9. As u end your points, say thank you 10. Strongly urge your audience to tow your line of argument.

title: NOUN CLAUSE
subject: English Language
rawText: SS1 English Language Handout Topic: Noun Clauses What is a Noun Clause? 📘 A noun clause is a group of words that acts as a noun in a sentence. It can be the subject, object, or complement in a sentence. Examples and Their Functions 📍 Sentence Function of the Noun Clause What you said is true. Subject I believe that she will come. Object The fact is that he passed. Complement Common Noun Clause Starters: 🧠 - that - what / whatever - who / whoever / whom - when, where, why, how - whether / if How to Identify a Noun Clause: 🛠 ✔ It begins with special words like "that," "what," or "who" ✔ It can be replaced with "something" or "someone" ✔ It answers what?, who?, or whom? ✏ Practice Exercises A. Underline the noun clause in each sentence and state its function: 1. What you did was wrong. 2. She knows that you lied. 3. That he is honest is clear to all. 4. The teacher asked who was absent. 5. I wonder if he will come. B. Fill in the blanks with a suitable noun clause: 1. I don’t know _____________________. 2. ___________________ makes me happy. 3. They said ____________________ was late. 4. My worry is ______________________. 5. The truth is _______________________.

title: ADJUNCT
subject: English Language
rawText:
Adjunct Adjunct is any adverb, adverbial clause, adverbial phrase or prepositional phrase that adds extra meaning/information to a sentence thus, if Adjunct is removed from a sentence, the sentence will still remain grammatically correct. Hence, adjunct is not an essentially part of a sentence but are there to make it more meaningful. Specifically, Adjuncts are usually adverbs used to modify verbs, another adverb or even a complement. Adjuncts when used as an adverb will usually indicate time, place, reason, frequency, manner or degree of action. Example; 1. Ada slapped Ike in the gallery (place) 2. My sister travelled to Abuja yesterday (time) 3. He screamed angrily (manner) In the examples stated above, the three sentences are still complete even without the underlined part. Adverbial is different from Adjunct in that, Adjunct is a type of Adverbial which add OPTIONAL information to a sentence while Adverbials add information that are RELEVANT to the overall meaning of a sentence. Example; 1. I put my bag on the floor = Adverbial 2. I dropped my bag next to my seat and sat down = Adjunct In the instances above, one will observe that the first sentence is incomplete without the extra information whereas, in the second sentence, the underlined information is not necessary in making the sentence complete thus it is a complete sentence even without the underlined aspect.  I put my bag (incomplete sentence). Thus, the Adverbial adds information relevant in making the sentence to be complete and meaningful.  I dropped my bag and sat down. (Complete sentence). Here, the sentence can stand with or without the underlined information Types of Adjuncts 1. Adjunct of Time Example; we shall meet after the break. In the morning I will cross the bridge. The alarm went off yesterday. 2. Adjunct of Place Example; Mr. Smith is having his leisure in the stadium. Thompson’s car is packed at the garage. Mum is relaxing outside the house.

Ere, te situation is completely different. 3. Adjunct of Manner Example; the news of his demise came as a thunderbolt. I travelled to Lagos in Obedience. She handled the case carefully. 4. Adjunct of Frequency or Degree Example; he comes to school always. He seldom visits his grandmother We occasionally travel together. 5. Adjunct of Reason Example; he did it for God’s sake. The little boy came to the field to play football. They were flogged because they fought. As its Friday, you can stay up another hour. 6. Adjunct of Degree: te structure (as + adverb + as) is used to express tat two persons or tins are equal or not equal in degree or intensity Example: you are not as poor as you could ave been. She is as smart as she is brilliant.

title: ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText:
Argumentative Essay Argument is the process of organizing and stating objectively and dispassionately the facts and reasons surrounding a particular stand or point of view. In many cases, the argumentative essay attempts to influence and persuade the reader/listener to the author’s opinions on a particular issue and even to effect a change in the behavior of others. For an argument to be effective, it must be relatively objective, well organized and logical. Similar principles apply in informal argument as in the different forms of daily arguments between classmates, brothers, sisters or market people. They each require that u list your reasons why or why not. Marshalling out your reasons ahead of time helps clarify your thinking, lends force and conviction to what you have to say as well as provide unity and coherence to your thought. Reasons for Argument 1. One may have a need to justify one’s opinions ad ideas o a particular issue or topic 2. A individual may hope to effect certain changes I a situation that one feels very strongly about. Eg electing a particular candidate, exposing injustice I a system, changing certain rules in an institution etc. 3. Most of the positive changes we see around us are as a result of someone’s argument for such changes to e made. Strategies for Effective Argument 1. Effective argument must be grounded on facts, verifiable and accurate statistics as arguments is weighed by reasons and not by verbosity. 2. Effective argument should be presented in a well organized form (introduction with a thesis, paragraphs that develops topic sentences of the thesis ad a conclusion that summarizes the argument ad restates the thesis). 3. An effective argument must be presented objectively without passion or vehemence. 4. An argument must be based on sound logic ie it must avoid any emotive language, personal attacks, over simplification and generalizations. Its conclusion must be valid and true. 5. An effective argument must anticipates the possible points of the opposition in order to conquer them by over whelming them with greater facts and figures. How to Organize an Argumentative Essay 1. Arrange your reasons in either a chronological or a logical order (according to relative importance, usually with the strongest point at the end for climatic effect). 2. Your introductory paragraph should include background information on the topic, a definition of ay important term. In the body of the essay, each major point should e developed I one or a number of paragraph to the ext

Presentation: the manner adopted in communicating ones ideas/views, there should be;  Content: sufficient information relevant to the topic  Organization: give a definite statement of facts supported by, experience, history or literature neatly presented on paragraphs. Let each paragraph end with a conclusion drawn from the fact. As usual, the normal debate greeting should be observed accordingly. While the introductory paragraph should be interesting and captivating enough to arrest the attention of the reader/audience.  Human elements used as examples  Expressing your argument should be as clear as possible. Figures of speech could be of great advantage if properly used. 3. Accuracy of points: your points must be generally acceptable with facts to support your views. 4. Elocution: oral delivery which involves adequate voice control, correct pronunciation. Your voice should be clear without fear. 5. Comportment: confidence to deliver with body movement without tension. 6. Appearance: your outlook, neatness and proper dressing Guidelines for Debate 1. The Greetings eg. Mr Chairman, Panel of Judges, Moderator, Accurate time keeper, Fellow students, Distinguished guests, Ladies and Gentlemen.

2. State your vocatives 3. Define content 4. Make sure you are convinced about the side you support if not, you will run out of points. 5. Do not draw conclusion from one example 6. Oppose or counter your opponents points 7. Use polite language 8. Use rhetorical questions 9. As u end your points, say thank you 10. Strongly urge your audience to tow your line of argument.

title: INFORMAL LETTER
subject: English Language
rawText: Informal Letter An Informal Letter is also known as a Personal Letter. It is a kind of letter that is often written to people that are related or close to us in one way or another. It could be letters written to our family members like our parents, siblings, our relatives and also friends. Just as the name implies, informal letters are usually informal in nature that is, the writer can chose to use words in an informal way since the reader is known to the writer and thus, certain degree of cordial relationship has already been established by both individuals. Features of Informal Letter 1. The Writers Address (At the right hand side of the paper) 2. Date 3. Salutation eg (Dear mother/father) etc 4. Body of the Letter 5. Complimentary Close 6. First name of the writer (At the right hand side of the paper) Semi-Formal Letter A semi-formal letter is a letter that falls in between formal and informal letters in terms of tone and language. The semi-formal letters can be written to your teachers, boss, colleagues, neighbors, business associate, etc. they include; complaint letters, request letters, etc Features of Semi-Formal Letter 1. Address; write the return address (your own address) at the top right hand side of the paper, followed by the date. 2. Salutation; if you do not know the name of the recipient, you may write the position as in ‘Dear Sir’ or ‘Dear Madam,’. But in a case where the recipient is known, it can thus be written as, ‘Dear Mrs Lucy’. 3. Introduction; the introductory sentence should not be too formal or informal. 4. Body; devout about four clear, direct and specific paragraphs to the body and present only one main idea per paragraph. 5. Complementary close; this ranges from more formal to less formal. Example; Your truly, respectfully yours, best regards, warmest regards, cordially, best wishes etc 6. The complementary close is immediately followed by your signature and your full name,

title: ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText:
Argumentative Essay 📘 An argumentative essay is a type of essay where you present your opinion about a topic and support it with strong reasons and evidence. In this essay, you: Choose a position (for or against) Give reasons to support your opinion Provide examples or facts Sometimes explain the opposite view and show why your view is better Structure of an Argumentative Essay 📝 1. Introduction Introduce the topic Give background information State your thesis statement (your main opinion) 2. Body Paragraphs Each paragraph should contain: A clear point (reason) Explanation Example or evidence 3. Counter-Argument (Optional but Important) Mention the opposite opinion Explain why you disagree with it 4. Conclusion Restate your opinion Summarize your main points End strongly ✏ Example of an Argumentative Essay

Topic: Should Students Use Mobile Phones in School? Mobile phones have become very important in our daily lives. However, many schools do not allow students to use them. I believe that students should be allowed to use mobile phones in school for learning purposes. Firstly, mobile phones help students to research information quickly. With internet access, students can look for meanings of words, solve mathematics problems, and learn new things. This makes learning easier and faster. Secondly, mobile phones help in communication. In case of emergency, students can contact their parents immediately. This makes both students and parents feel safe. Some people argue that mobile phones distract students during lessons. This may be true if students misuse them. However, teachers can make rules to control how phones are used in school. In conclusion, mobile phones should be allowed in schools because they help learning and improve communication. Proper rules can prevent distraction. title: STRESS
subject: English Language
rawText:
WORD STRESS Word stress means giving more emphasis (strength) to one syllable in a word. The stressed syllable is said louder, longer, and clearer than the others. Why word stress is important It helps people understand you clearly Wrong stress can change meaning or sound incorrect in English Examples TAble → /ˈteɪ.bəl/ aBOUT → /əˈbaʊt/ DOCtor → /ˈdɒk.tər/ ( Capital letters show the stressed syllable) 👉 Types / Rules of Word Stress 1. Two-syllable nouns & adjectives Stress is usually on the first syllable PREsent (noun) HAPpy TAble 2. Two-syllable verbs & prepositions Stress is usually on the second syllable preSENT (verb) reLAX aBOVE 3. Words ending in –tion, –sion Stress is on the syllable before the ending eduCAtion

disCUSsion 4. Words ending in –ic, –ical Stress comes before the ending geoGRAphic POlitical Stress can change meaning PREsent (gift – noun) preSENT (to give – verb) Simple practice Say these aloud: COMfort imPORtant TEAcher
