title: SPEECH WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText:
Speech writing is the process of preparing a spoken message for an audience. A good speech is clear, engaging, and easy to understand—especially when you are speaking to people directly. Here’s a simple guide you can follow: 1. Understand Your Purpose Ask yourself: Why am I giving this speech? Do I want to inform, persuade, or entertain? Example: Inform → teaching about health Persuade → encouraging people to vote Entertain → telling a story or joke 2. Know Your Audience Think about: Age (young or old) Education level Language (simple English or advanced) Since your English is still growing, using simple and clear words is best. 3. Structure of a Good Speech a. Introduction Greet your audience Introduce your topic Example: “Good morning everyone. Today, I want to talk about the importance of education.” b. Body Present your main points (2–3 points is enough) Give examples Example: “First, education helps us gain knowledge. Second, it opens doors to better jobs.”

c. Conclusion Summarize your points End with a strong message Example: “In conclusion, education is the key to success. Let us all take it seriously. Thank you.” 4. Use Simple Language Avoid long and difficult words Speak clearly and slowly 5. Practice Read your speech aloud Practice in front of a mirror Time yourself ✍ Example of a Short Speech “Good afternoon everyone. Today, I want to talk about cleanliness. Cleanliness is very important in our daily life. First, it helps us stay healthy. Second, it makes our environment look neat and beautiful. In conclusion, we should always keep our surroundings clean. A clean place is a healthy place. Thank you.”

title: ANTONYMS
subject: English Language
rawText: Antonym An antonym is a word that has the opposite meaning of another word. Examples: 📘 Hot ↔ Cold Big ↔ Small Happy ↔ Sad Light ↔ Dark Rich ↔ Poor So, if someone asks for the antonym of happy, the answer is sad.

title: PHRASE
subject: English Language
rawText: A phrasal verb is a verb plus one or two small words (called particles—usually a preposition or adverb) that work together to give a new meaning. Examples look + up → look up (to search for information) I look up new words in the dictionary. give + up → give up (to stop trying) Don’t give up. Common Phrasal Verbs (with simple meanings) wake up – stop sleeping sit down – take a seat turn on – switch on turn off – switch off carry on – continue put off – postpone pick up – lift / learn / collect run out of – have no more Types of Phrasal Verbs Separable (object can come in the middle) Turn off the light. Turn the light off. Inseparable (object cannot separate them) Look after the baby. Look the baby after. No object The plane took off.

title: STRESS
subject: English Language
rawText: Word Stress Word stress can be defined as the relative loudness in pitch and length associated with the pronunciation of a particular syllable in a word. A stressed syllable is a syllable that is louder, longer and higher in pitch than the other syllables in a word. What is a syllable? A syllable is a unit of human speech that can be interpreted as a single sound and is often produced with one puff of breath. Examples of words of three syllables stressed on the first syllable  Policy  Delicate  FORtunate  Secondary  CANdidate  QUANtity  ADvertise Examples of words of three syllables stressed on the second syllable 1. coMEdian 2. emPHAtic 3. aDDItion 4. draMAtic 5. tuTOrial 6. poSItion 7. aTTENtion 8. toMOrrow 9. deMOnic 10. adVIsor 11. roTAtion 12. deCIsion Stress can also be the emphasis in the production or pronunciation of a particular syllable that are louder or longer than other syllables in a word. It is often marked by the use of capitalisation as expressed above. The syllables without stress are called unstressed syllable and they do not affect one syllable words (mono syllabic)

title: SPEECH
subject: English Language
rawText:
GOVERNMENT SECONDARY SCHOOL, GWARINPA ENGLISH FIRST TERM SCHEME OF WORK 1. SPEECH: consonant sounds /j/, /z/, /Ʒ/. Vocabulary: words associated with home and family. Structure: nouns – types of nouns. Comprehension: reading to comprehend main story line. Writing: narrative composition. 2. SPEECH: consonant sounds /ᵭ/, /Ө/. Vocabulary: words associated with agriculture. Comprehension: reading to comprehend main story line II. Structure: Nouns – revision. Writing: expository composition. 3. SPEECH: consonants followed by /w/. Structure: noun phrases. Comprehension: reading to comprehend supporting details. Writing: mechanics in writing i.e. paragraphing, punctuation and spelling. 4. SPEECH: consonants followed by /j/. Comprehension: reading to comprehend supporting details II. Writing: mechanics in writing II. 5. SUMMARY: introduction to summary through identifying key words. Structure: countable and non-countable nouns. Writing: writing of articles. 6. SPEECH: syllabic consonants /l/. Structure: introducing nominalisation of adjectives and verbs. Summary: introduction to summary (continued). 7. SPEECH: syllabic consonant /n/. Structure: pronoun. Writing: letter writing (informal). Vocabulary: words associated with animal husbandry. 8. SPEECH: words of two syllables. Structure: possessive pronoun. Comprehension: reading to comprehend word meaning through context. Summary: reading to assign a title to context. 9. SPEECH: words of two syllables II. Vocabulary: words associated with religion – Traditional. Structure: regular and irregular verbs. Comprehension: reading to make notes. 10. SPEECH: listening to tell the meaning of words I context. Structure: complex tense forms. Writing: descriptive composition. Comprehension: reading to identify writer’s mood, tone and purpose. 11. SPEECH: consonant sounds followed by /k/+/w/. Structure: demonstrative pronouns. Vocabulary: words associated with religion – Islaam and Christianity. Writing: formal letter.

12. SPEECH: listening to identify a speaker’s style. Writing: semi-formal letter. Structure: differences between phrase and clause. Summary: writing a summary of a passage in a specified number of sentences. 13. Revision. 14. Examination. SPEECH: Consonant Sounds /j/, /z/, /Ʒ/ There are 44 speech sounds in the English language whereby, 20 of the sounds are termed ‘vowels’, whilst the other 24 sounds are considered ‘consonants’. Vowels and consonants differ depend on their parameters of production. Vowels are produced with free-flow of air, i.e. without any obstruction of airflow, while consonants are produced with a complete or partial obstruction of air at one place or the other from the vocal tract. The following are some selected few consonant sounds: /j/ as in y ou, y am, y es, y acht, y oung /z/ as in z ip, z ebra, z ero, increa s e, ari s e, tho s e, buse s , churche s , bag s /ʒ/ as in plea s ure, mea s ure, trea s ure, vi s ion, confu s ion, divi s ion, televi s ion Vocabulary: Words Associated with Home and Family Family related words:  Ancestor: predecessor in family  Care-giver: a person who cares for someone who is sick or disabled  Heir: a person who inherits or has a right of inheritance in the property of another following the latter’s death  Hereditary: descending or capable of descending to succeeding generations by inheritance, derived from one’s ancestors  Infant: a child during the earliest period of its life, especially before he or she can walk; baby  Juvenile: young, youthful or immature  Kin: a person of the same family; related  Kinship: family relationship

 Kith: blood relatives  Lineage: direct descent from a particular ancestor  Matriarch: a woman who rules a family, clan or tribe  Offspring: children or young of a particular parent or progenitor  Paternal: relating to or characteristic of a father or fatherhood; fatherly  Patriarch: a man who rules a family, clan or tribe  Progeny: the immediate descendants of a person  Sibling: a person’s brother or sister Structure: Nouns – Types of Nouns Noun: is a word that identifies a person, place or thing. In short; noun is a naming word, anything that has name it is a noun. Another way of recognising a noun is by its: ending, position and function. Noun Ending There are certain word endings that show that a word is a noun, for example: - -ity = nationality - -ment = appointment - -ness = happiness - -tion = relation - -hood = childhood Noun Position in Sentence A noun can be often recognised by its position in the sentence. Nouns often come after a determiner (a, an, the, this, my, such, etc). for example: - A relief - An afternoon - The doctor - This word - My house - Such stupidity

Noun Function in Sentence Nouns have certain functions (jobs) in a sentence, for example: - Subject of verb; Doctors work hard. - Object of verb; he likes coffee. - Subject and object of verb; teachers teach students. Types of Nouns Proper Nouns Names of people, places or organisations are proper nouns. Your name is a proper noun. Egypt is a proper noun. United Nations is a proper noun. Rule: proper nouns always start with a capital letter. Examples: Auwal, Nigeria, Friday, Shakespeare. - Isa introduced himself. - He is the chairman of Algeria Broadcasting Corporation. - The capital of Saudi is Ryadh. - He was born in November. Concrete Nouns All things that are physical and one can touch or otherwise sense is termed as concrete nouns. Examples: rice, car, furniture, mobile phone, etc. - Many books do you have? - Pour the water. - Give me the computer. Abstract Nouns These are the opposite of concrete nouns. They are things that one cannot touch. Abstract nouns are idea, concepts and feelings. Examples: happiness, courage, danger, truth, etc. - He has great strength. - Who killed Kennedy is a real mystery. - Sometimes it takes courage to tell the truth. - Their lives were full of sadness.

Collective Nouns A collective noun denotes a group of individuals. Examples: class (group of students), pride (group of lions), crew (group of sailors), etc. Rule: collective nouns can be treated as singular or plural. - His family live in different countries. - The new company is the result of a merger. - The board of directors will meet tomorrow. Common Nouns Most nouns are common nouns. Common nouns refer to people and things in general like chair or cat. Any noun that is not a name is a common noun. Examples: teacher, car, receipt, etc. - Have you seen his cat? - The books are on your desk. - The phone is ringing. Noun Countability The major division of English nouns is into ‘Countable’ and ‘Non-countable’ nouns. Countable nouns are easy to recognise. They are things that we can count. For example: ‘pen’ we can count pens. We can have one, two, three or more pens. Here are some more countable nouns: Dog, cat, animal, bottle, box, coin, note, cup, plate, spoon, table, chair, bag, etc. Countable nouns can be singular or plural: - His cat is playing. - His cats are playing. We can use the indefinite article (‘a’ or ‘an’) with countable nouns: - A cat is an animal. Non-Countable Nouns

Unlike countable nouns, non-countable nouns are substances, concepts, etc that we cannot divide into separate elements. We cannot ‘count’ them generally. For example: milk. We can count bottles of milk, or litres of milk, but we cannot count milk itself. Here are some more non-countable nouns: Art, happiness, information, furniture, electricity, work, power, advice, news, luggage, rice, sugar, gas, water, butter, currency, etc. we usually treat non- countable nouns as singular, and use singular verb. For example: - This news is very important. - Your luggage looks heavy. Comprehension: reading to comprehend main story line Comprehension is involves constructing mental representations of the information presented. Connecting it to existing knowledge, and making inferences to fill in gaps. Comprehension goes beyond mere decoding of words; it encompasses the understanding of idea, concepts and relationships conveyed through language. Some reading practical exercises are found in the following categories: - Reading for kids - Short stories - Reading about interests; sport, art, history, legends, etc - Reading about movies; horror, sci-fi, drama, action, documentaries, etc - Reading about recent historical events - Reading about environmental issues - Reading about health issues - Reading classical texts; religious books, ancient books; like Shakespearean works Writing: Narrative Composition A narrative essay could be fiction (unreal, imaginative) or non-fiction (true life). A good narrative essay involves correct spellings and real life conditions. Meanwhile, in exam conditions a guided topic or theme is given for the student to write a story. Also, the number of words is not less than 450 prescribed. This makes a narrative essay in this context a flash fiction or a short story.

Features of Narrative Essay Note that a good narrative essay must have: a. Title and paragraphs as well as conversations which are indented and put in speech marks (‘ ’ or “ ”). b. Characters c. Settings. d. Plot. Since it involves story-telling, the storyline or plot can either be: 1) Chronological: Here, the story goes from beginning to middle which captures the conflict and climax and then to the end which includes the resolution or denouement and anti-climax. 2) Non-Chronological: another word for this is episodic. Here, the story is structured anticlockwise. It is pertinent to note that what makes a narrative essay very interesting and attract good marks is its literary embellishments with figures of speech such as metaphor, simile, irony, hyperbole, personification, euphemism etc. Also, note that in an instance where a topic is not given, you are expected to coin a topic from the subject matter you are to write about which can either be a word which in most cases can be a name of a character in the story, or a phrase. However, when a topic is given then adopt it as your topic. SPEECH: Consonant Sounds /j/, /z/, /Ʒ/ There are 44 speech sounds in the English language whereby, 20 of the sounds are termed ‘vowels’, whilst the other 24 sounds are considered ‘consonants’. Vowels and consonants differ depend on their parameters of production. Vowels are produced with free-flow of air, i.e. without any obstruction of airflow, while consonants are produced with a complete or partial obstruction of air at one place or the other from the vocal tract. The following are some selected few consonant sounds: /j/ as in y ou, y am, y es, y acht, y oung /z/ as in z ip, z ebra, z ero, increa s e, ari s e, tho s e, buse s , churche s , bag s /ʒ/ as in plea s ure, mea s ure, trea s ure, vi s ion, confu s ion, divi s ion, televi s ion Vocabulary: Words Associated with Home and Family Family related words:  Ancestor: predecessor in family  Care-giver: a person who cares for someone who is sick or disabled  Heir: a person who inherits or has a right of inheritance in the property of another following the latter’s death  Hereditary: descending or capable of descending to succeeding generations by inheritance, derived from one’s ancestors  Infant: a child during the earliest period of its life, especially before he or she can walk; baby  Juvenile: young, youthful or immature  Kin: a person of the same family; related  Kinship: family relationship

 Kith: blood relatives  Lineage: direct descent from a particular ancestor  Matriarch: a woman who rules a family, clan or tribe  Offspring: children or young of a particular parent or progenitor  Paternal: relating to or characteristic of a father or fatherhood; fatherly  Patriarch: a man who rules a family, clan or tribe  Progeny: the immediate descendants of a person  Sibling: a person’s brother or sister Structure: Nouns – Types of Nouns Noun: is a word that identifies a person, place or thing. In short; noun is a naming word, anything that has name it is a noun. Another way of recognising a noun is by its: ending, position and function. Noun Ending There are certain word endings that show that a word is a noun, for example: - -ity = nationality - -ment = appointment - -ness = happiness - -tion = relation - -hood = childhood Noun Position in Sentence A noun can be often recognised by its position in the sentence. Nouns often come after a determiner (a, an, the, this, my, such, etc). for example: - A relief - An afternoon - The doctor - This word - My house - Such stupidity

Noun Function in Sentence Nouns have certain functions (jobs) in a sentence, for example: - Subject of verb; Doctors work hard. - Object of verb; he likes coffee. - Subject and object of verb; teachers teach students. Types of Nouns Proper Nouns Names of people, places or organisations are proper nouns. Your name is a proper noun. Egypt is a proper noun. United Nations is a proper noun. Rule: proper nouns always start with a capital letter. Examples: Auwal, Nigeria, Friday, Shakespeare. - Isa introduced himself. - He is the chairman of Algeria Broadcasting Corporation. - The capital of Saudi is Ryadh. - He was born in November. Concrete Nouns All things that are physical and one can touch or otherwise sense is termed as concrete nouns. Examples: rice, car, furniture, mobile phone, etc. - Many books do you have? - Pour the water. - Give me the computer. Abstract Nouns These are the opposite of concrete nouns. They are things that one cannot touch. Abstract nouns are idea, concepts and feelings. Examples: happiness, courage, danger, truth, etc. - He has great strength. - Who killed Kennedy is a real mystery. - Sometimes it takes courage to tell the truth. - Their lives were full of sadness.

Collective Nouns A collective noun denotes a group of individuals. Examples: class (group of students), pride (group of lions), crew (group of sailors), etc. Rule: collective nouns can be treated as singular or plural. - His family live in different countries. - The new company is the result of a merger. - The board of directors will meet tomorrow. Common Nouns Most nouns are common nouns. Common nouns refer to people and things in general like chair or cat. Any noun that is not a name is a common noun. Examples: teacher, car, receipt, etc. - Have you seen his cat? - The books are on your desk. - The phone is ringing. Noun Countability The major division of English nouns is into ‘Countable’ and ‘Non-countable’ nouns. Countable nouns are easy to recognise. They are things that we can count. For example: ‘pen’ we can count pens. We can have one, two, three or more pens. Here are some more countable nouns: Dog, cat, animal, bottle, box, coin, note, cup, plate, spoon, table, chair, bag, etc. Countable nouns can be singular or plural: - His cat is playing. - His cats are playing. We can use the indefinite article (‘a’ or ‘an’) with countable nouns: - A cat is an animal. Non-Countable Nouns

Unlike countable nouns, non-countable nouns are substances, concepts, etc that we cannot divide into separate elements. We cannot ‘count’ them generally. For example: milk. We can count bottles of milk, or litres of milk, but we cannot count milk itself. Here are some more non-countable nouns: Art, happiness, information, furniture, electricity, work, power, advice, news, luggage, rice, sugar, gas, water, butter, currency, etc. we usually treat non- countable nouns as singular, and use singular verb. For example: - This news is very important. - Your luggage looks heavy. Comprehension: reading to comprehend main story line Comprehension is involves constructing mental representations of the information presented. Connecting it to existing knowledge, and making inferences to fill in gaps. Comprehension goes beyond mere decoding of words; it encompasses the understanding of idea, concepts and relationships conveyed through language. Some reading practical exercises are found in the following categories: - Reading for kids - Short stories - Reading about interests; sport, art, history, legends, etc - Reading about movies; horror, sci-fi, drama, action, documentaries, etc - Reading about recent historical events - Reading about environmental issues - Reading about health issues - Reading classical texts; religious books, ancient books; like Shakespearean works Writing: Narrative Composition A narrative essay could be fiction (unreal, imaginative) or non-fiction (true life). A good narrative essay involves correct spellings and real life conditions. Meanwhile, in exam conditions a guided topic or theme is given for the student to write a story. Also, the number of words is not less than 450 prescribed. This makes a narrative essay in this context a flash fiction or a short story.

Features of Narrative Essay Note that a good narrative essay must have: a. Title and paragraphs as well as conversations which are indented and put in speech marks (‘ ’ or “ ”). b. Characters c. Settings. d. Plot. Since it involves story-telling, the storyline or plot can either be: 1) Chronological: Here, the story goes from beginning to middle which captures the conflict and climax and then to the end which includes the resolution or denouement and anti-climax. 2) Non-Chronological: another word for this is episodic. Here, the story is structured anticlockwise. It is pertinent to note that what makes a narrative essay very interesting and attract good marks is its literary embellishments with figures of speech such as metaphor, simile, irony, hyperbole, personification, euphemism etc. Also, note that in an instance where a topic is not given, you are expected to coin a topic from the subject matter you are to write about which can either be a word which in most cases can be a name of a character in the story, or a phrase. However, when a topic is given then adopt it as your topic. rawText: Phrasal Verb A verb phrase is a verb that is made up of a main verb together with an adverb or preposition. Typically, the meaning of a phrasal verb is not obvious from the meaning of the underlined words themselves. The phrasal verbs are important because they are in everyday spoken language. Example : Show up = arrive Wake up = awake Blow up = explode Cal off = cancel Set up = arrange Throw away = discharge Fill out = complete a form Do over = repeat a job Leave out = omit Find out = discover/investigate  Choose (no modifier) Would have died  Come (no modifier) Was being beaten  Am writing Would have been done .  Were sleeping Decides to marry  Have eaten Wants to go  Am going to attend Has been done

4. Narrative Composition (Planning) Narrative writing = telling a story. Basic structure: Setting → Where/when (e.g., “In a small village…”) Characters → Who (e.g., “Tunde, his mother, and a dog…”) Plot → Events (Beginning → Middle → End). Example outline: ✅ Setting: A school playground Character: Musa, a student Plot: Musa finds a lost book → he returns it → the teacher praises him. 5. Reading Comprehension Passage (Short Example): "Ada loves reading storybooks. Every evening, she sits under the mango tree to read. One day, her friend Tolu joined her, and together they read a new story about a brave hunter." Questions: 1. Who loves reading storybooks? 2. Where does Ada sit to read? 3. Who joined Ada one day? 4. What kind of story did they read?

title: FALLING TUNE
subject: English Language
rawText:
USES OF THE FALLING TUNE The falling tune is used to make: Statement of fact. Examples: Mary’s mother is a police woman. Bello is my friend. Give commands. Examples: Get out of my class. Shut the door. 3. Make exclamations Examples: What a rainy day! What a pleasant surprise! 4. Ask Wh-Questions. Examples: Where do you live? How was your bag stolen? title: INTONATION: FALLING & RISING
subject: English Language
rawText:
Intonation: Falling and Rising Intonation means the rise and fall of the voice when speaking. It helps to show meaning, emotion, or attitude in speech. There are two main types of intonation patterns: falling and rising intonation. 1. Falling Intonation 🌻 The voice goes down at the end of a sentence. It is used in: Statements: → She is my teacher. Commands: → Close the door. Wh-questions: → Where are you going? End of a conversation: → Goodbye. Example ( ↓ ): > “I live in Lagos.” (The pitch falls at the end.) 2. Rising Intonation The voice goes up at the end of a sentence. It is used in: Yes/No questions: → Are you coming? Unfinished thoughts: → I bought apples, oranges, and...

Polite or uncertain statements: → Maybe later? Example ( ↑ ): > “Are you okay?” (The pitch rises at the end.) Type of Intonation Voice Direction Common Use Example Falling ↓ Down Statements, commands, Wh-questions Where is my book? Rising ↑ Up Yes/No questions, uncertainty Do you like it?

title: STOCK EXCHANGE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Stock Exchange Stock Exchange is an organized market for buying and selling corporate and other securities. It is a place where people buy and sell shares in companies, Persons associated with the stock exchange. Bull Jobber market maker Bear Bond holder Share holder Stock holder Other Words associated with the stock exchange Flow Trade Float Gain Grey market Pit Raid Bid Bear market Share: A share is the part ownership of a company and represents a claim on the company’s assets and earnings. It fluctuates up or down depending on several different market factors and is exchangeable at stock exchanges. As you acquire more stock, your ownership stake in the company becomes greater. Shareholder: An individual, institution or corporation that legally owns one or more shares of stock in a public or private corporation are called shareholder. Shareholders have a claim on the company’s ownership. Primary market: Also known as New Issue Market (NIM). It is the market place where new shares are issued and the public buys shares directly from the company, usually through an IPO. The company gets the amount on the sale of shares. Secondary Market: It is the place where formerly issued securities are traded. The second market involves indirect purchasing and selling of shares among investors. Brokers are Intermediary and the investors get the amount on the sale of shares. Intraday: When you buy and sell the share on the same day, then it is called intraday trading. Here the shares are not purchased for investing, but to get profits by harnessing the movement in the market. Delivery: When you buy a share and hold it for more than one day, then it is called delivery. It doesn’t matter whether you sell it tomorrow, after 1 week, 6 months or 5 years. If you hold the stock for more than one day, then it is called delivery. Bull market: This is a term used to describe the scenario of the market. A bull market is when the share prices are rising and the public is optimistic that the share price will continue to rise. Bear Market: When the share prices are falling and the public is pessimistic about the stock market, then it’s a bear market. The public is fearful and thinks that the market will continue to fall and hence, selling increases in this market. IPO: When a privately listed company offers its sharers first time to the public to enter the share market, then it is called initial public offering.

Blue chip stocks: These are the stocks of those reputed companies who are in the market for a very long time, financially strong and have a good track record of consistent growth and returns in the past many years. Their stocks have low risk compared to mid cap and small cap stocks. Broker: A stockbroker is an individual/organization who is a registered member of the stock exchange and are given license to participate in the securities market in place of its clients. Stockbrokers can directly buy & sell stocks in the share market on behalf of their clients and charge a commission for this service. Portfolio: A stock portfolio is grouping all the stocks that you are holding. A portfolio shows the different stocks and the quantities that you are holding. It’s important to build a good portfolio to maintain risk-reward in the stock market. Stock Exchange: Just like a vegetable market, exchanges act as a market where the stock buyers connect with stock sellers. Dividend: Whenever a company (whose shares you are holding) is in profit, the company can either reinvest the profit or distribute the amount among its shareholders. This share of the profit that you get from the company is called dividend. Index: Since there are thousands of company listed on a stock exchange, hence it’s really hard to track every single stock to evaluate the market performance at a time. Therefore, a smaller sample is taken which is the representative of the whole market. This small sample is called Index and it helps in the measurement of the value of a section of the stock market. The index is computed from the prices of selected stocks. Limit Order: Limit order means to buy/sell a share with a limit price. If you want to buy/sell a share at a given price, then you place a limit order. For example, if the current market price of ‘Tata motors’ is Rs 425, however you want to buy it at Rs 420, then you need to place a limit order. When the market price of Tata motors falls to Rs 420, then the order is executed. Market order: When you want to buy/sell a share at the current market price, then you need to place a market order. For example, if the market price of ‘Tata Motors’ is Rs 425 and you are ready to buy the share at the same price, then you place a market order. Here, the order is executed instantaneously. Good till cancellation (GTC) order: This order can be placed when an investor is willing to buy/sell the shares at a specific price and the order remains active till it is executed or canceled. Day order: This order can be placed when an investor is willing to buy/sell shares on a particular day and the order gets automatically canceled if not fulfilled on that day. Trading volume: It is the total number of shares being traded at a particular period of time. When securities are more actively traded, their trade volume is high. Higher trade volumes for a stock mean higher liquidity, better order execution and a more active market for connecting a buyer and seller.

Volatility: It means how fast a stock price moves up or down. More volatile assets are considered riskier than less volatile assets because the price is expected to be less predictable and may fluctuate dramatically. Liquidity: Liquidity means how easily you can buy/sell a share without affecting the share price. A highly liquid share means that it can easily be bought or sold. A low liquid stock means that the buyers/sellers are hard to find. Short selling: It is a practice where the trader sells share first (which he doesn’t even own at that time) and hope that the price of that share starts falling. He will make a profit by buying back those shares at a lower price. Overall, both selling and buying are done here, however, it’s sequence is opposite to the regular transactions to get the profit of the falling share prices. Going long: This is buying the shares in expectations that the share price is going to increase. When a trader say I am “Going long…” or “Go long”, it indicates his interest in buying a particular share. Average down: This is an approach that investors use to buy more shares when the share price starts falling. This results in an overall lower average price for that share. For example, you bought a stock at Rs 100. Then the stock price starts falling. You bought the stock again at Rs 80 and Rs 60. Hence, the average price of your investment will be lower i.e. Rs 80. This is the approach used in averaging down. Public float (free float): Public float or free float represents the portion of shares of a company that is in the hands of public investors. Market capitalization: It refers to the total rupee value of the company’s share. It is calculated by multiplying the total number of shares by its present market share price. We define large cap, mid cap or small cap companies based on their market capitalization. Bid: The bid price represents the maximum price that the buyer/buyers are willing to give to buy a share. Ask: This is the minimum price that the seller/sellers are willing to receive to sell their shares. Bid-Ask spread: This is the difference between the ‘bid’ and ‘ask’ price of a share. Basically, its the difference between the highest price that the buyers are willing to buy a share and the lowest price that the sellers are willing to sell their shares. Demat account: It is the short form for ‘Dematerialised account’. The demat account is similar to a bank account. Just as money is kept in your saving account, similarly bought stocks are kept in your demat account. Trading Account: This is a medium to buy and sell shares in a stock market. In simple words, the trading account is used to place buy or sell order for a share in the stock market. Margin: Trading on margin means borrowing money from your stock brokers to purchase stock. It allows the traders to buy more stocks than you’d normally be able to.

title: WORD STRESS
subject: English Language
rawText:
WORDS STRESS IN FIRST SECOND AND THIRD SYLLABLES STRESS Stress is the force with which the part of a word or part of a sentence is articulated. SYLLABLES A syllable is a word or parts of a word that can be pronounce as a single unit of sound. WORDS STRESS ON THEIR FIRST SYLLABLES 1. The following words take their stress in their first syllables: a. Noun ending with –“URE” takes their stress in their first syllables e.g Furniture – FUR-ni-ture, Temperature – TEM-pe-ra-ture, Literature – LI-te-ra-ture. b. Noun and adjective ending with –“TUDE” take their stress in their first syllables e.g Attitude – AT-ti-tude, Gratitude- GRA-ti-tude, Multitude – MUL-ti-tude. WORDS STRESS ON THEIR SECOND SYLLABLES 1. The following words take their stress in their second syllables: a. Noun and adjectives that ends with “ant/ent” take their stress in their second syllable. E.g defendant – de-FEN-dent, expectant –ex-PEC-tent. b. Verbs that ends with “ISH” take their stress in second to the last syllables e.g demolish – de-MO-lish, admonish – ad- MO-nish, relinguish – re-LIN-guish, . accomplish- ac-COM-plish. c. Adjective that ends with “UAL” take their stress in second to the last syllables e.g continual – con-TI-nual, perpetual – pe-PE-tual. d. Adjective that ends with “IOUS” take their stress in second to the last syllables e.g malicious – ma-LI-TIOUS, contentious – con-TEN-tious. e. Adjective that ends with “EOUS” take their stress in second to the last syllables e.g advantageous – ad-van-TA-geous, courageous –cour-RA-geous. f. Noun and verbs that ends with “AGE” take their stress in second to the last - syllables e.g advantage – ad-VAN-tage, discourage – dis-COU-rage. WORDS STRESS ON THEIR THIRD SYLLABLES 1. The following words take their stress on their third syllables: a. Adjective that ends with “-ENT” take their stress in third to the last syllables and noun ending with “-ENCE” also take their stress in third to the last syllables e.g magnificient/ence – mag-ni-FI-cient/ence, equivalent/ence –e-qui-VA-lent/ence. b. Verbs ending with”-ate” take their stress in third to the last syllables e.g congratulate – con-gra-TU-late, appreciate –ap-PRE-ci-ate.

c. Verb ending with “-IZE” or “-ISE” take their stress in third to the last syllables e.g commercialize/ ise. – com-mer-CIA-lize/ise, apologize – a-po-LO-gize. d. Noun ending with “-SIS” take their stress in third to the last syllables e.g hypothesis- hy-PO-the-sis, photosynthesis – pho-to-SYN- the-sis. e. Noun ending with “-ty” take their stress in third to the last syllables e.g nationality- na-tion-NA-li-ty, quantity – QUAN-ti-ty. Possibility –po-ssi-BI-li-ty.

title: WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText:
ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY DEFINITION Argumentative writing is a type of essay in which the writer attempts to make the reader or audience accept his views as a valid option. It can also be defined as a type of writing that involves expression of one’s independent views or opinion on a topic that has been opened to a debate. NATURE OF AN ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY SIDES TO EVERY ARGUMENT There are two sides to every argument. 1. The Proposition which is the side to argue in favour or support of a given topic. 2. The Opposition which is the side to present opinion against the topic. FEATURES OF AN ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY. A) It requires no topic. The motion moved represents the topic and the speaker’s interest.(speak for or against). B) INTRODUCTION For instance, in a school setting, one can have the following introduction : The Principal, Vice Principal, members of Staff, invited guests, panel of Judges, accurate time keeper, co debaters and fellow students. I am here to speak against the motion which states that…………. C) Body of the Essay. This is a focus to back up points for your motion. E.g. provision of infrastructural facilities, To debate a point. To defend an idea, policy or proposal. To defend an accused in a court of law. To convince your parents or others to do certain things

promotion of games, etc. in short, you must support or oppose with valid reasons and figures if need be.  The use of apt words i.e relevant registers or vocabularies and phrases as the case may be is very important. Whichever stand you intend to take, the use ofpersuation is very important.  There must be clarity of argument.  There must be logical presentation of ideas or points. That is, the essay must be well organized to attract valuable marks from the examiner. D) Conclusion: In concluding this type of essay, reference must be made to your listeners while giving a summary of all your points. A typical conclusion may end like this: The Principal, Vice Principal, Panel of Judges, Ladies and Gentlemen and my Listeners, I hope you will all agree with my logical presentation of views that …………….. MORE TECHNIQUES  Audience inclusion  Alliteration  Acknowledging the opposing view….. then showing that it is wrong’  Use powerful language to really get your point across.  Use a variety of sentence types and lengths.

title: MULTIPLE TOPICS
subject: English Language
rawText:
Concord The word ‘concord’ simply means agreement or harmony. It is the agreement which must exist between the subject of a sentence; whether a noun, noun phrase or pronoun and the verb. The basic rule of concord is that singular subject must be followed by a singular verb wile a plural subject must be followed by a plural verb. Applications of Concord 1. Any time [either or/neither nor] correlates two subjects, the verb to use will be determined by the subject nearest to the verb. E.g; either James or you is sick. 2. [many a/many an] must be followed by a singular noun in a sentence, followed also by a singular verb. E.g; many a student does not read anymore. 3. A plural noun which is the subject of a sentence will take a singular verb if it is referring to time, distance, money or measurement. Plural nouns relating to time include seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, years, etc. Plural nouns relating to money include Naira, Dollars, Cedes, Rands, Rupees, etc. While the plural nouns relating to measurement include grammes, kilogrammes, yards, litres, etc. E.g; Ten million Naira is needed for his trip. 4. Anytime collective is used as the subject of a sentence, it must go with a plural noun followed by a singular verb. E.g; A battalion of soldiers has moved to Kano. Words Associated with Advertisement 1. Ad = is a short form of advertisement 2. Advertisement = item of publicity on media that is meant to persuade people to buy 3. Advertising agency= a company specialising in producing and placing advertisements for clients 4. Benefit = advantage of a product or service 5. Billboard = a large signboard, usually outdoors, on which a poster-style ad is displayed 6. Coupon = a part of advertisement used for ordering goods or getting a discount 7. Eye-catcher = something that especially at tracts one’s attention Speaking to Persuade Speaking to persuasion is a method of getting someone to do, believe or accept something by means of the words. It involves reasoning with the listener, using sound arguments or a compelling entreaty.

Persuasion is usually about gaining agreement and support. It is about creating a common ground where you and others can come together in purpose of thought. In contrast, manipulation involves controlling or influencing a person or group of people through unfair or unscrupulous means. Record Keeping Record Keeping refers to the process of collecting, organizing, storing, and maintaining records or information for future reference. It is an essential part of personal, business, and government operations. Types of Record Keeping 1. Manual Record Keeping – Records are kept using paper files, notebooks, or registers. 2. Electronic Record Keeping – Records are stored using computers and digital systems like databases or spreadsheets. Importance of Record Keeping  Provides accurate information for decision-making.  Helps track financial transactions , such as income and expenses.  Ensures legal compliance and accountability.  Improves efficiency in managing resources and activities.  Helps in planning and budgeting. Examples of Records to Keep  Financial records (receipts, invoices, bank statements)  Academic records (report cards, admission forms)  Employment records (contracts, salary slips)  Medical records  Inventory records Intonation Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice when speaking. It helps to express emotions, attitudes, and the meaning of sentences beyond just the words. Types of Intonation 1. Rising Intonation: The voice rises at the end of the sentence. Common in yes/no questions. Example: Are you coming? 2. Falling Intonation: The voice falls at the end of the sentence. Used in statements, commands, and wh-questions.

Examples: I am going home. What is your name? 3. Rising-Falling Intonation: The voice rises and then falls. Used to show strong feelings or surprise. Example: Really?! 4. Falling-Rising Intonation: The voice falls and then rises. Often shows uncertainty, hesitation, or politeness. Example: I guess so... Importance of Intonation: Helps listeners understand the speaker’s mood. Clarifies the speaker’s intentio n. Makes speech more natural and interesting. Reading for Words in Context Reading for words in context means understanding the meaning of unfamiliar words or phrases by examining how they are used in a sentence or passage. Importance: Helps improve vocabulary without using a dictionary. Enhances reading comprehension. Makes reading smoother and more enjoyable. How to Understand Words in Context: 1. Look at the surrounding words: The words before and after can give hints about the meaning. 2. Identify context clues: Definition Clues: The word’s meaning is explained in the sentence. Example: Photosynthesis, the process by which plants make food, requires sunlight. Synonym Clues: A similar word is used. Example: He was elated, or very happy, about his results. Antonym Clues: An opposite word is used. Example: Unlike his stingy brother, John is very generous. Example Clues: Examples are given to explain the word. Example: Celestial bodies, such as the sun, moon, and stars, light up the sky. General Sense of the Passage: Use the overall idea of the sentence or paragraph. 3. Guess and Confirm: Make an educated guess, then check if the word makes sense in that context. Practice Tip: While reading, underline unfamiliar words and try to figure out their meanings from context before checking the dictionary. Oral Composition

Oral composition is the process of expressing ideas, thoughts, or stories verbally in a structured and coherent manner. It involves speaking clearly and logically, often for an audience, without necessarily writing it down first. Types of Oral Composition 1. Narrative: Telling a story or recounting an event. 2. Descriptive: Describing a person, place, object, or event. 3. Argumentative: Expressing an opinion and supporting it with reasons and evidence. 4. Expository: Explaining a concept or process clearly and logically. 5. Dialogue/Conversation: A spoken exchange between two or more people. Features of a Good Oral Composition Clear structure (Introduction, Body, Conclusion) Logical flow of ideas Fluency and accuracy Appropriate language and tone Confidence and audibility Good eye contact and body language Tips for Effective Oral Composition Plan your speech before speaking. Use linking words to connect ideas (e.g., firstly, however, therefore). Avoid fillers like “um” or “you know.” Practice speaking in front of a mirror or peers. Listen to good speakers and learn from them. Types of Sentences 1. Declarative Sentence  Definition : A sentence that makes a statement or expresses an opinion.  Ends with : A full stop (.)  Example : o She loves reading books. o The sky is blue. 2. Interrogative Sentence  Definition : A sentence that asks a question.  Ends with : A question mark (?)  Example : o What is your name? o Are you coming to school tomorrow? 3. Imperative Sentence  Definition : A sentence that gives a command, instruction, or request.

 Ends with : A full stop (.) or exclamation mark (!)  Example : o Close the door. o Please sit down. o Stop talking! 4. Exclamatory Sentence  Definition : A sentence that shows strong emotion or excitement.  Ends with : An exclamation mark (!)  Example : o What a beautiful dress! o I can’t believe it! Words Associated with Stock Exchange 1. Stock  Meaning : A share or part of ownership in a company. 2. Shareholder  Meaning : A person who owns shares (stocks) in a company. 3. Dividend  Meaning : The profit a company pays to its shareholders, usually in cash or more shares. 4. Stock Exchange  Meaning : A marketplace where people buy and sell stocks and shares. 5. Broker  Meaning : A person or company that buys and sells stocks for others and earns a commission. 6. Bull Market  Meaning : A market where prices of shares are rising and investors are confident. 7. Bear Market  Meaning : A market where share prices are falling and investors are cautious or fearful.

8. Portfolio  Meaning : A collection of different investments (stocks, bonds, etc.) owned by a person or company. 9. Capital Gain  Meaning : The profit made when a stock is sold for more than it was bought. 10. IPO (Initial Public Offering)  Meaning : The first time a company sells its shares to the public on the stock exchange. Emphatic Stress Emphatic Stress is the special force or emphasis placed on a word in a sentence to show importance, contrast, or strong feeling. It helps to highlight the exact meaning the speaker wants to convey. Why We Use Emphatic Stress  To correct wrong information  To show surprise or emotion  To make a contrast Examples of Emphatic Stress Consider this simple sentence: "She passed the exam." By stressing different words, the meaning changes: 1. " She ** passed the exam."** – Emphasis: It was she , not someone else. 2. "She passed the exam." – Emphasis: She passed , not failed. 3. "She passed the exam." – Emphasis: That specific exam. 4. "She passed the exam ." – Emphasis: She passed an exam , not a test or assignment. How It's Used in Speech In spoken English, emphatic stress is applied by:  Raising your voice slightly on the word

 Slowing down to make it clearer  Sometimes using gestures or facial expressions Synonyms Word Synonym(s) Happy Glad, joyful, cheerful Big Large, huge, massive Small Tiny, little, miniature Fast Quick, rapid, speedy Smart Intelligent, clever, bright Sad Unhappy, sorrowful, gloomy Start Begin, commence, launch End Finish, conclude, terminate Help Assist, aid, support Say Speak, tell, express Look See, glance, observe Beautiful Pretty, lovely, attractive Strong Powerful, sturdy, tough Quiet Silent, calm, peaceful Angry Mad, furious, annoyed

Types Of Clauses 1. Main Clause (Independent Clause)  Can stand alone as a complete sentence.  Expresses a complete thought. Examples:  She sings beautifully.  The boy ran away. 2. Subordinate Clause (Dependent Clause)  Cannot stand alone as a complete sentence.  Depends on the main clause to make sense. There are three major types of subordinate clauses: a. Noun Clause  Functions like a noun (subject, object, or complement). Examples:  What she said was true. (Subject)  I know that he is lying. (Object) b. Adjective Clause (Relative Clause)  Describes or gives more information about a noun.  Begins with relative pronouns like who, whom, whose, which, that . Examples:  The girl who won the prize is my sister.  This is the book that I borrowed . c. Adverbial Clause  Acts like an adverb; tells when, where, why, how , etc.  Begins with subordinating conjunctions like because, although, when, if, since, after, before, while , etc. Examples:  I left because it was late . (Reason)

 When the bell rings , we will go for lunch. (Time) Simple/Polite Request And Simple Greetings Simple/Polite Requests A request is when we ask someone to do something for us. When we add polite words like please or use respectful expressions, it becomes a polite request . Common Phrases for Polite Requests: 1. Can you…? / Could you…? o Can you help me with my homework, please? o Could you pass me the salt, please? 2. Would you mind…? o Would you mind opening the window? o Would you mind helping me with this bag? 3. Would you please…? o Would you please sit down? o Would you please be quiet? 4. Do you mind…? o Do you mind if I use your pen? o Do you mind if I join you? Simple Greetings Greetings are polite expressions used when meeting or speaking to someone. Types of Greetings: A. Formal Greetings (Used with elders, strangers, or in official situations)  Good morning.  Good afternoon.  Good evening.  How do you do?  It’s a pleasure to meet you. B. Informal Greetings (Used with friends, family, or people of the same age)  Hi!  Hello!  Hey!  What’s up?  How are you?

In Summary: - Use polite words like please , could , and would when making requests. - Choose formal or informal greetings depending on the person and situation. - Always respond to greetings with respect and friendliness. Antonyms Antonyms are words that have opposite meanings . Examples of Antonyms: Word Antonym Hot Cold Big Small Happy Sad Fast Slow Open Close Up Down Early Late Light Dark Win Lose NOUN CLAUSE A noun clause is a group of words that acts as a noun in a sentence. It usually contains a subject and a verb , but cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. Functions of a Noun Clause: A noun clause can function as: 1. Subject of a sentence o What she said was surprising. (Noun clause as subject) 2. Object of a verb o I know that he is honest . (Noun clause as object) 3. Object of a preposition o They are worried about what might happen . (Noun clause as object of a preposition) 4. Complement of a sentence

o The truth is that she lied . (Noun clause as complement) Common Introducers of Noun Clauses: Noun clauses often begin with these words: that , what , whatever , who , whom , whoever , whomever , whether , if , why , when and how Examples: Sentence Function of Noun Clause What you did was wrong. Subject I believe that she will come. Object of the verb "believe" They are interested in what he said. Object of a preposition The fact is that he was late. Complement Tip: If a group of words answers “what?” or “who?” in the sentence and contains a verb, it's likely a noun clause . Adjectival Clause An adjectival clause (also called a relative clause ) is a group of words that describes or gives more information about a noun or pronoun in the main clause. It functions like an adjective in a sentence. Key Features:  It begins with a relative pronoun : o who (for people) o whom (formal, for people – object position) o whose (possession) o which (for things and animals) o that (for people or things)  It is usually placed directly after the noun it describes. Examples: 1. The boy who won the prize is my cousin. → "who won the prize" describ es "the boy". 2. I saw the dog that barked all night . → "that barked all night" describes "the dog". 3. The woman whose car was stolen is crying. → "whose car was stolen" describes "the woman".

4. They hired the man whom we interviewed yesterday . → "whom we intervi ewed yesterday" describes "the man". Types of Adjectival Clauses: 1. Defining (Restrictive) Clauses o Give essential information. o No commas are used. o Example:  The student who studies hard will pass. 2. Non-defining (Non-restrictive) Clauses o Add extra information (not essential). o Use commas to separate them. o Example:  My brother, who lives in Lagos , is a doctor. Omitting the Relative Pronoun: Sometimes, the relative pronoun can be left out when it refers to the object of the clause. Example:  The book that I bought is interesting.  The book I bought is interesting. ✅ Functions in the Sentence: Adjectival clauses describe nouns and act like adjectives, answering "Which one?" or "What kind?" Quick Exercise: Identify the adjectival clause 1. The girl who sang at the party is my friend. 2. I found the key that opens the garage . 3. The man whom you met is a teacher. Argumentative Essay An argumentative essay is a type of essay that presents arguments for or against a particular topic. The writer takes a clear stance on an issue and supports it with logical reasoning, facts, examples, and evidence . Purpose To convince or persuade the reader to accept a particular point of view or take a specific action. Features of an Argumentative Essay 1. Clear Thesis Statement – States your position on the issue. 2. Introduction – Introduces the topic and gives background information. 3. Arguments For or Against – Based on the side you are supporting. 4. Evidence and Examples – To support each argument. 5. Counterarguments – Acknowledge the other side and refute it.

6. Conclusion – Summarizes the points and restates your position clearly. Structure 1. Introduction o Hook: Catch the reader’s attention. o Background: Brief information on the topic. o Thesis Statement: Your main argument or position. 2. Body Paragraphs o Point 1 : Topic sentence, explanation, evidence/example. o Point 2 : Topic sentence, explanation, evidence/example. o Point 3 : Same structure. o (Include a paragraph for counterargument and refutation.) 3. Conclusion o Restate thesis. o Summarize main points. o End with a strong closing statement. Useful Expressions  In my opinion…  I strongly believe that…  It is often argued that…  On the other hand…  However, it is important to note that…  In conclusion… Sample Topics  Should students wear school uniforms?  Is social media beneficial or harmful?  Should mobile phones be allowed in schools?  Is online learning better than traditional learning? Tips for Writing a Good Argumentative Essay  Choose a debatable topic.  Do proper research.  Be clear and logical.  Use linking words to connect ideas.  Avoid emotional language.  Proofread for grammar and spelling errors. Active/Passive Tense Definitions  Active Voice : The subject performs the action of the verb. Example : The teacher taught the lesson.  Passive Voice : The subject receives the action of the verb. Example : The lesson was taught by the teacher. Structure

Active Voice Structure Subject + Verb + Object Example: John (subject) wrote (verb) a letter (object). Passive Voice Structure Object + form of “to be” + past participle + by + subject (optional) Example: A letter (object) was written (verb) by John (subject). Tense Changes in Passive Voice Tense Active Voice Passive Voice Simple Present He writes a letter. A letter is written by him. Present Continuous He is writing a letter. A letter is being written by him. Present Perfect He has written a letter. A letter has been written by him. Simple Past He wrote a letter. A letter was written by him. Past Continuous He was writing a letter. A letter was being written by him. Past Perfect He had written a letter. A letter had been written by him. Future (will) He will write a letter. A letter will be written by him. Modal + verb He can write a letter. A letter can be written by him. When to Use Passive Voice  When the doer of the action is unknown: Example : The window was broken.  When the focus is on the action, not the subject: Example : The road was repaired yesterday.  In formal or scientific writing: Example : The experiment was conducted in a lab. Common Passive Voice Indicators  Forms of the verb “to be” : is, am, are, was, were, be, been, being.  Past participle (e.g., eaten , written , done ). Examples Active Passive The chef cooks the food. The food is cooked by the chef. The police arrested the thief. The thief was arrested by the police.

Active Passive She will deliver the message. The message will be delivered by her. Tips  Not all verbs can be used in the passive voice (intransitive verbs like sleep , go , arrive can’t).  Use active voice for clearer and more direct writing unless passive voice is necessary. British And American Spellings British and American English use different spellings for certain words, even though the meanings are usually the same. Why the Difference?  British English is the original form of the language.  American English developed its own spellings after the U.S. became independent.  Influenced by dictionary makers (e.g., Noah Webster in America simplified many spellings). Common Differences British Spelling American Spelling Example in a Sentence colour color The sky is full of colour. / color. favour favor She did me a favour. / favor. centre center The town centre / center is crowded. theatre theater We went to the theatre / theater. travelling traveling She is travelling / traveling abroad. cancelled canceled The flight was cancelled / canceled. realise realize I realise / realize the mistake. organise organize They organise / organize meetings. defence defense The team’s defence / defense was strong. licence (noun) license He got his driving licence / license. Rules and Patterns 1. -our (British) → -or (American) e.g. colour → color, favour → favor 2. -re (British) → -er (American) e.g. centre → center, metre → meter 3. Double L in verbs (British) → Single L (American) e.g. travelled → traveled, cancelled → canceled 4. -ise (British) → -ize (American) e.g. organise → organize, realise → realize 5. -ce vs. -se endings o British : licence (noun), practise (verb) o American : license (both noun and verb), practice (both) Why is this Important?  Exams, essays, and writing tasks may require consistency in one form.

 British English is used in Nigeria, the UK, and most Commonwealth countries.  American English is used in the USA and is common online and in software. Tips for Students  Stick to British spelling for schoolwork in Nigeria unless told otherwise.  Be consistent : don’t mix both styles in one essay.  Use dictionaries to check correct spellings (e.g., Oxford for British, Merriam-Webster for American).

Formal Greetings (Used with elders, strangers, or in official situations)  Good morning.  Good afternoon.  Good evening.  How do you do?  It’s a pleasure to meet you. B. Informal Greetings (Used with friends, family, or people of the same age)  Hi!  Hello!  Hey!  What’s up?  How are you?

In Summary: - Use polite words like please , could , and would when making requests. - Choose formal or informal greetings depending on the person and situation. - Always respond to greetings with respect and friendliness. Antonyms Antonyms are words that have opposite meanings . Examples of Antonyms: Word Antonym Hot Cold Big Small Happy Sad Fast Slow Open Close Up Down Early Late Light Dark Win Lose NOUN CLAUSE A noun clause is a group of words that acts as a noun in a sentence. It usually contains a subject and a verb , but cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. Functions of a Noun Clause: A noun clause can function as: 1. Subject of a sentence o What she said was surprising. (Noun clause as subject) 2. Object of a verb o I know that he is honest . (Noun clause as object) 3. Object of a preposition o They are worried about what might happen . (Noun clause as object of a preposition) 4. Complement of a sentence

o The truth is that she lied . (Noun clause as complement) Common Introducers of Noun Clauses: Noun clauses often begin with these words: that , what , whatever , who , whom , whoever , whomever , whether , if , why , when and how Examples: Sentence Function of Noun Clause What you did was wrong. Subject I believe that she will come. Object of the verb "believe" They are interested in what he said. Object of a preposition The fact is that he was late. Complement Tip: If a group of words answers “what?” or “who?” in the sentence and contains a verb, it's likely a noun clause . Adjectival Clause An adjectival clause (also called a relative clause ) is a group of words that describes or gives more information about a noun or pronoun in the main clause. It functions like an adjective in a sentence. Key Features:  It begins with a relative pronoun : o who (for people) o whom (formal, for people – object position) o whose (possession) o which (for things and animals) o that (for people or things)  It is usually placed directly after the noun it describes. Examples: 1. The boy who won the prize is my cousin. → "who won the prize" describ es "the boy". 2. I saw the dog that barked all night . → "that barked all night" describes "the dog". 3. The woman whose car was stolen is crying. → "whose car was stolen" describes "the woman".

4. They hired the man whom we interviewed yesterday . → "whom we intervi ewed yesterday" describes "the man". Types of Adjectival Clauses: 1. Defining (Restrictive) Clauses o Give essential information. o No commas are used. o Example:  The student who studies hard will pass. 2. Non-defining (Non-restrictive) Clauses o Add extra information (not essential). o Use commas to separate them. o Example:  My brother, who lives in Lagos , is a doctor. Omitting the Relative Pronoun: Sometimes, the relative pronoun can be left out when it refers to the object of the clause. Example:  The book that I bought is interesting.  The book I bought is interesting. ✅ Functions in the Sentence: Adjectival clauses describe nouns and act like adjectives, answering "Which one?" or "What kind?" Quick Exercise: Identify the adjectival clause 1. The girl who sang at the party is my friend. 2. I found the key that opens the garage . 3. The man whom you met is a teacher. Argumentative Essay An argumentative essay is a type of essay that presents arguments for or against a particular topic. The writer takes a clear stance on an issue and supports it with logical reasoning, facts, examples, and evidence . Purpose To convince or persuade the reader to accept a particular point of view or take a specific action. Features of an Argumentative Essay 1. Clear Thesis Statement – States your position on the issue. 2. Introduction – Introduces the topic and gives background information. 3. Arguments For or Against – Based on the side you are supporting. 4. Evidence and Examples – To support each argument. 5. Counterarguments – Acknowledge the other side and refute it.

6. Conclusion – Summarizes the points and restates your position clearly. Structure 1. Introduction o Hook: Catch the reader’s attention. o Background: Brief information on the topic. o Thesis Statement: Your main argument or position. 2. Body Paragraphs o Point 1 : Topic sentence, explanation, evidence/example. o Point 2 : Topic sentence, explanation, evidence/example. o Point 3 : Same structure. o (Include a paragraph for counterargument and refutation.) 3. Conclusion o Restate thesis. o Summarize main points. o End with a strong closing statement. Useful Expressions  In my opinion…  I strongly believe that…  It is often argued that…  On the other hand…  However, it is important to note that…  In conclusion… Sample Topics  Should students wear school uniforms?  Is social media beneficial or harmful?  Should mobile phones be allowed in schools?  Is online learning better than traditional learning? Tips for Writing a Good Argumentative Essay  Choose a debatable topic.  Do proper research.  Be clear and logical.  Use linking words to connect ideas.  Avoid emotional language.  Proofread for grammar and spelling errors. Active/Passive Tense Definitions  Active Voice : The subject performs the action of the verb. Example : The teacher taught the lesson.  Passive Voice : The subject receives the action of the verb. Example : The lesson was taught by the teacher. Structure

Active Voice Structure Subject + Verb + Object Example: John (subject) wrote (verb) a letter (object). Passive Voice Structure Object + form of “to be” + past participle + by + subject (optional) Example: A letter (object) was written (verb) by John (subject). Tense Changes in Passive Voice Tense Active Voice Passive Voice Simple Present He writes a letter. A letter is written by him. Present Continuous He is writing a letter. A letter is being written by him. Present Perfect He has written a letter. A letter has been written by him. Simple Past He wrote a letter. A letter was written by him. Past Continuous He was writing a letter. A letter was being written by him. Past Perfect He had written a letter. A letter had been written by him. Future (will) He will write a letter. A letter will be written by him. Modal + verb He can write a letter. A letter can be written by him. When to Use Passive Voice  When the doer of the action is unknown: Example : The window was broken.  When the focus is on the action, not the subject: Example : The road was repaired yesterday.  In formal or scientific writing: Example : The experiment was conducted in a lab. Common Passive Voice Indicators  Forms of the verb “to be” : is, am, are, was, were, be, been, being.  Past participle (e.g., eaten , written , done ). Examples Active Passive The chef cooks the food. The food is cooked by the chef. The police arrested the thief. The thief was arrested by the police.

Active Passive She will deliver the message. The message will be delivered by her. Tips  Not all verbs can be used in the passive voice (intransitive verbs like sleep , go , arrive can’t).  Use active voice for clearer and more direct writing unless passive voice is necessary. British And American Spellings British and American English use different spellings for certain words, even though the meanings are usually the same. Why the Difference?  British English is the original form of the language.  American English developed its own spellings after the U.S. became independent.  Influenced by dictionary makers (e.g., Noah Webster in America simplified many spellings). Common Differences British Spelling American Spelling Example in a Sentence colour color The sky is full of colour. / color. favour favor She did me a favour. / favor. centre center The town centre / center is crowded. theatre theater We went to the theatre / theater. travelling traveling She is travelling / traveling abroad. cancelled canceled The flight was cancelled / canceled. realise realize I realise / realize the mistake. organise organize They organise / organize meetings. defence defense The team’s defence / defense was strong. licence (noun) license He got his driving licence / license. Rules and Patterns 1. -our (British) → -or (American) e.g. colour → color, favour → favor 2. -re (British) → -er (American) e.g. centre → center, metre → meter 3. Double L in verbs (British) → Single L (American) e.g. travelled → traveled, cancelled → canceled 4. -ise (British) → -ize (American) e.g. organise → organize, realise → realize 5. -ce vs. -se endings o British : licence (noun), practise (verb) o American : license (both noun and verb), practice (both) Why is this Important?  Exams, essays, and writing tasks may require consistency in one form.

 British English is used in Nigeria, the UK, and most Commonwealth countries.  American English is used in the USA and is common online and in software. Tips for Students  Stick to British spelling for schoolwork in Nigeria unless told otherwise.  Be consistent : don’t mix both styles in one essay.  Use dictionaries to check correct spellings (e.g., Oxford for British, Merriam-Webster for American).

title: WEEK 2: VERBS (REGULAR AND IRREGULAR).
subject: English Language
rawText:
FCT School for the Gifted, Gwagwalada Subject: English Language Class: SSS 1 (A & B) Term: Second Term Week: 2 Teacher: Mrs. Naadzenga Mgbede Grace Topic: Verbs (Regular and Irregular Verbs) 1. Definition of a Verb A verb is a word that shows action , state of being , or occurrence in a sentence. Without a verb, a sentence cannot be complete. Examples: • She runs every morning. (action) • They are happy. (state of being) • The accident happened yesterday. (occurrence) 2. Types of Verbs (Based on Past Tense Formation) Verbs can be classified into Regular Verbs and Irregular Verbs , based on how they form their past tense and past participle . 3. Regular Verbs Definition: Regular verbs are verbs that form their past tense and past participle by adding – ed or – d to the base form. Formation Rules: 1. Most verbs → add -ed o walk → walked

o play → played 2. Verbs ending in -e → add -d o love → loved o like → liked 3. Verbs ending in consonant + y → change y to i and add -ed o carry → carried o study → studied Examples in Sentences: • She cleaned the classroom yesterday. • We visited our grandparents last holiday. • The teacher marked the scripts carefully. 4. Irregular Verbs Definition: Irregular verbs do not form their past tense by adding -ed . Instead, their past forms change completely , change partially , or remain the same . Characteristics: • There is no fixed rule for forming their past tense. • They must be memorized . Common Irregular Verb Forms: Base Form Past Tense Past Participle go went gone eat ate eaten see saw seen come came come take took taken write wrote written

Base Form Past Tense Past Participle cut cut cut Examples in Sentences: • She went to school late yesterday. • I have seen that movie before. • They ate rice for lunch. • The boy cut the rope with a knife. 5. Differences Between Regular and Irregular Verbs Regular Verbs Irregular Verbs End with -ed / -d in past tense Do not follow -ed rule Easy to form Must be memorized Example: talk → talked Example: speak → spoke 6. Summary • A verb shows action or state of being. • Regular verbs form their past tense by adding -ed . • Irregular verbs change form in the past tense and do not follow a fixed rule. • Correct use of verbs helps improve grammar accuracy and sentence clarity . 7. Class Exercise 1. Identify the verbs in the following sentences and state whether they are regular or irregular : o She opened the door quietly. o They ran very fast. o He finished his assignment. o We drank water after the match. 2. Write five (5) regular verbs and five (5) irregular verbs. Use each in a sentence.

Prepared by: Mrs. Naadzenga Mgbede Grace English Language Teacher

title: COMPREHENSION
subject: English Language
rawText: Topic: Comprehension: Comprehending words meanings in context/ Activity- Page 104 section A. CONTENT: Meaning. How to comprehend the meanings of words in context. Comprehension: means understanding. To comprehend words in context means to understand the meaning of a given word used in the context or passage. USEFUL HINTS: Before the meaning of a word can be given, the contextual usage must be considered, this might be quite different from the general meaning of the word. When replacing a given word in a passage, test your equivalent in the passage to see if the original meaning of the passage or sentence has been retained. The equivalents should be exact equivalents. For example, you should retain the tense of the original verb; E.g. 'stared' should be replaced by 'gazed'. you must also retain the word class I.e if a word is a noun, it equivalent must also be a noun and vice versa. E.gprobity(noun)- honesty, decency, intergity, uprightness,saintliness. All these are nouns. Vehemently (adverb)-strongly{adverb}, forcefully etc. Jealous (adjective)-envious(adjective). The word given must be equivalent to the word in the context.

title: RISING TUNE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Intonation In linguistics, Intonation is the variation in pitch used to indicate the speaker's attitudes and emotions. In other words iit is the rise and fall in the voice while speaking. There are two basic intonation patterns, namely Rising Tune Falling Tune Intonation patterns are indicated in writing using arrows. Falling tune Rising tune USES OF THE RISING TUNE A) Yes or No questions that require yes or no answer. Example 1) Is English your best subject? 2) Are you going to eat that? B) Incomplete Statement , 1) As soon as the rain stops .......... 2) Although I had never met the senator, ........... 3) Since the cost of books has risen,. ........ C,) Simple polite requests. Examples: 1) Could you pass the sugar, please? 2) A minute of your time please? 3) Could you me your pen ? D) Surprise questions Examples:

1) She eats cockroaches? 2) She is the younger sister? E) Confirmation questions 1) You are from FCT, right? 2) We meet at six, right? F) Expressing uncertainty / doubts . Examples: 1) You think so? 2) He did what? G) Listing items 1) We bought apples, oranges and bananas. 2) I invited Mary, John and Paul.

title: STRUCTURE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Types of Sentence According to Structure A sentence is a group of words with a subject and a predicate that has a finite verb and makes a complete sense or thought on its own. It starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop (.), a question mark (?) or an exclamation mark (!) *CHARACTERISTICS OF A SENTENCE* It is a group of words. It has a subject and a predicate. It has a finite verb. It starts with a capital letter. It ends with a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark. It makes a complete sense or thought on its own. *Study these:* I have Kola. Proverbs are the palm oil with which words are eaten. Is he staying long with us? Do what you are told, woman! The words above starts with capital letters and end with a full stop, a question mark and an exclamation mark respectively. They also possess subjects, predicates and finite verbs. *TYPES OF SENTENCE ACCORDING TO STRUCTURE* This is the classification of sentences according to their grammatical structures. *SIMPLE SENTENCE:* This is a kind of sentence with one main verb. It consists of one subject and one predicate and makes a single thought. It may possess auxiliary verbs but has only one main verb. *Study these:* She travelled to Akure. I was left with no one at home. The captain of the team elected by the coaching crew scored a goal at the last match. The above sentences have one main verb each, which are underlined respectively.

*COMPOUND SENTENCE:* This is a kind of sentence that is made up of two simple sentence joined with a coordinating conjunction – and, but, yet, or, etc. It possesses two subjects and two predicates joining the two thoughts. *Study these:* a. John likes mangoes. b. Mark likes oranges. Sentences (a) and (b) are simple sentences but can be joined with a coordinating conjunction. John likes mangoes but Mark likes oranges *More examples:* a. They told him but he did not believe. b. She saw her mother and her brother arrive. *When the subjects are the same, the second subject is usually omitted but when they differ, they are both written.* c. The boy came home. d. The boy washed his clothes Joining them to form a compound sentence, it will be written thus: *The boy came home and washed his clothes.* *3. COMPLEX SENTENCE:* lt is a kind of sentence with one simple sentence and one or more subordinate clause joined with a subordinating conjunction – when, after, while, where, immediately, because, etc. *Study these:* a. I met the girl when she was crying b. He was dismissed because of his fraudulent acts. c. After he arrived, Bode came to see me because he needed some money. The underline words are the main or simple sentences, while the ones not underlined are the subordinate clauses. 4. *COMPOUND COMPLEX SENTENCE:* This is a kind of sentence with two or more simple sentences and one or more subordinate clauses. It has more than one simple sentence with one or more than one subordinate clause.

*Study these:* a. The boy is fluent and brilliant because he attends a private school. b. The boy came to then stream and washed his clothes because it was dirty. c. The man shot at the bird, he fried it but he was unable to eat it because he felt sick after he left the farm. *Note that a simple sentence differs not from a main clause.*

SCHEME OF WORK ENGLIGH LANGUAGE SS1 1 ST TERM 2025/2026 SESSION WEEK 1 SPEECH - Selected Consonant Sounds /j/, /z/ and /ӡ/ Vocabulary Development – Vocabulary associated with home and family STRUCTURE - Nouns -Types of nouns COMPREHENSION - Reading to comprehend main or storyline WEEK 2 SPEECH -Selected consonant sounds/ð/, /θ/ VOCABULARY DEVELOPMENT -Vocabulary associated with agriculture COMPREHENSION -Reading to comprehend main ideas or storyline STRUCTURE -Nouns continued CONTINUOUS WRITING -Writing for effective communication in given length. WEEK 3 SPEECH -Consonants followed by /w/. STRUCTURE -Noun phrases.
