title: CONCORD
subject: English Language
rawText:
CONCORD AND COLLOCATION The word 'concord' simply means agreement or harmony. It is the agreement which must exist between the subject of a sentence; whether a noun, noun phrase or pronoun, and the verb. The rule of concord is that singular subject must be followed by a singular verb while a plural subject must be followed by a plural verb. Talking about singular and plural subjects or nouns and singular and plural verbs, it is important to state here that plural nouns can be recognised by the addition of 's', 'es', 'ies' to them. Conversely, verbs that have these letters added to them are in the singular form, not plural. This is the first step towards students' mastery of concord. Consider the illustration below: DIFFERENT APPLICATIONS OF CONCORD (1) Any time either or /neither nor correlates two subjects, the verb to use will be determined by the subject nearest to the verb, that is, the subject that immediately follows nor/or. Let us take a look at the following sentences: (i) Either James or you are sick (correct). Either James or you is sick (wrong). (ii) Either Udoh or the boys are foolish (correct). Either Udoh or the boys is foolish (wrong). (2) When a percentage or fraction is the subject of a sentence, followed by of, it is the noun or pronoun that follows the percentage or fraction that determines the verb to use, not the percentage or fraction. If the percentage or fraction is singular, then a singular verb follows, and vice versa. (i) Three quarters of the students have packed in (correct) Three quarters of the students has packed in (wrong). (ii). Sixty per cent of the class is absent (correct).

Sixty per cent of the class are absent (wrong). (3) Many a or many an must be followed by a singular noun in a sentence, followed also by a singular verb: Many a/an + singular noun + singular verb. (i) Many a student does not read anymore (correct). Many a student do not read anymore (wrong). (ii) Many an egg has been eaten today (correct). Many an egg have been eaten today (wrong). (iii) Many a preacher has died lately (correct). Many a preacher have died lately (wrong). (4) Anytime the word number is the subject of a sentence and is followed by of, it takes a plural verb if number is preceded by the indefinite articles a, and a singular verb if preceded by the definite article the. Eg: (i) A number of students have been arrested (correct). A number of students has been arrested (wrong). (ii) The number of students is not known (correct). The number of students are not known (wrong). (5). A plural noun which is the subject of a sentence will take a singular verb if it is referring to time, distance, money or measurement Plural nouns relating to time include seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, years, etc. Plural nouns relating to distance include metres, kilometers, miles, etc. Plural nouns relating to money include dollars, nȧira, shilling, pounds, etc. while plural nouns relating to measurement include grammes, kilogrammes, yards, litres, etc. Examples: (i) Ten minutes was allocated to prayers (correct).

Ten minutes were allocated to prayers (wrong). (ii)Ten yards of lace material is just enough (correct). Ten yards of lace material are just enough (wrong). (iii) Ten kilometres of trekking needs to be done (correct). Ten kilometres of trekking need to be done (wrong). (iv) Ten million naira is needed for his trip (correct). Ten million naira are needed for his trip (wrong). 6. Any time any of the collectives is used as the subject of a sentence, it must go with a plural noun followed by a singular verb. Examples: (i) A battalion of soldiers has moved to Kano (correct). A battalion of soldiers have moved to Kano (wrong). (ii) A troupe of dancers is needed for the ceremony (correct). A troupe of dancers are needed for the ceremony (wrong). (iii) A swarm of locusts has been sighted from afar (correct). A swarm of locusts have been sighted from afar (wrong). (iv) A flock of sheep has invaded his farm (correct). A flock of sheep have invaded his farm (wrong). When a collective name is used to denote a category (of people), it goes with a plural verb. Examples: (i) The rich also cry (correct). The rich also cries (wrong). (ii) The blind need assistance (correct). The blind needs assistance (wrong). (iii) The poor always feel cheated (correct). The poor always feels cheated (wrong). 8. A collective noun may take a singular or plural verb depending on the notion

one has in mind. When a collective noun is seen as an entity, it takes a singular verb but when it is seen from the angle of the individual items that constituted the entity, it takes a plural verb Again, a collective noun that is not performing any action takes a singular verb and a plural verb when it is performing an action. Examples: (i) The police are searching for criminals (correct). The police is searching for criminals (wrong). (The action here is 'searching') (ii) The police is your friend (correct). The police are your friend (wrong). (Police' here is an entity) (iii) The audience is too large (correct). The audience are too large (wrong). ('Audience' not performing any action). 9. When all means 'everything' it takes a singular verb but when it refers to a collection of people or actions, it takes a plural verb. Examples: (i) All want to travel abroad (correct). All wants to travel abroad (wrong). (All' here refers to people) (ii) All is set for the inauguration (correct). All are set for the inauguration (wrong). (All' here refers to everything) (iii) All that glitters is not gold (correct). All that glitters are not gold (wrong). (All' above means everything)

(iv) All is not well here (correct). All are not well here (wrong). (All' here also means everything) (v) All have agreed to pay promptly (correct). All has agreed to pay promptly (wrong). (All' here refers to a collection of people). 10. When a singular number or noun follows 'every' or 'each' as is always the case, a singular verb is used. Examples: (i) Every man wants to be the boss (correct). Every man want to be the boss (wrong). (ii) Each biro costs ten naira (correct). Each biro cost ten naira (wrong). However, when every or each is used in a sentence and a coordinator and links two or more subjects, a singular verb is used. (i) Every pastor, deacon and elder needs to attend (correct). Every pastor, deacon and elder need to attend (wrong). (ii) Every boy and girl knows the reason (correct). Every boy and girl know the reason (wrong). Again, each of and everyone of must be followed by a plural number and a singular verb: Examples: (i) Each of the boys has a friend (correct). Each of the boys have a friend (wrong). (ii) Everyone of the members was fined for lateness (correct). Everyone of the members were fined for lateness (wrong).

title: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH HOME AND FAMILY
subject: English Language
rawText: Words Associated with Home and Family A home is a place of residence or refuge. It is usually a place in which an individual or a family can rest and store/keep personal property. A family is a group of people who are related by birth or marriage. Vocabularies Associated with the Home and Family under the following headings Family relations: Siblings, next of kin, grandparents, uncle, aunt, children, mother, father, nephew, niece, brother, sister, etc. cousin Items found in the home: Kitchen utensils, e.g. pots, plates, cutleries, cup, gas cooker, stove, blender, etc. wardrobe, bed, bed-sheet, pillows, standing fan, air conditioner etc. cushion, television, centre table, photo frames, dining table etc., washing hand basin, water system, soap-dish, bathing towel etc. Sentence samples My father’s brother is my uncle My mother has a lot of kitchen utensils The tailor made twelve beautiful pillow cases My son broke the standing mirror in my bedroom The plumber has not fixed the water closet Assignment Refer to unit 1 of new concept English 1 on register home and family

title: COMPLEX TENSES
subject: English Language
rawText:
In English grammar, complex tenses refer to verb forms that combine auxiliary (helping) verbs with the main verb to show different times, actions, or situations. These tenses help convey more specific details about when an action took place, whether it’s finished, ongoing, or will happen in the future. Understanding complex tenses can improve your ability to express actions in the past, present, or future, as well as ongoing or completed actions. 1. Present Perfect Tense Structure: Subject + has/have + past participle of the main verb. Use: It talks about an action that happened at an unspecified time before now and may still be relevant. Example: "She has finished her homework." 2. Past Perfect Tense Structure: Subject + had + past participle of the main verb. Use: It expresses an action that was completed before another action or event in the past. Example: "By the time we arrived, they had already left." 3. Future Perfect Tense Structure: Subject + will have + past participle of the main verb. Use: It describes an action that will be completed before a specific time in the future. Example: "By next year, I will have graduated." 4. Present Perfect Continuous Tense Structure: Subject + has/have + been + present participle of the main verb (verb + ing). Use: This tense describes an action that started in the past and is still continuing or has just finished, often with a focus on the duration. Example: "I have been studying for two hours." 5. Past Perfect Continuous Tense Structure: Subject + had + been + present participle of the main verb (verb + ing).

Use: This tense describes an action that was ongoing in the past before another past event happened. Example: "He had been working all day when I called him." 6. Future Perfect Continuous Tense Structure: Subject + will have been + present participle of the main verb (verb + ing). Use: This tense shows an ongoing action that will be happening until a certain point in the future. Example: "By the end of this year, I will have been living here for 10 years."

title: CONSONANT SOUNDS
subject: English Language
rawText: LESSON NOTE Selected Consonant Sounds /j/, /z/, /ʒ/ consonant sounds is speech sounds produced with an obstruction of the air stream. When a consonant sound is produced, the flow of air from the lungs is obstructed somewhere in the mouth by either the tongue, teeth or lips. In the English language, there are twenty four (24) consonant sounds Consonants are divided into two parts, namely; (a) Voiced Consonants (b) Voiceless Consonants The voiced consonants are the consonants that the vocal cords vibrate when they are produced. title: STRUCTURE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Complex Tense Forms Meaning of Tense Tense refers to the form of a verb that shows the time an action happens. There are three main tenses in English: Present Tense – action happening now Past Tense – action that has already happened Future Tense – action that will happen later Complex tense forms are tenses that use more than one verb (helping verbs + main verb). Types of Complex Tense Forms 1. Present Continuous Tense Structure Subject + am/is/are + verb + ing Uses Actions happening now Temporary actions Examples I am reading a book. She is cooking. They are playing football. 2. Past Continuous Tense Structure Subject + was/were + verb + ing Uses Action that was going on in the past Interrupted past action

Examples I was sleeping when you called. They were dancing yesterday. She was writing a letter. 3. Future Continuous Tense Structure Subject + will be + verb + ing Uses Action that will be happening in the future Examples I will be travelling tomorrow. She will be studying tonight. They will be playing by noon. Perfect Tenses Perfect tenses show completed actions. 4. Present Perfect Tense Structure Subject + has/have + past participle Uses Action completed recently Experience Examples I have eaten. She has finished her work. They have travelled to Lagos.

5. Past Perfect Tense Structure Subject + had + past participle Uses Action completed before another past action Examples He had left before I arrived. They had eaten before the meeting started. She had written the test earlier. 6. Future Perfect Tense Structure Subject + will have + past participle Uses Action that will be completed before a future time Examples I will have finished the work by Friday. She will have arrived before noon. They will have completed the project soon. Perfect Continuous Tenses These tenses show actions that continue over a period of time. 7. Present Perfect Continuous Tense Structure Subject + has/have been + verb + ing Uses Action that started in the past and is still continuing

Examples I have been reading for two hours. She has been singing since morning. They have been working all day. 8. Past Perfect Continuous Tense Structure Subject + had been + verb + ing Uses Continuous action before another past action Examples He had been sleeping before the noise started. They had been waiting for hours. She had been teaching before she retired. 9. Future Perfect Continuous Tense Structure Subject + will have been + verb + ing Uses Continuous action that will continue up to a point in the future Examples By next year, I will have been working here for five years. She will have been studying for hours by then. They will have been travelling all day. Summary Table Tense Structure

Example Present Continuous am/is/are + ing She is singing Past Continuous was/were + ing They were dancing Future Continuous will be + ing I will be reading Present Perfect has/have + past participle He has gone Past Perfect had + past participle She had left Future Perfect will have + past participle They will have finished Present Perfect Continuous has/have been + ing I have been reading Past Perfect Continuous had been + ing He had been working

Future Perfect Continuous will have been + ing She will have been teaching Important Notes Helping verbs are important in complex tense forms. The main verb may appear as: Present participle (-ing) Past participle (eaten, gone, written) Time expressions often help identify tense: now, yesterday, since, for, tomorrow, by next week Exercise Change the verbs in brackets to the correct complex tense form. She _________ (read) for two hours. They _________ (finish) the work before noon. I _________ (wait) when he arrived. We _________ (travel) tomorrow morning. He _________ (study) since morning. Answers has been reading will have finished was waiting will be travelling has been studying

title: PHRASES
subject: English Language
rawText: Topic: PHRASE A phrase is a group of words that stands together as a single grammatical unit, typically as part of a clause or a sentence. It does not contain a verb. Often, phrases are used for description of people, things or events. Types of phrase 1. Noun phrase 2. verb phrase 3. adjective phrase 4. adverb phrase 5. prepositional phrase 6. gerund phrase 7. infinitive phrase 8. participial phrase.

title: ARTICLE
subject: English Language
rawText: Article Writing Content Definition, Features, Sample Question,Outline An article is a type of writing that is meant to be published in a school magazines, a newspaper or a journal. Basic Features It must have a heading It must have an introductory paragraph Its body should contain at least three well development paragraphs which should serve as the content of the writing. When added to the introductory and concluding paragraphs, the writing should not be less than five paragraphs. But it can be more It must contain a concluding paragraph Write your full name and your class, school, town or city as the situation may require. Outline: Women in Politics Topic/Heading Introduction: Men have dominated the political space for long The effects of men’s domination The need for women’s involvement (equality, less corruption, compassionate, talent use, example from other countries) Conclusion: challenge the audience

title: STRUCTURE - NOUN
subject: English Language
rawText:
Structure Noun: Types of Nouns Definition of Noun: A noun is a naming word. It can name Persons. For example: Ada, Olu, Adamu Places: Lagos Abuja Things: Book, classroom Ideas and concepts: e.g. beauty, happiness Animals e.g goat, ewe Types of Noun Proper Noun: This refers to the specific names of persons. Example Kemi, Charles etc. Cities: Lagos, Abuja Countries: Nigeria, United States of America Institutions: Central Bank of Nigeria, University of Nigeria Nsukka. Months and Days: January, Monday Note: It should be noted that all proper noun must begin with a capital letter including the personal pronoun “I” irrespective the position in a sentence. rawText:
1 SCHOOL FOR THE GIFTED GWAGWALADA ENGLISH LANGUAGE SS1 – THIRD TERM FULL LESSON NOTES Teacher: Mrs. Naadzenga Mgbede Grace WEEK 1 Speech: Intonation Patterns Intonation refers to the variation in the pitch level of the voice when speaking. It plays a crucial role in conveying meaning beyond the literal interpretation of words. In English, intonation helps to distinguish between statements, questions, commands, and emotions such as surprise, anger, or excitement. There are two major types of intonation patterns. The falling intonation is used when the voice drops at the end of a sentence, typically in statements, commands, and WH-questions. For example, in the sentence “She is coming,” the voice falls at the end to indicate completion. Rising intonation, on the other hand, occurs when the pitch rises at the end of an utterance, commonly used in yes/no questions such as “Are you coming?” Learners must understand that incorrect intonation can distort meaning. For instance, using rising intonation in a statement may unintentionally turn it into a question. Structure: Types of Sentences Sentences are classified based on their function. A declarative sentence makes a statement and ends with a full stop. An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark. An imperative sentence gives a command or request, while an exclamatory sentence expresses strong emotion. Understanding sentence types helps students construct meaningful and grammatically correct expressions in both spoken and written communication.

2 Writing: Speech Writing Speech writing involves preparing a structured presentation intended for oral delivery. A good speech begins with an introduction that captures attention, followed by a body that develops ideas logically, and ends with a conclusion that reinforces the message. Effective speech writing must consider audience, purpose, tone, and clarity. The use of rhetorical devices such as repetition, rhetorical questions, and vivid examples enhances engagement. WEEK 2 Speech: Oral Composition Oral composition involves expressing ideas verbally in a clear and organized manner. It requires proper pronunciation, logical sequencing of ideas, and appropriate use of language. Students are trained to speak fluently on given topics, maintaining coherence and clarity while avoiding unnecessary pauses and repetition. Vocabulary: Words Associated with Advertising Advertising vocabulary includes terms such as “promotion,” “brand,” “consumer,” “slogan,” and “marketing.” These words are used in contexts related to selling products or services. Understanding such vocabulary enhances comprehension of media messages and improves communication in commercial contexts. Comprehension and Summary: Summarising a Passage Summarising involves reducing a passage to its essential points without altering the original meaning. Students must identify key ideas, eliminate repetition, and express the summary in their own words. Structure: Types of Sentences (Continued) Further emphasis is placed on recognizing sentence types in complex texts and using them appropriately in writing and speech.

3 WEEK 3 Speech: Intonation Patterns (Continued) Students engage in practical exercises to master intonation through dialogue reading and role play. Emphasis is placed on how intonation conveys attitudes and emotions. Structure: Complex Sentences A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one subordinate clause. The subordinate clause cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. Examples include sentences introduced by conjunctions such as “because,” “although,” and “when.” Mastery of complex sentences improves writing sophistication. Writing: Descriptive Essay (Oral Composition) A descriptive essay focuses on vividly portraying a person, place, object, or event. It relies heavily on sensory details, including sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Students are encouraged to organize their descriptions logically and use figurative language to create imagery. WEEK 4 Speech: Emphatic Stress Emphatic stress involves placing extra force on certain words to highlight importance or contrast. For example, in the sentence “I said now , not later,” the stressed word changes the meaning. Students learn how stress affects meaning and improves clarity in communication.

4 Vocabulary: Synonyms Synonyms are words that have similar meanings. For example, “happy” and “joyful.” Learning synonyms enriches vocabulary and prevents repetition in writing. Structure: Clauses (Independent and Dependent) An independent clause expresses a complete thought, while a dependent clause relies on another clause for meaning. Understanding clauses helps in constructing complex sentences. Writing: Article Writing Article writing involves presenting information or opinions on a topic in a structured format. It requires a clear introduction, detailed body, and logical conclusion. WEEK 5 Speech: Polite Requests and Greetings Politeness in speech involves using expressions such as “please,” “thank you,” and “excuse me.” Greetings vary depending on context and time of day. Students are taught appropriate social expressions to enhance communication etiquette. Vocabulary: Antonyms Antonyms are words with opposite meanings, such as “hot” and “cold.” Learning antonyms improves understanding of word relationships. Comprehension: Contextual Meaning Students learn to derive the meaning of unfamiliar words from context rather than relying solely on dictionaries.

5 Structure: Noun Clauses A noun clause functions as a noun within a sentence. It can serve as subject, object, or complement. WEEK 6 Speech: Expository Oral Composition Expository speaking involves explaining or informing. It requires clarity, factual accuracy, and logical organization. Vocabulary: Investment Terms Words such as “capital,” “interest,” “dividend,” and “profit” are introduced to familiarize students with financial language. Comprehension: Note-Making Students learn to extract key information and present it in concise note form using headings and subheadings. Structure: Adjectival Clauses Adjectival clauses describe nouns and are introduced by relative pronouns such as “who,” “which,” and “that.”

6 WEEK 7 Speech: Persuasive Speaking Persuasive speaking aims to convince the audience. It involves presenting arguments, evidence, and appealing to emotions or logic. Structure: Adjectival Clauses (Continued) Further exercises focus on identifying and constructing adjectival clauses correctly. WEEK 8 Comprehension: Reading Speed and Accuracy Students practice reading quickly while maintaining understanding. This skill is essential for examinations. Vocabulary: Political Register Words related to politics such as “democracy,” “election,” and “governance” are introduced. Writing: Argumentative Essay An argumentative essay presents a claim supported by evidence. It includes introduction, arguments, counterarguments, and conclusion. WEEK 9 Speech: Oral Description Students describe events or objects verbally, focusing on clarity and vividness.

7 Structure: Commonly Misspelt Words Attention is given to frequently misspelt words to improve writing accuracy. Vocabulary: Photography Terms Words such as “lens,” “focus,” and “exposure” are taught. WEEK 10 Speech: Identifying Speaker’s Style Students learn to recognize tone, mood, and style in spoken language. Structure: Active and Passive Voice In active voice, the subject performs the action, while in passive voice, the subject receives the action. Vocabulary: British and American Spelling Differences such as “colour” and “color” are examined. WEEK 11 Speech: Listening for Main Ideas Students practice identifying key points in spoken passages, improving listening comprehension.

8 WEEK 12 Speech: Revision of Consonant Sounds Students revise consonant sounds, focusing on correct pronunciation and articulation. Structure: Synonyms Further reinforcement of synonyms is provided. Writing: Formal and Informal Letters Students learn the differences in tone, format, and language between formal and informal letters. Formal letters are structured and polite, while informal letters are conversational.

title: SPEECH
subject: English Language
rawText:
Intonation Pattern: Rising Tune. Intonation refers to the pattern of changes that take place during speech production. In connected speech, intonation is the variation (the rise and fall) in the pitch of the voice. Intonation enables the listener to interpret an utterance accurately and get the correct information passed across. There are two basic intonation patterns namely; Rising Tune Falling Tune Intonation patterns are indicated in writing using arrows. Falling tune Rising tune FUNCTIONS OF INTONATION. Intonation has two basic functions: grammatical and attitudinal. The grammatical function refers to the ability of voice pitch to indicate to a listener the grammatical classification of an utterance. This means that specific intonation patterns are associated with specific sentence types. For example: statements, commands, exclamations are said with a falling tune while questions demanding a yes/ or are rendered with a rising tune. The attitudinal function conveys to the listener information relating to the speaker’s emotional attitude either to the listener or the topic of discussion. For example: a speaker’s intonation might reveal surprise, doubt, or warmth. USES OF THE RISING TUNE The rising tune is used to make: 1. Simple polite requests. Examples: Please sit down.

A minute of your time please. 2. Simple greeting Examples: Good morning. Hello 3. Questions that require Yes/No answer. Examples: Must you go with them? Do you like apples? 4. Questions without formal question markers such as who, what, when, etc. Examples: He is going home? Kemi is ill? 5. Incomplete statements. Examples: As soon as the rains stops, I’ll ………. Since the price of crude oil has fallen, African countries need to ………… 6. Listing items. Examples: She bought carrots, green pepper, peas, green beans, cabbage, and spring onions. 7. Express surprise or doubts. Examples: You did this yourself?

title: SYLLABIC CONSONANTS /L/ AND /N/
subject: English Language
rawText:
A syllabic consonant is a phonetic element that normally patterns as a consonant, but may fill a vowel slot in a syllable. In other words a syllabic consonant is a consonant that can form an entire syllable on its own, without any vowels. Ususally, a syllable contains a vowel. Syllabic / l/ and /ņ/ typically occur in an unstressed syllable immediately following the alveolar consonants, /t/, /s/, /z/, as well as /d/. Examples: :bottle /ba:t|/, cattle /'kæt|/, chisel /s / cotton /ka:tn:/, button /bAtn/. listen /IIsn/, fasten /fæsn/ risen /rizn/, prison 'prizn/ saddle /'sædļ/, poodle /pu:d/ sadden /'sædn/, burden /badn/ Syllabic /l/can also follow /st/ or plain /n/ or-- Examples: pistol /pist|/ tunnel /tan|/ mantle /mæntl Syllabic consonants are consonants that can form a syllable on their own, replacing schwa sounds in unstressed syllables. Though /l/ and /n/ are the noticeable syllable consonant in English syllable /l/ ... The syllabic /n/ is common after alveolar plosives and fricatives. syllabic consonants l/ and /n Syllabic consonants are consonants that form a syllable by themselves, without a vowel sound. In English, the sounds /n/ and /l/ can act as syllabic consonants, most commonly in unstressed

syllables. Syllabic /n/ The /n/ sound carries the syllable after an alveolar consonant like /t/ or /d/. Examples: button: /ˈbʌt.n̩ / listen: /ˈlɪs.n̩ / sadden: /ˈsæd.n̩ / often: /ˈɔf.n̩ / (note that "often" has a silent 't' and the 'n' is syllabic) didn't: /dɪd.n̩ / Syllabic /l/ How it works: The /l/ sound carries the syllable after certain consonants like /t/, /d/, /s/, /z/, /n/, or /nt/. Examples: bottle: /ˈbɑːt.l̩ / saddle: /ˈsæd.l̩ / puddle: /ˈpʌd.l̩ / pistol: /ˈpɪs.təl/ mantle: /ˈmæn.tl̩ / tunnel: /ˈtʌn.l̩ / Important considerations Unstressed syllables: Syllabic consonants usually occur in unstressed syllables. Phonetic transcription: In phonetic transcriptions, a small vertical line under the consonant (e.g., [n̩ ] or [l̩ ]) indicates that it is syllabic. Natural speech: While you might see a vowel written in words like "button," native speakers produce the word without an extra vowel sound, making the syllabic consonant the only "vowel" sound in that syllable. syllabic consonant, the syllabic consonant may

either be retained as such or it simply becomes the initial consonant of the extra syllable. Examples: Listening /lisnın/ going /'gowIn/ Pronouncing Syllabic Consonants: /l/ and /n/ in English ... Syllabic Consonants: /l/ and /n/ · 1. sound the final /n/ · 2. avoid putting in a vowel before the Examples of consonants followed by the /j/ sound /j/ sound spelled with "u" In many words, the /j/ sound is represented by the letter "u" and follows a consonant. cute during music popular tune value computer Common consonant + w blends dw: dwell, dwarf, dwindle sw: sweep, swing, swift tw: twist, twin, twelve Words with initial consonant + w Dw-: dwell, dwarf, dwindle, dwelt Sw-: sweet, sweat, sweep, swim, swing, swoosh, swoop Tw-: twist, twig, twelve, twin, twine, twenty, twirl Qu- (/kw/ sound): quit, quiet, queen, quiz, quick, quilt

title: FORMAL LETTER
subject: English Language
rawText:
Formal Letter A letter is a written message sent from one person to another. Letters can be formal or informal depending on the relationship between the writer and the receiver. A formal letter is written to people in official positions or to people we do not know personally. Examples include letters written to: The principal A company manager A government official An editor of a newspaper Definition of Formal Letter A formal letter is an official letter written to someone in authority or for official purposes using polite and formal language. Features of a Formal Letter A formal letter has the following parts: 1. Writer's Address This is the address of the person writing the letter. Example: 15 Unity Street Wuse Zone 3 Abuja 2. Date This is written below the writer’s address. Example: 10th March, 2026 3. Receiver's Address This is the address of the person receiving the letter.

Example: The Principal Government Secondary School Garki, Abuja 4. Salutation This is the greeting used in the letter. Examples: Dear Sir, Dear Madam, 5. Heading / Title This shows the purpose of the letter. Example: Application for Permission to Organize a Debate 6. Body of the Letter This contains the main message. It is usually written in paragraphs. Introduction paragraph Main explanation Conclusion 7. Complimentary Close This is the polite way to end the letter. Examples: Yours faithfully Yours sincerely 8. Signature and Name

The writer signs and writes their name. Example: Yours faithfully (Signature) Victory Ojeba Characteristics of Formal Letters Use formal language. Avoid slang and contractions. Be clear and direct. Be polite and respectful. Follow the correct format. Example of a Formal Letter 15 Unity Street, Wuse Zone 3, Abuja. 10th March, 2026 The Principal, Government Secondary School Garki, Abuja Dear Sir, APPLICATION FOR PERMISSION TO ORGANIZE A DEBATE I write to request permission to organize a debate competition in our school. The purpose of the debate is to improve students’ speaking skills and build their confidence. The debate will involve students from different classes and will take place in the school hall next month. We believe this activity will help students develop their communication abilities and critical thinking. I will be grateful if my request is granted.

Yours faithfully, (Signature) Gambo Salami.

title: MECHANICS IN WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText:
Mechanics in Writing Mechanics in writing refers to the rules and conventions that help us write clearly, correctly, and in a way that others can easily understand. It deals with how writing looks on the page — the technical aspects of writing. Main Elements of Writing Mechanics 1. Capitalization Use capital letters for: The first word in a sentence. Proper nouns (names of people, places, days, months, etc.). The pronoun “I”. Example: My name is Victory. ✅ my name is victory. ❌ 2. Punctuation Punctuation marks help to separate ideas and show meaning. Examples: Full stop (.) – Ends a sentence. Comma (,) – Shows a short pause. Question mark (?) – Ends a question. Exclamation mark (!) – Shows strong feeling. Apostrophe (’) – Shows possession or missing letters. Quotation marks (“ ”) – Show direct speech or titles. 3. Spelling Words must be spelled correctly to avoid confusion. Example: Because not becos ✅

Beautiful not beautifull ✅ 4. Paragraphing Each paragraph should contain one main idea. Indent or leave a space at the beginning of each new paragraph. Helps organize ideas and make writing neat. 5. Abbreviations and Numbers Use abbreviations correctly (e.g., Mr., Dr., etc.). Write numbers appropriately: Spell out small numbers (one to nine). Use figures for larger ones (10, 20, 100). Importance of Mechanics in Writing Makes writing clear and understandable. Helps readers follow your ideas easily. Shows that the writer is careful and educated. Improves the overall quality of writing.

Exclamation mark (!) – Shows strong feeling. Apostrophe (’) – Shows possession or missing letters. Quotation marks (“ ”) – Show direct speech or titles. 3. Spelling Words must be spelled correctly to avoid confusion. Example: Because not becos ✅

Beautiful not beautifull ✅ 4. Paragraphing Each paragraph should contain one main idea. Indent or leave a space at the beginning of each new paragraph. Helps organize ideas and make writing neat. 5. Abbreviations and Numbers Use abbreviations correctly (e.g., Mr., Dr., etc.). Write numbers appropriately: Spell out small numbers (one to nine). Use figures for larger ones (10, 20, 100). Importance of Mechanics in Writing Makes writing clear and understandable. Helps readers follow your ideas easily. Shows that the writer is careful and educated. Improves the overall quality of writing.

title: STRESS
subject: English Language
rawText:
TOPIC: SPEECH: WORDS OF THREE SYLLABLES STRESSED ON THE 2ND SYLLABLE Stress is the degree of force by which a word is pronounced. Words are broken into tiny units called syllables. A syllable is the pronounced unit of a word. It is on a syllable that stress is placed. Stressing a syllable therefore means giving it more force, such that it is louder, longer and higher in pitch than other syllables. A stressed syllable like in the dictionary is indicated by placing a stroke at the beginning of the syllable, but here, a stressed syllable should be written in capital letters. THREE SYLLABLE WORDS Three syllable words are parts of polysyllable words which have their different stress patterns with some guiding rules. These rules help us to identify when to stress the word on the first, second, third or fourth syllable. For three syllable words stressed on the second syllable, the rule guiding it says Stress the second syllable from the end of a word if it ends in : - cient, - ion, - ic, - ial, - ian. Examples suf-FI-cient ef- FI-cient ic stra-TE-gic dra-MA-tic -ion o-CCA-sion pro-JEC-tion

dis-CU-ssion con-VIC-tion in-JEC-tion star-VA-tion con-VER-sion con-STRUC-tion fru-STRA-tion o-VA-tion -ial co-LO-nial of-FI-cial com-MER-cial -ian ci-VI-lian Examples of the three syllable words in a sentence The fru-STRA-tion in that job is too much She is at the venue for col-LA-tion of results The people in overalls are con-STRUC-tion workers Something dra-MA-tic happened yesterday I am a ci-VI-lian not a soldier

title: ADVERTISING
subject: English Language
rawText:
Advertising is a means of communication with the users of a product or service. Advertisements are messages paid for by those who send them and are intended to inform or influence people who receive them. Advertising is the act or practice of calling public attention to one's product, service, need, etc., especially by paid announcements in newspapers and magazines, over radio or television, on billboards, etc. Advertising is the profession of planning, designing, and writing advertisements. In today's world, advertising uses every possible media to get its message through. It does this via television, print (newspapers, magazines, journals etc), radio, press, internet, direct selling, hoardings, mailers, contests, sponsorships, posters, clothes, events, colours, sounds, visuals and even people (endorsements). The advertising industry is made of companies that advertise agencies that create the advertisements, media that carries the ads, and a host of people like copy editors, visualizers, brand managers, researchers, creative heads and designers who take it the last mile to the customer or receiver. A company that needs to advertise itself and/or its products hires an advertising agency.. title: SPEECH
subject: English Language
rawText:
Four Syllable Words with Stress on the First, Second and Third Syllable. A syllable is a word or that part of a word which represent the minimum unit of pronunciation; it contains one vowel sound and may be preceded or followed by one or more consonants. Stress on the other hand is the emphasis or force that one syllable carries in a word or sentence. In other words, stress is the degree of force with which a syllable is uttered. When the degree of force is high, we say the syllable is stressed, but when the degree of force is low, we say that the syllable is unstressed. Syllables stressed on first, second and third syllable are notalways easy to identify the syllable that is stressed. Therefore the following rules will be used as a guide: Most 4 syllable words that end in ... ABLE have their primary stress on the first syllable. Examples: Lamentable LA-men-ta-ble Applicable AP-pli-ca-ble lamentable LA-men-ta-ble Most 4 syllable words that end in... ATE have their primary stress on the second syllable. Examples: Communicate com-MU-ni-cate Comfortable COM-for-ta-ble Admirable AD-mi-ra-ble Eradicate e-RA-di-cate Accelerate a-CE-re-late Articulate ar-TI-cu-late Congratulate con-GRA-tu-late on the second syllable. Most 4 syllable words that end in ... LITY... SITY... MITY/...NITY have their primary stress Examples:

Calamity ca-LA-mi-ty Totality to-TA-li-ty Fidelity fi-DE-li-ty Finality fi-NA-li-ty Maternity ma-TER-ni-ty Pomposity pom-PO-si-ty Most 4 syllable words that end in. ARY have their primary stress on the second syllable. Examples: Judiciary ju-DI-cia-ry Obituary o-BI-tua-ry Most 4 syllable words that end in ... TIVE have their primary stress on the second syllable. Examples: Evocative E-VO-ca-tive Affirmative A-FIRR-ma-tive Demonstrative de-MONS-tra-tive Most 4 syllable words that end in... NAL have their primary stress on the second syllable. Examples: Professional pro-FES-sio-nal Additional ad-DI-tio-nal Occasional oc-CA-sio-nal Rotational ro-TA-tio-nal Intentional in-TEN-tio-nal Most 4 syllable words that end in ... TION have their primary stress on the third syllable. Examples: Federation fe-de-RA-tion Jubiliation ju-bi-LA-tion

Institution ins-ti-TU-tion Population po-pù-LA-tion Most 4 syllable words that end in ... TIC have their primary stress on the third syllable. Examples: Democratic de-mo-CRA-tic Automatic au-to-CRA-tic Systematic sys-te-MA-tic Diplomatic di-plo-MA-tic Energetic e-ne-GE-tic.

title: DEBATE
subject: English Language
rawText:
TOPIC 4: CONTINUOUS WRITING DEBATE A debate is an argument between two persons or group of persons over an issue or a topic. It is an argumentative essay where the writer is expected to argue logically in support or against a topic. It aims at convincing the audience or the reader to share the opinion or view points of the writer. A debate could be written or delivered orally. FEATURES/FORMAT OF A DEBATE The Topic: The topic should be clearly stated and should be underlined if written in small letters The Vocatives: This is the greetings to acknowledge the presence of the members of the panel and the audience. Examples: The Moderator/Chairman, Panel of Judges, Accurate Time Keeper, Co-Debators, Fellow Student/The audience The Introduction: The speaker/writer is expected to introduce himself (if it is oral debate) state the topic and take a stand whether in support or against the motion. The key words in the topic could be defined, quoting from a reliable source. The Body: The speaker/writer should state at least three strong points in favour of his stand to persuade the judges and win them to his side. Also a paragraph should have one point well explained. It is good to counter the opinion of the opponent with good reasons. The Conclusion: Summarize the points raised to re-affirm your position earlier taken by stating that your view points are better than your opponent.

CLASS ACTIVITY You are the Chief speaker representing your school on a debate topic. Technology has done more harm than good. Write in support or against the topic. This should be not less than 350 words

pages.text: TOPIC 4: CONTINUOUS WRITING DEBATE A debate is an argument between two persons or group of persons over an issue or a topic. It is an argumentative essay where the writer is expected to argue logically in support or against a topic. It aims at convincing the audience or the reader to share the opinion or view points of the writer. A debate could be written or delivered orally. FEATURES/FORMAT OF A DEBATE The Topic: The topic should be clearly stated and should be underlined if written in small letters The Vocatives: This is the greetings to acknowledge the presence of the members of the panel and the audience. Examples: The Moderator/Chairman, Panel of Judges, Accurate Time Keeper, Co-Debators, Fellow Student/The audience The Introduction: The speaker/writer is expected to introduce himself (if it is oral debate) state the topic and take a stand whether in support or against the motion. The key words in the topic could be defined, quoting from a reliable source. The Body: The speaker/writer should state at least three strong points in favour of his stand to persuade the judges and win them to his side. Also a paragraph should have one point well explained. It is good to counter the opinion of the opponent with good reasons. The Conclusion: Summarize the points raised to re-affirm your position earlier taken by stating that your view points are better than your opponent.

CLASS ACTIVITY You are the Chief speaker representing your school on a debate topic. Technology has done more harm than good. Write in support or against the topic. This should be not less than 350 words

title: SENTENCE BY FUNCTION
subject: English Language
rawText:
A sentence is a group of words with a subject and a predicate that has a finite verb and makes a complete sense or thought on its own. It starts with a capital letter and ends with either a full stop (.), a question mark (?) or an exclamation mark (!) CHARACTERISTICS OF A SENTENCE* It is a group of words. It has a subject and a predicate. It has a finite verb. It starts with a capital letter. It ends with a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark. It makes a complete sense or thought on its own. *Study these:* I have Kola. Proverbs are the palm oil with which words are eaten. Is he staying long with us? Do what you are told, woman! The sentences above start with capital letters and end with a full stop, a question mark and an exclamation mark respectively. They also possess subjects, predicates and finite verbs. TYPES OF SENTENCE There are two broad types of sentences, namely; *i Types of sentences according to function* *ii. Types of sentences according to structure* One is the grouping of sentences based on the functions they are used to perform, while the other is the grouping of sentences based on their structures. *TYPE OF SENTENCE ACCORDING TO FUNCTIONS* This is the grouping of sentences according to the function they are used to perform. *DECLARATIVE SENTENCE*: This is a kind of sentence that is used to express a thought, an idea or a statement e.g.

a. The boy closed the door. b. The car is for sale. c. A banker bought the new house. *INTERROGATIVE SENTENCE:* These kinds of sentences are used for asking question or making an enquiry e.g. a. Do you know his father? b. Have they built their house? c. Who are his parents? *IMPERATIVE SENTENCE:* This is a kind sentence that is used to make a command, request or suggestion e.g. a. Open the door at once! b. May I use your phone? c. We should help the poor. *DEMONSTRATIVE SENTENCES:* This kind of sentence points out the position of objects (things or person) a. This is the man. b. Those managers are corrupt. c. These are my books. *EXCLAMATORY SENTENCE:* This kind of sentence expresses some strong or sudden feeling. a. What a beauty! b. How brilliant Victoria is! c. What a shame! *OPTATIVE SENTENCE:* This kind of sentence expresses a wish, supposition or probability.

a. We wish she could be with us b. He ought to have been married by now. c. If wishes were horses, beggars would ride.

title: COMPREHENSION
subject: English Language
rawText:
What is Comprehension? Comprehension means understanding what you read. In exams (WAEC / NECO), comprehension tests: how well you understand a passage how well you can answer questions from it What you see in a Comprehension passage A passage (story or article) Questions based on the passage Types of Comprehension Questions 1. Factual questions Answers are directly in the passage. Example: Where did the boy go? 2. Inferential questions You think from the passage, not direct. Example: Why was the man angry? 3. Vocabulary questions Meaning of words as used in the passage. Example: What is the meaning of “rapid” as used in paragraph 2? Steps to Answer Comprehension Questions (Very Important ) ✅ Read the passage carefully Read the questions Go back to the passage and underline answers

Answer in your own words (do not copy too much) Use correct grammar and spelling Common Mistakes to Avoid ❌ Copying the passage word for word Writing long stories Wrong tense Bad spelling and grammar Example Passage: Ade went to school early. He wanted to meet his teacher. Question: Why did Ade go to school early? Answer: Ade went to school early because he wanted to meet his teacher.

title: ARTICLE WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText:
Theme: Continuous Writing. Unit topic: article writing Lesson Topic: Article witting (introduction, illustration and practice). An article is a piece of writing on national or regional issues of public Interest, usually meant for publication in of magazine of a newspaper. Note that in writing an article, the writer expresses his /her views or opinion on a given topic with good and logical points or facts. Features/format of an Article A. The title: It should be clearly written. Eg: The falling standard of Edicatan in Nigeria B. Introduction: This paragraph should introduce your topic or review whether people had written previously on the topic C. Body: This should contain relevant points discussed extensively and logically to give a clear understanding of the topic in question points raised should be discussed and arrange Paragraphs D. Conclusion: This is where the writer makes suggestions for solutions. E. Closure: It requires only the name of the writer and location where he/she is writing from Furthermore, your location should be your class in the school if the article is meant for a school publication. On the other hand d, your location should be the state from which you write if the article is meant for a national publication, Note that Signature is not needed! NOTE, the language of an article is formal and straight forward. Slangs are not required. Some article topics for publication include: 1. Insecurity in Nigeria. 2. Unemployment problem in the country. 3. High rate of kidnapping / human trafficking in Nigeria. 4. the falling standard of education in Nigeria. 5 Drug abuse among Nigeria youths. Assignment write an article suitable for publication in a national newspaper on the growing Incidence of drug abuse among the youth, Stating the causes and Suggesting the way It can be curbed.

Question and Answer WASSCE 2019.

title: EXPOSITORY ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText: B. ESSAY WRITING: EXPOSITORY Content Format (Sample Outline) An expository essay is one that requires you to explain a thing or a process fully. The explanation demands writing a great deal about what distinguishes the subject of the essay from all other things. It may also involve some description. Sample Outlines on Expository Essay Write an article for publication in one of your local newspapers on the need to improve sanitation in your area. Paragraph Introduction: The state of sanitation / definition The need for sanitation First way to improve (detailed) Second way to improve (detailed) Third way to improve (detailed) Conclusion: Hope that the new measures offered will be used “A Friend in Need is a Friend Indeed” Write an article to illustrate this saying Introduction: Say who your friend is How friendly you are Another proof that you are good friends,an incident to prove the saying

title: ADJECTIVAL PHRASE AND THEIR GRAMMATICAL FUNCTION
subject: English Language
rawText:
Adjectival Phrase and Their Grammatical Function Meaning of Adjectival Phrase ✅ An adjectival phrase is a group of words that performs the work of an adjective. It describes or gives more information about a noun or pronoun. Grammatical Functions of Adjectival Phrase ✅ 1. To describe or qualify a noun It tells us more about a noun. Examples: The girl in the red gown is my sister. The phrase describes the girl. 👉 The house near the market is beautiful. The phrase describes the house. 👉 2. To identify or specify a noun It helps to show exactly which person or thing we are talking about. Examples: The boy with curly hair is crying. It shows which boy. 👉 The book on the table is mine. It shows which book. 👉 3. To give additional information about a pronoun It can also describe a pronoun. Example: He in the black shirt is my teacher. The phrase describes he. 👉 How to Recognize Adjectival Phrase ✅

It usually comes after the noun or pronoun it describes. Example: The woman with a baby is waiting. Summary ✅ An adjectival phrase: 👉 Is a group of words Works like an adjective Describes or gives more information about nouns or pronouns

title: SYNONYM
subject: English Language
rawText: A synonym is a word which very nearly has the same meaning as some other words, and which can replace the word in a sentence, without changing the meaning in the sentences. It helps to avoid monotony in writing . Note the following synonyms and the different shade of meanings: Synonyms: odour, scent, smell, stench, aroma, fragrance. Aroma: refers to a pungent, spicy odour e.g the aroma of peppers Fragrance : Describes a smell that is sweet and agreeable e.g the fragrance of the rose flower odour and smell: refer to something that may be either pleasant or unpleasant e.g. the odour of ol leather, the smell of hydrogen sulphide. Scent: is less strong than odour or smell as in the scent of lilac Stench: is an offensive foul smell as the stench of burning rubber. Typical Synonyms Word Synonyms Confess admit, own Abandon give up, relinquish Dangerous risky, perilous Surrender resign, yield Expensive dear, costly Disaster misfortune, calamity Aloof shy, withdrawn Dishonest unjust, deceptive Compensate requite, atone Dull gloomy cheerless Reject expel, emit Protagonist hero, star Obliterate efface destroy Generous liberal open-handed Famous renowned eminent

title: SENTENCES
subject: English Language
rawText:
Types of sentence by structure YPES OF SENTENCE ACCORDING TO STRUCTURE* This is the classification of sentences according to their grammatical structures. *SIMPLE SENTENCE:* This is a kind of sentence with one main verb. It consists of one subject and one predicate and makes a single thought. It may possess auxiliary verbs but has only one main verb. *Study these:* She travelled to Akure. I was left with no one at home. The captain of the team elected by the coaching crew scored a goal at the last match. The above sentences have one main verb each, which are underlined respectively. *COMPOUND SENTENCE:* This is a kind of sentence that is made up of two simple sentence joined with a coordinating conjunction – and, but, yet, or, etc. It possesses two subjects and two predicates joining the two thoughts. *Study these:* a. John likes mangoes. b. Mark likes oranges. Sentences (a) and (b) are simple sentences but can be joined with a coordinating conjunction. John likes mangoes but Mark likes oranges *More examples:* a. They told him but he did not believe. b. She saw her mother and her brother arrive. *When the subjects are the same, the second subject is usually omitted but when they differ, they are both written.* c. The boy came home. d. The boy washed his clothes

Joining them to form a compound sentence, it will be written thus: *The boy came home and washed his clothes.* *3. COMPLEX SENTENCE:* lt is a kind of sentence with one simple sentence and one or more subordinate clause joined with a subordinating conjunction – when, after, while, where, immediately, because, etc. *Study these:* a. I met the girl when she was crying b. He was dismissed because of his fraudulent acts. c. After he arrived, Bode came to see me because he needed some money. The underline words are the main or simple sentences, while the ones not underlined are the subordinate clauses. 4. *COMPOUND COMPLEX SENTENCE:* This is a kind of sentence with two or more simple sentences and one or more subordinate clauses. It has more than one simple sentence with one or more than one subordinate clause. *Study these:* a. The boy is fluent and brilliant because he attends a private school. b. The boy came to then stream and washed his clothes because it was dirty. c. The man shot at the bird, he fried it but he was unable to eat it because he felt sick after he left the farm. *Note that a simple sentence differs not from a main clause.*

title: AN ADVERB
subject: English Language
rawText: An adverb is a word that describes or gives more information about a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. It tells us how, when, where, how often, or to what extent something happens. Examples of Adverbs How (manner) – quickly, slowly, happily She ran quickly. When (time) – now, yesterday, soon I will come tomorrow. Where (place) – here, there, everywhere Come here. How often (frequency) – always, often, never He always studies. To what extent (degree) – very, too, quite The water is very cold. Note Many adverbs end in -ly, but not all. Slowly (adverb) ✅ Very (adverb) ✅ Fast (adverb without -ly) ✅ Simple Sentences She sings beautifully. They arrived late. He is very tall. title: CONSONANT SOUNDS
subject: English Language
rawText:
Speech on Consonant Sounds /j/, /z/. /Ӡ/ Consonant Sounds: A speech sound produced in the oral cavity with either partial or total obstruction to the oral cavity pulmonic aggressive air stream coming from the lungs is called consonant sound. There are actually twenty four consonant sounds in the English language. Here’s the chart below Manner of articulation, state of the glottis. Manner of Articulation State of Glottis Place of Articulation Voiceless Voiced PLOSIVE p t k b d g Bilabial Aiveola Velar FRICATIVE f Ø s S h v ǝ z Ӡ Labio-dental Dental Alveolar Palato-Alveolar Glottal AFFRICATES ts dӡ Palato-Alveolar or post Alveolar LATERAL l Alveolar ROLLS r Alveolar SEMI-VOWEL w Bilabial J Palatal NASAL m n Ղ Bilabial Alveolar Velar Palatal

/j/ sound is a semi vowel sound. Examples of words include: toy, suit, tune, year, few, view, Europe, educate, student, union, use, onion, queue, stew, new, pure, yeast, yes, yatch etc. There is a very important point to note about this particular sound. In some words, it can be found before /u/ or /u:/ and in such words it may or may not be represented by any letter of the alphabet. Such words include: cure /kjuǝ/ huge /hju:dӠ/ tune /tju:n/ few /fju:/, university /ju:nivӠsǝti/ beauty /bjuti/ ewe /ju:/ Europe /juǝrǝup/ etc. /z/ This is a voiced alveolar. This sound in the following: has, is, does, rose, ooze. boys, tells, phrase, examination, exact etc. /Ӡ/ The /Ӡ/ sound is voiced palatal alveolar fricative: This sound is found in words such as: pleasure, seizure, prestige, television, conclusion, casual, measure, invasion, provision, leisure etc. Assignment Study the consonant chart in your note

title: PHRASAL VERBS CONTINUED
subject: English Language
rawText:
Phrasal Verb Phrasal verbs are combinations of a verb and one or more particles (typically prepositions or adverbs) that function together as a single semantic unit, often with a meaning that is different from the individual meanings of the verb and the particle(s) alone. Examples include "turn up," "give in," and "take off." Structure of a Phrasal Verb The structure of a phrasal verb typically consists of a main verb followed by one or more particles, which are usually prepositions or adverbs. These particles can come before or after the verb, depending on the specific phrasal verb. Here are the basic structures: 1. Verb + Preposition Example: "Look up" (verb + preposition) Example sentence: "I need to look up that word in the dictionary." 2. Verb + Adverb Example: "Turn off" (verb + adverb) Example sentence: "Please turn off the lights before leaving. 3. Verb + Adverbial particle + Preposition Example: "Make up for" Examples of Phrasal Verbs and their meanings. 1. Turn off: Meaning to stop the operation or flow of something. - Example: "Please turn off the lights before leaving." 2. Look up: Meaning to search for information in a reference source. - Example: "I need to look up that word in the dictionary."

3. Take care of: Meaning to be responsible for someone or something. - Example: "She takes care of her younger brother." 4. Put on: Meaning to place something on oneself, typically clothing or accessories. - Example: "He put on his coat before going outside." 5. Give up: Meaning to stop doing or trying something because it seems too difficult. - Example: "Don't give up on your dreams." 6. Break down: Meaning to stop working properly or to fail. - Example: "The car broke down on the highway." 7. Come across: Meaning to find or encounter unexpectedly. - Example: "I came across an old photo while cleaning out the attic." 8. Go on: Meaning to continue or proceed. - Example: "The meeting will go on as scheduled." 9. Turn down: Meaning to reject or refuse something. - Example: "She turned down the job offer." 10. Look forward to: Meaning to anticipate with pleasure. - Example: "I'm looking forward to seeing you again."

title: PHRASES
subject: English Language
rawText:
TOPIC 2: PHRASES TYPES OF PHRASES A phrase is a group of words that do not contain a finite verb. A phrase cannot stand on its own to make meaning. It only form part of a sentence. Types of phrases Noun phrase: This is the phrase that does the work of a noun or pronoun in a sentence. Example: John the driver is dead. The big ugly girl is quarrelsome. Adjectival phrase: This is the phrase that describes a noun or a pronoun in a sentence. Examples: The coat made of cotton is very lovely. The girl with dirty hands ate the food. Adverbial phrase: this is the phrase that modifies a verb in a sentence. It answers the question “why, where, when, how? etc. Examples: The head boy lives near the church. The old man walked slowly across the road. Prepositional phrase: This is a phrase that begins with a preposition. Examples Sani was beaten with a cane. The woman drowned in the river. Identification of phrases

If the verbs in the expression given is preceded by ‘to’ that verb is non-finite, therefore the expression is a phrase. Example He is always ready to fight anybody. To pass examination involves hard work. If the verb in the expression functions as an adjective, it is a non-finite verb and therefore the expression becomes a phrase. Example I have boiled yam in my pot. He has replaced the broken bottle. If the verb in the expression is in the ‘-ing’ form, the verb is non-finite and the expression becomes a phrase. Example I saw the boy going to the library. Eating supper late is what I don’t like. If the expression underlined in the sentence cannot make meaning when standing alone. Example She is sleeping in the room. They are standing outside the gate.

title: PRONOUNS
subject: English Language
rawText:
1 FCT School for the Gifted: SS1 2 nd Term English Notes_Mrs. Naadzebga Mgbede Grace FCT SCHOOL FOR THE GIFTED SUBJECT: ENGLISH LANGUAGE – SS1 TOPIC: PRONOUNS Prepared by: Mrs. Naadzenga Mgbede Grace (Subject Teacher) 1. Meaning of Pronouns A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun to avoid repetition. Example: • Instead of saying “John came and John took John’s bag,” • we say “John came and he took his bag.” 2. Functions of Pronouns Pronouns help to: • make sentences shorter and clearer, • avoid repeating the same noun many times, • show ownership, number, gender, and person. 3. Types of Pronouns a. Personal Pronouns These refer to specific persons or things. Person Subject Form Object Form Possessive 1st singular I me my/mine 2nd singular you you your/yours 3rd singular he/she/it him/her/it his/hers/its 1st plural we us our/ours 3rd plural they them their/theirs Examples • I love English. • The teacher called me . • They finished their work. b. Possessive Pronouns They show ownership and stand-alone without a noun. Examples: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs • This book is mine . • The house is theirs .

2 FCT School for the Gifted: SS1 2 nd Term English Notes_Mrs. Naadzebga Mgbede Grace c. Demonstrative Pronouns They point out nouns. Forms: this, that, these, those • This is my pen. • Those are the new students. d. Relative Pronouns They introduce relative clauses. Forms: who, whom, whose, which, that • The boy who won is my friend. • The car which was stolen has been found. e. Interrogative Pronouns Used to ask questions. Forms: who, what, which, whom • Who is at the door? • Which do you prefer? f. Reflexive Pronouns They refer back to the subject. Forms: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves • She blamed herself . • We did the work ourselves . g. Indefinite Pronouns They do not refer to specific nouns. Forms: everyone, somebody, nobody, few, many, all, some • Everyone is happy. • Nobody came late. 4. Position of Pronouns in Sentences Subject Position • He is my brother. • We are learners. Object Position • The pastor blessed them . • I greeted her . 5. Common Errors to Avoid • Do not mix subject and object forms: ❌ Me went to school ✔ I went to school • Do not use reflexive pronouns wrongly: ❌ Myself and John came ✔ John and I came

3 FCT School for the Gifted: SS1 2 nd Term English Notes_Mrs. Naadzebga Mgbede Grace 6. Summary • Pronouns replace nouns. • There are many types with different uses. • Correct choice of pronoun depends on function in the sentence. 7. Class Activity Exercise 1: Fill in the gaps 1. Mary is kind; ____ helps everyone. 2. The students saw the doctor and greeted ____. 3. This seat is not yours; it is ____. Exercise 2: Identify the pronoun type • The girl who sang is my sister. • This is better than that. • He hurt himself. Take Note: Understanding pronouns will improve your speaking and writing in English. title: PHRASAL VERBS
subject: English Language
rawText:
A phrasal verb is a verb that contains two or three words where the first word is a verb and the second or third word is a particle. The particle here is either an adverb or a preposition. Examples: turn on, carry out, make up, etc. PHRASAL VERBS. MEANING Ask after To request about somebody’s health. Ask out. To invite out Break down. To stop working because of a fault Break in To enter a by force. Break up. To building end a relationship Call on. To visit a person Give up. To stop , to abandon Put off. To postpone, to be upset Put up with. To tolerate, endure Set up. To establish, to trick somebody Take on. To employ Write off. To cancel a task Take down To write/ to bring low Cut in To interrupt Call off. To stop Turn on. To excite or interest/ To start From the words or group of words lettered Ato D, choose the word or group of words that best completes each of the following sentences. She set ------- preparing lunch when I came. A. on B. at C. about D. for My friend and I quarreled last week and haven’t ------ yet. A. made it out B. made up C. made out. D. made it 3. Bassey was ------- by the girl’s story

A. taken away B. taken on C. taken in D.taken up. 4. The plane --------- at 2 O’clock. A. take off B took up C.take up D took off 5. it was a long time before his surprise wore……… A. out B. off. C. through D. down Assignment Give the meaning of the following phrasal verbs Round off Round up

title: NOUN TYPES
subject: English Language
rawText: Types of nouns 1. A proper noun is a name that refers to a single or specific person, place, or thing. It always begins with a capital letter. Nigeria, Alex, Asorock 2. A common noun is a noun that's not the name of any particular or a name for something which is common for many things, person, place or thing (for instance, singer, river, and tablet). Example: Country (it can refer to any country, nothing in particular 3. Abstract Noun: An abstract noun is a word for something that cannot be seen but is there. It has no physical existence. Generally, it refers to ideas, qualities, and conditions. Example: Truth, lies, happiness, sorrow, time, friendship, humor, patriotism, etc. 4. A concrete noun is the exact opposite of abstract noun. It refers to the things we see and have physical existence. Example: Chair, table, bat, ball, water, money, sugar, etc. 5. Countable Noun :The nouns that can be counted are called countable nouns. Countable nouns can take an article: a, an, the.. Example: Chair, table, bat, ball, etc. (you can say 1 chair, 2 chairs, 3 chairs – so chairs are countable) 6. Uncountable Noun : The nouns that cannot be counted are called non-countable nouns. Example: Water, sugar, oil, salt, etc. (you cannot say “1 water, 2 water, 3 water” because water is not countable) 7. Collective Noun:: A collective noun is a word for a group of things, people, or animals, etc. Example: family, team, jury, cattle, etc. Collective nouns can be both plural and singular. 8. Compound Noun:: Sometimes two or three nouns appear together, or even with other parts of speech, and create idiomatic compound nouns. Idiomatic means that those nouns behave as a unit and, to a lesser or greater degree, amount to more than the sum of their parts. Example: six- pack, five-year-old, and son-in-law, snowball, mailbox, etc. 9. Singular Noun: : Singular Nouns are namely, singular in number. The base form of any noun is naturally singular and so that is the Singular Noun. Examples:: Duck, Bush, Man, Mouse, Child, Fish etc. are Singular Nouns. 10. Plural Noun:: The plural forms of the Singular Nouns are Plural Nouns. These nouns determine more than one element. Examples:: Belts, Boxes, Mice, Sheep, People etc. are examples of Plural Noun.

Countable nouns can take an article: a, an, the.. Example: Chair, table, bat, ball, etc. (you can say 1 chair, 2 chairs, 3 chairs – so chairs are countable) 6. Uncountable Noun : The nouns that cannot be counted are called non-countable nouns. Example: Water, sugar, oil, salt, etc. (you cannot say “1 water, 2 water, 3 water” because water is not countable) 7. Collective Noun:: A collective noun is a word for a group of things, people, or animals, etc. Example: family, team, jury, cattle, etc. Collective nouns can be both plural and singular. 8. Compound Noun:: Sometimes two or three nouns appear together, or even with other parts of speech, and create idiomatic compound nouns. Idiomatic means that those nouns behave as a unit and, to a lesser or greater degree, amount to more than the sum of their parts. Example: six- pack, five-year-old, and son-in-law, snowball, mailbox, etc. 9. Singular Noun: : Singular Nouns are namely, singular in number. The base form of any noun is naturally singular and so that is the Singular Noun. Examples:: Duck, Bush, Man, Mouse, Child, Fish etc. are Singular Nouns. 10. Plural Noun:: The plural forms of the Singular Nouns are Plural Nouns. These nouns determine more than one element. Examples:: Belts, Boxes, Mice, Sheep, People etc. are examples of Plural Noun.

title: NARRATIVE ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText:
Narrative Essay A narrative essay is a type of essay that tells a story. It is written from the writer’s point of view and often describes personal experiences, events, or incidents in a chronological order (the order in which they happened). Features of a Narrative Essay 1. Storytelling – It tells a story with a beginning, middle, and end. 2. Characters – There are people (real or imagined) involved in the story. 3. Setting – The place and time where the story happens. 4. Plot – The sequence of events or actions in the story. 5. Conflict – A problem or challenge that makes the story interesting. 6. Point of View – Usually written in first person (“I”, “we”) to make it personal. 7. Description – Uses descriptive language to create clear pictures in the reader’s mind. 8. Moral or Lesson – Often ends with what the writer learned from the experience. Structure of a Narrative Essay 1. Introduction Introduces the story or event. Captures the reader’s attention. May include background information. 2. Body Describes the main events in order. Builds up to the climax (the most exciting part). Uses paragraphs for each main event or stage. 3. Conclusion Brings the story to an end. States the outcome or lesson learned.

Examples of Narrative Essay Topics The day I will never forget My first day at school How I overcame a challenge An accident I witnessed A visit to the village

title: MECHANICS IN WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText:
Mechanics in Writing! Writing mechanics refer to the technical aspects of writing, ensuring clarity, coherence, and effectiveness. Here are key mechanics to master: *Grammar* 1. Verb tenses (past, present, future) 2. Subject-verb agreement 3. Pronoun usage (e.g., who/whom, its/it's) 4. Clause structure (independent, dependent) 5. Sentence types (simple, compound, complex) *Punctuation* 1. Commas (separating items, clauses) 2. Semicolons (joining independent clauses) 3. Colons (introducing lists, explanations) 4. Apostrophes (possessive nouns, contractions) 5. Quotation marks (dialogue, quotes) *Spelling and Capitalization* 1. Word spelling (correct usage) 2. Capitalization (proper nouns, titles) 3. Abbreviations (e.g., acronyms, initialisms) *Syntax and Sentence Structure* 1. Sentence length and variety 2. Active and passive voice 3. Parallel structure 4. Modifiers (adjectives, adverbs) 5. Clause and phrase arrangement *Style and Tone*

1. Formal and informal tone 2. Audience consideration 3. Purpose and intent 4. Point of view (first person, third person) 5. Figurative language (metaphors, similes) *Common Errors to Avoid* 1. Fragments and run-on sentences 2. Misused words (e.g., affect/effect, accept/except) 3. Lack of subject-verb agreement 4. Inconsistent verb tense 5. Overuse of adverbs

title: PHRASES AND TYPES
subject: English Language
rawText:
PHRASES AND TYPES A phrase is a group of words without a finite verb that works together as a unit in a sentence. Types of Phrases (with simple examples) 1. Noun Phrase A noun phrase has a noun as its head word. Examples: the tall boy my new book a beautiful dress Used as subject or object in a sentence. 👉 Example: The tall boy is my brother. 2. Verb Phrase A verb phrase has a main verb and sometimes helping verbs. Examples: is running has eaten will go Example: She is reading a novel. 3. Adjective Phrase An adjective phrase describes a noun. Examples: very happy full of joy quite tall Example: She is very happy today.

4. Adverbial Phrase An adverbial phrase modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb. Examples: very quickly in the morning with great care Example: He ran very quickly. 5. Prepositional Phrase A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and ends with an object. Examples: in the room on the table under the tree Example: The bag is on the table. 6. Gerund Phrase A gerund phrase starts with a verb ending in -ing and acts as a noun. Examples: reading novels playing football Example: Playing football is fun. 7. Infinitive Phrase An infinitive phrase begins with to + verb. Examples: to read a book to win the match

Example: She wants to become a teacher.
