WEEK 8 I. SPEECH: Vowel /e/ and / Ȝ :/ /e/ is a front short vowel. The jaw position is half close and half open. The sound is produced when the lips are spread and the front of the tongue is raised. The spelling symbols includes: “e” as in bed, lend, recent, let. “a” as in many, ate, any. “u” as in bury. “ay” as in say/sez/. “ai” as in said. “ie” as in friend. “ue” as in guess/gez/ “eo” as in leopard, jeopardize, jeopardy. “eՁ” as in head, weapon, threat, heavy, bread, instead, pleasant,/feznt/ / Ȝ :/ is a long central vowel. It is produced with the lips in a fairly neutral position-half closed and half open. It is neither spread nor round and the centre of the tongue is raised. The spelling symbols includes: “ir” as in girl, firm, bird, dirt, stir, whirl, third, shirk, birth. “ur” as in urgent, occur, nurse, return, purr, burn, church, urn/3:n/ “o” as in colonel/k3:nl/ “or” as in word, work, worthy, worst, world, worship, worse. “er” as in serve, her, err/3:/, desert, germ, concern, mercy, perch. “ear” as in earn, early, pearl, heard, search. ”our” as in journey, sourge, adjourn. The minimal pairs includes /e/ / Ȝ :/

Bed Gem Head Said Ate Wed West Bend End Lens Bed Nest Death debt Bird Germ Herd Search Earth Word Worse Burned Earned Learns birth nursed dearth dirt ii. STRUCTURE: Adverbial phrase and their functions An adverbial phrase is a group of related words that modifies a verb in a sentence. It performs the work of an adverb. It answers the questions “when?, where?, why? And how?”. The infinitive and prepositional phrase can also serve as an adverbial phrase. Examples 1. Mr mark visited his brother in the morning(when). 2. I met him at the marking centre (where). 3. The old man walked quickly across the road(how). 4. His father refused to give him the car because he is reckless. (reason) 5. Mr joseph came here last Monday.(when) 6. The three women arrived early in the morning.(when)

7. I will see you later in the day.(when) 8. He played the ball over the bar.(where) 9. She played the drum extremely well.(how) 10. He enlisted to become an aviator (why). FUNCTIONS OF THE PHRASES ABOVE 1. prepositional phrase acting as adverbial phrase of time modifying the verb “visited’. 2. prepositional phrase as adverbial phrase of place modifying the verb ’met’. 3. Adverbial phrase of manner, modifying the verb ‘walked’. 4. Adverbial phrase of reason, modifying the verb ‘refused’. 5. Adverbial phrase of time modifying the verb’came’. 6. Adverbial phrase of time modifying the verb ‘played’. 7. prepositional phrase as adverbial phrase of time modifying the verb ‘see’. 8. prepositional phrase as adverbial phrase of time modifying the verb ’played’. 9. Adverbial phrase of manner modifying the verb ‘played’. 10. Infinitive phrase as adverbial phrase modifying the verb ‘enlisted’. Some prepositional phrases are used either as adverbial phrase or adjectival phrase depending on how they are used in a sentence. Examples A. I saw the man in the garden(adverbial phrase of place modifying the verb ‘saw’). B. The man in the garden has gone (adjectival phrase modifying the noun ’man’). III) COMPREHENSION; Reading books and marking notes- reading ton take and mark notes .

Marking notes (note-taking)is an essential part of reading to comprehend. It is a form of summarizing and extracting the relevant points from the whole book or story. meetings, lectures, or in other activities such as listening to a sermon, it is impossible to write everything. In these circumstances, good note taking is important. Note taking is a technique or method used for recording important information for future use. Good note should be as brief as possible without leaving out important points and essential details. When you read to take notes, it is necessary to jot down the name of the author, the title of the book(lecture, sermon or story) the name of the publisher, the dates of publication, the n8mber of pages, the edition of the book then state the ideas etc. when you take notes, use your own words, relating the ideas to one another. Your notes should be arranged in an appropriate form. Notes can be taken during a talk, immediately afterwards or when reading a text but it should not be delayed more than necessary. A note that is not taken may lose some of the vital points and accuracy will be lost. STRATEGIES FOR NOT-TAKING AND MAKING FROM ORAL SOURCE. While taking notes from verbal presentations such as talk, lectures, sermon etc. 1. Do not write the complete words. Abbreviation and symbols will help you to save time, space, and energy. Remember how you write your text messages, for example ‘2’ can be used in place of to/too/two. 4(for/four/fore). E.g r(are) u or ur (you or your) etc. be careful not to over do this or extend it to your essays and compositions. 2. Your notes will be more effective if they are recorded and transcribed later. 3. Organize your notes well and arrange your ideas in order, do not jumble up ideas. 4. Even though your notes are personal, a good layout will help you to recall and use materials more readily and 5. Do not forget that notes can become easy or composition later. READING FOR MARKING NOTES Note-taking while reading simply means texts, marking, underling or highlighting the important Ideas or points in the margins you may underline or highlight the: - Main subject matter/ideas of the text.

- Examples of these main ideas in the text. - Unfamiliar vocabulary or definitions encountered in the text. As you read, jot down paraphrases, questions and summaries. Avoid time wasting while doing this. STEPS FOR MAKING NOTES WHEN READING 1. Read to understand the section of the book (or materials)you need before the significant points can be written(noted). 2. Review the material and make sure you locate the main ideas and other subsidiary points. 3. Without using the book, paraphrase the points or ideas which you think are useful for you. Except where it is necessary, unimportant words, illustrations and examples are not included. 4. Write the paraphrased work/ideas as your notes. Do not copy words for word or verbatim. 5. Review and compare your notes with the text and ask yourself if you have family represented the ideas of the text in your notes. The general tips for note taking and note making. 1. Do not use small scraps of papers to write your notes. It is easier to keep track of your notes if you use size of your regular school books. 2. Always start a new note on a new page with its own title. It will help you to store and identify them later. Keep the topic separately. Have them clearly titled and labeled to enable you to make easy recall. 3. Write out the sub- topics boldly and always remember to leave wide margins where you can make further comments later. 4. Notes must be highly selective. Only significant points should be written (noted). 5. As you write, use your own English expressions. 6. Write boldly and legibly. Do not load too many words on a page. 7. The ideas in the notes should relate to one another orderliness is important, cohesion and coherence are necessary.

8. Always leave a space between each set of notes. If you keep the items separately, they will be easier to find. 9. When you make notes, use the front of the sheet of paper only. When you do this, the back will always be available for future corrections and additions. 10. Always number the pages of your notes. In brief, marking notes is the same as summarizing in the sense that in both, brevity is the watch word. As brief as the note is, it should contain important points and must have a clear organizational pattern. Your notes should be easy to understand by anyone who reads them III) Continuous Writing - Letter Topic: Formal Letter A formal letter is a letter written to someone or a group of people in official positions. It is also called an Official Letter. It includes letters to the Press Crew Paper or magazines, companies, offices, school. Types of formal letter. 1) Letter of enquiry 2) Order letter 3) Promotion letter. 4) Sales letter. 5) Recovery Letter Features of a formal letter 1) Writer's address/date: This should be written at the top of a letter on the right hand corner. It includes the name of your school, post office number, state, date, etc. Write the date in full and put a dot after each abbreviation Government Secondary School, P.M.B. 227. Kubwa,

Abuja. 28th October, 2017. 2) The recipient's address: this is written as the left hand side below the writer's address. Example: The Commissioner of Education Abia State. E.g: The Registrar, University of Abuja, Abuja. 3) Salutation: This is followed by Comma e.g: Dear Sir, 4) Title: A formal letter should have a tille underlined if written in small letter or with initial of each headword in capital letters. But not underlined when written in capital letters. E.g: Application for the Post of a Secretary 5) Introduction: This gives a brief account of what the letter talks about. 6) The body of the letter: Write clear and simple English. Mind your tenses. Pay attention to spelling and punctuations. 7 Conclusion: This draws together the ideas and the relationships with the major points. 8 Subscription: This comes at the end of the letter followed by a comma. Only the letter in "Your" is written with a capital letter. E.g: Yours faithfully, 9 Signature and name: Name should be written below the signature. Sign

Ayo Obi Musa The situations that demand for formal letters includes a job transfer, admission, leave of absence, promotion, scholarship, application for loan, etc. The tone of a formal letter must be official. Do crack jokes or discuss personal affairs. Be precise, direct and business like. The language used must be acceptable expressions, use polite and official language. Avoid slangs, short forms or abbreviations etc.

7. I will see you later in the day.(when) 8. He played the ball over the bar.(where) 9. She played the drum extremely well.(how) 10. He enlisted to become an aviator (why). FUNCTIONS OF THE PHRASES ABOVE 1. prepositional phrase acting as adverbial phrase of time modifying the verb “visited’. 2. prepositional phrase as adverbial phrase of place modifying the verb ’met’. 3. Adverbial phrase of manner, modifying the verb ‘walked’. 4. Adverbial phrase of reason, modifying the verb ‘refused’. 5. Adverbial phrase of time modifying the verb’came’. 6. Adverbial phrase of time modifying the verb ‘played’. 7. prepositional phrase as adverbial phrase of time modifying the verb ‘see’. 8. prepositional phrase as adverbial phrase of time modifying the verb ’played’. 9. Adverbial phrase of manner modifying the verb ‘played’. 10. Infinitive phrase as adverbial phrase modifying the verb ‘enlisted’. Some prepositional phrases are used either as adverbial phrase or adjectival phrase depending on how they are used in a sentence. Examples A. I saw the man in the garden(adverbial phrase of place modifying the verb ‘saw’). B. The man in the garden has gone (adjectival phrase modifying the noun ’man’). III) COMPREHENSION; Reading books and marking notes- reading ton take and mark notes .

Marking notes (note-taking)is an essential part of reading to comprehend. It is a form of summarizing and extracting the relevant points from the whole book or story. meetings, lectures, or in other activities such as listening to a sermon, it is impossible to write everything. In these circumstances, good note taking is important. Note taking is a technique or method used for recording important information for future use. Good note should be as brief as possible without leaving out important points and essential details. When you read to take notes, it is necessary to jot down the name of the author, the title of the book(lecture, sermon or story) the name of the publisher, the dates of publication, the n8mber of pages, the edition of the book then state the ideas etc. when you take notes, use your own words, relating the ideas to one another. Your notes should be arranged in an appropriate form. Notes can be taken during a talk, immediately afterwards or when reading a text but it should not be delayed more than necessary. A note that is not taken may lose some of the vital points and accuracy will be lost. STRATEGIES FOR NOT-TAKING AND MAKING FROM ORAL SOURCE. While taking notes from verbal presentations such as talk, lectures, sermon etc. 1. Do not write the complete words. Abbreviation and symbols will help you to save time, space, and energy. Remember how you write your text messages, for example ‘2’ can be used in place of to/too/two. 4(for/four/fore). E.g r(are) u or ur (you or your) etc. be careful not to over do this or extend it to your essays and compositions. 2. Your notes will be more effective if they are recorded and transcribed later. 3. Organize your notes well and arrange your ideas in order, do not jumble up ideas. 4. Even though your notes are personal, a good layout will help you to recall and use materials more readily and 5. Do not forget that notes can become easy or composition later. READING FOR MARKING NOTES Note-taking while reading simply means texts, marking, underling or highlighting the important Ideas or points in the margins you may underline or highlight the: - Main subject matter/ideas of the text.

- Examples of these main ideas in the text. - Unfamiliar vocabulary or definitions encountered in the text. As you read, jot down paraphrases, questions and summaries. Avoid time wasting while doing this. STEPS FOR MAKING NOTES WHEN READING 1. Read to understand the section of the book (or materials)you need before the significant points can be written(noted). 2. Review the material and make sure you locate the main ideas and other subsidiary points. 3. Without using the book, paraphrase the points or ideas which you think are useful for you. Except where it is necessary, unimportant words, illustrations and examples are not included. 4. Write the paraphrased work/ideas as your notes. Do not copy words for word or verbatim. 5. Review and compare your notes with the text and ask yourself if you have family represented the ideas of the text in your notes. The general tips for note taking and note making. 1. Do not use small scraps of papers to write your notes. It is easier to keep track of your notes if you use size of your regular school books. 2. Always start a new note on a new page with its own title. It will help you to store and identify them later. Keep the topic separately. Have them clearly titled and labeled to enable you to make easy recall. 3. Write out the sub- topics boldly and always remember to leave wide margins where you can make further comments later. 4. Notes must be highly selective. Only significant points should be written (noted). 5. As you write, use your own English expressions. 6. Write boldly and legibly. Do not load too many words on a page. 7. The ideas in the notes should relate to one another orderliness is important, cohesion and coherence are necessary.

8. Always leave a space between each set of notes. If you keep the items separately, they will be easier to find. 9. When you make notes, use the front of the sheet of paper only. When you do this, the back will always be available for future corrections and additions. 10. Always number the pages of your notes. In brief, marking notes is the same as summarizing in the sense that in both, brevity is the watch word. As brief as the note is, it should contain important points and must have a clear organizational pattern. Your notes should be easy to understand by anyone who reads them III) Continuous Writing - Letter Topic: Formal Letter A formal letter is a letter written to someone or a group of people in official positions. It is also called an Official Letter. It includes letters to the Press Crew Paper or magazines, companies, offices, school. Types of formal letter. 1) Letter of enquiry 2) Order letter 3) Promotion letter. 4) Sales letter. 5) Recovery Letter Features of a formal letter 1) Writer's address/date: This should be written at the top of a letter on the right hand corner. It includes the name of your school, post office number, state, date, etc. Write the date in full and put a dot after each abbreviation Government Secondary School, P.M.B. 227. Kubwa,

Abuja. 28th October, 2017. 2) The recipient's address: this is written as the left hand side below the writer's address. Example: The Commissioner of Education Abia State. E.g: The Registrar, University of Abuja, Abuja. 3) Salutation: This is followed by Comma e.g: Dear Sir, 4) Title: A formal letter should have a tille underlined if written in small letter or with initial of each headword in capital letters. But not underlined when written in capital letters. E.g: Application for the Post of a Secretary 5) Introduction: This gives a brief account of what the letter talks about. 6) The body of the letter: Write clear and simple English. Mind your tenses. Pay attention to spelling and punctuations. 7 Conclusion: This draws together the ideas and the relationships with the major points. 8 Subscription: This comes at the end of the letter followed by a comma. Only the letter in "Your" is written with a capital letter. E.g: Yours faithfully, 9 Signature and name: Name should be written below the signature. Sign

Ayo Obi Musa The situations that demand for formal letters includes a job transfer, admission, leave of absence, promotion, scholarship, application for loan, etc. The tone of a formal letter must be official. Do crack jokes or discuss personal affairs. Be precise, direct and business like. The language used must be acceptable expressions, use polite and official language. Avoid slangs, short forms or abbreviations etc.

Theme: this means the main idea, the subject matter or the central point of view from which a story is developed. Example One good turn deserves another. A stitch in time saves another. 2. Plot: this is the sequential arrangement of events in a chronological order in which the events occurred. It is the story-line, the order that the story follows to develop the theme. 3. Setting: this refers to where the event’s happened(place) and when(time). It is the geographical location and the daily manner of living of the characters as well as the period during which the action occurs, it may be urban or rural area. 4. Tone/mood: This is the way or attitude that the author/writer delivers the message to his reader. It is the expression of the emotional attitude of the writer towards his subjects. It may be pleasant, apologetic, anger, sorrowful, humorous etc. 5. Characters: These are the people who participate in the action of the story. They could be human beings or inanimate objects of animals. The story will appear real if you give the characters names and interaction among them through dialogue. E.g “animal farm” by George Orwell. 6. Characterization: this is the manner of exposing the imaginary being created in your writing so that they appear to your readers if they exist. 7. Language/ Diction: this is the writer’s choice of words. It may be simple, straight forward, native language etc. the tense of the narration must be in the past, but when dialogue is brought In the tense can be present. 8. Style: this is simply writers method of expression which distinguishes his work from others. E.g Chinua Achebe combine English and Igbo 9. Figures of speech: these are the literary devices used in expressing ones thought in writing. E.g simile, personification, metaphor, Hyperbole etc

title: INTONATION PATTERN
subject: English Language
rawText:
SS 2 ENGLISH LANGUAGE NOTE Topic: Speech – Intonation Pattern (Falling Tone) 1. Meaning of Intonation Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice when speaking. It helps to express meaning, feelings, and attitude in speech. 2. Meaning of Falling Tone A falling tone (↘) is when the voice falls or goes down at the end of a sentence. It is commonly used in: 1. Statements 2. WH-questions (who, what, where, when, why, how) 3. Commands 4. Exclamations 5. Completed ideas 3. Examples and Explanation 1. There will be a match at the National Stadium tomorrow. ↘ This is a statement, so the voice falls at the end. 2. There will be a class quiz tomorrow evening. ↘ Also a statement. The voice falls on evening because the information is complete. 3. Where are you going? ↘ This is a WH-question. Unlike Yes/No questions, WH-questions take a falling tone. 4. Other Examples of Falling Tone 1. I am coming now. ↘ 2. Close the door. ↘ 3. What is your name? ↘ 4. Stop talking. ↘

5. That is wonderful! ↘ 5. Features of Falling Tone • The voice drops at the end of the sentence. • It shows completeness or certainty. • It is used in giving information. • It sounds firm and confident. 6. Difference Between Rising and Falling Tone Falling Tone (↘) Rising Tone (↗) Used in statements Used in Yes/No questions Used in WH-questions Used in polite requests Shows certainty Shows doubt or expectation of response Example: Where are you going? ↘ (falling tone – WH-question) Are you going out

WEEK 1 - SPEECH: Listening comprehension- I) listening to answer questions on a given passage. Listening comprehension is defined as one’s ability to comprehend spoken language. it requires attention, comprehension of the passage being read and recollection of what has being said. To listen, we need to make a conscious effort not to just hear what people said but to take it in, digest it and understand. Listening enhances one’s ability to understand better and evaluate what one hears. The passage is taken from ’animal farm ’written by George orwell. It is a satire – a piece of writing that criticizes either a person or an institution by using humour to show their faults or weaknesses. It is a satire on Nigerian readers. The characters are animals that are given names used by humans (page 254). Answer to the passage on animal farm. ii) Vocabulary development: words associated with the human internal body system and functions: the human body system consist of many system that works together to function properly. This System consist of organs. The organs are made up of tissues which are a collection of cells ˃ body- system - organ - tissue – cells. The Systems includes: a) Digestive system. b) Respiratory system. c) Excretory system. d) Endocrine system. e) Reproductive system. f) Circulatory system. g) Nervous system. h) Skeletal system a) The digestive system is responsible for the breaking down of food. It Consist of mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestine and anus. b) The respiratory system is responsible for the intake and absorption of oxygen from the surrounding environment, and also the transport of oxygen to the individual cells in the body.

c) The excretory system is responsible for the removal of waste substances from the body of a living organism. It consists of kidney, lungs, liver, Skin. d) The skeletal system is responsible for providing the foundational framework, support, shape and protection of the whole body system and internal organs. It consists of (1) Axial skeleton – the skull, sternum, vertebral column and rib cage. (2) Appendicle skeleton – the forelimbs and the hind limbs. e) The reproductive system is responsible for the production of young offspring through the fusion of gametes sexually or other means such as asexual fragmentation, spore formation, binary fusion, vegetative propagation. f) The circulatory system is responsible for the rapid mass and other materials such as digested food, water and other nutrients. This system also transports excretory products such as carbon dioxide, and urea and lastly water, oxygen and hormones. h) The nervous system together with the endocrine system is responsible for co-ordinating all the other activities of the body like locomotion, digestion, respiration and excretion. The organs- • Heart: The heart supplies oxygenated blood to the cells in the body. • Kidney: It excretes urea and urine from blood. • Lungs: Used for gaseous exchange. • Liver: To neutralize toxic substances in the body. • Brain: The organ that control, receives and send signals to the other organs through the nervous system and through secreted hormones. • Bladder: Hold urine until it goes out of the body. • Intestine: The long tube through which food passes after it leaves the stomach. iii) STRUCTURE: Noun phrases- position and functions. A phrase is a group of related words that forms part of a large sentence but has no finite verb and therefore cannot stand alone and makes complete sense. E. g – In the Market. -- The man at the door. -- Within the compound. A noun phrase is a group of words that has a noun as its headword. It performs the work of a noun in sentences.

E. g - my English teacher is hard working. - Igbo people are in the east. FUNCTIONS OF A NOUN PHRASE 1) As subject of a verb: when a noun phrase occupies the initial position in a sentence, it functions as the subject. In this case, the verb comes after the noun. E. g – A huge tree fell across the street. - The short boy in choir is my brother. 2) As object of a verb: when a noun phrase comes after a verb in a sentences, it functions as the object of that verb. E. g - she destroyed the car. -- He bought a long note. 3) As subject compliment: It links the subject to something that describes the subject. E. g – John may become our hero. -- Our principal may become a commissioner. 4) As object complement: it links the object to something that describes it. E. g - The house girl called her mistress a savior. - The class made her the class prefect. CHARACTERISTICS OF A NOUN PHRASE 1. The head in a noun phrase can be pre-modified by articles, possessives, demonstratives or/and adjectives or a combination of these. E. g • A student”, the people”, (pre - modified by article.) • My father”, their farms”, (pre -modified by possessives.) • Beautiful house”, easy question”,(pre -modified by adjective.) • This book”, that bag”, (pre -modified by demonstrative.) • The boy ugly girl is quarrelsome (combination of all.) 2. The head in a noun phrase can be post modified by prepositional phrase or clause.

• E. g – “the boy in the room”, “the house of the mother” (post modified by prepositional phrase.) • “a man who stammers”, ”the book I told you about” (post modified by clause.) title: OTHER TYPES OF PRONOUNS
subject: English Language
rawText:
Pronouns Pronouns are words used in place of nouns. They are used in a piece of writing or speech to avoid repeating a previously stated noun referred to as the antecedent of the pronoun. Types of pronouns 1. Personal Pronouns are those used in place of names of people. Here are some examples : I/m e we/us, you/you He/him, she/her, it/it, they/them 2. Possessive Pronouns Possessive pronouns are used to show possession. That is, showing that something belongs to someone or something. They are used instead of mentioning the items of possession. Person Singular Plural Subject Object Subject Object 1st person my mine Our Ours 2nd person Your Yours Your Yours 3rd person His, Her, Its His, hers, its Their Theirs 3. Relative pronouns are pronouns that connect relative clauses to independent clauses . Often, they include these words: that, which, who, whom, whose, 4. Demonstrative pronouns are only four demonstrative pronouns. We use them to point out particular people or things. this, that, these, those 5. Reflexive Pronoun: A reflexive pronoun is one that refers back to the subject of a sentence. Reflexive pronouns always end in – ‘self’ (for singular) and - ‘selves’ (for plural). They appear as: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, oneself (for singular) and ourselves, yourselves, themselves 6. Emphatic or Intensive Pronouns : Emphatic pronouns too end in ‘self’ or ‘selves’ . However, whereas reflexive pronouns are used to show that the action by the verb in the sentence goes back to the doer of the action, emphatic pronouns are used to make what is said stronger. In other words, they are used for emphasis. They appear as: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, oneself (for singular) and ourselves, yourselves, themselves 7. Indefinite Pronouns are not definite. We don't know whom or what these refer to! Example: anyone, something, all, most, some anybody, anyone, anything, each, either, everyone, everybody, everything nobody neither no one, nothing, somebody, one, someone, something, few, many, both, several, any, all, some, most, none. 8. Interrogative Pronouns are pronouns that are used to make questions. Interrogative pronouns often begin interrogative sentences and they start with ‘ wh’ . Example are: what, whom, whose, who, how, which 9. Reciprocal pronouns are only two reciprocal pronouns: Each other One another 10. Distributive pronouns : refer to people, animals, and objects as individuals within larger groups. They enable you to single out individuals while acknowledging that they’re part of a larger group. They are: Either, Each Neither Any None

Type Pronouns in this category Example sentences Personal I/me, they/them, he/him, she/her, it, we/us, you • I brought all the snacks. • We weren’t planning on staying over. Relative That, what, which, who, whom • My car, which is twenty years old, doesn’t connect to Bluetooth. • The professor who ran the meeting ended it promptly Demonstrative That, this, these, those • You’ve seen clear quartz and smoky quartz, but have you seen these stones? • I ordered Hawaiian pizza. I like that a lot. Indefinite One, other, some, none, everybody, anybody, no one, nobody, both • We need cashiers up front. Anybody who’s available, please report to the front end. • “Why can’t we fix this?” I asked nobody in particular. Reflexive Myself, ourselves, yourself/yourselves, /themselves, herself, himself, oneself, itself, ourselves • The car began to swerve, then corrected itself. • He made himself a sandwich. Intensive Myself, yourself/yourselves, /themselves, himself, oneself, itself, ourselves • You did all of this yourself? • She did the entire group project by herself. Possessive My, your, his, her, their, our, its, whose • We’re lounging out by our pool. • His car is green. Interrogative Who, what, which, whose • Whose bike is this? • What is the answer? Reciprocal Each other, one another • We ran into each other on the subway. • They’ve been fighting with one another for decades. Distributive Either, each, neither, any, none • Peanut butter or chocolate? I’m good with either. • There were four cats, and none had long hair.

title: VOCABULARY
subject: English Language
rawText:
VOCABULARY: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH THE HUMAN INTERNAL BODY SYSTEM AND FUNCTION Meaning of Vocabulary Vocabulary refers to the group of words we use or understand. In this topic, we learn words that are related to the human internal body systems and how they function. 1. CIRCULATORY SYSTEM Function: Transports blood, oxygen, and nutrients around the body. Key Vocabulary: • Heart – pumps blood through the body • Artery – carries blood away from the heart • Vein – carries blood back to the heart • Capillary – tiny blood vessel connecting arteries and veins • Blood – fluid that carries oxygen and nutrients • Pulse – heartbeat felt through the arteries • Circulation – movement of blood in the body • Oxygen – gas that supports breathing and life 2. DIGESTIVE SYSTEM Function: Breaks down food into nutrients for energy and growth. Key Vocabulary: • Mouth – where food enters and chewing begins • Tongue – helps in tasting and swallowing • Saliva – liquid in the mouth that helps break down food • Esophagus – tube that carries food to the stomach • Stomach – organ that digests food with acid and enzymes • Liver – produces bile to help digestion • Intestine – absorbs nutrients from food • Anus – where waste leaves the body • Digestion – process of breaking down food • Enzyme – chemical that helps digestion 3. RESPIRATORY SYSTEM Function: Helps in breathing and supplying oxygen to the body. Key Vocabulary: • Nose – passage for air to enter the body • Trachea (windpipe) – carries air to the lungs • Lungs – main organs of breathing • Bronchi – air passages inside the lungs • Diaphragm – muscle that helps in breathing • Inhale – to breathe in • Exhale – to breathe out • Oxygen – gas needed for respiration • Carbon dioxide – waste gas breathed out

4. EXCRETORY SYSTEM Function: Removes waste products from the body. Key Vocabulary: • Kidney – filters blood and removes waste • Bladder – stores urine • Urethra – passage for urine to leave the body • Urine – liquid waste from the body • Sweat – water and salt removed through the skin • Excretion – process of removing waste • Toxin – harmful substance in the body 5. NERVOUS SYSTEM Function: Controls and coordinates body activities. Key Vocabulary: • Brain – control center of the body • Spinal cord – carries messages between brain and body • Nerves – carry signals throughout the body • Neuron – nerve cell • Reflex – quick automatic response • Impulse – electrical message carried by nerves • Sense organs – eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin 6. SKELETAL AND MUSCULAR SYSTEMS Function: Provide support, shape, and movement. Key Vocabulary: • Bone – hard structure forming the skeleton • Skeleton – framework of bones • Joint – point where two bones meet • Muscle – tissue that helps movement • Tendon – connects muscle to bone • Ligament – connects bone to bone • Movement – act of changing position • Posture – position of the body when sitting or standing 7. REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM Function: Enables humans to produce offspring. Key Vocabulary: • Sperm – male reproductive cell • Egg (Ovum) – female reproductive cell • Uterus – where a baby develops • Vagina – female reproductive passage • Penis – male reproductive organ • Testes – produce sperm • Menstruation – monthly discharge in females • Fertilization – joining of sperm and egg

8. ENDOCRINE SYSTEM Function: Controls growth, metabolism, and hormones. Key Vocabulary: • Hormone – chemical messenger in the body • Gland – organ that produces hormones • Thyroid – gland that controls metabolism • Insulin – hormone that controls blood sugar • Adrenaline – hormone that helps the body react to danger • Pituitary gland – master gland controlling others ACTIVITY/EXERCISE Match each system to its function: 1. Circulatory system 2. Digestive system 3. Nervous system 4. Excretory system 5. Respiratory system Functions: a. Helps in breathing b. Breaks down food c. Removes waste d. Pumps blood e. Controls body activities (Answers: 1–d, 2–b, 3–e, 4–c, 5–a)

title: NOUN PHRASE.
subject: English Language
rawText:
NOTE ON NOUN PHRASE In the English language, nouns are the words used to refer to people, places, or things. A noun phrase is a group of words, usually a noun in addition to a modifier—such as an adjective, determiners or modifiers—that functions just as a noun would. Grammatically, a noun phrase can be the subject, object, subject complement, or object complement, complement of a preposition or function as an appositive to a noun in the sentence in which it appears. Simply put, a noun phrase consists of one or more words that function together to name a person, place, thing, or idea and can include modifiers to provide more information about that noun. Examples of noun phrases in sentences: 1. The gigantic, ancient oak tree stood majestically in the centre of the forest. 2. My best friend's fluffy, white cat always greets me with a purr and a nuzzle. 3. The sparkling, turquoise waters of the Caribbean Sea were breath- taking. 4. The old, leather-bound book on the shelf contained many fascinating stories. 5. The delicious, homemade apple pie filled the kitchen with a warm, sweet aroma. 6. The bustling, colourful marketplace was filled with vendors selling exotic spices and handmade crafts. 7. The brave and fearless fire-fighter rushed into the burning building to rescue the trapped family. 8. The sleepy, picturesque village nestled in the valley was a perfect retreat for city dwellers. 9. A shiny, silver key unlocked the mysterious door hidden in the attic . 10. The talented, young musician played a hauntingly beautiful melody on her violin. The main components of a noun phrase are: Noun: The core of the noun phrase is, of course, the noun itself, which is the word that represents the person, place, thing, or idea. Examples of nouns: Cat: The cat is sleeping. Mount Everest: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world. Love: Love can conquer all. Determiner (Optional): A determiner is an optional word that comes before a noun to specify or clarify it. Common determiners include articles (a, an, the), demonstratives (this, that, these, those), possessive pronouns (my, your, his, her, its, our, their), and quantifiers (some, many, few). Examples:

The cat: The definite article "the" specifies which cat we are referring to. My book: The possessive pronoun "my" shows ownership. Some cookies: The quantifier "some" indicates an unspecified quantity of cookies. Adjectives (Optional): Adjectives are words that describe or modify the noun by providing additional information. They can describe the size, color, shape, or other qualities of the noun. Examples: Beautiful sunset: "Beautiful" is an adjective describing the sunset. Three big balloons: "Three" and "big" are adjectives describing the balloons. Round table: "Round" describes the shape of the table. Prepositional Phrases (Optional): Prepositional phrases consist of a preposition and a noun (or pronoun) object and can be used to modify the noun. Examples: The book on the shelf : "On the shelf" is a prepositional phrase that provides additional information about the book. The girl with the red backpack : "With the red backpack" is a prepositional phrase that describes the girl. Relative Clauses (Optional): Relative clauses are dependent clauses that provide more information about the noun. They often start with relative pronouns like "who," "which," or "that." Examples: The cat that chased the mouse… : "That chased the mouse" is a relative clause describing the cat. The house where I grew up… : "Where I grew up" is a relative clause modifying the house. Appositives (Optional): An appositive is a noun or noun phrase that renames or explains another noun in the sentence. Examples: Tom, my friend …: "my friend" is an appositive renaming "Tom." The city, New York : "New York" is an appositive explaining "the city." In a noun phrase, you can have any combination of these components to add detail and description to the noun it modifies. The specific components used depend on the context and what you want to convey. d what you want to convey. Types of Noun Phrases According to English grammar rules, noun phrases are equivalent to nouns, but depending on their placement in the sentence, they can have various grammatical roles. pages.text: NOTE ON NOUN PHRASE In the English language, nouns are the words used to refer to people, places, or things. A noun phrase is a group of words, usually a noun in addition to a modifier—such as an adjective, determiners or modifiers—that functions just as a noun would. Grammatically, a noun phrase can be the subject, object, subject complement, or object complement, complement of a preposition or function as an appositive to a noun in the sentence in which it appears. Simply put, a noun phrase consists of one or more words that function together to name a person, place, thing, or idea and can include modifiers to provide more information about that noun. Examples of noun phrases in sentences: 1. The gigantic, ancient oak tree stood majestically in the centre of the forest. 2. My best friend's fluffy, white cat always greets me with a purr and a nuzzle. 3. The sparkling, turquoise waters of the Caribbean Sea were breath- taking. 4. The old, leather-bound book on the shelf contained many fascinating stories. 5. The delicious, homemade apple pie filled the kitchen with a warm, sweet aroma. 6. The bustling, colourful marketplace was filled with vendors selling exotic spices and handmade crafts. 7. The brave and fearless fire-fighter rushed into the burning building to rescue the trapped family. 8. The sleepy, picturesque village nestled in the valley was a perfect retreat for city dwellers. 9. A shiny, silver key unlocked the mysterious door hidden in the attic . 10. The talented, young musician played a hauntingly beautiful melody on her violin. The main components of a noun phrase are: Noun: The core of the noun phrase is, of course, the noun itself, which is the word that represents the person, place, thing, or idea. Examples of nouns: Cat: The cat is sleeping. Mount Everest: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world. Love: Love can conquer all. Determiner (Optional): A determiner is an optional word that comes before a noun to specify or clarify it. Common determiners include articles (a, an, the), demonstratives (this, that, these, those), possessive pronouns (my, your, his, her, its, our, their), and quantifiers (some, many, few). Examples:

The cat: The definite article "the" specifies which cat we are referring to. My book: The possessive pronoun "my" shows ownership. Some cookies: The quantifier "some" indicates an unspecified quantity of cookies. Adjectives (Optional): Adjectives are words that describe or modify the noun by providing additional information. They can describe the size, color, shape, or other qualities of the noun. Examples: Beautiful sunset: "Beautiful" is an adjective describing the sunset. Three big balloons: "Three" and "big" are adjectives describing the balloons. Round table: "Round" describes the shape of the table. Prepositional Phrases (Optional): Prepositional phrases consist of a preposition and a noun (or pronoun) object and can be used to modify the noun. Examples: The book on the shelf : "On the shelf" is a prepositional phrase that provides additional information about the book. The girl with the red backpack : "With the red backpack" is a prepositional phrase that describes the girl. Relative Clauses (Optional): Relative clauses are dependent clauses that provide more information about the noun. They often start with relative pronouns like "who," "which," or "that." Examples: The cat that chased the mouse… : "That chased the mouse" is a relative clause describing the cat. The house where I grew up… : "Where I grew up" is a relative clause modifying the house. subject: English Language
rawText:
LISTENING COMPREHENSION Definition: Listening comprehension is the ability to understand and make meaning from spoken words or recorded messages. It involves paying attention, understanding the message, and answering questions based on what is heard. PURPOSE OF LISTENING COMPREHENSION 1. To develop the ability to understand spoken English. 2. To test the learner’s concentration and memory. 3. To improve vocabulary and pronunciation. 4. To help students respond correctly to real-life communication. 5. To teach listening skills useful in everyday life situations. SKILLS REQUIRED IN LISTENING COMPREHENSION 1. Concentration: Focus your attention on what is being said. 2. Understanding main ideas: Identify the central message of the passage. 3. Noting specific details: Listen for names, dates, figures, or facts. 4. Recognizing tone and attitude: Understand the speaker’s mood or feeling. 5. Taking notes: Jot down important points to help recall later. 6. Answering questions: Respond clearly and accurately based on what you heard. TYPES OF PASSAGES USED Listening comprehension passages can be on topics such as: 1. HIV/AIDS: Causes, prevention, effects, and care of infected persons. 2. Drug Abuse: Meaning, examples of abused drugs, effects, and prevention. 3. Real-life situations: Daily experiences, moral lessons, or short stories that teach values like honesty, hard work, and discipline. EXAMPLES OF QUESTIONS ASKED AFTER LISTENING 1. What is the passage mainly about? 2. Mention two effects of drug abuse mentioned in the passage. 3. According to the passage, how can HIV/AIDS be prevented? 4. What lesson can be learned from the story? 5. State two pieces of advice given by the speaker. TIPS FOR ANSWERING LISTENING COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS 1. Listen attentively from the beginning to the end. 2. Do not be distracted during the reading. 3. Take quick notes of key points. 4. Do not depend on memory alone. 5. Read the questions carefully before and after listening. 6. Give short and direct answers. EXAMPLE THEMES (a) HIV/AIDS Passage:

• Definition and causes of HIV/AIDS • How it is transmitted • Prevention methods (e.g., abstinence, use of sterile needles) • Caring for infected people (b) Drug Abuse Passage: • Meaning of drug abuse • Examples of abused drugs (e.g., cocaine, marijuana, tramadol) • Effects on health, family, and society • How to avoid drug abuse (c) Real-Life Situation Passage: • A story about honesty, discipline, or helping others • A report about a community event or accident • A conversation between two people teaching moral or social lessons

title: SUFFIX
subject: English Language
rawText:
Lesson Note: Suffix 1. Definition of Suffix A suffix is a group of letters added at the end of a word to change its meaning, function, or grammatical category .  It is different from a prefix , which is added at the beginning of a word. Example:  Care → Careful (Suffix -ful changes a noun to an adjective)  Act → Action (Suffix -ion changes a verb to a noun) 2. Functions of Suffixes Suffixes can perform different roles in English. The main functions include: 1. Forming Nouns (from verbs or adjectives) o Hunger → Hungering o Create → Creation o Common noun suffixes: -ness, -ion, -ment, -ity, -er, -ist 2. Forming Adjectives (from nouns or verbs) o Beauty → Beautiful o Hope → Hopeful o Common adjective suffixes: -ful, -less, -able, -ous, -ish, -ic 3. Forming Verbs (from nouns or adjectives) o Strength → Strengthen o Modern → Modernize o Common verb suffixes: -en, -ize, -ify 4. Forming Adverbs (usually from adjectives) o Quick → Quickly

o Happy → Happily o Common adverb suffix: -ly 3. Examples of Common Suffixes Suffi x Word Formed Function / Meaning -ness Kindness Forms nouns from adjectives -ion Celebration Forms nouns from verbs -ment Enjoyment Forms nouns from verbs -er Teacher Person who performs action -ist Artist One who specializes -ful Beautiful Full of (adjective) -less Hopeless Without (adjective) -able Washable Can be done (adjective) -ous Courageous Full of (adjective) -ic Poetic Relating to (adjective) -en Strengthen To make (verb) -ify Beautify To make (verb) -ize Modernize To make (verb) -ly Quickly Forms adverbs from adjectives

4. Rules to Remember 1. Most suffixes do not change the base spelling of the word, e.g., hope → hopeful . 2. Some suffixes may require spelling changes : o Drop the final e before adding a suffix starting with a vowel: hope → hoping o Double the final consonant if the word ends in a single vowel + consonant: run running → o Change y to i before adding a suffix: happy happiness → 5. Exercises A. Identify the suffix in each word: 1. Careful 2. Happiness 3. Modernize 4. Quickly 5. Artist B. Form new words using the correct suffix: 1. Joy ______ → 2. Hope ______ → 3. Strong ______ → 4. Teach ______ → 5. Magic ______ →

WEEK 10 I. SPEECH: Vowel sounds /i/ and /i:/ /i/ is a short vowel produced by raising the front teeth. It is a front vowel and the position of the jaw during its production in half-close. The spelling symbols include: 1. “I” as in sit, with, misfit, simple. 2. “e” as in e.g precede/prisi:d/, Bucket enforce Examination epitome Market college Engagement 3. “ą” as in village, manage, orange, coltage, advantage. 4. “u” as in busy, minute, business. 5. “y” as in city, rhythm, hymn, myth. 6. “Ie” as in ladies /leidiz/ 7. “ui” as in built. /i:/ is a long front vowel. It is produced by raising the front of the tongue behind the front of the lower teeth. The jaw position during its production is closed. The spelling symbols include; 1. “I” as in machine, police, prestige, chlorine. 2. “e” as in epoch(era)/i:pok/ eke/i:k/, ego, complete. 3. “ee” as in breeze/bri:z/, fee/fi:/, agree, wheel/wi:l/. 4. “ea” as in beat, deal, teach, league/li:g/, lead(verb) /li:d/. 5. “ei” as in conceive, seize, protein, receipt, caffeine. 6. “ey” as in key, donkey, geyser /gi:z/. 7. “eo” as in people /pi:pl/. 8. “ie” as in belief, brief/bri:f/, field /fi:ld/, chief, siege, shield. 9. “oe” as in foetus/fi:tə s/, amoeba, phonix/fi:niks/. 10. “uay” as in quay. /i/ /i:/

STRUCTURE: DETERMINERS Determiners are the other class of grammatical parts of speech which modify noun’s and preposition of phrases to convey partitive (part of a whole) or whole meanings. TYPES OF DETERMINERS 1. Partitive determiners: they are so called because they convey part of a whole meaning and includes many, some, much, little, few, each and any. 2. Non partitive determiners: they are so called because they convey whole meanings. They include all, both and every. All determiners can stand alone in a sentence as subject, object of a verb or complement. USES OF DETERMINERS 1.”any” it is used to refer to a part of an unstated countable noun or prepositional phrase. Example - Any member of staff can invigilate. -Any of the students may answer the question ”any” may be used to express nothingness.

e.g – we have not got any food to waste. - He has not any good to deliver. 2. Each: The determiner may be used to refer to any number of things taken separately with a singular verb. Examples: - Each of the students is to be caned. - Each question’s attracts some marks. - Each other as a determiner refers to each of the two people. Example -The two boys hugged each other. -The twins lied against each other. 3. Few: few may be used with “a” in front as in few, followed by a plural verb. Examples -A few days have passed since he died. -A few of them have registered. “The” can also be used with few as in the few, followed by a plural verb. Examples - The few who came were fed. - The few ladies in the meeting left in time. NOTE: “A” or ”The” cannot be used with few when the reference is to number that is too small or not many at all or together, insignificant or negligible, in such cases, few is used alone. Example; - Few students attended the Principals party. - Few were employed, out of the thousands that applied. - Many were called, but few were choosen.

4. Little: when reference is to an uncountable noun, the articles “ a” or “the” may be used with little as in a little. Examples; - I used a little time tp summarize. - Children need a little milk for healthy growth. - The little sand in the soup made me abandon it. When reference is to a part of an uncountable noun which is either not much or insufficient, little should not be used with “a” or “the”. Example - He had little or no experience when he came. 5. MUCH: can be used with so and too as in so much and too much. When much modifies abstract noun, a singular verb is used after the determiner. E.g - Too much love is not good Ii) Much can also modify an adjective in the comparative form to show a higher comparative degree. Examples -I feel much better now I have eaten. -A Peugeot car is much more expensive than a Toyota. iii) Much can also modify verbal adjectives in their ordinary form (adjectives ending in”ing” or “ed”) Examples - The god seems much appeased now the king is dead. - - Soccer is much exciting to watch alive 6. MANY: Many can modify a plural noun or plural prepositional phrase at the subject or object position within a sentence. Example - Many players were wounded in the match. - Many of the players are yet to resign.

Ii) Alone: many can be used either as a subject or an object of plural verb. Examples: - Many are preached to, few repent. - Many ere remanded in custody by the judge. iii) Many can be used with a singular noun phrase, preferably, an article plus singular noun such as a boy, a time . Such a noun phrase is not singular but plural, hence, it will go with a plural verb. Example; - Many a boy have died taking a risk. - Many a child contracted diseases during birth. iv) Just as in the above usage, many can be used with a plus time as in many a time. In this case, time must be used in the singular sense, not plural; Example - Many a time, the principal has warned him. - Many a time, Cameroun has beaten Nigeria in soccer. 7. SOME: Modifies an uncountable noun. In this sense it is used within a singular verb. Examples - Some fruit juice is okay for breakfast. - Some petrol is needed to burn the rubble. ii) When some modifies a countable noun which is in the plural form, then a plural verb must be used, Example; - Some teachers have just been sacked. - Some children are more stubborn than others. iii) When some is used alone as the subject of a complex sentences whose second clause contains any other determiner in the singular form, then a singular verb must be used; Examples - Some was destroyed, but much was still saved. - Some was expanded, but a little was realized. 8. All: all is used in the plural sense when used with countable nouns. Here, plural verb must be used. Examples

- All the stubborn children have been expelled. - All guests are to be seated before a: am. II) When used as subject of the verb or with an uncountable noun. “All” is used in the singularsense and must go with a singular verb. Examples; - All the sand has been used up. - All is well which ends well. 9. EVERY: Generally, every indicates a whole group. Every modifies such words as are, time etc. As such words do not separately from them, as in every one, every time, as such words do not express universal meaning. What they actually mean is every person or each time. Examples - Every one of the students loves me. - I will always feel relieved every time I sleep. ii) Every is used with a singular countable noun and a singular verb, Examples: - Every worker is to pay fifty naira. - Every plan he made to pass was futile. iii)Every can also be used to express a countable period of time. Example - The injection is to be given every six hours. 10. BOTH: Always take a plural verb as it is always use in the plural sense if it is used alone as the subject of a verb or as a modifier of a plural noun. Both is also used to show too many things which are complete. Examples - Both have to be surcharged. - Both of them have passed the interview. - Both lecturers are one of a kind.

Example; - Many a boy have died taking a risk. - Many a child contracted diseases during birth. iv) Just as in the above usage, many can be used with a plus time as in many a time. In this case, time must be used in the singular sense, not plural; Example - Many a time, the principal has warned him. - Many a time, Cameroun has beaten Nigeria in soccer. 7. SOME: Modifies an uncountable noun. In this sense it is used within a singular verb. Examples - Some fruit juice is okay for breakfast. - Some petrol is needed to burn the rubble. ii) When some modifies a countable noun which is in the plural form, then a plural verb must be used, Example; - Some teachers have just been sacked. - Some children are more stubborn than others. iii) When some is used alone as the subject of a complex sentences whose second clause contains any other determiner in the singular form, then a singular verb must be used; Examples - Some was destroyed, but much was still saved. - Some was expanded, but a little was realized. 8. All: all is used in the plural sense when used with countable nouns. Here, plural verb must be used. Examples

- All the stubborn children have been expelled. - All guests are to be seated before a: am. II) When used as subject of the verb or with an uncountable noun. “All” is used in the singularsense and must go with a singular verb. Examples; - All the sand has been used up. - All is well which ends well. 9. EVERY: Generally, every indicates a whole group. Every modifies such words as are, time etc. As such words do not separately from them, as in every one, every time, as such words do not express universal meaning. What they actually mean is every person or each time. Examples - Every one of the students loves me. - I will always feel relieved every time I sleep. ii) Every is used with a singular countable noun and a singular verb, Examples: - Every worker is to pay fifty naira. - Every plan he made to pass was futile. iii)Every can also be used to express a countable period of time. Example - The injection is to be given every six hours. 10. BOTH: Always take a plural verb as it is always use in the plural sense if it is used alone as the subject of a verb or as a modifier of a plural noun. Both is also used to show too many things which are complete. Examples - Both have to be surcharged. - Both of them have passed the interview. - Both lecturers are one of a kind.

title: INTONATION PATTERN: EXPRESSING
subject: English Language
rawText:
SS 2 ENGLISH LANGUAGE NOTE Topic: Speech – Intonation Pattern (Expressing Surprise / Disbelief – Exclamation) 1. Meaning of Intonation Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice when speaking. It shows the speaker’s feelings or attitude. There are three main types of intonation: 1. Falling intonation (↘) 2. Rising intonation (↗) 3. Fall–rise intonation 2. Intonation for Surprise or Disbelief When expressing surprise or disbelief, we usually use: • A rising intonation (↗) • Sometimes a sharp fall–rise tone • Strong emphasis (stress) on important words This makes the statement sound emotional or shocked. 3. Examples 1. Ade is a witch? ↗ 2. Really?! ↗ 3. Musa is a millionaire?! ↗ 4. You must be joking! ↗ 5. Richard is a spy?! ↗ 6. I don’t believe it! ↗ 7. Ibrahim is dead?! ↗ 8. Is he?! ↗ In these examples, the voice rises sharply to show shock, doubt, or disbelief.

4. Explanation of the Examples • “Ade is a witch?!” – The speaker is shocked and does not believe it. • “Musa is a millionaire?!” – The speaker finds it hard to believe. • “You must be joking!” – The speaker thinks it is a joke. • “I don’t believe it!” – Direct expression of disbelief. • “Is he?!” – Rising tone shows doubt and surprise. 5. Features of Intonation for Surprise • Voice rises sharply at the end. • Important words are stressed. • Facial expression usually shows shock (wide eyes, raised eyebrows). • Sometimes repeated words (Really?! What?!). 6. Dialogue (Acting Practice) Dialogue 1 Bola: Have you heard the news? Tunde: What news? Bola: Musa is a millionaire. Tunde: Musa is a millionaire?! ↗ Bola: Yes, he won a business award. Tunde: Really?! I can’t believe it! Dialogue 2 Aisha: Ibrahim is dead. Fatima: Ibrahim is dead?! ↗ Aisha: Yes, it happened yesterday. Fatima: Oh no! Is he?! That’s shocking! Dialogue 3 John: Richard is a spy. Mary: You must be joking! ↗ John: I’m serious. Mary: Richard? A spy?! I don’t believe it!

7. Class Activity Students should: 1. Form pairs. 2. Create a short dialogue expressing surprise. 3. Use rising intonation correctly. 4. Act it out in front of the class.

Consonant cluster is also known as consonant blend. Consonant Cluster vs Consonant Digraph • A consonant cluster is a group or sequence of consonants that appear together in a syllable without a vowel between them. In consonant cluster each letter represents a single sound sp eak, sk y, st ick, sn ail, sw im, • Consonant digraphs are groups of two consonants that make a single sound. title: SUFFIX
subject: English Language
rawText:
W r i t i n g & L a n g u a g e D e v e l o p m e n t C e n t e r S u f f i x e s f o r E n g l i s h L a n g u a g e L e a r n e r s Adding suffixes to the base, or root, of existing words to form new words is common in English. Suffixes are added to the back of the base word to create a new word with a different meaning. For example, if you add the verb suffix - en to the adjective awake , you get awaken , a verb. Suffixes usually change the part of speech of the base word. Suffixes are not words in their own right and cannot stand on their own in sentence; if we print them on their own we place a hyphen before them (- en ). Suffixes that create verbs Common suffixes used in academic English create verbs. If you add a verb suffix to a noun or adjective, it becomes a verb. For example, adding - ate to the noun pollen creates the verb pollinate (or pollenate, an alternate spelling). If you add the suffix - en to the adjective short , you get the verb shorten , to become short. Suffix Meaning Example -ate become differentiate, liquidate, pollinate, duplicate, fabricate -en become awaken, fasten, shorten, moisten -ify make or become classify, exemplify, simplify, justify -ise /-ize become compromise, stabilize, characterize, symbolize, visualize Suffixes that create nouns The following suffixes create nouns. For instance, if you take the verb demonstrate and add the noun suffix - tion , you get the noun demonstration . Similarly, if you add the noun suffix - ship to the noun citizen , you get the noun citizenship , holding the position of being a citizen. Suffix Meaning Example -age result of breakage, wastage, package -al action or process of denial, proposal, refusal -ant /-ent agent or performer of an action assistant, consultant, student -cy state or quality urgency, efficiency, frequency -ence /-ance state of quality of preference, dependence, interference, attendance, acceptance, endurance -er person or object that does a specified action advertiser, dancer, teacher, driver, computer, silencer -ism doctrine or belief Marxism, Maoism, Thatcherism -ity quality of ability, similarity, responsibility, curiosity -ment condition development, punishment, unemployment -ness state of being darkness, preparedness, consciousness -ship position held friendship, citizenship, leadership -tion /-sion condition or state of alteration, demonstration, expansion, inclusion, admission

Suffixes that create adjectives These suffixes create adjectives. As an example, adding the adjective suffix - ful to the noun peace gives you an adjective, peaceful . Adding the adjective suffix - ous to the verb danger gives you the adjective dangerous , characterized by danger. Suffixes that create adverbs A few suffixes create adverbs. For instance, adding the adverb suffix - ly to the adjective happy gives you happily , an adverb. Or adding - ward to the noun west gives you the adverb westward , in the direction of the west. Prefixes and Suffixes used together Prefixes and suffixes are often used together. The following words use both the prefix mis - (wrongly or badly) and the noun suffix - tion (condition of) with different base words: inform misinformation communicate miscommunication interpret misinterpretation The following base words are changed by using both the prefix un - (not) and the adjective suffix - able (capable of being): comfort uncomfortable imagine unimaginable available unavailable These use the prefix dis - (not) and the noun suffix - ment (condition): agreement disagreement arm disarmament Contributed by Kelly Cunningham This Yuba College Writing & Language Development Center Tip Sheet is made available under a Creative Commons Attribution- NonCommercial 4.0 International License . To view a copy of this license, visit http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0 Suffix Meaning Example -able capable of being drinkable, countable, avoidable -al having the form or character of central, political, national, optional, professional -ent tending toward different, dependent, excellent -ful notable for beautiful, peaceful, careful -ive having the nature of attractive, effective, imaginative, repetitive -less without endless, homeless, careless, thoughtless -ous characterized by continuous, dangerous, famous Suffix Meaning Example -ly / -ily related to or quality softly, happily, sleepily, quickly -ward/ -wards direction toward, afterwards, backwards, westward -wise in relation to otherwise, likewise, clockwise

Unit Topic: clause Lesson topic: Adverbial clause and function An adverbial clause is the clause that performs the work of an adverb in a sentence. The adverbial clauses are classified according to the meaning they Convey in sentence They answers questions like when, where, how why, etc. The functions of adverbial clause is to modifies verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs in a sentence Types and functions of adverbial clause 1. Adverbial clause of time: This expresses the time of the action-contained in the main clause .It answers the question when, and is often Introduced by while, since, after, when, as, before, untill during etc. Examples. a. It was raining when I woke up . when I woke up modifies the verb "raining" in the main Clause b. I will not go away until he comes back until he comes back modifies the verb "go away". 2. Adverbial clause of place: This shows the place where the action occurs. It answers the question where and is often introduced by where, whenever anywhere, everywhere, etc Examples a. my father left the money where it could be seen Where it could be seen modifies the verb "left". b. He eats anywhere he sees food. (anywhere he Sees food) modifies the verb "left" 3. Adverbial clause of manner: An adverbial Clause of manner is used to express the way. in which the action in the mam clause is carried out. It answers the question "how" and is often Introduced by as, as if, as though, etc. Eg a. she sang as if she was a solost. as if she was a soloist modifies the verb "sang". b. He parades himself as though he is the president of the whole world. as though he is the president of the whole world modifies the verb "Parades

4. Adverbial clause of reason. An adverbial clause of reason explains the cause of the action in the mam clause. It is an expression for justification for something that has happened. It answer the question why and it is introduced by because, since for, as, seeing that etc. Eg: a. The teacher punished the student because he Came late to class. because he came Lode to School modifies the verb "punished" b. . We left Since he was not ready to Increase our Salary.Since he was not ready to Increase our Salary modifies the verb "Left"! 5. Adverbial Clause of result: An adverbial clause of result mentions the Consequence the action in the main clause. It is Introduced by that, So that, Such that Example a. she sang in a manner that made every body to admire her.. that made everybody to admire her, modifies to verb sang! Her. b. It rained heavily such that vehicles stopped moving .Such that vehicles stopped moving modifier the aduerb "heavily. 6. Aduerbial clause of purpose: An adverbial clause purpose expresses the aim of the action in the many Clause: It answers the question for what purpose? and is usually Introduced by So that, in order that In case, should, etc. Examples. a. He prays so that God will hear him... So that God will hear him modifies the verb 'prays in the main clause. b. Truth is necessary so that people will have Confidence In you. so that people will have confidence in you modifies the verb is in the main clause. 7. Adverbial clause of degree. An adverbial clause of degree expresses the weight (gravity or level) of the action in the main clause. It is introduce by then, as... as. Examples a. He is more dangerous than you think... than you think modifies the verb is' in the main clause. b. He works longer than his boss permits. than his boss permits modifier the verb "Works in the main clause. 8 Adverbial clause of Condition: An adverbial Clause of Condition states the situation (Condition) under which the action in the mains clause will take place. It is introduced by the conditional words if, unless, except, provided, until, once. Examples. a. I will not let you go unless you bless me. Unless you bless me modifies the verb "will not let go in the main clause.

b. If you do not marry me, I will die. If you do not marry me modifies the verb "will die in the main clause. Unit Topic : better writing Lesson topic: Informal letter features and Language Informal letters are private or personal Letters. They are letters written to people who are very familiar to us such as our parent’s relatives, friends, classmate, brothers and sisters, husband and wives and other people with whom we have close relationship. Unit Topic: clause Lesson topic: Adverbial clause and function An adverbial clause is the clause that performs the work of an adverb in a sentence. The adverbial clauses are classified according to the meaning they Convey in sentence They answers questions like when, where, how why, etc. The functions of adverbial clause is to modifies verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs in a sentence Types and functions of adverbial clause 1. Adverbial clause of time: This expresses the time of the action-contained in the main clause .It answers the question when, and is often Introduced by while, since, after, when, as, before, untill during etc. Examples. a. It was raining when I woke up . when I woke up modifies the verb "raining" in the main Clause b. I will not go away until he comes back until he comes back modifies the verb "go away". 2. Adverbial clause of place: This shows the place where the action occurs. It answers the question where and is often introduced by where, whenever anywhere, everywhere, etc Examples a. my father left the money where it could be seen Where it could be seen modifies the verb "left". b. He eats anywhere he sees food. (anywhere he Sees food) modifies the verb "left" 3. Adverbial clause of manner: An adverbial Clause of manner is used to express the way. in which the action in the mam clause is carried out. It answers the question "how" and is often Introduced by as, as if, as though, etc. Eg a. she sang as if she was a solost. as if she was a soloist modifies the verb "sang". b. It rained heavily such that vehicles stopped moving .Such that vehicles stopped moving modifier the aduerb "heavily. 6. Aduerbial clause of purpose: An adverbial clause purpose expresses the aim of the action in the many Clause: It answers the question for what purpose? and is usually Introduced by So that, in order that In case, should, etc. Examples. a. He prays so that God will hear him... So that God will hear him modifies the verb 'prays in the main clause. b. Truth is necessary so that people will have Confidence In you. so that people will have confidence in you modifies the verb is in the main clause. 7. Adverbial clause of degree. He is more dangerous than you think... than you think modifies the verb is' in the main clause. b. title: NOMINALIZATION
subject: English Language
rawText:
NOMINALISATION NOTE Nominalization is a linguistic process in which a word that is not a noun is transformed into a noun. This often involves converting verbs, adjectives, or other parts of speech into nouns. For example, turning the verb "to run" into the noun "running" or the adjective "beautiful" into the noun "beauty" are instances of nominalization. It's a common technique in language to create nouns from other words to express abstract concepts or make sentences more concise Simply put, Nominalisation is the process of turning a verb or adjective into a noun. This linguistic technique is often used to refer to actions, qualities, or concepts as nouns, allowing for clearer communication and a more versatile use of language. Verbs into Nouns (Nominalization) Verbs can be turned into nouns through nominalization. This is achieved by adding 1. suffixes, or changing the word form. 2. using gerunds, Nominalization of Verbs Suffixes Verbs can be turned into nouns by adding suffixes. Common suffixes for nominalization of verbs include: -tion -ment -ance Examples: 1. Verb: Create Nominalized Noun: Creation Example: The creation of this artwork is impressive. 2. Verb: Develop

Nominalized Noun: Development Example: The development of technology has revolutionized our lives. 3. Verb: Communicate Nominalized Noun: Communication Example: Effective communication is essential in a team. 4. Verb: Perform Nominalised Noun: Performance Example: The performance of the troup was top notch. 5. Verb: Perform Nominalized Noun: Performance Example: Her piano performance was outstanding at the concert. 6. Verb: Investigate Nominalized Noun: Investigation Example: The police conducted a thorough investigation into the case. 7. Verb: Contribute Nominalized Noun: Contribution Example: Your contribution to the charity made a significant impact. 8. Verb: Explore Nominalized Noun: Exploration Example: The exploration of outer space has always fascinated scientists Nominalisation of Verbs through Gerunds. (-ing). Using gerunds (verbs ending in -ing) as nouns is another form of nominalization. Example: 1. Verb: Teach Gerund/Nominalized Noun: Teaching

Example: Teaching requires patience and dedication. 2. Drink Nominalsed Noun: Drinking Example: Drinking a hot cup of coffee is a good way of keeping awake. 3. Verb: Sing Nominalised Noun: Singing Example: Her singing is so melodious. Nominalisation of Adjectives Adjectives can also be transformed into nouns by using them to describe a group or category of people or things. Examples: 1. Adjective: Responsible Noun Form: Responsibility Example: Taking on this project is a big responsibility. 2. Adjective: Generous Noun Form: Generosity Example: His generosity touched the hearts of many. 3. Adjective: Creative Noun Form: Creativity Example: She has a unique creativity that shines through her art. 4. Adjective: Available Noun Form: Availability Example: Her availability to duty is unmatched. 5. Adjective: Content Noun Form: Contentment Example: Godliness with contentment is great gain.

Why Use Nominalization? Clarity : Nominalization can make sentences clearer and more concise. Variety : It adds variety to your writing and allows you to express ideas in different ways. Example: Original Sentence - "They decided to investigate the matter thoroughly." Nominalization: "Their decision to conduct a thorough investigation was wise." Conciseness : It helps you to make sentences in fewer words. Example: Original Sentence - "She made a suggestion that we should go on a vacation." Nominalization: "Her suggestion of a vacation is enticing." Formality : Nominalization is often used in formal writing and academic contexts. Example: Original Sentence (Casual): "She discovered how to solve the problem." Nominalization (Formal): "She arrived at a solution to the problem." Precision : Nominalization can make it easier to discuss abstract concepts. It also removes ambiguity. Example: Original Sentence - "The decision to cancel the project is a possibility." Nominalization: "The possibility of project cancellation exists." Sentences with nominalised verbs and adjectives 1. The acceleration of the car impressed everyone. 2. His constant complaining became tiresome. 3. The destruction caused by the hurricane was devastating. 4. Her singing was enchanting to all who listened.

5. The exploration of outer space requires significant resources. 6.The selection of candidates for the job was challenging. 7. The presentation of the award made her feel proud. 8. The analysis of the data revealed interesting patterns. 9. The construction of the new bridge is underway. 10. The completion of the project was a major accomplishment. 11. His kindness is one of his most admirable qualities. 12. The beauty of the landscape took my breath away. 13. The purity of her intentions was evident to everyone. 14. The darkness of the night concealed all movement. 15. The simplicity of the design appealed to minimalists. 16. The importance of education cannot be overstated. 17. The depth of his knowledge was unmatched. 18. The rarity of such a gem made it highly valuable. 19. The elegance of her dress was the talk of the evening. 20. The severity of the storm caused significant damage. Created by Ewuzie Jacinta Njideka GSS Jabi

Theme : speech Unit topic: Consonant sounds. Lesson Topic: Nasal sounds/n//m/and/g/ Nasal sounds are consonants which are produced when the soft oft palate is lowered to close the oral cavity so that air-Steam passes through the nasal cavity (The nose) The nasal are /n//m//sand /g/ and they are all voiced /m/ is a voiced bilabial nasal which is produced when upper and lower lips come together, you breathe out through the nose and add some voice to the breaths Stream. The spelling Symbol includes. m as in man, meat march, move, mat Mas. mm as in Commit, summon recommend. mb as in tomb bomb, Comb, Thumb. mn as in damn, column, Solemn . /n/ is a voiced alveolar nasal sound and for the production to it, the tip of the tongue forms a closure with the alveolar ridge, allowing the air stream pass through the nasal Cavity (the nose). The vocal Cords Vibrate during the articulation of /n/ which makes if a voiced Sound. The spelling symbols for the /n/ sound are. 'n' as in-nail, neat, never, noon, Snake. Nn as in funny, annoy, dinner kn as in know, knot, knit, knife "gn" as in gnat, gnaw, gnarle, gnash. Dz/ is a voiced velar nasal produced with the basis of the tongue forming a closure with the Velum and the air stream passing through the nasal cavity (noise). There is a vibration at the vocal Cords during the Production of/dz/ The /dz/ Sound does not occur at the beginning of a word. The spelling Symbol Includes:" /ng/ as in bring, anger, tongue, wing, sing, ring, king, Spring, morning. When 'n' occurs before 'g' in a word that is more than one syllable, it is pronounced as/g/while the g' is pronounced as /g/ to give the two Sounds /dg/. Eg: bangle, angle dangle, finger, hungry, Jungle ete... Note that not all 'ng' letter become /g/in word like fringe, Stingy, revenge, do not have the /g/ sound because the sound realized there is /n/

Theme: Structure Unit Topics: Concord Lesson topic : Concord-agreement between subject and verb Concord means agreement between the subject and the verb m any sentence both im number and person. A sentence will always be wrong if the subject and verb do not agree. Concord has rules guiding it which must be known For Correct sentence Constructions. 1. When the subject is Singular It takes a Singular verb and when the subject is plural, if takes a plural verb. Examples. a. The Lecturer comes to class every Tuesday!! b. she has a very good hand writing. c. Some students want to pass without reading. d. They come here every day. Note that when the pronoun I is used it uses a plural verb "have" even though it is a singular person. Example. a. I have some work to do. b. I have finished cooking the food. 2. When two or more subjects are connected by 'and' a plural verb is used Example. a. John and Adamu play football every day. b. The Woman and her twins were honored. If the subjects are connected by each' or 'every, a singular verb is required. Examples. a. Each boy and girl is to bring a hoe. b. Every man and woman has a role to play in fighting corruptions.

If two singular subjects Connected by "and" refer to the same personal, a Singular verb is used. Example. a. My Sister and friend is very good to me. b. He is your husband and mentor. 3. When two or more singular subjects are joined by neither now, either or not only-but, take a Singular verb. Eg. a. Neither the man nor his wife qualifies for the award. b. Either the principal or the vice gives out the certificates. C. Not only the robbers but the policeman was responsible for the theft.
