Lesson Topic: Nasal sounds/n//m/and/g/ Nasal sounds are consonants which are produced when the soft oft palate is lowered to close the oral cavity so that air-Steam passes through the nasal cavity (The nose) The nasal are /n//m//sand /g/ and they are all voiced /m/ is a voiced bilabial nasal which is produced when upper and lower lips come together, you breathe out through the nose and add some voice to the breaths Stream. The spelling Symbol includes. m as in man, meat march, move, mat Mas. mm as in Commit, summon recommend. mb as in tomb bomb, Comb, Thumb. mn as in damn, column, Solemn . /n/ is a voiced alveolar nasal sound and for the production to it, the tip of the tongue forms a closure with the alveolar ridge, allowing the air stream pass through the nasal Cavity (the nose). The vocal Cords Vibrate during the articulation of /n/ which makes if a voiced Sound. The spelling symbols for the /n/ sound are. 'n' as in-nail, neat, never, noon, Snake. Nn as in funny, annoy, dinner kn as in know, knot, knit, knife "gn" as in gnat, gnaw, gnarle, gnash. Dz/ is a voiced velar nasal produced with the basis of the tongue forming a closure with the Velum and the air stream passing through the nasal cavity (noise). There is a vibration at the vocal Cords during the Production of/dz/ The /dz/ Sound does not occur at the beginning of a word. The spelling Symbol Includes:" /ng/ as in bring, anger, tongue, wing, sing, ring, king, Spring, morning. When 'n' occurs before 'g' in a word that is more than one syllable, it is pronounced as/g/while the g' is pronounced as /g/ to give the two Sounds /dg/. Eg: bangle, angle dangle, finger, hungry, Jungle ete... Note that not all 'ng' letter become /g/in word like fringe, Stingy, revenge, do not have the /g/ sound because the sound realized there is /n/

subject: English Language
rawText: POLYSYLLABIC WORDS Polysyllabic words are simple or complex words of more than one syllable. They can have more than one stress, i.e., a primary, a secondary stress and unstressed syllables. Examples of polysyllabic words are: Sum-ma-ry, con-so-nant, temp-ta-tion, cul-tu-ral, e-mo- tion, de-li-cious, con-duc-tor, e-du-cate, re-vi-sion, frus-tra-tion, etc. STRESS RULES In linguistics, stress is referred to as the relative emphasis that may be given to certain syllables in a word, or certain words in a phrase or sentence. Stress is typically signaled by such properties as increased loudness and vowel length, full articulation of the vowel, and changes in pitch. 1. Words ending in … CIAN or TIAN have their primary stress on the syllable before the … cian or tian : ma-the-ma-TI-cian, e-lec-TRI-cian, tech-NI-cian, tac-TI-cian, co-ME-dian, ci-VI-lian, etc. 2. Words ending in … OUS have their primary stress on the syllable before the ... ous : nuMERous, de-LI-cious, tre-MEN-dous, in-DUS-trous, tre-MEN-dous fa-LLA-cious, con-TA-gious, etc. 3. Some syllabic words ending in … NAL have their primary stress on the syllable before the ... nal : in-TER-nal, ex-TER-nal, etc. note: three syllabic words with TION in their middle always have the first syllable stressed: OP-tion-al, FUNC-tion-al, RA-tion-al, NO- tion-al, etc. 4. Words ending in… IC have their primary stress on the syllable before the …ic : fan-TA-Stic, at-LAN-tic, o-LYM-pic e-LEC-tric sy-LLA-bic, or-GA-nic ar-CHA-tic, pla-TO-nic, syn-THE-tic dia-BE-tics, pae-DIA-trics etc. 5. Words ending in… TION/SION have their primary stress on the syllable before the …tion/sion , e.g, temp-TA-tion, ag-GRE-sion, per-MI-ssion, a-DAP-tion, e-MO-tion, de-CI-sion, a- TTEN-tion con-NEC-tion ex-HAUS-tion 6. Words ending in … SIVE have their primary stress on the syllable before the ...sive : ex- PEN- sive, ag-GRE-ssive, ten- TA- tive, dis- TIN C-tive, a-TTRAC-tive , etc. 7. Words ending in … ABLE/IBLE have their primary stress on the syllable before …able/ible : vi-SI-ble, ter-RI-ble, etc. 8. Words ending in… MENT have their primary stress on the syllable before …ment : in- STRU-ment, a-MAZE-ment, com-PLE-ment, do-CU-ment,

subject: English Language
rawText:
Week 3 I. Speech: making a toast - meaning of toast and occasions for a toast. A toast can be a brief speech is congratulations, appreciation and remembrance for a person by a drink. However, the purpose for making a toast is, to thank someone, wishing someone good luck weeks celebrating an achievement. Occasions that require making a toast 1. Birthday party. 2. Wedding party. 3. Celebrating good health. 4. Celebrating an achievement. 5. Success in examination. 6. Celebrating admission into school. 7. Employment. 8. Celebrating survival of accident. Steps required in making a toast 1. To write a toast: it should be short, appealing and personal. The use of humerous language and quotation is required. The target is your toast is to make your friend is the person concerned as well as his guest happy. 2. Making notes: it is not ideal to write the entire speech on a book or read entirely from a note. This will look awkward. Rather, note some key words or phrases that will guide your thoughts and help you to remember what you want to say. Example: the first time you met your friend, how friendly you have been with each other, what you share in common etc. Short expressions like; first meeting, our friendship, our joy etc. The purpose of the note is to stimulate your memory. 3. When it is time, stand up to toast. 4. Raise your glass to the person to whom you are making the toast to. 5. Announce your relationship with the celebrant. 6. Propose your toast. As you do this, look at the person to whom you are toasting.

7. End your toast on a positive note. Example: let us now drink a toast to joy and many more happy years of celebration. When you say this, wave your glass to all. Then tip it towards the person you are toasting. You may clink his glass if you are close enough with the people around you. Do this gently to avoid breaking a glass. It is rude to do so. 8. Get back to your seat. Note that your toast must be very short e.g. 5 minutes. Toast making is not an avenue for you to show off your skills in comedy. This avoid unnecessary jokes and your wine should be sip not gulp. II. Comprehension: Reading for Implied Meaning Reading for implied meaning means reading to fill in certain gaps in which some explanations are left out. The reader is expected to fill the gaps in order to get the full understanding of the passage. Tips needed while reading for implied meaning includes: 1. Keep asking questions at you read. Questions such as where, why, how will shed more light on the content is the passage. 2. You will note that subtle expression are laden with deeper meaning. 3. Keep linking ideas as you read on, to understand the writer's line is development. This will enable you notice when a gap in information occurs or is created. 4. Your background knowledge of a topic may assist you too decipher a hidden or implied meaning in the passage. 5. If something is amiss, you assume what has happened. This assumption will help you draw conclusion and subsequently help you locate the implied meaning. Page "80" the determined mother. III. STRUCTURE - NOMINALIZATION: Nominalism is the formation of noun from adjectives, verbs or other nouns using syllable. Suffixes are unstressed syllables added to a root-word which then changes the meaning or class of the word to another. Formation of Noun: common suffixes used for nouns : -ity, -ness, -ist, -ancy/ency, -ster, -ment, - age, -ance/ence, -ism, -hood. How best to form nouns using suffixes. Examples: a. Adjective: add -ity to form nouns and add -ant, -ment to adjective exchange for -ancy and ency to also form nouns.

Example: Adjective + ity Noun i) Final + ity = finality II) Curious + ity = curiosity III) Sensitive + ity = sensitivity Iv) Able + ity = ability V) Expectant + ity = expectancy Vi) Redundant + ancy = redundancy Vii) Fluent + ency = fluency Viii) Efficient + ency = efficiency Note: ity when added to adjective that ends with -al, -ble, -cal, -ous, -ive, turns to nouns. b. Verbs: add -ment, -age, -ance, or -ence to some verbs to form nouns. Example: Verb Noun I) Entertain + ment = Entertainment Ii) Retire + ment = Retirement III) Settle + ment = settlement Iv) Advance + ment = advancement V) Move + ment = movement Vi) Carry + age = carriage Vii) Spoil + age = spoilage Viii) Use + age = usage Ix) Def + ence = defence X) Repent + ance = repentance Xi) Adhere + ence = adherence Xii) Prefer + ence = preference c. Nouns can also be form from other nouns. Example: nouns can be formed by adding -ship, hood, -ish etc.

Noun Noun II) Friend + ship = friendship II) Court + ship = courtship III) Adult + hood = adulthood Iv) Brother + hood = brotherhood V) Boy + ish = boyish Vi) Girl + ish = girlish Vii) Child + ish = childish IV. CONTINUOUS WRITING - Writing speeches for specific purposes (Introduction, Purpose, Feature) A speech is a written material meant to be read to a group of listeners. Speeches are meant to entertain, educate and inform people. It is also to motivate people to action. Features of a Speech 1. The title: there must be a title for the speech you are meant to deliver. The title should indicate the mark of identification. Such as: The purpose. Name and title of speaker. Occasion. Place. Date and time. For example: 1. A farewell speech presentation by Gideon John, the head boy of Government secondary school, Kubwa on the welcoming party of our new principal, Mr Okechukwu Kunle Musa, at the assembly hall this day 20th January, 2024 at. 10:00am. 2. The introduction: this must be interesting and captivating so as to elicit the interest of the listeners. It must start with salutation. Example: Good morning the chairman, the principal, the school management, the PTA... Ladies and gentlemen. I feel highly honored to stand here today to deliver my speech on... You write your topic and say your topic.

3. The body of the speech: this is the stage that contains the actual message. Start by giving your main points and the support each points with relevant details, comparisons and contrast etc. explaining who, when, where, why and how. The ideas must be stated in good and clear sentences. 4. The conclusion: Here you summarize your points. It is important to end in a memorable way by: 1) making a forceful and shocking statement. 2) urging your audience to follow a certain line of action or thought etc. 3) Ending in an interesting and captivating manner

A farewell speech presentation by Gideon John, the head boy of Government secondary school, Kubwa on the welcoming party of our new principal, Mr Okechukwu Kunle Musa, at the assembly hall this day 20th January, 2024 at. 10:00am. 2. The introduction: this must be interesting and captivating so as to elicit the interest of the listeners. It must start with salutation. Example: Good morning the chairman, the principal, the school management, the PTA... Ladies and gentlemen. I feel highly honored to stand here today to deliver my speech on... You write your topic and say your topic.

3. The body of the speech: this is the stage that contains the actual message. Start by giving your main points and the support each points with relevant details, comparisons and contrast etc. explaining who, when, where, why and how. The ideas must be stated in good and clear sentences. 4. The conclusion: Here you summarize your points. It is important to end in a memorable way by: 1) making a forceful and shocking statement. 2) urging your audience to follow a certain line of action or thought etc. 3) Ending in an interesting and captivating manner

title: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH HUMAN INTERNAL ORGANS
subject: English Language
rawText:
NOUN PHRASE AND FUNCTIONS A noun phrase is a group of words which has its headword as a noun or pronoun. It usually begins with an article such as ‘a’, ‘an’ or ‘the’. FUNCTIONS OF A NOUN PHRASE 1. Subject of the verb : When the noun phrase occupies the first position in a sentence, it functions as the subject of the verb that follows it. Examples: a. An old man is at the door. ( subject of the verb “is”) b. Sleeping without light is not something I enjoy. (subject of the verb is) c. An old music box is on the table. d. Your uncle is coming here. 2. Subject complement: When the noun phrase is the same thing or person as the subject, it functions as subject complement. Examples: a. Susan is the doctor.( complement of the subject Susan) b. My dad is a film director. (complement of the subject “my dad”) c. David was a naughty boy. d. I will soon become the head boy. 3. Object of the verb : When the noun phrase comes after the verb of action in the sentence, it functions as the object of the verb. Examples: a. Sunday received an award for excellence.( object of the verb received) b. An old man broke the door. ( object of the verb broke) c. Fatima has a kind heart. d. Stella bought a beautiful silver necklace. 4. Object complement: When the noun phrase is the same person or thing as the object, it functions as the object complement. Examples : a. My father calls my brother a hero. ( complement of the object my brother) b. The students calls the teacher a wizard.( complement of the object the teacher) c. My mother calls me the best. d. The principal named my friend the new representative. 5. Object of the preposition: When the noun phrase occurs after the preposition, it is governed by the preposition. Hence, it is the object of the preposition. Examples : a. An award of excellence was given to the teacher. ( object of the preposition to) b. An old man is at the door.( object of the preposition at) 6. Apposition: this is when a phrase tells us more about the noun that comes before it or when two noun phrases lie side by side without any word between them. Examples:

a. My brother, the teacher, was given an award. (the teacher is in apposition to my brother) b. Mr. Jones, the prince, was here last week. (the prince is in apposition to Mr. Jones)

title: CONTINUOUS WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText: FORMAL LETTER Formal letters are letters written to offices rather than persons, and so are recognized as impersonal letters. As such, they should contain neither personal greetings nor discussion or personal issues. Types of Formal Letter 1. Letters to offices and business houses Applying for jobs Making requests Replying to official letters Complaining about a product Placing an order 2. Invitations, Notices, Memos, Advertisement, Circular letters 3. Letter to instruct, requesting for admission, making complaints 4. Letter to editors of Newspaper, Magazine Guidelines for a Formal Letter a. The date should be punctuated and should appear in this form – 14th June, 1999. Note that ‘th’ touches the line. There is a comma after the month and full stop after the year. b. The address must always be written in block form. c. The address of the recipient should start immediately following the date. d. Start with ‘Dear Sir’ or Dear Madam’ as appropriate or simply ‘Sir’ or ‘Madam’. Note that either of the two start with a capital letter. Remember that a comma ends the salutation. e. If every letter of the words constituting the title is in capital letter, do not underline the heading. Underline if only the first letters of the key words are in capital letters. Article, conjunction and prepositions are not key words, so should begin in small letters, except where any starts the title. f. Write your points in paragraphs. g. Close with ‘Yours’ faithfully’. Note that ‘Y’ of ‘Yours’ is capital and there is no apostrophe either before or after‘s’ the ‘f’ starting faithfully is small letter. A comma should follow faithfully. h. The writer should sign his signature after the subscript. i. Write out full name and end with a full stop.

subject: English Language

Theme: Speech Unit topic: Stress in sentences Lesson Topic: sentential/Emphatic stress. Emphatic stress is also known as sentential stress or contrastive stress. It is the act of stressing a particular word more than other words in a sentence such a stress is important in conveying the appropriate meaning or information. Emphatic stress is different from primary Stress because while a whole word is stressed in a sentence to indicate emphatic Stress, just a syllable is stressed on a word to Indicate primary stress. Note that a Lexical item such as noun, verb, adjective, or adverb is usually stressed in sentences. Grammatical such as Pronouns, determiners, auxiliary verbs, Conjunctions, etc are not usually stressed that notwithstanding, any class of word can be stressed in a sentence if any important or special emphasis or message is intended. Examples 1. The child broke the MIRROR (not the plate) 2 James BORROWED my shirt ( he did not steal nor buy it) 3. I placed the cup on the table (not under) 4. We cooked the food (not any other person) 5. John bought NEW bicycle (not an old one) To indicate emphatic stress, a sentence is given and a word is written in capital Letter (indicating stress). Some questions an asked from which an appropriate option is selected as the best question meant for the Statement given. Examples: 1. Students must study HARD to pass their exams. a. Why must study hard to pass their exams? b. Why must students study hand? c. How must students study to pass their exams d. when must students study to pass their exams 2. Honesty is Always the best policy.

a. Is honesty always the best policy? b. Is honesty always the worst policy? C.is dishonesty always the best policy? d. Is honesty seldom the best policy? Theme: Comprehension Unit Topic: Reading Comprehension Lesson Topic: Reading for Implied meaning Reading for implied meaning means reading to fill in Certain gaps in which some explanation are left out. the reader is expected to fill the gaps in order to get full understanding of the Passage. The tips needed while reading for Implied meaning Include: 1. Keep asking question as you reads; question such as where, when? why?, How ?, will shed more light to the content of the passage. 2. You will note that subtle expressions αre laden with deeper meaning. keep linking ideas as you read on to understand the writer's line of development. This will enable you know when a gap is created 3. Your background knowledge of a topic or your past experience may assist you to decipher a hidden or implied meaning in the Passage 4. If something is amiss you assume what has happened. This assumption will help you draw Conclusions and subsequently help you locate the implied meaning. The Passage titled “Writing English composition. Unit 8 Theme: Structure Unit Topic: Clauses Lesson Topic : Adjectival clauses and their functions Adjectival clause is a subordinate Clause that performs the function of adjectives in a sentence. This means that It qualifies or tells us more about a noun or pronoun in the sentence.

Therefore, any clause which l gives more information about a noun or pronoun is an adjectival clause. It can also be called a relative clause. It is introduced by the following (wh) words. who, whom, which, whose, where, when thats etc. Eg 1. Adamu followed the road which was very rough function of qualifies the noun "road" 2. Okoye met the girl who insulted his father It qualifies the noun girl" 3. He showed me the place where his friend kept the bag: function It qualities the noun places. 4. These are the books which I bought last week . It qualifies the noun books". Theme: Continuous Writing. Unit topic : article writing Lesson Topic: Article witting (introduction, illustration and practice). An article is a piece of writing on national or regional issues of public Interest, usually meant for publication in of magazine of a newspaper. Note that in writing an article, the writer expresses his /her views or opinion on a given topic with good and logical points or facts. Features/format of an Article A. The title: It should be clearly written. Eg: The falling standard of Edicatan in Nigeria B. Introduction: This paragraph should introduce your topic or review whether people had written previously on the topic C. Body: This should contain relevant points discussed extensively and logically to give a clear understanding of the topic in question points raised should be discussed and arrange Paragraphs D. Conclusion: This is where the writer makes suggestions for solutions. E. Closure: It requires only the name of the writer and location where he/she is writing from Furthermore, your location should be your class in the school if the article is meant for a school

publication. On the other hand d, your location should be the state from which you write if the article is meant for a national publication, Note that Signature is not needed! NOTE, the language of an article is formal and straight forward. Slangs are not required. Some article topics for publication include: 1. Insecurity in Nigeria. 2. Unemployment problem in the country. 3. High rate of kidnapping / human trafficking in Nigeria. 4. the falling standard of education in Nigeria. 5 Drug abuse among Nigeria youths. Assignment write an article suitable for publication in a national newspaper on the growing Incidence of drug abuse among the youth, Stating the causes and Suggesting the way It can be curbed. Question and Answer WASSCE 2019.

title: RELATIVE AND DEMONSTRATIVE PRONOUNS
subject: English Language
rawText:
DATE: 3 rd October, 2023 THEME: Structure UNIT TOPIC: pronouns (II) LESSON TOPIC: types of Pronouns (relative and demonstrative) TIME: 8.00 -11.10 DUR: 120 minutes INSTRUCTIONAL OBJECTIVE: at the end of the lesson students should be able to; i explain the meaning of pronoun ii list the types of pronoun iii relative pronoun and meaning) iv define demonstrative pronoun and types INSTRUCTIONAL RESOURCES: teacher presents a cardboard paper containing a list of the identified pronouns to be treated STEP I : Identification of prior knowledge MODE : Individual TEACHER’S ACTIVITIES : Teacher began the day’s topic by recalling students’ memory of previous topic taught on pronoun types. 1. List types of pronouns 2. Write their meanings 3. Explain personal and reciprocal pronoun STUDENTS’ ACTIVITIES : Students respond to the questions asked by the teacher. STEP II : Exploration MODE : Entire class TEACHER’S ACTIVITIES: Teacher discusses the day’s topic in the order below • Define pronoun • List the types of pronoun • Explain relative pronoun with examples • Demonstrative pronoun and types • Asking of questions by students for clarification and • Copying of note on the board STUDENTS’ ACTIVITIES : Students listen to the teacher as she explai ns. STEP III : Discussion Mode : Entire class TEACHER : Teacher discusses the day’s topic with the brief note below Structure Pronoun A pronoun is a word that can be used instead of a noun. Pronouns refer to nouns that has been previously mentioned or does not need to be named specifically. Eg- he, she, you, i, we, they, that, these, this, it, them, us, something, anybody, whoever, nobody, who, whoever, etc. Types of Pronouns 1. The relative pronoun 2. The demonstrative pronoun 3. The indefinite pronoun 4. Personal pronouns 5. Reflexive pronouns 6. Demonstrative pronoun 7. Interrogative pronouns 8. Reciprocal pronouns etc a) The relative pronoun: they are pronouns that refer to nouns which have been previously mentioned. Eg- who, which, that, whose, whom, where, etc. It connects relative clauses to independent clauses. They usually appear after a noun to help clarify the sentence or give extra information. Example:- Look at the girl who has just been named the best student. The relative pronoun ‘who’ acts to refer back to the noun phrase ‘the girl ’. Example:- the cup which Bayo picked is flammable. In the example above, the relative pronoun ‘which’, helps in identifying the particular cup being talked about, ie not just any cup but the one that is flammable, thus giving more information to the noun ph rase, ‘the cup ’. Example:- This is the woman whose key you found. The relative pronoun, ‘whose’ in the example above, refers back to the noun phrase, ‘the woman’. b) Demonstrative pronoun: the demonstrative pronoun is used to point at something specific within a sentence. There are only four demonstrative pronouns, they are; Singular demonstrative pronouns plural demonstrative pronouns this, these, that, and those. c) Examples: ‘ this’ is singular demonstrative pronouns. ‘th ese ’ plural demonstrative pronouns. 1. I prefer this

2. These are beautiful 3. Those belong to Mary 4. I can ’t beli eve she said that. Grammatical Functions of Pronouns: Pronouns can perform the following functions 1. Pronoun as subject of verb in a sentence: a pronoun is said to be the subject of the verb when it is used in place of a noun and comes before the main verb in a sentence Eg- I gave the man his money. We know where we came from. He is a lawyer You have to go now They recognised him. 2. Pronouns as object of the verb: it is used as the object of the verb when it comes after the verb and receives the action of the verb in a sentence. Eg-the dog bit me The woman insulted them James trained her. 3. Pronouns as complement of the verb: in this instance, the pronoun comes after a linking verb but receives no action from the verb. Eg- it was I who called the police. 4. Pronoun as object of preposition: a pronoun functions as object of preposition when it comes after the preposition. Eg- I gave the book to her. I have lost my trust in him. Can you leave it with me? STUDENTS’ ACTIVITIES: Students copy the note on the board. STEP IV : Application MODE : Individual TEACHER’S ACTIVITIES : Teacher asks students to elaborate more on demonstrative pronouns with examples STUDENTS’ ACTIVITIES : Students respond to the questions asked by the teacher STEP V : Evaluation MODE : Individual TEACHER’S ACTIVITIES : Teacher evaluates students’ understanding of the day’s topic with the following questions. 1. Meaning of pronoun 2. Types of pronouns 3. Examples of relative pronouns 4. Grammatical functions of pronouns STUDENTS’ ACTIVITIES : Students respond to the questions asked by the teacher ASSIGNMENT : read on Essay (expository essay) REFERENCE : Essential English Language for Senior Secondary by Latilo T.A and Oluuku A.T. List types of pronouns 2. Write their meanings 3. Explain personal and reciprocal pronoun STUDENTS’ ACTIVITIES : Students respond to the questions asked by the teacher. STEP II : Exploration MODE : Entire class TEACHER’S ACTIVITIES: Teacher discusses the day’s topic in the order below • Define pronoun • List the types of pronoun • Explain relative pronoun with examples • Demonstrative pronoun and types • Asking of questions by students for clarification and • Copying of note on the board STUDENTS’ ACTIVITIES : Students listen to the teacher as she explai ns. STEP III : Discussion Mode : Entire class TEACHER : Teacher discusses the day’s topic with the brief note below Structure Pronoun A pronoun is a word that can be used instead of a noun. Pronouns refer to nouns that has been previously mentioned or does not need to be named specifically. Eg- he, she, you, i, we, they, that, these, this, it, them, us, something, anybody, whoever, nobody, who, whoever, etc. Types of Pronouns 1. The relative pronoun 2. The demonstrative pronoun 3. The indefinite pronoun 4. Personal pronouns 5. Reflexive pronouns 6. Demonstrative pronoun 7. Interrogative pronouns 8. Reciprocal pronouns etc a) The relative pronoun: they are pronouns that refer to nouns which have been previously mentioned. Eg- who, which, that, whose, whom, where, etc. It connects relative clauses to independent clauses. They usually appear after a noun to help clarify the sentence or give extra information. Example:- Look at the girl who has just been named the best student. The relative pronoun ‘who’ acts to refer back to the noun phrase ‘the girl ’. Example:- the cup which Bayo picked is flammable. In the example above, the relative pronoun ‘which’, helps in identifying the particular cup being talked about, ie not just any cup but the one that is flammable, thus giving more information to the noun ph rase, ‘the cup ’. Example:- This is the woman whose key you found. The relative pronoun, ‘whose’ in the example above, refers back to the noun phrase, ‘the woman’. b) Demonstrative pronoun: the demonstrative pronoun is used to point at something specific within a sentence. There are only four demonstrative pronouns, they are; Singular demonstrative pronouns plural demonstrative pronouns this, these, that, and those. c) Examples: ‘ this’ is singular demonstrative pronouns. ‘th ese ’ plural demonstrative pronouns. 1. I prefer this

2. These are beautiful 3. Those belong to Mary 4. I can ’t beli eve she said that. Grammatical Functions of Pronouns: Pronouns can perform the following functions 1. Pronoun as subject of verb in a sentence: a pronoun is said to be the subject of the verb when it is used in place of a noun and comes before the main verb in a sentence Eg- I gave the man his money. We know where we came from. He is a lawyer You have to go now They recognised him. 2. Pronouns as object of the verb: it is used as the object of the verb when it comes after the verb and receives the action of the verb in a sentence. Eg-the dog bit me The woman insulted them James trained her. 3. Pronouns as complement of the verb: in this instance, the pronoun comes after a linking verb but receives no action from the verb. Eg- it was I who called the police. 4. Pronoun as object of preposition: a pronoun functions as object of preposition when it comes after the preposition. Eg- I gave the book to her. I have lost my trust in him. Can you leave it with me? STUDENTS’ ACTIVITIES: Students copy the note on the board. rawText: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH GOVERNMENT Government is a body that makes and enforces laws to control a country, land area, people or organization, e.g. Nigeria. There are different types of government which include: Democratic, Aristocratic, Dictatorship, Monarchy. 1. Administration– a body that is entrusted with the execution of laws and the superintendence of public affair 2. Official Gazette – an official journal published periodically by the government containing legal and state notices 3. Memorandum – a short note sending as a reminder 4. Minutes – an official notes taken during a meeting 5. Constitution – The formal or informal system of primary principles and laws that regulates a government or other institutions 6. Legislature– a governmental body with the power to make, amend and annul laws 7. Constituency – A district represented by one or more elected individual. It also means the voters within a district 8. Bureaucracy – Structure and regulations put in place to control activities in government 9. Policy – A principle of behavior thought to be desirable, especially as formally expressed by a government 10. Election – a process of choosing a leader by popular vote

subject: English Language
rawText:
PLOSIVE CONSONANTS Consonant sounds are sounds produced with obstruction of air at certain points between the lungs and the mouth. While plosives are consonants made when the air flowing out of the lungs is stopped somewhere in the mouth before it is suddenly released. There are six plosives in the English sounds: /p, b, t, d, k, g/. For /p,b/: the stop is at the lip which are closed and then open to release the air, hence they are called bilabial plosive , /t,d/ are called alveolar plosive because the air stopped at the alveolar ridge and for /k,g/, the back of the tongue rests on the soft palate forming a closure at the back of the mouth, hence they are called velar plosive. /p/ - This sound has the following spelling forms; pie, pepper, pea, pipe, pot, stop, pen, pin, purple, people, pet, pain, tap, peace, please, peak, priest, lip, deep, past. /ph/ as in shepherd However, /p/ is silent, that is, not pronounced in words like, psalm, psychology, corps, coup, pneumonia, receipt, cupboard, psyche, ptomaine, psychedelic etc. it is pronounced as /f/ in ‘ph’ spelling as phase, pharmacy, physics, nephew, etc. /b/ which is counterpart of /p/ has the following spelling forms B – as in bomb, boy, belt, bell, build, ban, belief, book, buy, board, but, baby, bottle, break, bet, bring, table, bush, bad, bat, ball, bubble, bliss, etc /b/ is silent that is, not pronounced in words like bomb, tomb, womb, plumber, subtle, subtlety, comb, debt, dumb, doubt, lamb, climb, limb, thumb, etc /t/ has a spelling forms like cut, top, cat, title, tame, bottle, kettle, little, battle, bat, test, rat, net, ten, take, fat, pot, tent, tin, list, bite, sit, set, vote, party, cast, stick, trip, etc /t/ is silent that is, not pronounced in words like listen, Christmas, castle, hasten, often, whistle, apostle, mortgage, nestle, pestle, depot, fasten, rapport, chalet, ballet, bouquet, sachet, etc /d/ which is counterpart of /t/ has the following spelling forms like dog, food, word, find, build, bad, reduce, depart, dare, day, drink, drum, do, dove, dine, drive, dead, mad, made, grandfather, paddle, etc /d/ is silent that is, not pronounced in words like Wednesday, handsome, handkerchief, grandchild, grandson, sandwich, etc. (most times, but not always, letter ‘d’ is silent when it occurs between letter ‘n’ and another consonant /k/ has the following spelling forms:

‘k’ - as in kettle, kite, cake, king, key kiss etc ‘c’ – cake, cat, come, car, concert, cup, climb, clean etc ‘ch’ – school, scheme, Christian, chemist ‘q’ - as in quick, queen, queue, request ‘x’ –taxi, text, mix, fix, ‘ck’ – sick, pick, cock, pack, kick, lick, suck /k/ is silent that is, not pronounced when it is followed by ‘n’ words for example, it is not pronounced in words like know, knight, knock, knead, kneel, knife, knot, knowledge /g/ which is counterpart of /k/ has the following spelling forms girl, game, give, God, get, giggle, goat, ugly, gear, get, gas, gasp, gain, gang, wriggle, garage, ignore, e.t.c ‘gh’ – ghost, ghastly, aghast /g/ is silent that is, not pronounced when it comes before ‘n’ at the beginning or at the end of a word for example, gnash, reign, sign, feign, resign, assign, sign, malign etc. it is not pronounced in poignant. It is also silent when it comes before letter ‘m’ at the end of a word as in phlegm, paradigm. Other instances where /g/ is silent include words like sight, ought, fight etc. CLASS-WORK Underline the letters that bear the plosive consonant sounds in the given words. 1. Category /k/ 2. Lead /d/ 3. Troops /p/ 4. Accent /k/ 5. Unique /k/ 6. Ghost /g/ 7. Bomb /b/ 8. Talk /t/ ASSIGNMENT Draw a page-sized standard phonemic chart

Theme: Speech Unit Topic Rhymes. Lesson Topic: Rhyming words. Rhyme occurs when two or more words end on the same Vowel Sound, the same Vowel plus Consonant sequence sound or in the same sequence of Consonant cluster. Rhyme does not occur when two word end in the same single final Consonant eg wood and did. This shows that sound determines rhyme, not spelling. This is because two word must have the same sound in the last syllable before they can be said to rhyme. The harmonization of sound rhymes Can either be in part of the words Involved or in the whole words. There are two types of rhyme. a. Total rhyme b. partial rhyme. a. In total Rhyme the similarity of the Sound of the words occur at both the Initial and final Positions .Eg- Sweet - Suite waist - waste hot - hut Root-route knot- nut Meat - meet born - burn Wood - Would b. In partial rhyme, the thyme is at the end of the word. Eg: rice - dice while-smile Purse- curse. keep-heap part - heart. fond - pond pure. - sure. some - come comb - tomb. Fright - tight

Theme: Structure Unit Topic: Adjuncts. Lesson Topre: Types of adjuncts Adjuncts are forms of adverbs which answer the questions how, where when, wing under what Condition, to what degree, how often, for how long.. etc. Adjunct is a word or group of words added to a sentence to modify the meaning of the verb, adjective other adverbs and Sometimes modify a whole sentence. Adjuncts in order words are adverbs of time, place, direction reason/cause, result, purpose, duration, frequency comparison, Condition and Concession. Some adjuncts appear as single words while other paper as adverbial phrases and clauses. Types of Adjuncts 1. Adjunct of time: It tells us when an action took place and it answer the question when? a. He was admitted into the college Last year. 2 Adjunct place; It tells us where an action took place. It answer the question where? a. the food is on the table b. I was in the office when my wife return. 3. Adjunct of degree /manner: It show how an action is done. Example. quickly, bravely, happily, hand, fast, well etc. a. He came back home as quickly as possible. b. He caught the Boll as if he were a good keeper. 4. Adjunct of Reason/ Purpose: It shows why an action is taking place. Examples. Since, because,hence etc. 1. the woman went to church since it was agree on 2. The minister was Sacked because of bribery. 5. Adjunct of frequency: describes how often an action happens. Example always, usually, normally, often Sometimes, rarely and never.

a. I have never insulted him. b. she comes here often 6. Adjunct of Condition: establish the condition in which an action occars or state holds. a. I would go to lagos, If I had the money. b. you will be jailed unless the president says otherwise. 7. Adjuncts of concession (in spite of) It offers a statement which Contrasts with the mam Idea. it offen starts with one of the following Subordinating Conjunctions: "though, although, even though, while, whereas or even if a. A Loud voice cannot compete with a clear vorce, even if it's a whisper b. She Laughed where as I told him not to. A noun clause can be replaced with a pronoun in the sentence In most cases, If answers the questions "what" The noun clause is usually introduced by words that, what wow, where, who which etc. Functions of Noun clause 1. Subject to a verb, 2 Object of a verb 3 Subject Complement 4 Object complement 5 Object to a preposition 1 Subject to a verb: A noun clause functions. as the subject to a verb's if it starts a sentence and comes before a verb in the sentence. Nobody knows where the old man was buried. It function as object of the verb "knows" b You should eat what you are given. Object of the verb "eat") C. He received what I sent him. Object of the verb received 3. As subject Complement: A noun clause function as the complement of subject when it refers to the same person or thing as the subject. eg. a. music is what we require. This pencil could be claimed by whoever wins It function as object to a proposition "by" b. Her success depends on who teaches her.

title: HOW TO IDENTIFY TOPIC SENTENCES IN PARAGRAPHS
subject: English Language
rawText:
Introduction The teacher writes a short paragraph on the board and asks students what the paragraph is mainly about. This leads into the idea of the topic sentence. Definition A topic sentence is the sentence in a paragraph that states the main idea or central thought of that paragraph. Positions of a Topic Sentence 1. Beginning – Most common position. 2. Middle – Sometimes appears after one or two sentences. 3. End – Acts as a summary of the paragraph. 4. Implied – Not directly stated but understood from the paragraph. Steps to Identify a Topic Sentence 1. Read the entire paragraph carefully. 2. Ask: “What is this paragraph mainly about?” 3. Look for a sentence that expresses this main idea. 4. Check if other sentences support or explain that sentence. 5. Ensure it is not just a detail or example.

Examples Example 1: Reading every day improves a student’s language skills. It increases vocabulary, improves spelling, and helps with comprehension. ➡ Topic sentence: Reading every day improves a student’s language skills. Example 2: Many students struggle in school. Some fail due to lack of concentration, while others fail because they do not complete their assignments. ➡ Topic sentence: Many students struggle in school. Example 3 (Topic sentence at the end): There are many reasons why students succeed in school, such as hard work, discipline, and good study habits. All these show that success depends on commitment. ➡ Topic sentence: All these show that success depends on commitment. Common Mistakes  Choosing a sentence that is only an example.  Selecting a sentence that is too narrow or too broad.  Ignoring the paragraph’s main idea. Evaluation 1. Define a topic sentence. 2. State two positions where a topic sentence can appear. 3. Identify the topic sentence in this paragraph: Sports help students stay healthy. They improve strength, coordination, and mental alertness.

Assignment Write one paragraph and underline the topic sentence.

title: ORAL ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText:
Introduction The teacher introduces the lesson by asking students to express their opinions on a simple issue (e.g., “Should students wear school uniforms?” ). This leads into the concept of arguing orally in a structured way. Definition An oral argumentative essay is a spoken composition in which a speaker presents and supports a point of view on an issue, aiming to convince listeners using facts, reasons, and examples. Features of an Oral Argumentative Essay 1. Clear Standpoint – The speaker must state their position clearly. 2. Logical Arguments – Points must be reasonable and well-arranged. 3. Supporting Evidence – Facts, examples, or experiences must support claims. 4. Persuasive Language – Words are chosen to influence the audience. 5. Proper Introduction and Conclusion – The speech must begin and end effectively. 6. Fluency and Confidence – The speaker should speak clearly and confidently. Structure 1. Introduction – Introduce the topic and state your position. 2. Body – Present arguments with reasons and examples. 3. Conclusion – Summarize points and restate your position. Oral Argumentative Essay Topic Topic: “School uniforms should be compulsory.”

Sample Introduction: I strongly believe that school uniforms should be compulsory because they promote discipline, unity, and reduce distraction among students Body: Firstly, uniforms encourage discipline because students appear neat and responsible. Secondly, they promote unity since all students look alike regardless of background. Finally, uniforms reduce competition in dressing, allowing students to focus on learning. Conclusion: In conclusion, school uniforms should be compulsory because they improve discipline, unity, and academic focus. Evaluation 1. Define an oral argumentative essay. 2. List three features of an oral argumentative essay. 3. Present a short oral argument on: “Mobile phones should be allowed in schools.” Assignment Prepare a one-minute oral argumentative essay on: “Examinations do more good than harm to students.

title: SUMMARY WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText:
SUMMARY WRITING DEFINITION: A Summary is a brief or concise account of an event that gives only the main point and not the details. This means that summary must be shorter than the original text. GUIDELINES FOR WRITING A SUMMARY 1. Read the passage carefully. 2. Extract the main ideas from the paragraphs through the identification of topic sentences if any. 3. Paraphrase the extracted ideas into required number of sentences. 4. Use synonyms. 5. Never exceed the required number of sentences. 6. Answer must be in sentences and not in phrases unless there is a preamble. NOTE: in summary there is no need for the following; a. Examples and illustrations. b. Analogy: comparison between two situations or processes that seem similar. c. Repetition. d. The use of flowery language (figures of speech or literary devices) e.g. “the man is dark as charcoal” is the man dark?”. e. The inclusion of details (unnecessary or irrelevant materials) f. The use of link words (connectives- moreover, however, furthermore, as a matter of fact, etc).

Note : summary should be clear, straight forward and without blemish. E.g. “In the time of myth during the period of magic, the destiny of a great kingdom rested on the shoulder of a young boy, his name is Merlin”

Theme: Structure Unit Topic: Figurative expression Lesson Topic: Figures of speech Figures of speech are special expression used to covey clear and brief impression than when expressed in ordinary works colorful, forceful, powerful and impressive. 1. SIMILE: It compares one thing with another using the words like or ‘as’ the two things in comparison are not similar but have similarity in the area being compared example : i. he is as dirty as a pig ii. she talks like a parrot 2. METAPHOR: a metaphor is a figure of speech that describes an object or action in a way that is not literally true but helps to explain an idea or idea or make comparison . Example: i. Emeka is a tiger ii. She has a hear of stone

3. HYPERBOLE: it is an exasperation of fact for the sake of emphasis or to lighten effect. Example i. All the water in the ocean cannot wash the dirt in his clothes. ii. I ate a mountain of food 4. PERSONIFICATION: It is giving of life and human attributes to inanimate objects or abstract things e.g i. The leaves are dancing to the tune of the wind ii. Evil walk in the shadow of night 5. OXYMORON: This is placing side by side two words that are contradict each other i. Etuk is a holy sinner ii. It is an open secret that Odo is an armed robber iii. Ada is an honest liar 6. ANTITHESIS: It is pairing of two opposite ideas in a sentence in order to heighten a sharp contract between the ideas example: i. Man proposes, God disposes ii. United we stand, divided we fall iii. To err is human, to forgive is divine 7. SYNECDOCHE: This is when a part used to represent a whole thing or a hole car be used to represent a part. Example: i. All fingers are not equal ii. The best brains are in my class iii. Two heads are better than one 8. METONYMY: It is the act of referring to something by the name of something else that is closely connected or associated with it example: i. The crown has summon elders for a meeting ii. All the speakers must get the chair iii. Judgments will start from the pulpit 9. EVPHENISM: It talks of harsh and unpleasant things in a mild or pleasant way. Eg i. Mr. Sunday kicked the bucket last night ii. The man of the underworld sent him to the world beyond iii. He fought with his better half 10. ONOMATOPOEA: It is the ability of words to echo their meaning e.g (i) The bell of the chock jingles (ii) The student hissed 11. Rhetorical question:- It is when a question that does not need an answer is asked just for the purpose of persuading and appealing to the mind of the audience (i) E.g My people, will I like myself for you (ii) Can a kettle call a pot black? (iii) Who will say that his mother soup is bitter.

12. APOSTROPHE: This is addressing an about person (abstract now) as if it were present, having life and listening to the speaker. Example:- a. Oh! Death where is thy sting? b. O! WAEC, why are you treating me badly. c. Hear me, O earth, hear me, O hills 13. PARADOX:- it is a self contrary statement which seems to appear meaningless and unreasonable in the first thought but if closely examined, it contains an element of truth e.g i. The best way to learn a subject is to teach it. ii. Cowards dies many times before their death iii. For whosever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel shall save it. Assignment Make sentence to show the following figure of speech in each of the sentences (i) Simile (ii) metaphor (iii) personification (iv) hyperbole (v) Oxymoron Theme: Comprehension Unit Topic: Reading for Structural Pattern Lesion Topic: Reading for Specific Structural Pattern Page 143 unit 7 - “ The Civil Service ” Structural pattern is the overall form organization of something. In this case we look at the structure of sentence in a passage and identify those that are simple sentences or compound sentences e.t.c. A sentence structure is also the arrangement of words, phrases and clauses in a sentence. And the grammatical meaning of a sentence is dependent of the structural organization. There are four basic types of sentence structures. They are the simple sentence, compound sentence, complex sentence and the compound – complex sentence. CLASS ACTIVITY Find and all the sentence structures used in each paragraph of the passage read and answer all the comprehension questions. Theme: Continuous writing Unit Topic: Speeches Lesson Topic: Writing speeches (An address given on a prize given day) A speech is a written material meant to be read to a group of listeners. Speeches are meant to entertain, educate and inform people.

It is also meant to motivate people to action. Features of a Speech 1. The title: there should be a title for the speech you are to deliver. The title should indicate the mark of identification such as the - The purpose - Name and the title of speaker - Occasion - Place - Date and time An Address give on a prize giving day, by Joy Okoli the Head girl of government secondary school, Kubwa, the school Assembly Hall this day with September, 2017. 2. The introduction: this must be interesting and captivating so as to elicit the interest of the listeners. It must start within salutation. For Example; Good morning the chairman, the principal, the school management, the P.T.A, ladies and gentlemen. I feel highly honored to stand here today to deliver my speech on ............... 3. The body: this is the stage that contains the actual message. Start by giving. Your main points and then support each point with relevant details, comparisons and contrasts e.t.c explain who, where, why, how. The ideas must be stated in good clear sentences 4. The conclusion: here you summarize your main points. It is important to end in a memorable way by: - Making a forceful and shocking statement - urging your audience to follow a certain line of action or thought e.t.c - Ending in an interesting and captivating manner. Guidelines Required for speech written 1. A speech is meant to be delivered to an audience. Hence the use of present tense is required. 2. A speech should be in four sentences viz, heading introduction, body and conclusion 3. Slangs and humor should be avoided since the speech is meant to be delivered to an audience superior to the writer. The use of humor is appropriate only in an informal situation like party. 4. No use of name(s) at the end of the speech since it would have been introduction at the heading. Assignment Prepare a speech to be delivered on the prize and award giving day of the final year students of the school.

Rhetorical question:- It is when a question that does not need an answer is asked just for the purpose of persuading and appealing to the mind of the audience (i) E.g My people, will I like myself for you (ii) Can a kettle call a pot black? (iii) Who will say that his mother soup is bitter.

12. APOSTROPHE: This is addressing an about person (abstract now) as if it were present, having life and listening to the speaker. Example:- a. Oh! Death where is thy sting? b. O! WAEC, why are you treating me badly. c. Hear me, O earth, hear me, O hills 13. PARADOX:- it is a self contrary statement which seems to appear meaningless and unreasonable in the first thought but if closely examined, it contains an element of truth e.g i. The best way to learn a subject is to teach it. ii. Cowards dies many times before their death iii. For whosever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel shall save it. Assignment Make sentence to show the following figure of speech in each of the sentences (i) Simile (ii) metaphor (iii) personification (iv) hyperbole (v) Oxymoron Theme: Comprehension Unit Topic: Reading for Structural Pattern Lesion Topic: Reading for Specific Structural Pattern Page 143 unit 7 - “ The Civil Service ” Structural pattern is the overall form organization of something. In this case we look at the structure of sentence in a passage and identify those that are simple sentences or compound sentences e.t.c. A sentence structure is also the arrangement of words, phrases and clauses in a sentence. And the grammatical meaning of a sentence is dependent of the structural organization. There are four basic types of sentence structures. They are the simple sentence, compound sentence, complex sentence and the compound – complex sentence. CLASS ACTIVITY Find and all the sentence structures used in each paragraph of the passage read and answer all the comprehension questions. Theme: Continuous writing Unit Topic: Speeches Lesson Topic: Writing speeches (An address given on a prize given day) A speech is a written material meant to be read to a group of listeners. Speeches are meant to entertain, educate and inform people.

It is also meant to motivate people to action. Features of a Speech 1. The title: there should be a title for the speech you are to deliver. The title should indicate the mark of identification such as the - The purpose - Name and the title of speaker - Occasion - Place - Date and time An Address give on a prize giving day, by Joy Okoli the Head girl of government secondary school, Kubwa, the school Assembly Hall this day with September, 2017. 2. The introduction: this must be interesting and captivating so as to elicit the interest of the listeners. It must start within salutation. For Example; Good morning the chairman, the principal, the school management, the P.T.A, ladies and gentlemen. I feel highly honored to stand here today to deliver my speech on ............... 3. The body: this is the stage that contains the actual message. Start by giving. Your main points and then support each point with relevant details, comparisons and contrasts e.t.c explain who, where, why, how. The ideas must be stated in good clear sentences 4. The conclusion: here you summarize your main points. It is important to end in a memorable way by: - Making a forceful and shocking statement - urging your audience to follow a certain line of action or thought e.t.c - Ending in an interesting and captivating manner. Guidelines Required for speech written 1. A speech is meant to be delivered to an audience. Hence the use of present tense is required. 2. A speech should be in four sentences viz, heading introduction, body and conclusion 3. Slangs and humor should be avoided since the speech is meant to be delivered to an audience superior to the writer. The use of humor is appropriate only in an informal situation like party. 4. No use of name(s) at the end of the speech since it would have been introduction at the heading. Assignment Prepare a speech to be delivered on the prize and award giving day of the final year students of the school.

title: POETRY
subject: English Language
rawText:
Definition of Poetry Poetry is a form of literature in which ideas, feelings, and experiences are expressed in a creative and imaginative way, using rhythm, lines, stanzas, imagery, and sometimes rhyme . It often appeals to the emotions and imagination of the reader. Types of Poetry 1. Lyric Poetry o Expresses personal feelings or emotions. o Usually short and musical. o Examples: Ode, Sonnet, Elegy. 2. Narrative Poetry o Tells a story in verse form. o Has characters and a plot. o Examples: Epic, Ballad. 3. Dramatic Poetry o Written in the form of a speech or dialogue meant to be acted on stage. o Examples: Dramatic monologue, plays written in verse. 4. Epic Poetry o A long narrative poem that tells the story of heroic deeds or historical events. o Examples: Odyssey , Paradise Lost . 5. Ballad o A song-like poem that tells a story. o Often simple in language and structure. 6. Sonnet o A poem of 14 lines with a fixed rhyme scheme. o Commonly about love or serious themes. 7. Ode o A formal poem that praises a person, object, or idea. 8. Elegy

o A poem written to express sorrow, especially for someone who has died. 9. Free Verse o Poetry without regular rhyme or rhythm. Assignment. Wrute a poem of fourteen lines.

title: ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText:
Argumentative Essay 📘 An argumentative essay is a type of essay where you present your opinion about a topic and support it with strong reasons and evidence. In this essay, you: Choose a position (for or against) Give reasons to support your opinion Provide examples or facts Sometimes explain the opposite view and show why your view is better Structure of an Argumentative Essay 📝 1. Introduction Introduce the topic Give background information State your thesis statement (your main opinion) 2. Body Paragraphs Each paragraph should contain: A clear point (reason) Explanation Example or evidence 3. Counter-Argument (Optional but Important) Mention the opposite opinion Explain why you disagree with it 4. Conclusion Restate your opinion Summarize your main points End strongly ✏ Example of an Argumentative Essay

Topic: Should Students Use Mobile Phones in School? Mobile phones have become very important in our daily lives. However, many schools do not allow students to use them. I believe that students should be allowed to use mobile phones in school for learning purposes. Firstly, mobile phones help students to research information quickly. With internet access, students can look for meanings of words, solve mathematics problems, and learn new things. This makes learning easier and faster. Secondly, mobile phones help in communication. In case of emergency, students can contact their parents immediately. This makes both students and parents feel safe. Some people argue that mobile phones distract students during lessons. This may be true if students misuse them. However, teachers can make rules to control how phones are used in school. In conclusion, mobile phones should be allowed in schools because they help learning and improve communication. Proper rules can prevent distraction. title: NOUN CLAUSE

rawText: SS1 English Language Handout Topic: Noun Clauses What is a Noun Clause? 📘 A noun clause is a group of words that acts as a noun in a sentence. It can be the subject, object, or complement in a sentence. Examples and Their Functions 📍 Sentence Function of the Noun Clause What you said is true. Subject I believe that she will come. Object The fact is that he passed. Complement Common Noun Clause Starters: 🧠 - that - what / whatever - who / whoever / whom - when, where, why, how - whether / if How to Identify a Noun Clause: 🛠 ✔ It begins with special words like "that," "what," or "who" ✔ It can be replaced with "something" or "someone" ✔ It answers what?, who?, or whom? ✏ Practice Exercises A. Underline the noun clause in each sentence and state its function: 1. What you did was wrong. 2. She knows that you lied. 3. That he is honest is clear to all. 4. The teacher asked who was absent. 5. title: NOUN CLAUSE
subject: English Language
rawText: Noun Clause A noun clause is a dependent clause that functions like a noun in a sentence. It can act as: - The subject of a verb - The object of a verb or preposition - The complement of a verb It usually starts with words like _that, what, who, whom, whose, which, when, where, how, why, whether, if_. Examples: 1. What he said is true. → _Noun clause as subject_ 2. I believe that she will win. → _Noun clause as object_ 3. The truth is that he was late. → _Noun clause as complement_ Key point: You can usually replace a noun clause with the pronoun _it_ or _something_ and the sentence still makes sense.

title: ADVERBIAL CLAUSES
subject: English Language
rawText:
Adverbial Clauses and their grammatical functions Adverbial clauses are dependent clauses that function like adverbs. They modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs, or the whole sentence by telling you _when, where, why, how, to what extent, or under what condition_ something happens. 1. How to spot them They start with subordinating conjunctions like: *when, while, before, after, since, until, because, since, as, if, unless, although, though, even though, so that, in order that, as if, as though* > *When the bell rang*, everyone stood up. > “When the bell rang” tells you _when_ everyone stood up. 2. Grammatical functions Adverbial clauses always function as *adverbials*. The exact function depends on the conjunction: Function Question it answers Example **Time** When? **After I eat**, I’ll call you. **Place** Where? Sit **where it’s comfortable**. **Reason/Cause** Why? I stayed home **because it was raining**. **Purpose** Why/For what purpose? She studied hard **so that she would pass**. **Condition** Under what condition? **If it rains**, we’ll cancel. **Concession/Contrast** Despite what? **Although he was tired**, he kept working. **Manner** How? She spoke **as if she knew everything**. **Result/Effect** What was the result? He was so tired **that he fell asleep**. **Comparison/Degree** To what extent? He’s taller **than I thought**. 3. Key features *a. Movable* Unlike adjectival clauses, adverbial clauses can usually move to the front or end of the sentence.

> *When it’s hot*, I drink cold water. > I drink cold water *when it’s hot*. *b. Always dependent* They can’t stand alone. If you remove the main clause, it becomes a sentence fragment: > _When the bell rang._ ✗ *c. Punctuation rule* If the adverbial clause comes first, use a comma. If it comes after, usually no comma. > *Because I was late*, I missed the start. > I missed the start *because I was late*. 4. Quick test Try replacing the clause with a single adverb. If it works, it’s an adverbial clause. > She left *when it got dark* → She left *then*. > He ran *as fast as he could* → He ran *quickly*.

title: CLAUSES AND TYPES OF CLAUSES
subject: English Language
rawText:
Topic: Clauses and types of clauses. A claus e is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb . It’s a building block of sentences. Unlike a phrase, a clause can express a complete thought. Types of Clauses 1. Independent/Main Clause - Can stand alone as a complete sentence. - Has a subject, verb, and complete meaning. - _Example_: She left early because it was raining. 2. Dependent/Subordinate Clause - Cannot stand alone. It depends on a main clause to make sense. - Starts with subordinating words like _because, although, when, if, that, who_. - _Example_: She left early because it was raining Types of dependent clauses: - Noun Clause Acts as a noun in the sentence. _Example_: What she said surprised everyone. Functions as subject, object, or complement. - Adjective/Relative Clause: Describes a noun or pronoun. Usually starts with _who, which, that, whose_. _Example_: The book that you borrowed is mine.

- Adverbial Clause: Acts like an adverb, telling _when, where, why, how, or under what condition_. _Example_: I’ll call you when I arrived Quick way to spot them: If you remove the clause and the sentence still makes sense → it’s independent. If it falls apart → it’s dependent. Want examples for a specific type or a quick test to practice?Top

title: EMPHATIC STRESS
subject: English Language
rawText: Emphatic Stress Emphatic stress is when you put extra force or loudness on a specific word in a sentence to show contrast, emotion, or to correct a misunderstanding. It changes the meaning based on _what_ you emphasize. 1. How it works You stress a word by saying it louder, longer, and with a higher pitch. > I *didn’t* take your book. → Someone else did > I didn’t take *your* book. → I took someone else’s book > I didn’t *take* your book. → I borrowed it, didn’t steal it 2. Main functions a. Contrast/Correction Highlight the difference between two things. > She likes _coffee_, not tea. b. Express emotion Show surprise, anger, excitement, disbelief. > That is *amazing*! > I *can’t* believe you did that. c. Avoid ambiguity Make your meaning clear when the sentence could be read multiple ways. > I said he _might_ go, not that he _will_ go. d. Emphasis on important info Draw attention to the key word for the listener. > The meeting is *tomorrow*, not today. 3. Common rule You don’t usually stress function words like _a, the, of, is_ unless you’re contrasting them: > I said *a* dog, not *the* dog.

Words Pertaining to Death.  Pathology: A doctor who examines dead bodies to find out the cause of death.  Corpse: The dead body of humans.  Carcass: The dead body of animals.  Cremation: Disposal of corpse through burning.  Embalm: Preservation of corpse from decaying.  Hearse /(hз:з): Vehicles for carrying corpse.  Ambulance: Vehicle with special gadgets for taking sick or injured people to the hospital. e. Other words  Anemia: lack of blood in the body.  Narcotic: Drugs that make one to relax and sleep.  Antiseptic: drugs that weakens or kills germ.  Dispenser: A person who dispenses drugs. iii) GRAMMAR- Pronouns: types, functions and position A pronoun is a word that is used instead of a noun in a sentences to avoid repetition. Types of pronoun  Personal pronoun  Indefinite pronoun  Possessive pronoun  Interrogative pronoun  Relative pronoun  Reflective pronoun

 Reciprocal pronoun  Emphatic pronoun. 1. Personal pronoun : they are called personal pronouns because they stand for three persons namely; a) The person speaking (The first person) b) The person spoken to or addressed (The second person) c) The person spoken about or being discussed (The third person). Examples: I, we, me, our, us (first person pronoun). You, Yours (second person pronoun). She, Her, He, It, him, They, Their (their person pronoun). I go to church every Sunday. You saw her in the market. 2. Possessive pronoun: They show possession or ownership. It includes mines, yours, her, his, ours and theirs. Examples: That book is mine. The school across the road is theirs. The food is yours. The difference between possessive pronouns and possessive adjective. I) possessive pronouns are pronouns indicating ownership but do not precede or come before a Noun or in a Noun phrase. For example, Mine, yours, hers, theirs, ours, it's. II) possessive adjective: it comes before a Noun or pronoun to show who and what owns it. It shows who or what something is to or is. It is an adjective that is used to show ownership. It comes before a Noun in the sentence and let use to know to whom, including my, your, his, her, it's, our, their. Each one corresponds to a subject pronoun. They are used alone. 3) Demonstrative pronoun: These are used to point out specific things, persons or places referred to. They include: this, that, those, these . Examples: This biro is mine, that is yours These are my students, those are yours. These are my friends.

4) Relative pronoun: This relates to other nouns or pronouns and it also function as a conjunction. It introduces a clause. It includes: who, whom, that, which, whose. Examples: The man who came here last week is my friend. The students who were publicly flogged have been expelled. I read the book that was given to me. Relative pronouns are pronouns that connect a descriptive expression (adjectival or relative clause) to the noun that is being described by the expression. They are always close to the nouns or pronouns they are describing. Relative pronoun is sub-divided into two: a) Those that are used to refer to human beings – who, whom, whose,that, whomever. They are the relative pronouns for people b) Those that are used to refer to animals/ inanimate objects or ideas – that, which. Other division of relative pronouns are I) ownership - whose. It indicates possession, the owner of something. II) places - where. POSITION OF RELATIVE PRONOUNS Relative pronouns can appear at the initial, medial. Penultimate and final positions of a sentence. FUNCTIONS OF A RELATIVE PRONOUNS Relative pronouns perform the following functions in a sentence; 1. It shows possession or ownership e.g The man whose car was stolen is here 2. It indicates the location being referred to, e.g Where I saw her. 3. Relative pronouns is used for specifications. It singles out an item from the rest, e.g That book( not others but that particular one is indicated). 4. Relative pronouns differentiate between animate objects and inanimate objects in a sentence.

5) Indefinite pronoun: this is not definite or specific but stands generally for a noun. It includes anyone, anybody, anything, everyone, somebody, someone, none, some, etc. It can also be referred to objects or people that are not specified they include all, any, some. Examples: Nobody wants him back as teacher. Each candidate has Master’s Degree. Many want to eat her food . 6) Reciprocal pronoun: This represents persons or things as being interactive. It is used when the action expressed by the verb is shared by those concerned. It includes: each other and one another. Examples: The students taught one another in the examination. John and Esther like each other. IV) Continuous Writing: Expository Essay: An expository essay is an explanatory essay where the writing aims to inform, instruct, explain, criticize, or analyze some concepts or situation to the reader. It allows the writer to how his capability for logical thoughts and reasoning. It is a factual essay and most times, makes judgment. Topics Related to Expository Essay 1. How my favorite food is prepared. 2. Dangers of drug abuse. 3. The dangers of premarital sex. 4. The future of Nigerian Youth. 5. Causes of indiscipline in Nigeria Secondary Schools. 6. The consequences of indecent dressing 7. Why prostitution is a crime 8. Managing population explosion in Nigeria 9. My English teacher: How I saw him/her 10. Controlling HIV/AIDS in Nigeria . Guidelines for writing an expository essay: 1. Think of the most logical way of presenting in order to avoid missing links that could hinder full understanding. 2. Follow a sequential order: organize your thoughts carefully 3. Concentrate on one main point at a time 4. Mention the particular moments when thing should be done 5. Develop your paragraphs. Example - Topic for class discussion: “Dangers of Premarital Sex”

a. Introduction: Definition of Premarital Sex : Who should engage in sex b. Body: Dangers: i. Why youths should avoid sex. ii. Unwanted pregnancy. iii. Sexually transmitted diseases. iv. School dropout. v. Stigmatization. vi. VVF – Vesico-vaginal fistula. c. Conclusion: Your advice to the youths. Sanctions to Youths who engage in premarital sex.

title: REGISTER OF HUMAN INTERNAL BODY SYSTEM
subject: English Language
rawText:
SCHEME BASED NOTE FOR FIRST TERM SS2 TOPICS WEEK 1 - SPEECH: Listening comprehension- I) listening to answer questions on a given passage. Listening comprehension is defined as one’s ability to comprehend spoken language. it requires attention, comprehension of the passage being read and recollection of what has being said. To listen, we need to make a conscious effort not to just hear what people said but to take it in, digest it and understand. Listening enhances one’s ability to understand better and evaluate what one hears. The passage is taken from ’animal farm ’written by George orwell. It is a satire – a piece of writing that criticizes either a person or an institution by using humour to show their faults or weaknesses. It is a satire on Nigerian readers. The characters are animals that are given names used by humans (page 254). Answer to the passage on animal farm. ii) Vocabulary development: words associated with the human internal body system and functions: the human body system consist of many system that works together to function properly. This System consist of organs. The organs are made up of tissues which are a collection of cells ˃ body- system - organ - tissue –cells. The Systems includes: a) Digestive system. b) Respiratory system. c) Excretory system. d) Endocrine system. e) Reproductive system. f) Circulatory system. g) Nervous system. h) Skeletal system a) The digestive system is responsible for the breaking down of food. It Consist of mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestine and anus. b) The respiratory system is responsible for the intake and absorption of oxygen from the surrounding environment, and also the transport of oxygen to the individual cells in the body.

c) The excretory system is responsible for the removal of waste substances from the body of a living organism. It consists of kidney, lungs, liver, Skin. d) The skeletal system is responsible for providing the foundational framework, support, shape and protection of the whole body system and internal organs. It consists of (1) Axial skeleton –the skull, sternum, vertebral column and rib cage. (2) Appendicle skeleton – the forelimbs and the hind limbs. e) The reproductive system is responsible for the production of young offspring through the fusion of gametes sexually or other means such as asexual fragmentation, spore formation, binary fusion, vegetative propagation. f) The circulatory system is responsible for the rapid mass and other materials such as digested food, water and other nutrients. This system also transports excretory products such as carbon dioxide, and urea and lastly water, oxygen and hormones. h) The nervous system together with the endocrine system is responsible for co-ordinating all the other activities of the body like locomotion, digestion, respiration and excretion. The organs-  Heart: The heart supplies oxygenated blood to the cells in the body.  Kidney: It excretes urea and urine from blood.  Lungs: Used for gaseous exchange.  Liver: To neutralize toxic substances in the body.  Brain: The organ that control, receives and send signals to the other organs through the nervous system and through secreted hormones.  Bladder: Hold urine until it goes out of the body.  Intestine: The long tube through which food passes after it leaves the stomach. iii) STRUCTURE: Noun phrases- position and functions. A phrase is a group of related words that forms part of a large sentence but has no finite verb and therefore cannot stand alone and makes complete sense. E. g – In the Market. -- The man at the door. -- Within the compound. A noun phrase is a group of words that has a noun as its headword. It performs the work of a noun in sentences. E. g - my English teacher is hard working. - Igbo people are in the east.

FUNCTIONS OF A NOUN PHRASE 1) As subject of a verb: when a noun phrase occupies the initial position in a sentence, it functions as the subject. In this case, the verb comes after the noun. E. g – A huge tree fell across the street. - The short boy in choir is my brother. 2) As object of a verb: when a noun phrase comes after a verb in a sentences, it functions as the object of that verb. E. g - she destroyed the car. -- He bought a long note. 3) As subject compliment: It links the subject to something that describes the subject. E. g – John may become our hero. -- Our principal may become a commissioner. 4) As object complement: it links the object to something that describes it. E. g - The house girl called her mistress a savior. - The class made her the class prefect. CHARACTERISTICS OF A NOUN PHRASE 1. The head in a noun phrase can be pre-modified by articles, possessives, demonstratives or/and adjectives or a combination of these. E. g  A student”, the people”, (pre- modified by article.)  My father”, their farms”, (pre-modified by possessives.)  Beautiful house”, easy question”,(pre-modified by adjective.)  This book”, that bag”, (pre-modified by demonstrative.)  The boy ugly girl is quarrelsome (combination of all.) 2. The head in a noun phrase can be post modified by prepositional phrase or clause.  E. g – “the boy in the room”, “the house of the mother” (post modified by prepositional phrase.)  “a man who stammers”, ”the book I told you about” (post modified by clause.)

title: STRUCTURE
subject: English Language
rawText: FIGURES OF SPEECH They are those words that are used in non-literal sense to express one’s thought in writing. It is a word or phrase that deviates from straightforward literal language. Some Common Figures of Speech 1. Simile 2. Metaphor 3. Hyperbole 4. Personification 5. Onomatopoeia 6. Apostrophe 7. Alliteration 8. Euphemism 9. Oxymoron 10. Metonyms 11. Paradox 12. Synedoche 13. Assonance 14. Irony 15. Rhetorical question 16. Pun 1. Simile – this is a comparison of two things, which share the same qualities with the use of as or like. Eg. (a). Mary looks like her mother (b). She is as huge as a giant 2. Metaphor - – This is the direct comparison of two things that share the same qualities without the use of as or like (a). Mary is an angel (b). the man was a lion in the battle 3. Hyperbole – This is used to exaggerate a fact to show how serious it is. Eg. (a). The whole world stood still to welcome the principal (b). the drowning boy almost finished the water in the pool 4. Personification – an inanimate thing is addressed as if it is living. Eg. (a). The earth is smiling (b). the moon is dancing 5. Onomatopoeia - this is the formation of words in initiation of the actual sound made. For example (a) I heard a loud sound ‘ booo------oooooo-mmm (b). The clock ticks like this ‘ tick-tock – tick- tock 6. Apostrophe – This refers to direct address or appeal to someone that is absent or to a non-human object. Eg. (a) Oh! Mother of Africa, thou art great (b). Dear dad, if you were alive, things would have been better 7. Alliteration – This refer to the repetition of consonant sounds in quick succession in a group of words sounds effect. Eg. (a). a plantain, planter, planted plantain in his plantain plantation (b). he gave me a long lingering look 8. Assonance - this is the repetition of same vowel sounds that are close together. E.g “Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers”. 9. Oxymoron-combination of words with opposite meanings to create new idea. E.g ‘old news’, ‘deafening silence’, ‘friendly fire’ 10. Rhetorical question- it is a question asked in order to make a statement that does not require an answer. E.g ‘Tell me Africa/ Are you that back that is bent?’
