title: PRONOUNS
subject: English Language
rawText: SUBJECT: English Language CLASS: VEI 2 TOPIC: Relative Pronouns Definition: Relative pronouns are words that connect a dependent clause to an independent clause, referring back to a noun or pronoun in the independent clause. Examples 1. Who: refers to people (e.g., "The student who won the award is happy."). 2. Which: refers to things (e.g., "The book which is on the table is mine."). 3. That: refers to people or things (e.g., "The person that is speaking is the CEO."). 4. Whom: refers to people (object of the verb) (e.g., "The person whom I met is nice."). 5. Whose: shows possession (e.g., "The student whose book is lost is worried."). Demonstrative Pronouns Demonstrative pronouns are words that point out specific nouns or things, indicating their proximity or distance. Examples 1. This: refers to something near the speaker (e.g., "This book is mine."). 2. That: refers to something farther away from the speaker (e.g., "That car is nice."). 3. These: refers to plural nouns near the speaker (e.g., "These shoes are comfortable."). 4. Those: refers to plural nouns farther away from the speaker (e.g., "Those flowers are beautiful."). Key Differences 1. Relative pronouns connect clauses and refer back to a noun, while demonstrative pronouns point out specific nouns. Eg. Grace is beautiful. She is beautiful. Pronoun= she 2. Relative pronouns introduce dependent clauses, while demonstrative pronouns stand alone as subjects or objects. How to use the pronouns/ functions: 1. Use relative pronouns to connect ideas and provide more information about a noun. 2. Use demonstrative pronouns to point out specific things or people, making your language more precise. By understanding and using relative and demonstrative pronouns correctly, you can improve your communication and express yourself more effectively.

Write your speech for against the motion Theme: Structure Unit topic: Suffixes Lesson Topic: Suffixes (-able, -age, -action, -en etc.) Suffixes are added at the end of a word to form another word, In actual fact, many of the words, either prefixes or suffixes, If you are able to add a suffix to a word, it becomes easier to identify the word classes ( parts of speech). Nouns, adjectives, adverb are easily identifiable in words bearing suffixes. Example; -able; Laugh – laughable Wash – washable Loud – loudable -age; Bond – bondage Waste – wastage Drain – drainage Mile – mileage Dose – dosage -ant; Assist – assistant Serve – servant Depend – dependant Aspire – aspirant -en; Loose – loosen Dead – deaden Tight – tighten Quick – quicken

-ful; Month – mouthful Sorrow – sorrowful care – careful Hope – hopeful Theme: Register Unit topic: Vocabulary Development Lesson topic: Words Associated with Law and Order - Order in the court, legal action e.t.c. Law is the whole system of rules that people in a particular country or area must obey. Order means a situation in which rules are obeyed and authority respected. The dictionary interpret the law of the nation which must be obeyed to maintain order in that nation. Words associated with law and order. 1.Accuse; To say that somebody has done wrong 2. Acquit: To give a legal decision 3. Adjournment; To postpone proceeding in a law court. 4. Adjudicate; To give official judgement or decision upon somebody (usually lawyer) 5. Advocate: A lawyer who speaks in favor of somebody in the court of law 6. Appeal: Taking the decision of a lower court to higher court. 7. Bail: To secure the release of somebody accused to higher court 8. Client; A person who gets help or advice from a lawyer. 9. Contempt of court; Breach or act of disloyalty or disrespect to a court. 10. Counsel: Advice, (also a lawyer). 11. Court; A person who commit crime. 12. Damage; Money paid by person or company for causing injury to another. 13. Defendant; A person against who a legal action is brought. 14. Equity; fairness, right, judgement 15. Legal action Assignment 1. List at least ten words associated with law and order. 2. Use those words in sentence.

Summary is a brief form of writing a long passage, after removing irrelevant information from the main points using one ’ s own words Useful tips in writing good summary i. Brief (ii). Relevance (iii). Clarity (iv). Identify the topic sentence (v). Originality (vi). Write answers in complete sentence Topic sentence is a sentence that expresses the main idea of the paragraph in which it occurs. Theme: Continuous writing Unit topic: Essay writing Lesson topic: Argumentative Essay (to prove a point) An argumentative essay is an essay in which the writer tries to persuade and convince the reader to accept and agree with his point of view. Topic in this form of essay demands that the writer should prove a point, express an opinion and support or oppose a given idea Example

1. Child training is the sole responsibility of a mother 2. Covid – 19 is a blessing in disguise 3. Modern technology has done harm than good 4. Female should be given leadership position in the society 5. Uniforms are important or why the are not. Guidelines for an argumentative essay 1. State the topic. 2. State your vocatives: This is the greeting to acknowledge the presence of the panel and the audience. For example; The moderator/chairman, panel of judges, accurate time keeper, co – debaters, fellow student/audience, 3. Introduction: Define a content and take a stand 4. Body: Make sure you are convinced about the side you are opposing or supporting. If you support the side you do not belief in, you will run out of points and ideas. 5. Conclusion: Do not draw a general conclusion from one example or a few points you need a number of points to reach a convincing conclusion. 6. Do not be illogical in your argument. 7. Be sure that your points can support the conclusion you want to reach. Example: Female leaders perform better in authority than their male counter parts; Points to support 1. Points use to oppose 1.Pregnancy and maternity leaves take women away from their role as leaders. 2. Expert advice husbands (good or bad) may be extended to leadership position. 3. Family responsibility.

Nouns, adjectives, adverb are easily identifiable in words bearing suffixes. Example; -able; Laugh – laughable Wash – washable Loud – loudable -age; Bond – bondage Waste – wastage Drain – drainage Mile – mileage Dose – dosage -ant; Assist – assistant Serve – servant Depend – dependant Aspire – aspirant -en; Loose – loosen Dead – deaden Tight – tighten Quick – quicken

Acquit: To give a legal decision 3. Adjournment; To postpone proceeding in a law court. 4. Adjudicate; To give official judgement or decision upon somebody (usually lawyer) 5. Advocate: A lawyer who speaks in favor of somebody in the court of law 6. Appeal: Taking the decision of a lower court to higher court. 7. Bail: To secure the release of somebody accused to higher court 8. Client; A person who gets help or advice from a lawyer. 9. Contempt of court; Breach or act of disloyalty or disrespect to a court. 10. Counsel: Advice, (also a lawyer). 11. Court; A person who commit crime. 12. Legal action Assignment 1. List at least ten words associated with law and order. 2. Use those words in sentence.

Theme: Continuous writing Unit topic: Essay writing Lesson topic: Argumentative Essay (to prove a point) An argumentative essay is an essay in which the writer tries to persuade and convince the reader to accept and agree with his point of view. Topic in this form of essay demands that the writer should prove a point, express an opinion and support or oppose a given idea Example

1. Child training is the sole responsibility of a mother 2. Covid – 19 is a blessing in disguise 3. Modern technology has done harm than good 4. Female should be given leadership position in the society 5. Uniforms are important or why the are not. Guidelines for an argumentative essay 1. State the topic. 2. State your vocatives: This is the greeting to acknowledge the presence of the panel and the audience. For example; The moderator/chairman, panel of judges, accurate time keeper, co – debaters, fellow student/audience, 3. Introduction: Define a content and take a stand 4. Body: Make sure you are convinced about the side you are opposing or supporting. If you support the side you do not belief in, you will run out of points and ideas. 5. Family responsibility.

Week 5 Theme: Speech Unit topic: Word stress Lesson topic: Monosyllabic and polysyllabic words. A. Stress is the exertion of breath effort (force) on some syllables during production. All the syllables do not have equal force in production because some are said with greater force and are louder while others are not. Therefore, those syllables produced with greater force and energy is the stressed sound. We have primary and secondary stress, shoe, erase, people, draw, above e.t.c B. Syllable is the breaking down of words into sections that contains the smallest vowel sound, or word that c an be produced at one heart beat e.g the word “Monday” contains two syllables Monday 1. Types of syllable monosyllabic words such words are usually stressed when pronounce in isolation. Example are; Go, do, gain, come, jump e.t.c load, ask, more, live, such. C. Bisyllabic: these are words that contain two syllables. When there is more than syllable in a word, one syllable will be pronounced louder than the other sounds e.g /law/yer. More examples of Bisyllabic are: Eng/lish, fa/ther, E/ffort e.t.c. C. Polysyllabic words are words with three or more syllables and they have their own stress. Pattern Example; (a) Words with three syllables are; (i). advantage – ad – vantage (ii). expertise – ex – per – tise (iii). disagree dis – a – gree (iv). understand – un – der – stand (v). character – cha – racter Words with four syllables (i). Confidential – Con – fi – den – tial (ii) communicate – com – mu – ni – cate (ii). imposible – im – po – si – ble (iv). political – po – li – ti – cal

A verb is a word that indicate a physical action (e.g drive), a mental action (e.g think) or a state of being (e.g exist). Verb is a very important element in a sentence because of it role, it tells you more about the actions, event, doing and state of being of a subject. The doer is the subject of verb e.g dance, walk, eat, and the object is regarded as the receiver. Example Mrs. Joy bought some pen Active voice of verb Identify the subject and the predicate in the sentences. i. she wrote the letter ii. Three students swept the class iii. The surgeon did the operation. iv. The teacher is teaching the student The above sentences are all in active voices. A verb is used in the active voice when the doer of an action is made to function as the subject here, it means that the writer or the speaker is more interested in the sentence Those sentences can be changed to passive voice. A verb is used in the passive form when the receiver (object) of an action is made to function as the subject. the focus is not more on the receiver of the action. Example; (i) The letter was written by her. ii. The class was swept by three students. iii. The operation was done by the surgeon To effect the changes correctly, these points must be taken note of;

i. Only the transitive verb can be made passive ii. The tense of the transitive verb in the sentence determines the tense in the passive sentence. iii. The passive sentence has an object that becomes the subject of the passive sentence. Assignment Change the order of the following sentences to make them passive 1. Joy slapped Shade 2. Nigerians love Russians 3. Seidu stood on the rooftop 4. Bisi did not drive the truck. Theme: Comprehension Unit topic; Reading for specific Structural Pattern. title: VOC.DEV.
subject: English Language
rawText: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH LAW AND ORDER Law is the body of rules and standards issued by a government to be applied by a court and similar authorities. Simply put, it is a written rule that concerns behaviours and the appropriate consequences thereof. Order means a state of being well arranged. The government is responsible for making laws, interpreting the law and executing it. 1. The legislative is responsible for making laws by which government is run 2. The Judiciary on the other hand interprets the law made by the legislature. The Judiciary is responsible for settling disputes and imposing punishment when necessary through, the Supreme court, Appeal court, High court, Magistrate court or Customary court or Sharia court. 3. Finally, the Executive implements laws made by the legislature. The executive arm of government is largely responsible for the day to day running of the affairs of government. 4. The constitution refers to the totality of fundamental laws, rules and legislations, customs, conventions and principles by which a country is governed. The constitution in effect regulates the activities of the government 5. The police, the army, the navy, custom and civil defense are all organizations that ensure laws and order in various sections of the government. Some words associated with law and order include: Government, the legislature, the executive, the judiciary, law, order, House of representative, the senate, the chief whip, clerk, bill, curt, chief judge, lawyers, decrees, plaintiff, prosecutor, Bye laws, constitution e.t.c. Classwork Make sentences with 3 words from the list.

title: NOUN PHRASE AND ITS FUNCTIONS
subject: English Language
rawText:
NOUN PHRASE AND FUNCTIONS A noun phrase is a group of words which has its headword as a noun or pronoun. It usually begins with an article such as ‘a’, ‘an’ or ‘the’. FUNCTIONS OF A NOUN PHRASE 1. Subject of the verb : When the noun phrase occupies the first position in a sentence, it functions as the subject of the verb that follows it. Examples: a. An old man is at the door. ( subject of the verb “is”) b. Sleeping without light is not something I enjoy. (subject of the verb is) c. An old music box is on the table. d. Your uncle is coming here. 2. Subject complement: When the noun phrase is the same thing or person as the subject, it functions as subject complement. Examples: a. Susan is the doctor.( complement of the subject Susan) b. My dad is a film director. (complement of the subject “my dad”) c. David was a naughty boy. d. I will soon become the head boy. 3. Object of the verb : When the noun phrase comes after the verb of action in the sentence, it functions as the object of the verb. Examples: a. Sunday received an award for excellence.( object of the verb received) b. An old man broke the door. ( object of the verb broke) c. Fatima has a kind heart. d. Stella bought a beautiful silver necklace. 4. Object complement: When the noun phrase is the same person or thing as the object, it functions as the object complement. Examples : a. My father calls my brother a hero. ( complement of the object my brother) b. The students calls the teacher a wizard.( complement of the object the teacher) c. My mother calls me the best. d. The principal named my friend the new representative. 5. Object of the preposition: When the noun phrase occurs after the preposition, it is governed by the preposition. Hence, it is the object of the preposition. Examples : a. An award of excellence was given to the teacher. ( object of the preposition to) b. An old man is at the door.( object of the preposition at) 6. Apposition: this is when a phrase tells us more about the noun that comes before it or when two noun phrases lie side by side without any word between them. Examples:

a. My brother, the teacher, was given an award. (the teacher is in apposition to my brother) b. Mr. Jones, the prince, was here last week. (the prince is in apposition to Mr. Jones)

Lesson Topic:- Reading for Main Gistin a Passage Text: New Oxford English Pg 134 - 135 “ A Wandering Stranger ” The main gist of any passage is the essential contents they are the main substance of what has been written. They do not contain unnecessary details. The main gist, therefore is the main idea, the summary or the aspect that is gripping and essential for the desired information. The main gist of the passage is the difficulty in finding places due to poor street naming, confusion caused by irregular house numbering, lack of proper town planning and frustration experienced by strangers in an unfamiliar environment. Key words used in the passage are:- 1. Locate, apparently, exasperation, inquiries, numerals, conspicuously. Assignment:- To answer the comprehension question in pg 135 of their text book. Example:- un, mis, il, in, im, dis, etc. A prefix added to a word usually does not change the word class (Part of Speech) of the word e.g material-immaterial(adjective) Behave-misbehave(verb) Personal-impersonal(adjective). with channel, co-editor, co-exist D. prefixes that are used to generate antonyms Un Unhealthy, untainted, unserious, unaided, uninformed, unfair, untie Mis Mislead, misquote, misspell, misunderstand Ill Illegal, illogical, illegitimate, illiterate In Indecision, inaudible, inaccessible, Im Improper, impossible, monorail, impolite, immature, immodest Assignment:- Generate two sentences using the following words and their antonyms:- Regular Unwanted Polite Decent Agree Manage Theme: Register Unit Topic: Vocabulary Development Lesson Topic: Words associated with the environment. title: SPEECH WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText:
Lesson Note on:Speech Writin Meaning A speech is a formal talk or address given to an audience to inform, persuade, entertain, or motivate them. Speech writing is the act of preparing and arranging words in written form before delivering them orally to an audience. Unlike an essay, a speech is written to be spoken ; therefore, it must be lively, clear, and engaging. Features of a Good Speech 1. Title/Topic – the subject of the speech (e.g., The Importance of Discipline in School ). 2. Salutation – greeting the audience (e.g., Good morning, the Principal, teachers, and fellow students ). 3. Introduction – state who you are, your purpose, and capture attention. 4. Body – main points explained in paragraphs with examples and illustrations. 5. Conclusion – summarize key points and end strongly. 6. Signature/Name – the speaker’s name, designation, and sometimes date. Qualities of a Good Speech  Clarity – use simple and clear language.  Audience awareness – speech must suit the audience (students, teachers, politicians, etc.).  Good organization – points arranged logically.  Persuasive/Appealing – able to convince or move the audience.  Use of rhetorical devices – rhetorical questions, repetition, proverbs, quotations.  Politeness – respectful and courteous language.  Coherence -unity in organisation of Speech

Types of Speeches 1. Informative Speech – gives information or explains something. o Example: Speech on the causes of malaria. 2. Persuasive Speech – convinces the audience to accept a viewpoint. o Example: Why students should say no to drug abuse. 3. Entertainment Speech – aims to amuse and relax the audience. o Example: Wedding or birthday speech. 4. Special Occasion Speech – given at ceremonies (welcome, farewell, prize-giving, campaign, etc.). Steps in Writing a Speech 1. Understand the topic – know what you are expected to talk about. 2. Identify your audience – adjust your language and tone to suit them. 3. Research – gather facts, statistics, or quotations. 4. Plan the outline – arrange your points in order: introduction, body, conclusion. 5. Write the speech – use simple, clear, and lively sentences. 6. Edit and rehearse – remove errors and practice delivery. Format of a Speech Title: (e.g., The Dangers of Examination Malpractice ) Salutation: Good morning, the Principal, teachers, and my fellow students. Introduction: I am here today to talk about… Body: Firstly… Secondly… Finally… (well-developed points). Conclusion: In conclusion, I want us to remember that… Name/Signature: Thank you. — Michelle Ejeh(Senior Prefect) Eg.S peech in an outline f orm) Topic: The Importance of Discipline in School  Salutation: Good morning, Principal, teachers, and fellow students.  Introduction: Discipline is the foundation of success. Without it, no student can achieve much.  Body: 1. Discipline builds good character.

2. It promotes academic excellence. 3. It creates respect for authority and order in society.  Conclusion: In conclusion, discipline is the key to both personal and academic success. Let us all embrace discipline to become responsible citizens.  Signature: Thank you. — (Lawal Aisha ) Senior Prefect. Summary  Speech writing is preparing words for oral delivery.  A good speech has a title, salutation, introduction, body, conclusion, and the writer’s name.  It must be clear, logical, persuasive, and suited to the audience.

title: EXPOSITORY ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText:
Lesson Note on:Expository Essay Meaning The word expository comes from the verb expose , which means to explain, describe, or make something clear . An Expository Essay is a type of essay that explains, describes, or gives information about a particular subject. It does not argue or try to persuade, but rather aims to educate the reader. It is one of the most common essay types in schools and examinations. Features of an Expository Essay 1. Clarity – Ideas must be presented in a clear and simple way. 2. Logical sequence – Points should follow one another in order. 3. Explanation and examples – Each point must be explained with facts, examples, or illustrations. 4. Neutral tone – The writer does not show bias or emotions. 5. Formal language – Use standard English, no slang or contractions. Types of Expository Essays 1. Definition Essay – explains the meaning of a word or concept. o Example: Explain what democracy means. 2. Process/How-to Essay – explains steps in doing something. o Example: How to prepare a cup of tea. 3. Cause and Effect Essay – explains the reasons something happened and its results. o Example: Causes and effects of drug abuse among youths. 4. Comparison and Contrast Essay – shows similarities and differences between two things. o Example: Compare and contrast village life and city life. 5. Problem and Solution Essay – identifies a problem and suggests solutions.

o Example: Problems of unemployment in Nigeria and how to solve them. Structure of an Expository Essay 1. Introduction o State the topic clearly. o Sometimes include a definition or background. o End with a thesis statement (the main idea). 2. Body o Develop your points in paragraphs. o Each paragraph should have a topic sentence followed by explanation and examples. o Use linking words like firstly, in addition, furthermore, therefore, finally . 3. Conclusion o Summarize the main points. o Restate the importance of the subject. o Avoid introducing new ideas. Functions of Expository Essays  To educate the reader.  To explain facts and ideas.  To provide information in a clear and logical way.  To develop critical thinking and communication skills in students. title: NOUN PHRASE
subject: English Language
rawText:
LESSON NOTE ON NOUN PHRASE NOUN PHRASE 1. Definition A noun phrase is a group of words centered around a noun (called the headword ), which may be accompanied by other words such as determiners, adjectives, quantifiers, and prepositional phrases. It functions as a noun in a sentence. Example:  The big black dog in the yard → Head noun = dog 2. Structure of a Noun Phrase The typical structure can be represented as: (Determiner) + (Pre-modifier) + Noun (Headword) + (Post-modifier)  Determiners : articles (a, an, the), demonstratives (this, those), possessives (my, our).  Pre-modifiers : adjectives or nouns placed before the headword (e.g., beautiful , wooden ).  Headword : the central noun (e.g., boy , house ).  Post-modifiers : words/phrases/clauses after the noun giving more detail (e.g., in the garden , who lives next door ). Example:  The tall man with a walking stick o Determiner = The o Pre-modifier = tall o Headword = man o Post-modifier = with a walking stick

3. Functions of a Noun Phrase in a Sentence Noun phrases can perform the functions of nouns in sentences. They can be: 1. Subject of a verb o The little boy with curly hair is playing football. 2. Object of a verb o The teacher punished the stubborn students . 3. Object of a preposition o He sat on a broken wooden chair . 4. Complement of a subject o My brother is a talented musician . 5. Complement of an object o They elected her the class representative . 4. Types of Noun Phrases 1. Simple noun phrase – only the head noun (e.g., Dogs bark ). 2. Expanded noun phrase – has modifiers (e.g., The small brown dog ). 3. Complex noun phrase – has post-modifying clauses or prepositional phrases (e.g., The car that my father bought last year ). 5. Examples of Noun Phrases  A tall building  The girl in a red dress  Several bags of rice  The story that she told us  My two best friends from Lagos 6. Importance of Noun Phrases  They enrich sentence structure by providing details.  They help in precise and descriptive communication.  They serve multiple grammatical functions.

✅ Quick Tip for Identification: If you can replace the group of words with a single noun/pronoun and the sentence still makes sense, then it is a noun phrase. Example:  The hardworking students in my class passed the exam.  Replace with pronoun → They passed the exam.  The tall beautiful lady danced greatly  Replace with -She danced greatly. Assignment. Give 5 examples (sentences) and replace them with a pronoun of your choice.

WEEK 9 I. Speech - Vowel Sounds Topic - Diphthongs Diphthongs are a sequence of two vowel sounds within the same syllables. Diphthongs are vowels but differ from the pure vowels for they contain two vowel sounds. They involve a glide from the first vowel sound to the second vowel sound to produce a double sound. E.g /e/ => /I/ => /e ɪ /. This marks the direction of movement during pronunciation. All Diphthongs are long vowels. There are 8 diphthongs - vowels 13 to 20. 13: /e ɪ / 14: /a ɪ / 15: / ɔɪ / 16: / əʊ / 17: /a ʊ / 18: / ɪə / 19: /e ə / 20: / ʊə / Diphthongs are classified into three categories namely: 1) Diphthongs that guide towards / ɪ /: /e ɪ /, /a ɪ /, / ɔɪ /. 2) Diphthongs that guide towards / ʊ /: / əʊ /, /a ʊ /. 3) Diphthongs that guide towards / ə /: / ɪə /, /e ə /, / ʊə /. Words associated with each sounds include: A) Vowel 13 /e ɪ / The spelling symbols include: 'ei' as in Eight: /e ɪt/ Neighbour: /ˈneɪ b ə r/ 'a' as in Gate: / ɡeɪt/ Lady: /ˈleɪdi/. 'ai' as in Paid: /pe ɪ d/ Rain: /re ɪ n/ 'ea' as in Break: /bre ɪ k/ Great: / ɡreɪt/ 'ay' as in Play: /ple ɪ / Pay: /pe ɪ / 'ey' as in Grey: / ɡreɪ/ They: /ðeɪ/ B) Vowel 14 /a ɪ / The spelling symbols include:

'ei ' as in Neither: /ˈnaɪ ð ər/ Either: /ˈiːðə r/ 'eigh' as in Height: /ha ɪ t/ 'y' as in Try: /tra ɪ / 'uy' as in Buy: /ba ɪ / 'ie' as in Fried: /fra ɪ d/ 'ye' as Dye: /da ɪ / C) Vowel 15 / ɔɪ / The spelling symbols include: 'oy' as in Toy: /t ɔɪ / 'uoy' as in Buoy: /b ɔɪ / 'oi' as in Noise: /n ɔɪ z/ D) Vowel 16 / əʊ / The spelling symbols include: 'ow' as in Bow: /bo ʊ /. 'o' as in Choose: /t ʃuːz/. 'ou' as in Soul: /so ʊ l/. 'oa' as in Coat: /ko ʊ t/. 'oe' as in Toe: /to ʊ /. E) Vowel 17 /a ʊ / The spelling symbols include: 'ough' as in Plough: /pla ʊ / 'ow' as in Fowl: /fa ʊ l/ 'ou' as in House: /ha ʊ s/

F) Vowel 18 / ɪə / The spelling symbols include: 'eer' as in Deer: /d ɪə r/ Beer: /b ɪə r/ 'ere' as in Here: /h ɪə r/ Mere: /m ɪə r/ ’ea' as in Hear: /hɪə r/ Tear: /t ɪə r/ 'eir' as in Weird: /w ɪə rd/ Pier: /p ɪə r/ 'ea' as in Idea: /a ɪˈ di ə / G) Vowel 19 /e ə / The spelling symbols include: 'eir' as in Heir: / ɛə r/ Their: /ð ɛə r/ 'air' as in Chair: /t ʃɛə r/ Fair: /f ɛə r/ 'are' as in Care: /k ɛə r/ Share: / ʃɛə r/ 'ear' as in Swear: /sw ɛə r/ Tear: /t ɛə / 'ere' as in There: /ð ɛə r/ H) Vowel 20 / ʊə / 'ur' as in Sure: / ʃʊə r/ Pure: /pj ʊə r/ 'oo' as in Poor: /p ʊə r/ Tour: /t ʊə r/ 'ur' as in Curious: /ˈkjʊə ri ə s/ Topic: Summary Passage Refer to page 27 (History and Scientific Knowledge)

title: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH MEDICINE
subject: English Language
rawText: VOCABULARY DEVELOPMENT; WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH MEDICINE Medicine has different definitions based on context, it can be course of study of the cause, diagnosis, prognosis and treatment of disease or illness; it can also be a substance which specially promotes healing when ingested or consumed in some way. It is also a profession or practice of physicians, including surgeons. Whichever way, it all boils down to a particular thing, treatment and wellness of the body system. Some of the words include: 1. Consultant: A person who gives expert advice or medicine and surgery 2. Bandage : Strip of materials for binding round a wound 3. Blood donor: A person who gives blood for blood transfusion 4. Clinic : Hospital or institution where medical advice and treatment are given 5. Dentist: A person whose work is filling, cleaning and taking out teeth and filling artificial teeth 6. Dermatology : Medical study of the skin e.g skin disease 7. Dispenser: A person who dispenses medicine 8. Doctor: A person who has been trained in medical science 9. Gynaecology : Science of diseases of women and pregnancies 10. Matron ; A woman who manages the domestic affairs and nursing staff of a hospital 11. Nurse : A person trained to take care of people who are ill or injured 12. Surgeon : A doctor who perform operation 13. Transfuse : Transfer of blood from one person to another 14. Theatre : A room in the hospital where surgical operations are performed 15. Fill : Tablet of medicine for swallowing whole

title: CREATIVE WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText: CREATIVE WRITING Creative writing or free writing allows the students to freely express or write up, in a story form any imaginary thing that comes to their mind or real event or incident they experience. In free writing, the students try to freely utilize the vocabulary, idioms, figure of speech, which they have acquired. The short story has to come originally from individual students and that is why it is creative. Some features of a short story as part of creative writing 1. There should be a title. 2. The story may be real or imaginary but it should be credible or believable. 3. The story must have an interesting plot i.e. sequence of events, which must be well organized to have a beginning, a climax and a conclusion. 4. The events should relate to one another 5. A good story has dialogue in it. 6. The language or diction, imageries etc. should reflect the atmosphere of the setting and the target audience or the readers. 7. The writer must have a good sense of imagination.

title: FORMAL LETTER: LETTER OF COMPLAINT
subject: English Language
rawText:
English Language Class: VEI 2 TOPIC: Formal Letter: Letter of Complaint Formal Letter: A formal letter is a type of written communication used for official or professional purposes, following a specific format and tone. It's used to convey information, request action, or express opinions in a professional or business setting. Letter of Complaint: A letter of complaint is a type of formal letter expressing dissatisfaction or grievance about a product, service, or situation. It outlines the issue, provides details, and requests resolution or action. Other types of formal letters: - Letter of Application (Job Application) - Letter of Inquiry (Request for Information) - Letter of Request (Asking for something) - Letter of Order (Placing an order) - Letter of Invitation (Inviting someone to an event) - Letter of Resignation (Notifying employer of resignation) - Letter of Acknowledgement (Acknowledging receipt of something) Structure of a Formal Letter of Complaint: 1. Sender's Address: Top right corner 2. Date: Below sender's address 3. Recipient's Address: Left side, below date 4. Salutation: Formal greeting (e.g., Dear Sir/Madam) 5. title: NOMINALIZATION
subject: English Language
rawText:
Lesson Note on :Nominalization Nominalization Meaning Nominalization is the process of changing a word (especially a verb or an adjective) into a noun . The word nominal means “related to a noun.” Writers often use nominalization to make their writing more formal, academic, or abstract.  Example: o Verb: decide → Noun: decision o Adjective: happy → Noun: happiness How Nominalization Works 1. From Verbs to Nouns o arrive → arrival o move → movement o choose → choice o develop → development 2. From Adjectives to Nouns o strong → strength o wise → wisdom o angry → anger o beautiful → beauty 3. By Adding Suffixes Common suffixes used to form nominalizations include: o -tion / -sion (inform → information, admit → admission) o -ment (develop → development, govern → government) o -ity (possible → possibility, active → activity) o -ness (kind → kindness, happy → happiness) o -ance / -ence (attend → attendance, depend → dependence) o -al (arrive → arrival, refuse → refusal)

Functions of Nominalization 1. To Avoid Repetition – Instead of repeating verbs, we use nouns. o Example: He failed because he did not prepare → His failure was due to lack of preparation. 2. To Achieve Formality – Academic and professional writing often uses nominalization. o Example: We investigated the problem → An investigation of the problem was carried out. 3. To Make Writing Concise – It allows long actions to be expressed in short noun phrases. o Example: They decided to cancel the event → The decision to cancel the event… 4. To Emphasize Ideas – Nominalization highlights the result of an action rather than the action itself. Advantages of Nominalization  Makes writing formal and professional.  Helps to express complex ideas in fewer words.  Focuses on concepts or results instead of people performing actions. Disadvantages of Nominalization  Can make writing heavy, dull, or less direct.  May cause confusion if overused.  Sometimes hides the “doer” of the action. Examples in Sentences 1. Verb → Noun o We must decide soon. → A decision must be made soon. 2. Adjective → Noun o She is very wise. → Her wisdom is great. 3. Using suffixes o The teacher explained the rule. → The teacher gave an explanation of the rule.

Practice Exercise 1. Change these verbs into nouns: o admit, govern, arrive, fail, choose. 2. Change these adjectives into nouns: o happy, strong, weak, angry, possible. 3. Rewrite the sentences using nominalization: o (a) The students argued. o (b) She refused the offer. o (c) He developed a new idea. ✅ Summary : Nominalization is turning verbs and adjectives into nouns. It is useful in formal and academic writing but should be used carefully to avoid making sentences unclear and ambiguous.

title: PRONOUN
subject: English Language
rawText:
Pronoun A pronoun is a word used in place of a noun to avoid repetition. Instead of repeating the same noun several times, we use pronouns to make sentences smoother and clearer.  Example: o Without pronoun: Ijeoma is a student. Ijeoma loves reading. Ijeoma is kind. o With pronoun: Ijeoma is a student. She loves reading. She is kind. Here, she is the pronoun replacing "Ijeoma". Types of Pronouns 1. Personal Pronouns o Refer to specific persons or things. o They have three cases :  Subjective case (I, we, you, he, she, it, they) – used as subject.  Objective case (me, us, you, him, her, it, them) – used as object.  Possessive case (my/mine, our/ours, your/yours, his, her/hers, its, their/theirs). o Example: She is my friend. I like her. 2. Demonstrative Pronouns o Used to point out specific things. o Examples: this, that, these, those. o Example: This is my book; those are yours. 3. Interrogative Pronouns o Used to ask questions. o Examples: who, whom, whose, which, what.

o Example: Who is at the door? 4. Relative Pronouns o Introduce subordinate clauses and refer to nouns mentioned earlier. o Examples: who, whom, whose, which, that. o Example: The boy who won the prize is my brother. 5. Reflexive Pronouns o Used when the subject and object of a verb are the same. o Formed by adding -self (singular) or -selves (plural). o Examples: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves. o Example: He hurt himself while playing football. 6. Emphatic Pronouns o Same form as reflexive pronouns but used for emphasis . o Example: I myself saw him. She herself cooked the food. 7. Indefinite Pronouns o Refer to people or things in a general, non-specific way. o Examples: someone, anyone, everyone, nobody, each, few, many, several, all. o Example: Everybody likes music. Few attended the meeting. 8. Reciprocal Pronouns o Show mutual action or relationship. o Examples: each other, one another. o Example: The boys love each other. o Possessive Pronouns Show ownership. o Examples: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. o Example: This book is mine.

10. Distributive Pronouns  Refer to persons or things one at a time.  Examples: each, either, neither.  Example: Each of the students passed. Neither of the boys came. Functions of Pronouns 1. As Subjects of Verbs o Example: She is my sister. 2. As Objects of Verbs o Example: I saw him at the market. 3. As Possessives (showing ownership) o Example: That pen is mine. 4. As Complements o Example: It is he. 5. As Connectives (joining clauses) o Example: This is the man who helped me. 6. As Emphasis o Example: I myself cleaned the room. Summary  A pronoun replaces a noun to avoid repetition.  Types include: personal, demonstrative, interrogative, relative, reflexive, emphatic, indefinite, reciprocal, possessive, and distributive.  Functions: subject, object, possession, complement, connective, and emphasis.

title: NOUN CLAUSE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Noun clause. A clause itself expresses a complete thought or meaning. A noun clause is a clause which performs the grammatical functions of a noun a sentence. Noun clauses are introduced by the following Subordinating conjunctions; what, how, that, who, whether, if, when and where" who and that Can equally begin adjectival clauses" whether, "If "when and where" can also introduce adverbial clauses. It is only “what and how” that can consistently introduce noun clauses without introducing any other clauses. N oun Clauses perform Six grammatical functions. 1. As the subject of a verb~ A noun clause is the subject of a verb when it comes before the verb in the main clause. Examples a) How he escaped police arrest surprises everybody. How he escaped police arrest is the subject of the verb. “Surprises” is the main clause. b) What you said led to the sudden disappearance of the girl. What you said is the subject of the verb. “Led” is the main clause. 2. As the object of the verb; When a noun clause comes immediately after a verb in a main clause. It is the object of the verb. Examples a) The lady thought that the man will marry her. That the man will marry her is the object of the verb “thought” b) He does what everybody likes. What everybody likes is the object of the verb “does” in the main clause. 3. As the complement of the object in the main clause~ Whenever a noun clause follows the object in the main clause, it is said to be the complement of the object. Examples. a) She gave the advice that we should work together as a team. That we should work together as a team is the object complement of “the advice” b) I have taken the decision that we shall all visit him. That we shall all visit him is the object complement “of decision “ 4. As the complement of the subject~ A noun clause is the complement of the subject when it is the same person or thing as the subject of the sentence. A main verb usually separates the phrase and the subject. Examples a) The problem at hand is how we can stop corruption in Nigeria… How we can stop corruption In Nigeria is a restatement of the subject so the clause is the subject complement of “the problem at hand” b) The answer is what I know already. What I know already is the subject complement “of the answer “ 5. As the complement (object) of preposition ~ A noun clause is the complement or object of a preposition if it directly follows a preposition in a sentence. Examples a) It has become a case of who will bell the cat…. “Who will bell the cat” is the complement of the preposition “of” b) He always concentrate on what he does… What he does is the complement of the preposition “on” 6. Apposive Function~ A noun clause can be apposition to a noun. It is called appositive function. It provides further explanation on the noun. There by becoming the same person or thing

as the noun. Examples a) The fact, that HIV/ AIDS has no cure, is enough warning. That HIV/AIDS has no cure is in apposition to the noun “fact” b) The rumor, that he is death, is unfounded. That he is death is the apposition in apposition to the noun “rumor” Appositive functions and subject complement can be identified thus; Apposition function comma is used to mark off the clause and the noun it explains. When it functions as the subject complement complement the main verb separates the subject and the clause.

title: LECTURE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Introduction A lecture is one of the common ways information is passed from one person to many people, especially in schools, seminars, conferences, and religious or professional gatherings. Teachers, lecturers, and experts often use lectures to explain ideas, teach concepts, or give instructions. Definition of Lecture A lecture is a formal oral presentation in which a speaker gives information, explains a topic, or teaches an audience, usually in an organized and systematic manner. Features of a Lecture 1. It is usually formal. 2. It involves one main speaker and many listeners. 3. It is well-organized and planned. 4. It focuses on educating or informing the audience. 5. Notes or visual aids may be used. Purposes of a Lecture  To teach or educate.  To explain complex ideas or topics.  To share knowledge or research findings.  To give instructions or guidance.

Examples of Lecture Situations  A university lecturer teaching students in a lecture hall.  A health officer giving a talk on hygiene.  A guest speaker addressing students during a seminar. Differences Between a Lecture and a Speech Lecture Speech Mainly for teaching Mainly for persuasion or inspiration Usually longer Often shorter Formal and academic Can be formal or informal Evaluation 1. Define the term lecture . 2. Mention three features of a lecture. 3. State two purposes of a lecture. Summary A lecture is a formal method of teaching or sharing information where one person speaks to many listeners in an organized way. It is commonly used in educational and professional settings. Assignment Write a short paragraph explaining why lectures are important in schools.

It is only “what and how” that can consistently introduce noun clauses without introducing any other clauses. N oun Clauses perform Six grammatical functions. 1. As the subject of a verb~ A noun clause is the subject of a verb when it comes before the verb in the main clause. Examples a) How he escaped police arrest surprises everybody. How he escaped police arrest is the subject of the verb. “Surprises” is the main clause. b) What you said led to the sudden disappearance of the girl. What you said is the subject of the verb. “Led” is the main clause. 2. As the object of the verb; When a noun clause comes immediately after a verb in a main clause. It is the object of the verb. Examples a) The lady thought that the man will marry her. That the man will marry her is the object of the verb “thought” b) He does what everybody likes. What everybody likes is the object of the verb “does” in the main clause. 3. As the complement of the object in the main clause~ Whenever a noun clause follows the object in the main clause, it is said to be the complement of the object. Examples. a) She gave the advice that we should work together as a team. That we should work together as a team is the object complement of “the advice” b) I have taken the decision that we shall all visit him. That we shall all visit him is the object complement “of decision “ 4. As the complement of the subject~ A noun clause is the complement of the subject when it is the same person or thing as the subject of the sentence. A main verb usually separates the phrase and the subject. Examples a) The problem at hand is how we can stop corruption in Nigeria… How we can stop corruption In Nigeria is a restatement of the subject so the clause is the subject complement of “the problem at hand” b) The answer is what I know already. What I know already is the subject complement “of the answer “ 5. As the complement (object) of preposition ~ A noun clause is the complement or object of a preposition if it directly follows a preposition in a sentence. Examples a) It has become a case of who will bell the cat…. “Who will bell the cat” is the complement of the preposition “of” b) He always concentrate on what he does… What he does is the complement of the preposition “on” 6. Apposive Function~ A noun clause can be apposition to a noun. It is called appositive function. It provides further explanation on the noun. There by becoming the same person or thing

as the noun. Examples a) The fact, that HIV/ AIDS has no cure, is enough warning. That HIV/AIDS has no cure is in apposition to the noun “fact” b) The rumor, that he is death, is unfounded. That he is death is the apposition in apposition to the noun “rumor” Appositive functions and subject complement can be identified thus; Apposition function comma is used to mark off the clause and the noun it explains. When it functions as the subject complement complement the main verb separates the subject and the clause.

title: NOTE TAKING
subject: English Language
rawText:
Introduction A lecture is one of the common ways information is passed from one person to many people, especially in schools, seminars, conferences, and religious or professional gatherings. Teachers, lecturers, and experts often use lectures to explain ideas, teach concepts, or give instructions. Definition of Lecture A lecture is a formal oral presentation in which a speaker gives information, explains a topic, or teaches an audience, usually in an organized and systematic manner. Features of a Lecture 1. It is usually formal. 2. It involves one main speaker and many listeners. 3. It is well-organized and planned. 4. It focuses on educating or informing the audience. 5. Notes or visual aids may be used. Purposes of a Lecture  To teach or educate.  To explain complex ideas or topics.  To share knowledge or research findings.  To give instructions or guidance.

Examples of Lecture Situations  A university lecturer teaching students in a lecture hall.  A health officer giving a talk on hygiene.  A guest speaker addressing students during a seminar. Differences Between a Lecture and a Speech Lecture Speech Mainly for teaching Mainly for persuasion or inspiration Usually longer Often shorter Formal and academic Can be formal or informal Evaluation 1. Define the term lecture . 2. Mention three features of a lecture. 3. State two purposes of a lecture. Summary A lecture is a formal method of teaching or sharing information where one person speaks to many listeners in an organized way. It is commonly used in educational and professional settings. Assignment Write a short paragraph explaining why lectures are important in schools.

title: ADVERBIAL PHRASES
subject: English Language
rawText:
Adjectival Phases and Their Grammatical Functions . A phrase is a group of words without a finite verb, that does not make complete sense. An expression is a phrase if: i. it does not contain a finite verb, and so makes incomplete sense examples: in the class, outside the room, behind the door, the man etc. ii. it contains a non – finite verb and yet makes incomplete sense A non – finite verb is the opposite of a finite verbs, it is that form of a verb which does not indicate the tense of an action or the subject verb agreement iii. we have four (4) types of Phrase Prepositional Phase, Noun Phrase, Adjectival Phrase and Adverbial Phrase Adjectival Phrase is Phrase that qualifies a noun or pronoun in a sentence. She guides the students in formation of adjectival Phases. An adjectival phrase can be formed using any of the following structures: (1) Preposition + article + noun: Example: in the car, across the roads, with an umbrella, on the table etc. These can be used in the following sentences v The man, in the car is my uncle v The boy with an umbrella stole the goat v The people across the road are the newly employed teachers. v The books on the table belong to Aminu (2) preposition + adjective + noun: Examples: in black gowns, in red, with tribal marks, on a plastic chair etc. The examples can be used in the sentences below: v People in red are usually, dreaded v The women in black gowns are mourning v That old man with tribal marks speaks Hausa v The boy on a plastic chair is Philip’s twin brother v Adjectival phrases beginning with grounds Examples: v The man lying down is tired v People living with HIV/AIDS should not be stigmatized v That boy fighting across the road is school drop – out v Those living in Britain are usually conservative (3) Adjectival Phrases can also begin with participles. Examples: v The thief surrounded the police wept profusely v The money given to us really helped us v The English Language examination, passed by all the students, speaks well of Mrs. Enai v The letter written to the girl by her mother made her cry

She guides the students on how to identify adjectival phrases. First, an adjectival phrase is recognized by the grammatical function its performs in a sentence All adjectival phrases qualify nouns or pronouns. As long as a given phrase describes a noun or pronoun in a sentences, it is adjectival The boy in front of the class is very intelligent. The adjectival phrase in the expression is “in front of the class” this is a reference to a particular boy who is exceptionally intelligent therefore, the reference in front of the class gives a definite and clearer picture of the boy being spoken about, thereby making it easier to trace him amidst other boys. Another method that can be used to identify adjectival phrases is their closeness to the nouns or pronouns they qualify some expressions function as adjectival phrases as well as adverbial depending on usage Example: the pencil on the table is mine the pencil is on the table The phrase on the table is repeated in the two sentences. Sentence a on the table is an adjectival phrase. It describes a particular pencil out of many others.

title: TOAST MAKING
subject: English Language
rawText:
LessonNote on :Toast Making (Speech Toasts) TOAST MAKING Meaning A toast is a short speech made in honour of a person, group, or event, usually during a social gathering such as a wedding, birthday, graduation, anniversary, or farewell. When giving a toast, the speaker expresses goodwill, appreciation, or congratulations and then invites others to raise their glasses in agreement. Features of a Good Toast 1. Politeness and Courtesy – use respectful and kind words. 2. Brevity (Shortness) – a toast should be brief (usually 1–3 minutes). 3. Clarity – use simple and clear language. 4. Focus – concentrate on the person(s) or event being celebrated. 5. Positivity – use words that inspire joy, love, appreciation, or hope. 6. Concluding Gesture – end by asking everyone to raise their glasses to honor the person/event. Functions of a Toast  To honor a person or group.  To celebrate special occasions.  To express goodwill and best wishes.  To unite people in joy and happiness. Steps in Toast Making 1. Greet and get attention – politely call the audience’s attention. 2. Introduce yourself (if necessary) – especially in formal settings. 3. State the purpose – say why you are giving the toast (birthday, wedding, farewell, etc.). 4. Say kind words – express admiration, gratitude, or goodwill. 5. Be brief and sincere – avoid long speeches.

6. Propose the toast – end with the actual toast, e.g., “Ladies and gentlemen, please raise your glasses to the health and happiness of the celebrant!” Qualities of a Good Toast  Warm and heartfelt.  Short and straight to the point.  Relevant to the occasion.  Spoken with confidence and a smile.  Ends with a unifying call ( “Cheers!” ). Examples of Toasts 1. Wedding Toast: “Ladies and gentlemen, let us raise our glasses to the bride and groom. May your marriage be filled with love, joy, and endless happiness. To Mr. and Mrs. Okeke!” 2. Birthday Toast: “Today we celebrate a wonderful friend. May this new age bring you good health, success, and laughter. Please raise your glasses to Chiamaka!” 3. Farewell Toast: “We are sad to see our dear colleague leave, but we are happy for the bright future ahead. We wish you success in all your endeavors. To Mr. Ade!” Summary  A toast is a short speech to honor someone or celebrate an event.  It must be polite, short, positive, and focused.  It ends with an invitation to raise glasses and say cheers .  Occasions include weddings, birthdays, farewells, graduations, anniversaries, and official ceremonies

title: READING TO SUMMARIZE IN SPECIFIC NUMBER OF SENTENC
subject: English Language
rawText:
WHAT IS SUMMARY? Summary involves writing down a brief and concise account of a long passage. In other words, summary can be described as a shortened form of a long passage after removing all irrelevant points from the main points and giving a short account of the passage using your own words. There are four main things students have to note in order to write a good summary. These are: 1. Brevity: This demand that they must be brief and concise in their answers. There is no room for the use of flowery language or any other additional information aside from the main points. 2. Relevance: This calls for a candidate's answers to be relevant to the points mentioned in the passage. Students are not expected in summary writing to give any fact or point outside the passage, however relevant they think the fact or point is. 3. Proper coverage of the passage: this demand that students must read and understand every aspect of the passage. This calls for proper understanding of the passage since the passage is unlikely to lend itself so easily to them. 4. Clarity: this means that the students are expected to put down their answers correctly. you should be ready to go back to the questions, and answer them. HOW TO PUT DOWN SUMMARY ANSWERS. Write in sentences: summary answers should be written in sentences. When the student writes a preamble (A kind of introduction to his sentences) to his answers, the preamble must flow into the sentences. For example, in a question where the student is asked to summarize the factors responsible for different levels of achievement in schools, the students will need to write a preamble to all his sentences. The preamble will be: "the factors responsible for different levels of achievement in school are........" this can be followed by his sentences summarizing the factors. e.g., the factors responsible for different levels of achievement in schools are; (I) Where the schools are located. (ii) Some schools are located in privileged areas where others are not. The above sentences are complete sentences because they have their distinct subjects and verbs and other elements of a sentence. Another important thing is that you should not write more than the number of the sentences you are asked to write. Where you are asked to write two sentences, don't write one sentence or three sentences. • Short and concise answers: summary answers should be short and concise. Avoid the inclusion of irrelevant/ extraneous materials in every scoring answer. Limit your answers only to information available in the passage. • Use your words: in writing down your answers, make use of your own words and expression as much as possible. You are not expected to engage in middles lifting of words and expressions from the passage. • Use good grammar: summary answers should be written down in good grammar and expression. Make sure that your answers are devoid of grammatical and expression errors. you should be ready to go back to the questions, and answer them. HOW TO PUT DOWN SUMMARY ANSWERS. title: FIGURES OF SPEECH
subject: English Language
rawText:
Figures of speech are expressive uses of language designed to convey meaning in a more vivid or imaginative way than straightforward literal language. They enrich the text and speech, making it more engaging, memorable, and persuasive. By appealing to various sensory experiences and emotions, figures of speech can clarify information, create imagery, and evoke sentiments, making the communication more impactful. ### Importance of Figures of Speech 1. **Enhancement of Imagery**: They create vivid pictures in the minds of the audience. 2. **Emotional Appeal**: Figures of speech can evoke emotions and connect with the audience on a personal level. 3. **Persuasiveness**: They can make arguments more compelling and memorable. 4. **Creativity**: They add a unique flair to writing and speeches, setting the speaker or writer apart. 5. **Clarity**: Certain figures can clarify complex ideas by comparing them with familiar concepts. ### 30 Figures of Speech with Examples 1. **Simile** - A comparison using "like" or "as". - *Examples*: 1. "Her smile was like the sun." 2. "He fought like a lion." 2. **Metaphor** - A direct comparison without using "like" or "as". - *Examples*: 1. "Time is a thief." 2. "The world is a stage." 3. **Personification** - Assigning human traits to non-human entities. - *Examples*: 1. "The wind whispered through the trees." 2. "The flowers danced in the breeze." 4. **Hyperbole** - Exaggeration for emphasis or effect. - *Examples*: 1. "I ’ m so hungry I could eat a horse." 2. "He ’ s older than the hills." 5. **Alliteration**

- The repetition of initial consonant sounds. - *Examples*: 1. "She sells seashells by the seashore." 2. "Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers." 6. **Onomatopoeia** - A word that imitates the sound it represents. - *Examples*: 1. "The bees buzzed in the garden." 2. "The thunder rumbled in the distance." 7. **Irony** - A contrast between expectation and reality. - *Examples*: 1. "A fire station burns down." 2. "The police station gets robbed." 8. **Oxymoron** - A combination of contradictory terms. - *Examples*: 1. "Deafening silence." 2. "Bitter sweet." 9. **Idioms** - Expressions that don ’ t make sense literally. - *Examples*: 1. "Kick the bucket" (to die). 2. "Let the cat out of the bag" (to reveal a secret). 10. **Euphemism** - A polite way of saying something unpleasant. - *Examples*: 1. "Passed away" instead of "died." 2. "Let go" instead of "fired." 11. **Litotes** - An understatement by using double negatives. - *Examples*: 1. "Not bad" (meaning good). 2. "He ’ s not the friendliest person" (meaning unfriendly). 12. **Synecdoche** - A part represents the whole or vice versa. - *Examples*:

1. "All hands on deck" (hands represent sailors). 2. "The White House issued a statement" (White House represents the president). 13. **Metonymy** - Replacing a word with something closely associated with it. - *Examples*: 1. "The pen is mightier than the sword" (pen represents writing, sword represents military power). 2. "Hollywood is known for movies" (Hollywood represents the film industry). 14. **Chiasmus** - A reversal in the order of words in two otherwise parallel phrases. - *Examples*: 1. "Ask not what your country can do for you, but what you can do for your country." 2. "Never let a Fool Kiss You or a Kiss Fool You." 15. **Anaphora** - The repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses. - *Examples*: 1. "I have a dream that one day..." (Martin Luther King Jr.). 2. "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times..." 16. **Epistrophe** - The repetition of a word or phrase at the end of successive clauses. - *Examples*: 1. "Of the people, by the people, for the people." 2. "See no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil." 17. **Antithesis** - Juxtaposing contrasting ideas in balanced phrases. - *Examples*: 1. "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times." 2. "To err is human; to forgive, divine." 18. **Assonance** - The repetition of vowel sounds within words. - *Examples*: 1. "Hear the mellow wedding bells." 2. "The engineer held the steering to steer the vehicle." 19. **Consonance** - The repetition of consonant sounds within words or phrases. - *Examples*: 1. "The lumpy, bumpy road."

2. "He struck a streak of bad luck." 20. **Paradox** - A statement that appears contradictory but reveals a truth. - *Examples*: 1. "Less is more." 2. "This statement is false." 21. **Apostrophe** - Addressing an absent person or a personified idea. - *Examples*: 1. "O death, where is thy sting?" 2. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you are!" 22. **Rhetorical Question** - A question asked for effect, not meant to be answered. - *Examples*: 1. "Is the Pope Catholic?" 2. "Are we really prepared to face this challenge?" 23. **Tautology** - Unnecessary repetition of the same idea. - *Examples*: 1. "Free gift." 2. "Advance planning." 24. **Climax** - A series of ideas arranged in increasing order of importance. - *Examples*: 1. "I came, I saw, I conquered." 2. "To err is human; to blame it on someone else is politics." 25. **Bathos** - An abrupt turn from the serious and poetic to the regular and silly. - *Examples*: 1. "He spent his last night of freedom in a cheap motel, dreaming of the bowl of cereal that awaited him in the morning." 2. "In the heat of battle, he remembered his training, and then he thought about lunch." 26. **Syllogism** - A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises. - *Examples*: 1. "All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore, Socrates is mortal." 2. "All mammals are warm-blooded; all whales are mammals; therefore, all whales are warm-

blooded." 27. **Enallage** - Using one part of speech for another. - *Examples*: 1. "They was all here." (was instead of were). 2. "Thou art my friend." (archaic use of ‘ art ’ for ‘ are ’ ). 28. **Prolepsis** - Anticipating a response before it's given. - *Examples*: 1. "You might be thinking that this is going to take too much time, but let me assure you..." 2. "You might say, 'That's impossible!' but consider this..." 29. **Polysyndeton** - The deliberate use of many conjunctions. - *Examples*: 1. "I want a pizza and a salad and a drink." 2. "We have ships and men and money and stores." 30. **Asyndeton** - Omission of conjunctions between parts of a sentence. - *Examples*: 1. "I came, I saw, I conquered." 2. "They spent the day wondering, searching, thinking, understanding." These figures of speech can significantly impact the effectiveness of speeches and writing by adding layers of meaning and enhancing audience engagement. Understanding and using them skillfully can elevate your communication to a compelling level.

title: MODIFIERS
subject: English Language
rawText:
Modifiers A modifier is a word that describes another word or group of words or restrict its/their meaning in some way. Modifier are descriptive words. They are used to convey the exact feelings, emotions etc. and to make what we say or write vivid or more specific. It is an optional element in either a phrase or clause structure. The removal of the modifier does not affect the grammatical correctness of the structure. Using modifier means using appropriate word to describe persons, places or things. Examples: i. a man ii. an old man iii. a dirty old man iv. a dirty poor old man v. a dirty poor old man under the bridge A. Articles as modifiers. Examples A man of honour An eye for an eye The armed robber B. Adjectives as modifiers. Examples Dirty old man Young rich fool Bright students Red car Dark horse Nigerian men Many adjectives are found within noun phrases and thus acts as members of that group. They are called pre-modifiers or attributive adjectives. Examples My younger brother is in the university. The young and dynamic lecturer is around Three blind men went to C. Demonstratives as modifiers. Examples: These girls……

That book….. Those men…… This classroom……. D. Possessives as modifiers. Examples Our school Their house His dog Her book E. Adverbs as modifiers. Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs. Examples Modify the verb: The sick man slept soundly The man was killed yesterday Serious students study regularly. Modifier Adjective: The politician is passionately concerned The killing was absolutely unnecessary You are quite right. The man is quite ambitious. Ngozi is extremely kind Modify Adverb: He spoke quite rudely to the old man Mikel obi plays football very well They moved rather sluggishly towards the scene John does things extremely slowly. F. Adverbial Phrase as modifier. Examples She learnt French some years ago He saw the dog in the garden G. Adverbial clause as modifier. Examples Mr. Obi sold the old car because it was too small for the family. While I was trying to sleep, Sarah came in. Started early to struggle

title: HIV/AIDS
subject: English Language
rawText:
Lesson Note on:HIV/AIDS Meaning of HIV and AIDS  HIV : Human Immunodeficiency Virus. It is a virus that attacks the body’s immune system, specifically the white blood cells (CD4 cells), making it hard for the body to fight infections.  AIDS : Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome. It is the most advanced stage of HIV infection, where the immune system is badly damaged and the body can no longer fight off common diseases. Causes  HIV is caused by a virus that is transmitted through certain body fluids (blood, semen, vaginal fluids, breast milk). Modes of Transmission 1. Unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected person. 2. Transfusion of contaminated blood. 3. Sharing sharp objects (razor blades, needles, syringes) with an infected person. 4. From mother to child during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding. Symptoms of HIV/AIDS  Persistent fever  Rapid weight loss  Night sweats  Chronic diarrhoea  Skin rashes  Constant tiredness  Frequent infections (e.g. tuberculosis, pneumonia) Prevention  Abstinence from premarital sex

 Being faithful to one uninfected partner  Use of condoms during sexual intercourse  Screening of blood before transfusion  Avoid sharing sharp objects  HIV-positive mothers should seek medical care to reduce risk of infecting their babies Treatment  There is no permanent cure for HIV/AIDS.  Antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) are used to control the virus, prolong life, and keep patients healthy. Effects on Society  Increase in death rate among young and middle-aged people  Reduction in workforce and national productivity  High cost of healthcare and burden on families  Stigmatization and discrimination against infected persons Lesson Note on;Drug Abuse Meaning  Drug Abuse is the excessive or wrong use of drugs (legal or illegal) without following medical instructions, leading to harmful effects on the body and mind. Examples of Abused Drugs  Alcohol  Cigarettes/tobacco  Marijuana (Indian hemp)  Cocaine  Heroin  Tramadol, Codeine, and other painkillers or cough syrups

Causes of Drug Abuse 1. Peer pressure and bad company 2. Curiosity and experimentation 3. Frustration and stress relief 4. Easy access to drugs 5. Lack of parental care and supervision Effects of Drug Abuse On the Individual  Mental illness and hallucinations  Poor academic/work performance  Addiction and dependence  Increased risk of accidents  Health problems such as liver damage, lung cancer, and brain damage On Society  Increase in crime rate and violence  Family breakdown  High rate of unemployment  Burden on healthcare system  Social vices (armed robbery, cultism, prostitution) Prevention of Drug Abuse  Good parental guidance and care  Proper education on dangers of drug abuse  Avoiding bad peer groups  Strict government laws against drug trafficking and sales  Counselling and rehabilitation centres for addicts

title: LISTENING TO DEBATE FOR MAIN POINTS AND PASSING JU
subject: English Language
rawText:
A debate is a formal contest of argumentation in which two opposing teams defend and attack a given proposition. It is a persuasive manner of speaking with the aim of converting the view of another person or an audience to your own point of view. In debate writing, the speaker speaks or argues for or against the issue being discussed How to Write a Debate. Step one: Giving a strong opening, a good debate must start with a strong opening line. If you are discussing on something that is emotionally charged as debate topics tend to be, then you should start with a similar emotional opening to attract the interest of your audience. For example, where you are arguing for your country to take in more refugees, then you should have an opening like “have you ever thought about what it will be like to be forced to leave your home? To be so scared of violence or other persecution that you and your family have to leave behind everything you’ve ever known and travel to a new country?”. Don’t get caught up in the idea that facts are completely separate from emotions. For example, if you are arguing that your school should increase “Suicide awareness” you could start with, “Did you know that close to 800,000 people die of suicide every year?”. If your topic is not clearly emotional then give a topic that is filled with surprises or a topic having statistics can also inject some feelings into your opening line to arouse the interest of your audience and the judges too. Step two : Defining the Topic. After giving your opening, you must make the subject or topic you are talking about crystal clear to your audience. For you to do this, you have to state your topic i.e if you are against the topic or supporting it. For example, “Today we are here to discuss on the topic or motion X. As the proposing or opposing side, my team or I firmly believe that Y(doctors are more important than teachers). You must also define any keyword that is in your topic. It must not be a literal dictionary definition but it should be your own view on what the word means as regards to the topic or issue at large. Step three: Signposting. Signposting may appear to be annoying and unnecessary. Signposting means using phrases and words to guide the reader or listeners through the content of your essay, argument /dissertation. That is after your introduction, from time to time, you state your main arguments to remind your audience of what you are discussing on and where you stand because your audience may loose interest in the cause of the debate but where you restate your points, in the order in which you want to deliver them, maybe twice or thrice in between your argument, your audience will be kept attentive and in line with the debate until the end. Step four: Rebuttal It is a very important technique used in debates. It means picking one of the points your opponent has made and shredding it into pieces i.e disagreeing with the point your opponent has made. For you to use this technique, you have to prepare your points very well and think or prepare also on the points your opponent is likely to state using facts and figures if necessary. You have to do a thorough research on the debate topic properly to be able to rebute your opponents argument. Step Five: Your Arguments. For you to achieve success in any debate, you must develop your arguments or points very well.

Your points will be written in paragraphs and for you to build up a good paragraph, you must discuss extensively on your points leaving no stone unturned for each point you raise or discuss on by first deciding on what to discuss or argue, making a layout i.e arranging your points in a chronological order and coherent sentences, finding evidence, using persuasive strategies etc. Step six: Conclusion. The conclusion to any piece of writing is very important. It sums up the points you have made in the body of your write – up and leaves the reader with a take home message that should make them feel as if they’ve gained something by reading your work.

title: VOWEL/E/ AND /3:/
subject: English Language
rawText:
Vowel /e/: The vowel sound /e/ is a short and closed sound. It is produced with the mouth slightly open and the tongue in a mid-front position. Examples: \"bed,\" \"pet,\" \"let.\" Vowel /3:/: The vowel sound /3:/ is a long and open sound. It is pronounced with the mouth more open and the tongue in a mid-central position. Examples: \"bird,\" \"hurt,\" \"learn.\" The key difference between /e/ and /3:/ lies in the mouth position and length of pronunciation. /e/ is a shorter sound, while /3:/ is longer. Identifying the sound differences : /e/ sound: Say \"bed\". Feel your mouth - your tongue moves to the middle and spreads a little towards the front. This is the /e/ sound, like in \"red\", \"pen\", \"check\" /3:/ sound: Now, say \"bird\". Feel your tongue move further back in your mouth, and your lips almost form a circle. This is the /3:/ sound, like in \"girl\", \"shirt\" \"world\". letters rep.by sound words containing it \'e\' met, read, bed, help \'ea\' dead, read, breathe \'a\' any, many /3:/ \'er\' term, verb, serve \'ear\' earth, heard, early \'ir\' bird, girl, skirt \'ur\' turn, hurt, church \'our\' journey, courtesy, scourge \'or\' word, worst, world, worm The teacher guides the students in the transcription of some words that sounds the same as /3:/ as in burn /b:n/, turn /t3:n/, herb /h3:b/, girl /g3:1/, mercy /m3:si/, herd /h3:d/, perch /p3:tJ/, her /h3:/, service /s3:vis/, verb /V3:b/, serve /s3:v/, thirst /03:st/ occur /s:k3:/, church /t{3:tf/ nurse /n3:s/, bird /b3:d/, dirty /d:t/, first /f3:st/ /e/ e - belt, set, net, peg, red, bed, best, help, end, tell. eo - leopard, Geoffrey ea - weapon, instead, . /3:/ Ir - girl, firm, shirt,bird, dirt, birth, stir Ur - nurse, return, burn, burst, turn, er - term, verb, internal, servant, service. ear - earth, heard, early, earnest, learn or - worm, worst, worse, word, work, worship she guides students to make sentences with some of the words listed example:

• That red car belongs to Mr. Chima • That is not the end of the road • Let me go and help my sister • The weapon used during the Biafra war is too strong • The man is having internal bleeding > I heard him singing • Mr. Uche promised to finish the work today > Next Sunday I will worship in your church. How can we get better at using these sounds? Here are some fun exercises: Minimal Pairs: These are word buddies that sound almost identical except for one vowel sound! Try saying: "bed" vs "bird" Can you hear the difference in the vowel sound? Look and Say: Read these word lists and try pronouncing them clearly: /e/pet, ten, neck, yes, best /3:/ burn, first, thirst, nurse, curve

title: HUMAN INTERNAL BODY SYSTEM
subject: English Language
rawText:
Lesson notes on: The Internal Human Body Systems The human body is a complex, well-organized structure made up of different organs and tissues that work together to sustain life. These organs are grouped into systems that perform specific functions. Each system depends on the others, making the body an integrated whole. 1. Circulatory System (Cardiovascular System)  Main Organs : Heart, blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries), blood.  Functions : o Transports oxygen, nutrients, and hormones to cells. o Removes carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes. o Helps regulate body temperature and pH balance. o Provides defense against infections (through white blood cells). 2. Respiratory System  Main Organs : Nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs, alveoli.  Functions : o Facilitates gas exchange (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out). o Provides oxygen for cellular respiration. o Helps regulate blood pH. o Assists in producing speech. 3. Digestive System  Main Organs : Mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, liver, pancreas, gallbladder.  Functions : o Breaks down food into simple nutrients. o Absorbs nutrients into the bloodstream. o Eliminates undigested waste. o Provides energy for growth, repair, and body functions.

4. Nervous System  Main Organs : Brain, spinal cord, nerves, sensory organs.  Functions : o Controls body activities through electrical signals. o Coordinates voluntary and involuntary actions. o Processes information from the environment. o Maintains balance (homeostasis) with the endocrine system. 5. Endocrine System  Main Organs (Glands) : Pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, ovaries, testes.  Functions : o Produces and releases hormones. o Regulates metabolism, growth, reproduction, and stress response. o Maintains homeostasis with the nervous system. 6. Muscular System  Main Organs : Skeletal muscles, smooth muscles, cardiac muscle.  Functions : o Enables movement of the body and internal organs. o Maintains posture. o Generates heat through muscle activity. o Works with the skeletal system for locomotion. 7. Skeletal System  Main Organs : Bones, joints, cartilage, ligaments.  Functions : o Provides structural support for the body. o Protects vital organs (e.g., skull protects brain, ribs protect heart and lungs). o Produces blood cells in bone marrow (hematopoiesis). o Stores minerals like calcium and phosphorus.

8. Excretory/Urinary System  Main Organs : Kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra.  Functions : o Removes metabolic waste (urea, uric acid, excess salts). o Regulates water and electrolyte balance. o Maintains blood pressure. o Assists in pH regulation. 9. Immune/Lymphatic System  Main Organs : Lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils, lymphatic vessels, white blood cells.  Functions : o Defends the body against infections, diseases, and foreign substances. o Maintains fluid balance by returning leaked fluid to the blood. o Helps absorb fats from the digestive system. 10. Integumentary System (Skin System)  Main Organs : Skin, hair, nails, sweat glands, oil glands.  Functions : o Acts as the first line of defense against infections. o Protects internal organs from injury. o Regulates body temperature through sweating. o Prevents dehydration by reducing water loss. o Provides sensation (touch, pain, temperature). 11. Reproductive System  Main Organs : o Male: Testes, penis, vas deferens, prostate gland. o Female: Ovaries, uterus, fallopian tubes, vagina.  Functions : o Produces sex cells (sperm and eggs). o Ensures fertilization and development of offspring.

o Produces sex hormones (testosterone, estrogen, progesterone). Interdependence of Body Systems  The respiratory system provides oxygen to the circulatory system , which delivers it to cells.  The digestive system supplies nutrients that circulate through the blood.  The excretory system removes wastes filtered from blood by the kidneys.  The nervous and endocrine systems coordinate all body activities.  The immune system protects all systems from disease-causing agents. ✅ In summary, the internal human body systems are highly interconnected, and the proper functioning of one system often depends on the efficiency of others. Any failure in one system can affect the whole body.
