pages.text: Vowel /e/: The vowel sound /e/ is a short and closed sound. It is produced with the mouth slightly open and the tongue in a mid-front position. Examples: \"bed,\" \"pet,\" \"let.\" Vowel /3:/: The vowel sound /3:/ is a long and open sound. It is pronounced with the mouth more open and the tongue in a mid-central position. Examples: \"bird,\" \"hurt,\" \"learn.\" The key difference between /e/ and /3:/ lies in the mouth position and length of pronunciation. /e/ is a shorter sound, while /3:/ is longer. Identifying the sound differences : /e/ sound: Say \"bed\". Feel your mouth - your tongue moves to the middle and spreads a little towards the front. This is the /e/ sound, like in \"red\", \"pen\", \"check\" /3:/ sound: Now, say \"bird\". Feel your tongue move further back in your mouth, and your lips almost form a circle. This is the /3:/ sound, like in \"girl\", \"shirt\" \"world\". letters rep.by sound words containing it \'e\' met, read, bed, help \'ea\' dead, read, breathe \'a\' any, many /3:/ \'er\' term, verb, serve \'ear\' earth, heard, early \'ir\' bird, girl, skirt \'ur\' turn, hurt, church \'our\' journey, courtesy, scourge \'or\' word, worst, world, worm The teacher guides the students in the transcription of some words that sounds the same as /3:/ as in burn /b:n/, turn /t3:n/, herb /h3:b/, girl /g3:1/, mercy /m3:si/, herd /h3:d/, perch /p3:tJ/, her /h3:/, service /s3:vis/, verb /V3:b/, serve /s3:v/, thirst /03:st/ occur /s:k3:/, church /t{3:tf/ nurse /n3:s/, bird /b3:d/, dirty /d:t/, first /f3:st/ /e/ e - belt, set, net, peg, red, bed, best, help, end, tell. eo - leopard, Geoffrey ea - weapon, instead, . /3:/ Ir - girl, firm, shirt,bird, dirt, birth, stir Ur - nurse, return, burn, burst, turn, er - term, verb, internal, servant, service. ear - earth, heard, early, earnest, learn or - worm, worst, worse, word, work, worship she guides students to make sentences with some of the words listed example:

title: HUMAN INTERNAL BODY SYSTEM
subject: English Language
rawText:
Lesson notes on: The Internal Human Body Systems The human body is a complex, well-organized structure made up of different organs and tissues that work together to sustain life. These organs are grouped into systems that perform specific functions. Each system depends on the others, making the body an integrated whole. 1. Circulatory System (Cardiovascular System)  Main Organs : Heart, blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries), blood.  Functions : o Transports oxygen, nutrients, and hormones to cells. o Removes carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes. o Helps regulate body temperature and pH balance. o Provides defense against infections (through white blood cells). 2. Respiratory System  Main Organs : Nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs, alveoli.  Functions : o Facilitates gas exchange (oxygen in, carbon dioxide out). o Provides oxygen for cellular respiration. o Helps regulate blood pH. o Assists in producing speech. 3. Digestive System  Main Organs : Mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, liver, pancreas, gallbladder.  Functions : o Breaks down food into simple nutrients. o Absorbs nutrients into the bloodstream. o Eliminates undigested waste. o Provides energy for growth, repair, and body functions.

4. Nervous System  Main Organs : Brain, spinal cord, nerves, sensory organs.  Functions : o Controls body activities through electrical signals. o Coordinates voluntary and involuntary actions. o Processes information from the environment. o Maintains balance (homeostasis) with the endocrine system. 5. Endocrine System  Main Organs (Glands) : Pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, ovaries, testes.  Functions : o Produces and releases hormones. o Regulates metabolism, growth, reproduction, and stress response. o Maintains homeostasis with the nervous system. 6. Muscular System  Main Organs : Skeletal muscles, smooth muscles, cardiac muscle.  Functions : o Enables movement of the body and internal organs. o Maintains posture. o Generates heat through muscle activity. o Works with the skeletal system for locomotion. 7. Skeletal System  Main Organs : Bones, joints, cartilage, ligaments.  Functions : o Provides structural support for the body. o Protects vital organs (e.g., skull protects brain, ribs protect heart and lungs). o Produces blood cells in bone marrow (hematopoiesis). o Stores minerals like calcium and phosphorus.

8. Excretory/Urinary System  Main Organs : Kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra.  Functions : o Removes metabolic waste (urea, uric acid, excess salts). o Regulates water and electrolyte balance. o Maintains blood pressure. o Assists in pH regulation. 9. Immune/Lymphatic System  Main Organs : Lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils, lymphatic vessels, white blood cells.  Functions : o Defends the body against infections, diseases, and foreign substances. o Maintains fluid balance by returning leaked fluid to the blood. o Helps absorb fats from the digestive system. 10. Integumentary System (Skin System)  Main Organs : Skin, hair, nails, sweat glands, oil glands.  Functions : o Acts as the first line of defense against infections. o Protects internal organs from injury. o Regulates body temperature through sweating. o Prevents dehydration by reducing water loss. o Provides sensation (touch, pain, temperature). 11. Reproductive System  Main Organs : o Male: Testes, penis, vas deferens, prostate gland. o Female: Ovaries, uterus, fallopian tubes, vagina.  Functions : o Produces sex cells (sperm and eggs). o Ensures fertilization and development of offspring.

o Produces sex hormones (testosterone, estrogen, progesterone). Interdependence of Body Systems  The respiratory system provides oxygen to the circulatory system , which delivers it to cells.  The digestive system supplies nutrients that circulate through the blood.  The excretory system removes wastes filtered from blood by the kidneys.  The nervous and endocrine systems coordinate all body activities.  The immune system protects all systems from disease-causing agents. ✅ In summary, the internal human body systems are highly interconnected, and the proper functioning of one system often depends on the efficiency of others. Any failure in one system can affect the whole body.

title: EXPOSITORY ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText:
CONTINUOUS WRITING EXPOSITORY ESSAY ❖ Expository essays aim to provide a straightforward and clear explanation of a particular topic. ❖ These essays maintain objectivity, avoiding personal opinions and emotions. ❖ They are typically organized with an introduction, body paragraphs, and a conclusion for a logical and easy-to-follow presentation. ❖ This essay focuses on conveying facts, details, and evidence to educate and inform the audience. ❖ They prioritize clarity and precision in language using concise and direct expressions to enhance understanding. The term ‘expose’ means to reveal, therefore the term expository means a detailed explanation of how something is done or made. Expository essay as an impersonal writing which seeks to enlighten or give information about a particular thing. Requirements for Writing Expository Essays 1. The writer must know the subject matter and also know exactly how a process works or how a system work 2. The content of the expository essay must be carefully selected and arranged in sequential order 3. Your essay must be exciting in such a way that the reader may carry out what you have explained 4. Clarity is of paramount importance in writing expository essay so that the reader will not be confused but to be well informed 5. Your language should simple, correct and straight forward 6. You must have mastery of the topic connected with the subjected question. This will help you to be precise and clear in the explanation provided. 7. Usually, the present tense is used in writing an expository essay. It will not be appropriate to explain a process in past tense. Errors Students Make When Writing Expository Essays 1. Lack of good knowledge of the subject matter which results in scanty essay. 2. Lack of step-by-step explanation and process which results in unnecessary repetition. 3. The use of opinion rather than factors. Expository essay depends on facts only. 4. Poor paragraphing is another error made by the students when writing expository essay. Students don’t often know how to organize their points in paragraphs. 5. Creation of unnecessary paragraphs on each step. Teacher explains that in writing expository. Some steps could be followed in order not to have too many scanty paragraphs. Students are asked some possible topics for an expository essay.

Suggested Expository Essay Topics 1. Write an expository on how a bicycle or radio works. 2. Carefully describe the preparation of your favourite food in not less than 450 words. 3. Give a description of a mobile phone and explain how it works. ESSAY OUTLINE 1. Introduction • Hook (Start with something interesting) • Background information (a bit) • Thesis statement (clearly state what your essay will be about) 2. Body Paragraphs • Topic sentence (start each paragraph with a main idea) • Evidence (give details or examples to support the idea) • Analysis (explain why the information is important) • Transition (move smoothly to the next idea) 3. Conclusion • Restate thesis (remind the reader of your main point) • Summary • Closing sentence (end with a final thought or suggestion)

title: COMPREHENSION READING ON HIV AIDS OR DRUG ABUSE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Lesson Note on:HIV/AIDS Meaning of HIV and AIDS  HIV : Human Immunodeficiency Virus. It is a virus that attacks the body’s immune system, specifically the white blood cells (CD4 cells), making it hard for the body to fight infections.  AIDS : Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome. It is the most advanced stage of HIV infection, where the immune system is badly damaged and the body can no longer fight off common diseases. Causes  HIV is caused by a virus that is transmitted through certain body fluids (blood, semen, vaginal fluids, breast milk). Modes of Transmission 1. Unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected person. 2. Transfusion of contaminated blood. 3. Sharing sharp objects (razor blades, needles, syringes) with an infected person. 4. From mother to child during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding. Symptoms of HIV/AIDS  Persistent fever  Rapid weight loss  Night sweats  Chronic diarrhoea  Skin rashes  Constant tiredness  Frequent infections (e.g. tuberculosis, pneumonia) Prevention  Abstinence from premarital sex

 Being faithful to one uninfected partner  Use of condoms during sexual intercourse  Screening of blood before transfusion  Avoid sharing sharp objects  HIV-positive mothers should seek medical care to reduce risk of infecting their babies Treatment  There is no permanent cure for HIV/AIDS.  Antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) are used to control the virus, prolong life, and keep patients healthy. Effects on Society  Increase in death rate among young and middle-aged people  Reduction in workforce and national productivity  High cost of healthcare and burden on families  Stigmatization and discrimination against infected persons Lesson Note on;Drug Abuse Meaning  Drug Abuse is the excessive or wrong use of drugs (legal or illegal) without following medical instructions, leading to harmful effects on the body and mind. Examples of Abused Drugs  Alcohol  Cigarettes/tobacco  Marijuana (Indian hemp)  Cocaine  Heroin  Tramadol, Codeine, and other painkillers or cough syrups

Causes of Drug Abuse 1. Peer pressure and bad company 2. Curiosity and experimentation 3. Frustration and stress relief 4. Easy access to drugs 5. Lack of parental care and supervision Effects of Drug Abuse On the Individual  Mental illness and hallucinations  Poor academic/work performance  Addiction and dependence  Increased risk of accidents  Health problems such as liver damage, lung cancer, and brain damage On Society  Increase in crime rate and violence  Family breakdown  High rate of unemployment  Burden on healthcare system  Social vices (armed robbery, cultism, prostitution) Prevention of Drug Abuse  Good parental guidance and care  Proper education on dangers of drug abuse  Avoiding bad peer groups  Strict government laws against drug trafficking and sales  Counselling and rehabilitation centres for addicts

title: READING FOR IMPLIED MEANING
subject: English Language
rawText:
Reading for Implied Meaning: Reading comprehension is the ability to understand and interpret a text, not just at face value but also to grasp implied meanings, hidden meanings, and deeper messages within the text. Reading for implied meaning is a crucial skill that goes beyond basic understanding. This type of reading requires one to read between the lines and it helps to sharpen the critical thinking skills of the learners. Expository composition is defined as a style of composition that exposes/explain a topic using facts. Examples of expository essay are scientific reports, academic essay and magazine article. State rules/features of expository composition. 1. Informative: it must contain adequate information. 2. Clarity: using words that clearly express the author's message. 3. Organization of text: it has to be well-written in order to focus on the topic and list events in chronological order. 4. Unbiased: understanding the topic to enable the writer to write with an unbiased mind Steps in writing an expository essay 1. To conduct an extensive research on the topic at hand. 2. Pick a structure for the essay. 3. Formulate a thesis statement. 4. Write the introductory paragraph 5. Write the body paragraph 6. Summarize the expository essays. Here's a brief note to help you improve your reading comprehension in this aspect: 1. Pay Attention: When you read, ask yourself questions like, "What's the author trying to tell me without saying it directly?" 2. Look for Clues: See if there are hints or clues in the story that help you figure out what is not said plainly. 3. Make Smart Guesses: Sometimes, you need to guess what is happening based on what you read around it. 4. Feel the Mood: Think about how the story makes you feel. That can give you a clue about what's hiding in the story. 5. Symbols and Secrets: Keep an eye out for special words or things in the story that might mean more than they seem. 6. Think About Characters: Try to understand why characters in the story do what they do. What are they not telling you? 7. What's Not Said: Sometimes, it's important to think about what the characters are not saying out loud. 8. Think About the Time and Place: Consider when and where the story happens. This can help you understand hidden meanings. 9. Read Again: Don't be afraid to read a story more than once. You might catch things you missed the first time. 10. Talk About It: - Share your thoughts with your small group, friends or a teacher. They might have cool ideas about

the story. 11. Keep Practicing: - The more you read and think like this, the better you'll get at finding hidden meanings. 12. Ask for Help: - If you ever get stuck, don't hesitate to ask your teacher or someone you trust for help.

title: READING TO IMPLIED MEANING
subject: English Language
rawText: Reading for Implied meaning Reading for implied meaning is reading to fill in certain gaps in which some explanations are left out. The essence of language use is to communicate and the essence of communication is to make meaning. However, while expressing our ideas, feelings and thoughts, some messages are stated openly while others are inferred. To infer means to form an opinion that something is true based on the information you have at your disposal. Therefore, when information is not stated openly, we may guess, assume, conclude or infer. In that same way, meanings can be stated openly or implied. In brief, implied meaning is what is deduced from the passage we read. What are the tips we must note to imply meaning from the passages we read? 1) Keep asking questions. Questions such as where? Why? When? How? Will shed more light in the content of the passage. 2) Keep linking ideas as you read on. This will help you to understand the writer's line of development, and to find out when a gap is created. 3) Your world view. Your background knowledge of a topic may assist you to decipher implied meaning. 4) When you notice something is amiss, you assumed what has happened. This assumption may make draw some conclusions which will in turn help you to locate the implied meaning. When implying meanings from the passage, we can use expressions such as; 1. It means that…….. 2. We can, then, say….. 3. We can deduct……… 4. This suggest that…… 5. It implies that…… 6. We can conclude that….. Read the passage on page 107-109 of Your New Secondary English Course Book 2. Discuss the passage in groups and then share your thoughts with group members. Answer the questions on the passage and do peers review with group members. Answers: a) Dr. Obioma frequently went on tour to supervise his clinics. b) She was shouting because she was anxious about her children's safety. c) i. The man in the three-piece suit was the leader of the robbery gang. ii. Mrs. Obioma decided not to report the matter because she thought it was unsafe to disclose the identity of the robbers. d) The discreet act was not revealing that the man in the three-piece suit was the thief. e) The robbers brought back everything they had stolen at the promised time. f) "…shocked to the marrow with fear". i. Grammatical name: Adjectival or Relative Phrase. ii. Function: it qualifies the noun phrase " The woman". G) i.take on----- challenge, face, confront, fight, oppose ii. uninhibited: ---- freely, unchallenged, unrestrained, iii. realised--- learnt, discovered, found out, noticed. iv. composed ---- relaxed, unruffled, calm v. resuscitate:--- revive, bring back to life

title: ANSWERS TO COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS
subject: English Language
rawText:
Question (i) What does the author mean when he says “make hay while the sun shines”?  It means students should take advantage of their time in school and study hard while they still have the opportunity, instead of wasting time. Question (ii) State two conditions which constitute students’ lack of seriousness in class.  Sleeping during lessons.  Engaging in negative or distracting activities instead of concentrating. (Other answers could be: not doing assignments, coming late to class, or gossiping during lessons.) Question (iii) What do the carefree students hope will finally save them?  They hope that luck, help from the invigilator, or some miracle will help them pass the examination. Question (iv) What grammatical name is given to this expression as it is used in the passage: “who do not heed this advice”  Grammatical name : It is a Relative Clause .

Question (v) What is its function?  It functions as an adjectival clause because it describes/qualifies the noun “students” . Question (vi) “When examinations come knocking at the door” 1. What figure of speech is contained in the above expression? o It is Personification (because examinations are given the human action of “knocking at the door”). 2. What does it mean? o It means that the period of examination is approaching or has arrived. ✅

title: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH COMMERCE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Words Associated with Commerce Commerce is the branch of production engaged in the distribution of goods and services on a large scale. It also includes all others that aid services which make mass distribution possible. Words associated with commerce Trade, Ware housing, Transport, Wholesale Banking, Labour Insurance, Capital, Advertising ,Retailer, Goods, Entrepreneur, Stock, Business, Marketplace, Bartering, Black market etc Meaning of some words related to commerce Bank – this is an institution set up purposely for safe keeping of money. Insurance – This is a provision made for the protection of persons or objects against risks. Advertising – This is a means of bringing the existence or production of new goods and services to the knowledge of members of the public and to persuade them to buy and use the goods and services. Warehousing – this is the act of storing goods produced ahead of demand until the time they will be needed. business : : a usually commercial or mercantile activity engaged in as a means of livelihood : trade , line in the restaurant business marketplace : : an open square or place in a town where markets or public sales are held trade : : the business of buying and selling or bartering commodities : commerce free trade : : trade based on the unrestricted international exchange of goods with tariffs used only as a source of revenue black market : : to buy or sell goods in the black market gray market : : a market employing irregular but not illegal methods dealings : : method of business : manner of conduct horse-trading : : negotiation accompanied by shrewd bargaining and reciprocal concessions a political horse trade e-tail : : retail business conducted online via the World Wide Web merchandising : : sales promotion as a comprehensive function including market research, development of new products, coordination of manufacture and marketing, and effective advertising and selling

retailing : : the activities involved in the selling of goods to ultimate consumers for personal or household consumption wholesaling : : the sale of commodities in quantity usually for resale (as by a retail merchant) bartering : : to trade by exchanging one commodity for another : to trade goods or services in exchange for other goods or services farmers bartering for supplies with their crops bartered with the store’s owner. sentences with words related to commerce i) They offered discounts to the traders. ii) The goods were damaged during transport. iii) I want to set up a business with a good capital. iv) John should go and check in the warehouse. v) Her mother sells in wholesale prices.

subject: English Language
rawText: WEEK 11 I. SPEECH: Selected vowel sounds /u/ and /u:/ sounds. /u/ is a short back vowel. The shape of the lip during its production is rounded while the position of the jaw is half open. The spelling symbols includes “o” as in w oman, bosom. “oo” as in w ood, foot, took, good, wool, stool etc. “ou” as in w ould, could, should, courier. “u” as in p ut, pull, pulpit, sugar. /u:/ Is a long and back vowel. The manner of the articulation is same as /u/ except that the position of the jaw is close. The spelling symbols include: “o” as in wh o, do, two, whose, lose etc. “oo” ss in p ool, fool, balloon, saloon, school. “ou” as In youth, c oup, rouge, group. “ew” as in m ew, stew, few, screw etc “ui” as in juice, fruit, suit. “oe” as in canoes, shoe. “eu” as in feud, queue, cl ue. “u” as in students, crucle, c lue etc /u/ /u:/ Full Fool Could womb Wool Cool Wound Wounds etc.

title: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH AGRICULTURE
subject: English Language
rawText: Words Associated with Agriculture and Horticulture. Agriculture is the science or practice of farming, including cultivation of soil, growing of crops and rearing of animal for human consumption. Horticulture is the cultivation of a garden, orchard, or nursery; the cultivation of flowers, fruits, vegetables, or ornamental plants. While agriculture and horticulture are very similar and often used together, there is a subtle difference between the fields. Horticulture is a sub-division of agriculture. Agriculture is the cultivation of both plants and animals, usually for consumption by humans. Horticulture focuses strictly on plants and also involves plant use for aesthetic purposes instead of just consumption. Words associated with Agriculture and horticulture agriculture, nursery, crop, maize, fruit, plants, bedding, fishing, harvest, crop rotation, good harvest, husbandry, mixed farming, pastoral farming, aquaculture, mono cropping, floriculture gardening, husbandry, garden , landscape, botany, landscaping, farming, vegetable, agricultural, arboriculture, horticultural, horticulturist, cultivation agronomy viticulture botanical entomology forestry handicraft sericulture hydroponics zoology dairying beekeeping bonsai aquaculture microbiology science botanic wildflower parasitology silviculture arboretum ecology grower livestock agribusiness museology agroforestry floristry Meaning 1. Crop; any plant cultivated by people 2. Garden; a plot of ground where herbs, fruits, flowers, or vegetables are cultivated. 3. Arboricultural; the cultivation of trees and shrubs especially for ornamental purposes. 4. Monocultural; the cultivation or growth of a single crop or organism especially on agricultural or forest land. 5. Farming; The practice of intentionally performing an agricultural activity, such as growing crops or raising livestock, on land dedicated to the purpose, known as a farm. 6. Mono-cropping; The practice of growing a single crop repeatedly on the same land for many consecutive growing seasons. 7. Nursery; A nursery is a place where plants are propagated and grown to a desired size.

title: MODAL AUXILIARY VERBS
subject: English Language
rawText:
*Modal auxiliary verb* is an auxiliary verb that comes before the main verb to show the speaker ’ s attitude or mood. It expresses ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice, willingness, or probability. Modal verbs have 3 special rules: 1 They do not change for person or tense. He can, not He cans 2 They have no infinitive or participle form 3 They are followed by the base form of the main verb. She must go, not She must goes All Modal Auxiliary Verbs in English The 9 core modals plus 1 marginal modal are: 1. Can Uses 1 Ability Example: I can ride a bicycle 2 Permission informal Example: Can I use your phone 3 Possibility Example: It can get very hot here 2. Could Uses 1 Past ability Example: She could speak French at age 5 2 Polite request Example: Could you pass me the salt 3 Possibility less certain than can Example: It could rain tonight 3. May Uses 1 Permission formal Example: May I come in 2 Possibility Example: He may be at home now 3 Wish Example: May you succeed 4. Might Uses 1 Less certain possibility than may Example: She might join us later 2 Polite suggestion

Example: You might want to rest 5. Will Uses 1 Future action Example: They will arrive tomorrow 2 Promise Example: I will help you 3 Willingness or offer Example: I will carry that for you 6. Would Uses 1 Habit in the past Example: He would visit us every Sunday 2 Polite request Example: Would you close the window 3 Conditional or imagined situation Example: I would travel if I had money 7. Shall Uses 1 Future with I and We formal Example: I shall be 30 next year 2 Offer or suggestion Example: Shall I open the door 3 Command or promise Example: You shall obey the rules 8. Should Uses 1 Advice Example: You should drink more water 2 Duty or expectation Example: Students should respect teachers 3 Probability Example: He should be here soon 9. Must Uses 1 Strong obligation or necessity Example: You must wear a seatbelt 2 Logical conclusion Example: She must be the manager she is giving orders

3 Prohibition in negative Example: You must not enter 10. Ought to Uses 1 Advice or moral duty Example: We ought to help the poor 2 Recommendation Example: You ought to see a doctor Good Comparison of All Modal Auxiliary Verbs The main differences are strength, time, and formality. *1 Comparison of Possibility and Certainty from strongest to weakest* Must shows strong certainty Example: He must be at work now I see his car Will shows future certainty Example: It will rain tomorrow Should shows strong probability but not 100 percent Example: She should pass the exam she studied hard May shows possibility 50 percent Example: It may rain this evening Might shows weaker possibility than may Example: It might rain this evening Could shows possibility but also doubt Example: He could be lying I am not sure *2 Comparison of Permission from formal to informal* May is most formal Example: May I speak to the principal Can is informal Example: Can I speak to the principal Could is polite informal Example: Could I speak to the principal *3 Comparison of Obligation from strongest to weakest* Must shows strong obligation or rule Example: You must submit your work today Ought to shows moral duty Example: You ought to apologize Should shows advice or weaker obligation Example: You should apologize *4 Comparison of Past forms*

Can becomes could for past ability Example: Now I can swim. When I was 5 I could swim Will becomes would for future in the past or habit Example: He said he will come. He said he would come. He would always sing after dinner *5 Comparison of Offers and Requests* Shall I is used for offers Example: Shall I make tea Will you is used for requests Example: Will you make tea Would you is more polite request Example: Would you make tea

pages.text: *Modal auxiliary verb* is an auxiliary verb that comes before the main verb to show the speaker ’ s attitude or mood. It expresses ability, permission, possibility, obligation, advice, willingness, or probability. Modal verbs have 3 special rules: 1 They do not change for person or tense. He can, not He cans 2 They have no infinitive or participle form 3 They are followed by the base form of the main verb. She must go, not She must goes All Modal Auxiliary Verbs in English The 9 core modals plus 1 marginal modal are: 1. Can Uses 1 Ability Example: I can ride a bicycle 2 Permission informal Example: Can I use your phone 3 Possibility Example: It can get very hot here 2. Could Uses 1 Past ability Example: She could speak French at age 5 2 Polite request Example: Could you pass me the salt 3 Possibility less certain than can Example: It could rain tonight 3. May Uses 1 Permission formal Example: May I come in 2 Possibility Example: He may be at home now 3 Wish Example: May you succeed 4. Might Uses 1 Less certain possibility than may Example: She might join us later 2 Polite suggestion

Example: You might want to rest 5. Will Uses 1 Future action Example: They will arrive tomorrow 2 Promise Example: I will help you 3 Willingness or offer Example: I will carry that for you 6. title: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH HEALTH
subject: English Language
rawText:
Lesson Note on: Words Associated with Health Health is a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. In English, many words are linked with health, covering areas such as diseases, body parts, medicines, treatments, and general wellness. 1. General Health Vocabulary  Health – the general condition of the body and mind.  Well-being – a state of being comfortable, healthy, or happy.  Fitness – being physically strong and in good condition.  Nutrition – the process of obtaining food necessary for health and growth.  Immunity – the body’s ability to resist diseases. 2. Common Health Professionals  Doctor – a person qualified to treat the sick.  Nurse – one who cares for the sick in a hospital or clinic.  Pharmacist – prepares and sells medicine.  Surgeon – a doctor who performs operations.  Dentist – a doctor who treats teeth and gums.  Surgeon -a doctor that carries out an operation on the body 3. Places Connected with Health  Hospital – a place where sick or injured people are treated.  Clinic – a small health center for treatment.  Pharmacy/Chemist – where medicines are dispensed.  Laboratory – a place for medical tests.  Ward – a room in a hospital for patients.

4. Sickness and Diseases  Illness – a general word for being sick.  Disease – a disorder of the body (e.g., malaria, diabetes).  Infection – caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi.  Injury – harm caused to the body (e.g., cut, burn, fracture).  Epidemic – widespread outbreak of a disease in a community.  Pandemic – a global outbreak of a disease. 5. Symptoms of Poor Health; This is how we can understand that we are not feeling very well.  Fever – high body temperature.  Cough – sudden expulsion of air from the lungs.  Headache – pain in the head.  Nausea – feeling of sickness with an urge to vomit.  Fatigue – extreme tiredness.  Pain – unpleasant feeling due to injury or illness. 6. Medicines and Treatment  Drug/Medicine – a substance used to cure or prevent disease.  Antibiotics – medicines that kill bacteria.  Vaccine – given to protect against diseases.  Surgery – treatment by operation.  Therapy – treatment for illness (e.g., physiotherapy, psychotherapy).  First Aid – immediate care given to an injured or sick person. 7. Healthy Living Practices  Exercise – physical activity to keep fit.  Hygiene – cleanliness to maintain health.  Balanced diet – eating all food groups in the right proportion.  Rest – relaxation and sleep.  Vaccination – taking preventive injections.  Sanitation – keeping the environment clean.

8. Words Associated with Mental Health  Stress – mental strain or pressure.  Depression – prolonged sadness and loss of interest.  Anxiety – nervousness or worry.  Counseling – professional advice and support.  Meditation – practice of calming the mind. Conclusion Words associated with health cover a wide range of vocabulary related to the body, diseases, doctors, hospitals, medicines, and healthy living. Knowing these terms helps us describe health issues clearly, communicate with medical professionals, and understand how to live a healthy life.

title: STRUCTURE :CLAUSE-FEATURES AND TYPES
subject: English Language
rawText:
*A clause* is a group of words that contains both a *subject* and a *predicate (verb)*. It’s the basic building block of a sentence. Think of it this way: if it has someone/something doing an action, it’s a clause. *Features of a clause* 1. *Has a subject*: The person, place, thing, or idea the clause is about Example: _The dog_ barked. 2. *Has a predicate/verb*: Says what the subject does or is Example: The dog _barked_. 3. *Expresses an idea*: Can be complete on its own or depend on another clause 4. *Different from a phrase*: A phrase doesn’t have both subject + verb Phrase: _in the morning_ — no subject, no verb Clause: _we left in the morning_ — has “we” + “left” *Types of clauses* There are 2 main types, based on whether they can stand alone: *1. Independent Clause / Main Clause* *Features*: - Has subject + verb - Expresses a complete thought - Can be a sentence by itself *Examples*:

- _Nigeria launched a satellite._ - _NASRDA develops space technology._ - _I studied all night._ *2. Dependent Clause / Subordinate Clause* *Features*: - Has subject + verb - *Does NOT* express a complete thought - Cannot stand alone — needs an independent clause - Usually starts with a subordinating word like _because, although, when, if, that, who, which_ *Examples*: - _Because Nigeria launched a satellite_ — incomplete, needs more - _When NASRDA develops space tech_ — incomplete - _If I study all night_ — incomplete Put them together: _Because Nigeria launched a satellite, communication improved._ *3 Common types of dependent clauses, by job* Type Job in sentence Subordinating words Example **Noun clause** Acts like a noun — subject, object, complement that, what, who, whether, if, why *What she discovered* surprised everyone. I know *that NASRDA was formed in 1999*. **Adjective clause** Describes a noun/pronoun — starts with relative pronouns who, whom, whose, which, that The agency *that built the satellite* is NASRDA. Students *who study space science* work here.

**Adverb clause** Describes verb, adjective, or adverb — tells when, where, why, how when, while, because, if, although, since *When the satellite launched*, we celebrated. She works hard *because she loves space research*.

Healthy Living Practices  Exercise – physical activity to keep fit.  Hygiene – cleanliness to maintain health.  Balanced diet – eating all food groups in the right proportion.  Rest – relaxation and sleep.  Vaccination – taking preventive injections.  Sanitation – keeping the environment clean.

8. Words Associated with Mental Health  Stress – mental strain or pressure.  Depression – prolonged sadness and loss of interest.  Anxiety – nervousness or worry.  Counseling – professional advice and support.  Meditation – practice of calming the mind. Conclusion Words associated with health cover a wide range of vocabulary related to the body, diseases, doctors, hospitals, medicines, and healthy living. Knowing these terms helps us describe health issues clearly, communicate with medical professionals, and understand how to live a healthy life.

title: PRESERVATIVE PREFIX
subject: English Language
rawText: Preservative prefix Preservative prefixes are those syllables added to the beginning of certain words to convey the meaning of an action that is repeated. This type of prefix is mostly introduced with the syllable "-re" Preservative prefix can be seen as tending to keep safe, sound or free from decay; just like the preservative quality of salt. The prefix that ensures the words remain in their quality or condition without changing is known as "RE". RE simply means to do it again a new or back. Preservative prefixes is a prefix that keeps the present quality of a word from changing. Preservative prefixes 'Re' as in: Work - rework Examine - reexamine Affirm - reassure Consider - reconsider Count - recount Cast - recast Elect - re-elect Form - reform Preservative prefixes are those syllables added to the beginning of certain words to convey the meaning of an action that is repeated. This type of prefix is mostly introduced with the syllable "-re" For example: visit → revisit cast → Recast elect → re-elect print → reprint do → redo count → recount set → rest take → retake assure → re-assure tell → retell run → Rerun assure → reassure occur → reoccur examine → re-examine build → rebuild make → remake sit → re-sit write → rewrite consider → reconsider affirm → reaffirm load → reload Examples: 1. Chidi was asked to resit for common Entrance Examination. 2. He tried to recall who had borrowed his book. 3. Due to ugly building, the landlord wants to repaint it before his wife burial.

title: PRONOUNS
subject: English Language
rawText:
Pronoun Pronouns are words used in place of nouns or noun phrases. They are used mainly to avoid repetition of nouns which makes a sentence or passage boring. Types of Pronoun. 1. Personal pronoun 2. Possessive pronoun 3. Demonstrative pronoun 4. Interrogative pronoun 5. Relative pronoun 6. Reflexive pronoun 1. A relative pronoun is that which introduces a clause known as relative clause and links it with the word which precedes it and to which it refers. It joins two parts of a sentence. Examples "Here is the money I promise to give to you" These two sentences can be joined with the use of relative pronoun to become "Here is the money which I promised to give to you." Examples of Relative pronouns are; who, which, whom, whose, that. NOTE: "who" is used for people and"which" for thing when a subject pronoun is needed. 1a. The woman thanked us b. we helped the woman The woman whom we helped thanked us. 2a. The car broke down b. David hired the car The car which David hired broke down. 2. Demonstrative Pronouns ; These are so called because they point out or demonstrates particular person, places or things. The English demonstrative Pronouns are; This, these, that and those. This and that are singular while these and those are plural. This and these are use for object that are near, while that and those are used for distant objects. Examples 1. This is my friend. 2. These are my children. 3. That is her shop. 4. Those are my cars. Functions of Pronoun Pronouns can serve as; 1. The subject of a sentence as; (i) I am a teacher (ii) These are my cousins. 2. Object of a verb (i) Mary loves him ( direct object) (ii) Musa gave me the book (indirect object) 3. Complement of a subject (i) Who are you? (ii) That's him standing on the main road. 4. Complement of an object (i) He considered the culprit to be you 5. Complement of a preposition

(i) Give the book to him. (ii) She does not want to come with us.

title: NASAL SOUNDS
subject: English Language
rawText:
Nasal sounds The m, n, and ng sounds are produced with air movement through the nose. If you hold your nose, you cannot produce these sounds in the same way. The M consonant sound (IPA symbol: /m/) is made by lightly pressing your lips together while making the sound with your vocal chords. Although most of the air moves over your soft palate, some air moves through the nose, and it feels like it is vibrating through your nasal passage. This is why the M consonant is referred to as a nasal sound. Practice the M sound by saying these words aloud: 1) m o m 2) co m e 3) m y 4) m iss 5) ti m e 6) m an 7) M ary 8) di m 9) m ay 10) ra m The N consonant sound (IPA symbol: /n/) is made by moving air through the nasal passage. Your lips will be slightly parted. The tongue touches the roof your mouth just behind your teeth. You should feel a vibration in your nose. Practice the N sound by saying these words aloud: 1) n ap 2) ma n 3) n o 4) n o n e

5) n ot 6) n i n e 7) te n 8) wi n 9) ti n y 10) ru nn i n g Can you feel the vibration in your nose? You can't study the N sound without also studying the ng sound (IPA symbol: / ŋ /). This is the third nasal sound in English. It is also produced by moving air through your nasal passage, but the tongue placement is different than the N sound. Your tongue is raised and further back in your mouth. Practice the ng sound by saying these words aloud: 1) si ng 2) si ng er 3) ri ng 4) thi ng 5) stri ng 6) wi ng s 7) bri ng 8) bri ng i ng 9) ha ng 10) E ng lish The M sounds are blue . The N sounds are green . The ng sounds are red .

1) M y m o m si ng s. 2) N o, the dog is n ot m i n e. 3) That ri ng is n ice. 4) Co m e here n ow! 5) What is the m a n 's n a m e? 6) Bri ng m e n i n e thi ng s. 7) N a n cy kn ows hi m . 8) Bri ng the ha ng ers to m e! 9) M ary si ng s at n ight. 10) Lear n i ng E ng lish is fu n !

title: EXPOSITORY ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText: Expository Essay An expository essay provides a clear, focused explanation of a particular topic, process, or set of ideas. It doesn't set out to prove a point, just to give a balanced view of its subject matter. Five of the most common types of expository writing are descriptive essays, process essays, comparison essays, cause/effect essays and problem/solution essays. Topics on Expository The Causes and Effects of Air Pollution. • How Bullying Affects the Well-being of Students. • The Impact of Fast Food Consumption on Health. • The Causes and Consequences of Deforestation. • The Effects of Video Games on Children's Behavior. • The Influence of Parental Divorce on Children. Most expository paragraphs do the following things: 1. Start with a topic sentence, which explains what the paragraph will be about. 2. Then, include 3–5 body sentences that provide supporting details for the topic sentence. 3. Finally, wrap things up with a closing sentence that summarizes what the paragraph has said.

WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH PLUMBING Plumbing is the process of pipe installation to allow water movement. Some words associated with plumbing : Sewage, suckaway, zinc, toilet, water, pipe, plumber, thread, overhead tank, borehole, engine, pumping machine, fixing, plastering, joining, cutting, welding, soldering, plumbing vent, snaking. PLUMBING EXERCISES Exercise 1: Plumbing is a vital aspect of modern living, ensuring the smooth flow of water and the efficient removal of waste from homes and buildings. Here are some questions to test your knowledge: 1. Plumbing systems often consist of __________, pipes, fixtures, and fittings. a) wires b) cables c) drains d) circuits 2. The primary material used for water supply pipes in plumbing is __________. a) copper b) wood c) plastic d) aluminum 3. One of the main purposes of a __________ is to prevent backflow of water into the main supply. a) faucet b) check valve c) showerhead d) hose 4. The process of joining two metal pieces together in plumbing is called __________. a) welding b) soldering c) bolting d) gluing 5. A device used to regulate water pressure in plumbing systems is called a __________. a) pressure cooker b) pressure gauge c) pressure valve d) pressure regulator 6. The most common type of pipe used for draining waste water in plumbing is __________. a) PVC b) PEX c) ABS d) HDPE 7. In plumbing, a device that controls the flow of water by opening or closing a passageway is called a __________. a) valve b) faucet c) regulator d) hose

8. The term "septic tank" refers to a __________ used for wastewater treatment in areas without centralized sewer systems. a) large pipe b) underground chamber c) water heater d) filtration unit 9. Plumbing vents are designed to __________. a) remove waste water b) supply clean water c) provide air circulation d) regulate water pressure 10. The process of removing clogs or blockages from pipes using specialized tools is called __________. a) excavation b) demolition c) snaking d) sealing Exercise 2: As a plumbing apprentice, Jake was eager to learn the ins and outs of the trade. His mentor, Mark, a seasoned plumber, took him under his wing to show him the ropes. 1. One of the first lessons Mark taught Jake was about the importance of using high-quality __________ in plumbing projects. a) screws b) pipes c) tiles d) nails 2. "Always remember," Mark said, "copper is the preferred material for water supply pipes due to its durability and resistance to corrosion. Plastic pipes may be suitable for certain applications, but they can't match the longevity of __________." a) steel b) copper c) aluminum d) PVC 3. As they inspected a leaky faucet in a client's kitchen, Mark explained the function of a __________, which controls the flow of water and mixes hot and cold water to achieve the desired temperature. a) sprinkler b) faucet c) showerhead d) valve 4. While repairing a burst pipe in the basement, Jake learned how to properly __________ two pieces of metal together using a blowtorch and solder. a) weld b) bolt c) glue d) solder

5. "A pressure regulator is crucial," Mark emphasized, "as it ensures that water flows at a consistent pressure throughout the plumbing system, preventing damage to __________ and appliances." a) pipes b) tiles c) faucets d) mirrors 6. Later that day, they tackled a drainage issue in the backyard. Mark explained that __________ pipes are commonly used for drainage systems due to their durability and resistance to chemicals. a) PVC b) copper c) steel d) aluminum 7. As they replaced an old valve under the sink, Jake asked about the purpose of a __________. Mark explained that it prevents backflow of water, ensuring that contaminated water doesn't enter the main supply. a) check valve b) gate valve c) ball valve d) pressure valve 8. "In areas without access to municipal sewer systems," Mark said, "a septic tank is essential for wastewater treatment. It acts as a __________, breaking down solids and allowing liquid to be absorbed into the soil." a) filtration unit b) water heater c) pressure gauge d) septic tank 9. Mark pointed to the pipes protruding from the roof and explained that those were plumbing vents. "Their primary purpose is to __________, ensuring that wastewater flows smoothly and preventing the buildup of gases in the pipes." a) remove waste water b) provide air circulation c) supply clean water d) regulate water pressure 10. After a long day of troubleshooting and repairs, Mark showed Jake how to use a plumbing snake to clear a stubborn clog in the main sewer line. "Snaking is a common technique for __________ blockages and restoring proper flow." a) excavating b) demolishing c) snaking d) sealing

title: CLAUSES
subject: English Language
rawText:
Clauses A Clause is a group of words containing one finite verb and a main subject. It is like a sentence when it is capable of standing alone. It could also, however be introduced by such words as who, that, which, when and so forth. It will be incapable of standing alone in this instance. The former is referred to as subordinate or dependent clause. THE MAIN CLAUSE: This can stand on its own to make a complete sense or sentence. Example;  I am going home now.  The choir came and ministered Subordinate clause Features:  It is a group of words  It always has a finite verb  It does not express a complete thought.it needs the main clause to make a complete sense or sentence  It only forms part of the sentence. Examples;  As soon as the boy saw the teacher, he took to his heels.  Unless he passes the examination, he will not travel abroad. TYPE OF SUBORDINATE CLAUSES There are three types of subordinate clauses, namely: noun clause, relative or adjectival clause and adverbial clause.

Noun or Nominal Clauses: this clause behaves like a noun or noun phrase. Therefore, it functions as subject of verbs, object of verb and object of preposition in a sentence. It is introduced by any of such typical words as that,why,whether,how,what and so forth. Examples; Subject of the verb How Sola passed the examination beets the imagination of her teachers Functions: Subject of the verb “beats” Why he refused to put in his letter of resignation is best known to him Functions: Subject of the verb “is known “ Subject complement Examples;  The good news is that he passed his ICAN examination  The underlined noun clause refers to the good news. It is the same thing as the good news Object of the verb Examples; The authority awarded what is termed punctuality award. Functions: Object of the verb “awarded”.

The suspect eventually accepted that he was guilty Function: The object of the verb “accepted” Object complement Examples: The authority gave the student what is termed award for excellence. Function: compliment of the object “student” The robbers killed the man because he did not give them what they demanded for. Functions: Compliment of the object “them” Adverbial clause: It behaves like an adverb, meaning it modifies verbs, adjectives an adverbs. It falls into several categories depending on the introductory word employed. Examples: Time: since, while, when, after, before, He had arrived since the rain started Function: It modifies the verb”arrived” Place:, whenever

The dog hid where the puppies slept Purpose: That, so that, in order that. He suffered insult so that he might have peace. Cause: Because, as, in as much as, that, Because she was impatient, I hurried home. Concession: Although, though, even, if, Although Ade is physically handicapped, he is very hardworking Condition: if, unless, provided, incase. I will present a paper, if I pay the registration fee. Comparison: as, than. She is more brilliant than I am.

It falls into several categories depending on the introductory word employed. Examples: Time: since, while, when, after, before, He had arrived since the rain started Function: It modifies the verb”arrived” Place:, whenever

The dog hid where the puppies slept Purpose: That, so that, in order that. He suffered insult so that he might have peace. Cause: Because, as, in as much as, that, Because she was impatient, I hurried home. Concession: Although, though, even, if, Although Ade is physically handicapped, he is very hardworking Condition: if, unless, provided, incase. I will present a paper, if I pay the registration fee. Comparison: as, than. She is more brilliant than I am.

title: EXPOSITORY ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText: Expository Essay An expository essay provides a clear, focused explanation of a particular topic, process, or set of ideas. It doesn't set out to prove a point, just to give a balanced view of its subject matter. Five of the most common types of expository writing are descriptive essays, process essays, comparison essays, cause/effect essays and problem/solution essays. Topics on Expository The Causes and Effects of Air Pollution. • How Bullying Affects the Well-being of Students. • The Impact of Fast Food Consumption on Health. • The Causes and Consequences of Deforestation. • The Effects of Video Games on Children's Behavior. • The Influence of Parental Divorce on Children. Most expository paragraphs do the following things: 1. Start with a topic sentence, which explains what the paragraph will be about. 2. Then, include 3–5 body sentences that provide supporting details for the topic sentence. 3. Finally, wrap things up with a closing sentence that summarizes what the paragraph has said.

title: ADVERBS OF COMPARISON
subject: English Language
rawText:
Structure - Comparison and functions of Adverbs. An adverb is a word that modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb in a sentence. They are words that supply answers to the questions when, how, where, to what extent or degree or how often, etc. Examples of adverbs include: quickly, beautifully, foolishly, wisely, well, occasionally, selfishly, much, soon, quiet. e.t.c. Adverbs have three degrees of comparison which are; the positive, comparative and superlative. A] Adverbs which ends in ;ly, have their comparative and superlative formed by adding more and most. Examples; (A) POSITIVE COMPARATIVE SUPARATIVE Quickly More quickly Most quickly Dangerously More dangerously Most dangerously Slowly More slowly Most slowly Fortunately More fortunately Most fortunately Carefully More carefully Most carefully Excitedly More excitedly Most excitedly Foolishly More foolishly Most foolishly Rampantly More rampantly Most rampantly Beautifully More beautifully Most beautifully Sensibly More sensibly Most sensibly Rashly More rashly Most rashly B] Regular adverbs take- er and- est in forming their comparative and superlative. E.g

Early earlier earliest Soon Sooner Soonest Hard Harder Hardest Fast Faster Fastest Far Farther/Further Farthest / Furthest C] Irregular adverbs do not have a fixed form for comparative and superlative. Egs. MUCH MORE MOST LITTLE LESS LEAST WELL BETTER BEST BADLY WORSE WORST Functions of adverbs. Basically, the major function of an adverb is to modify the verb in the sentence. Eg;1] The teacher teaches well. [ WELL modifies the verb TEACHES] 2] The children went with the nanny reluctantly. [ RELUCTANTLY modifies the verb WENT] 3] Ade drives carefully [Carefully modifies the verb ’ drives ’ ] 4] She sings beautifully.[ Beautifully modifies ‘ sings ’ ] Other functions of the adverb A] When it comes before or after another adverb, it modifies the adverb. Eg; The girl danced very well during the competition [ very modifies the adverb ‘ well ’ which modifies the verb ‘ danced ’ ] B] An adverb also modifies an adjective. Eg; 1] The girl is too fat for her age.[ ‘ too ’ modifies the adjective ‘ fat ’ ] 2] The food is quite tasty. [quite modifies the adjective ‘ tasty ’ ]

Assignment : Write out the comparative and superlative forms of these adverbs: foolishly, fortunately, soon, sensibly, early. Reference : Essential English Language for Senior Secondary Schools, by Latilo .T. A et al

title: ADJECTIVE CLAUSE
subject: English Language
rawText: Adjectival clause as a subordinate clause that describes a noun or a pronoun. It does the work of an adjective in a sentence. Adjectival clauses are usually introduced by the following relative pronouns – who, whom, which, that, whose, where The Collins Dictionary defines an adjective clause as “a relative clause that modifies a noun or pronoun, as who saw us in It was she who saw us”, and the Merriam-Webster Dictionary defines an adjective clause as “an clause introduced by a relative pronoun expressed or suppressed, relative adjective, or relative adverb and having either a purely descriptive force (as in John, who often tells fibs) or a limiting one (as in boys who tell fibs)”. According to the Oxford Learner’s Dictionary, a relative clause is one “referring to an earlier noun, sentence, or part of a sentence”. . Examples: 1. Adamu wore the coat which he bought yesterday 2. We set out for the next town where we had planned to stay the night. 3. This is a fine opportunity which should not be lost. 4. That is the man whom Adaeze married. functions of adjectival clauses. Examples 1. The driver followed the road which was very rough It modifies the noun road. 2. The teacher punished the girl who insulted him. It modifies the noun girl 3. He showed me the place where he kept the key. It modifies the noun place. 4. I helped the woman whose money was stolen. It modifies the noun woman 5. That millionaire on whom we relied for help disappointed us. It modifies the noun millionaire

rawText:
AUXILIARY VERBS These are verbs which go with lexical/main/principal verbs, to which they serve as helpers. Hence, they are also called helping verbs. A verb having another verbal item after it is an auxiliary verb. It helps the principal verbal item which follows it to function. There are two types of auxiliary verbs which are; 1. Primary auxiliary verbs and 2. Modal auxiliary verbs. 1. The primary auxiliary verbs has three verb types. A. The ‘be’ form: ‘be’ is the base and it has the branches given below: BE – is, am, be, was, are, were, being, been B. The ‘do’ form: the branches are as given below: DO – does (singular present), do (plural present), did (past for both ‘do’ and ‘does’), and done (is used as past participle) C. The ‘have’ form – have is the base form other forms generated from it are as given below HAVE – has (singular present), have (plural present), had (past and past participle of both ‘has and have’) 2. Modal auxiliary verbs – These verbs may represent ideas or notions such as: possibility, probability, ability, condition, order, obligation, request, futurity, advice, offers, certainty, permission, capability, willingness, questioning Modal auxiliary verbs are – Shall, should, will, would, ought to, must, can, could, dare, may or might, need, used to, Examples a) The ‘be’ form: ‘be’ is the base and it has the branches given below BE – is, am, be, was, are, were, being, been 1. Your baby is crying 2. I am eating 3. The rude students are being flogged 4 . Be thinking of how to do it 5. He was writing when the guest came 6. They were preparing to leave when the rain started. b) The ‘do’ form: the branches are as given below DO – does (singular present), do (plural present), did (past for both ‘do’ and ‘does’), and done (is used as past participle). For example: 1. It does not speak well 2. I do not trust him 3. They did not register their name

c) The ‘have’ form – have is the base form other forms generated from it are as given below HAVE – has (singular present), have (plural present), had (past and past participle of both ‘has and have’ 1. The programme has ended 2. They have been counted 3. They had elected their officers before we joined them 4. They have been disgraced twice today Auxiliary verb used as main verb: 1. The woman is a nurse 2. They are ready 3. She is a nurse 4. He is a Nigerian 5. My Uncle was once a soldier 6. Tobi has two oranges 7. Judith does her homework regularly 8. Eniola and John have Bible storybooks 9. Tunde is here now 10. We are all ready

title: SPEECH WORK :WORD STRESS
subject: English Language
rawText: Word stress! It's like the rhythm of words, where one syllable is emphasized more than the 😊 others. Let's break it down: *What is word stress?* Word stress is the way we pronounce a word with emphasis on a particular syllable(s). It's like giving more "oomph" to one part of the word. *Rules on word stress:* 1. *Two-syllable nouns and adjectives:* Stress usually falls on the first syllable. - Example: Happy (Ha-ppy), London (Lon-don), clever (cle-ver) 2. *Two-syllable verbs:* Stress usually falls on the second syllable. - Example: Decide (de-CIDE), enjoy (en-JOY), relax (re-LAX) 3. *Words ending in -tion, -sion, -cian:* Stress falls on the penultimate syllable (the one before the suffix). - Example: Education (ed-u-CA-tion), decision (de-CI-sion), musician (mu-SI-cian) 4. *Words ending in -ic, -ical, -ian:* Stress falls on the penultimate syllable. - Example: Historic (his-TOR-ic), logical (log-I-cal), Canadian (ca-NA-di-an) 5. *Compound words:* Stress usually falls on the first part of the compound. - Example: Blackbird (BLACK-bird), toothbrush (TOOTH-brush), birthday (BIRTH-day) These are general rules, and there are exceptions. The best way to learn word stress is to listen to native speakers and practice.

title: EMPHATIC STRESS
subject: English Language
rawText: Stress in language: Stress is level of emphasis given to a word, syllable, or phrase when using language. Stress can involve changes in volume, tone, accent, or pitch. Changes in vowel sounds can also be involved in stress in language. Answer and Explanation: Emphatic stress is the placing of emphasis on a particular word of a sentence. This is typically used to connect, clarify, compare, or highlight ideas. Using emphatic stress can significantly change the meaning of a sentence. For example, if the word do is stressed in the sentence " What does she do here," it changes the meaning from a simple question asking for information to an implied questioning of the subject's efficacy or contribution. If one were to say, " Eat the red apple," while stressing the word red, it potentially adds the implication of " not one of the other colors of apple" to the intended meaning. Emphatic stress may be used in a sentence to compare, connect, or clarify things. Usually, emphatic stress singles out the word that the speaker considers the most important, and in this case, even a function word may become stressed. Emphatic stress is the placement of articulatory prominence or emphasis on a word in a sentence. In responding to questions on emphatic stress in examinations, interrogative sentences will be provided as options. The interrogative sentence that contradicts the emphasized word is the correct option.

title: REGISTER: ENVIRONMENT
subject: English Language
rawText:
Sure! Here are fifty key terms associated with the environment, along with brief explanations for each: 1. **Ecosystem**: A community of living organisms and their physical environment, interacting as a system. 2. **Biodiversity**: The variety of life in a particular habitat or ecosystem, including species diversity, genetic diversity, and ecosystem diversity. 3. **Sustainability**: Meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. 4. **Climate Change**: Long-term alterations in temperature, precipitation, wind patterns, and other elements of the Earth's climate system, primarily driven by human activity. 5. **Pollution**: The introduction of contaminants into the natural environment, causing adverse effects on ecosystems and human health. 6. **Deforestation**: The large-scale removal of trees from forests, often resulting in damage to the quality of the land. 7. **Renewable Energy**: Energy generated from natural resources that are replenished over shorter time frames than fossil fuels, such as solar, wind, and hydroelectric power. 8. **Greenhouse Gases**: Gases that trap heat in the atmosphere, contributing to the greenhouse effect and global warming (e.g., CO2, methane). 9. **Habitat**: The natural environment in which a particular species lives, grows, and thrives. 10. **Conservation**: The careful management and protection of natural resources to prevent their depletion or destruction. 11. **Erosion**: The process by which soil and rock are worn away and removed from one location to another, often exacerbated by human activities. 12. **Biomass**: Organic material derived from plants and animals, which can be used as a source of energy. 13. **Ozone Layer**: A region of Earth's stratosphere that contains a high concentration of ozone, which protects life by absorbing the majority of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation. 14. **Acid Rain**: Precipitation that has a lower pH than normal, often resulting from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides released into the atmosphere, which can harm ecosystems.

15. **Invasive Species**: Non-native species that spread rapidly in a new environment, often harming local ecosystems and biodiversity. 16. **Organic Farming**: Agricultural practices that avoid synthetic pesticides and fertilizers, focusing instead on sustainable farming techniques. 17. **Carbon Footprint**: The total amount of greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide, emitted directly and indirectly by an individual, organization, or product. 18. **Waste Management**: The collection, transport, processing, recycling, or disposal of waste materials to minimize their impact on the environment. 19. **Composting**: A natural process of recycling organic matter, such as food waste and yard debris, into a valuable fertilizer that can enrich soil. 20. **Sustainable Agriculture**: Farming practices that maintain soil health, protect water resources, and promote biodiversity while providing food. 21. **E-waste**: Discarded electronic devices and components, which can contain harmful substances and require proper recycling processes. 22. **Fossil Fuels**: Natural fuels formed from the remains of ancient organisms, primarily coal, oil, and natural gas, associated with significant greenhouse gas emissions. 23. **Natural Resources**: Materials and components found in the environment that are valuable to humans, including water, minerals, and timber. 24. **Urbanization**: The process of population movement from rural areas to cities, often leading to environmental challenges such as habitat loss and pollution. 25. **Climate Action**: Initiatives and strategies to mitigate climate change and its impacts, often involving policy changes and community engagement. 26. **Water Scarcity**: A situation where water availability is insufficient to meet the demands of a given area or population. 27. **Ecosystem Services**: The benefits that humans derive from ecosystems, including clean water, pollination, and climate regulation. 28. **Green Infrastructure**: A network of natural and semi-natural features, designed to deliver environmental, economic, and social benefits, such as parks and green roofs. 29. **Metropolitan Area**: A region consisting of a densely populated urban core and its less- populated surrounding territories, often facing unique environmental challenges.

30. **Carbon Sequestration**: The process of capturing and storing atmospheric carbon dioxide in vegetation, soils, and geological formations to mitigate climate change. 31. **Photovoltaics**: Technology that converts sunlight directly into electricity using solar cells. 32. **Sustainable Development**: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, linking economic growth with environmental stewardship. 33. **Greenwashing**: The practice of promoting an organization's products or policies as environmentally friendly while making misleading claims. 34. **Ecodesign**: A design approach that considers the environmental impacts of a product throughout its entire lifecycle, from production to disposal. 35. **Restoration Ecology**: The science and practice of renewing and restoring degraded ecosystems and habitats. 36. **Protected Areas**: Regions of land or water dedicated to the conservation of nature, often established to safeguard biodiversity and ecosystem services. 37. **Sustainable Tourism**: Tourism that respects local cultures, environments, and economies, allowing for conservation and community benefit. 38. **Land Use Planning**: The process of regulating how land is used and developed to minimize environmental impact and ensure sustainable practices. 39. **Carbon Offset**: A reduction in emissions of carbon dioxide or other greenhouse gases made in order to compensate for emissions produced elsewhere. 40. **Zero Waste**: A philosophy that encourages the redesign of resource life cycles to ensure that all products are reused and no waste is sent to landfills. 41. **Agroforestry**: A land-use management system that combines agriculture and forestry practices to create more sustainable and productive land-use systems. 42. **Climate Resilience**: The ability of a system, community, or individual to anticipate, prepare for, respond to, and recover from climate-related shocks and stresses. 43. **Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)**: A process used to assess the potential environmental effects of a proposed project or development before it is carried out. 44. **Tipping Point**: A critical threshold at which a small change can lead to significant and

often irreversible impacts on an ecosystem. 45. **Natural Capital**: The world's stocks of natural assets, including geology, soil, air, water, and all living things, which provide ecosystem services. 46. **Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK)**: Indigenous and local knowledge about the relationships between living beings and their environment, developed over time. 47. **Aquifer**: A geological formation that can store and transmit water, often tapped for groundwater supply. 48. **Soil Degradation**: The decline of soil quality due to factors such as erosion, compaction, nutrient depletion, and contamination. 49. **Pay-per-use Tiers**: Payment systems designed to incentivize energy or resource conservation by charging users based on their consumption levels. 50. **Ecotourism**: Responsible travel to natural areas that conserves the environment and improves the well-being of local people. These terms represent a broad spectrum of concepts important for understanding environmental science, policy, and conservation efforts.

management and protection of natural resources to prevent their depletion or destruction. 11. **Erosion**: The process by which soil and rock are worn away and removed from one location to another, often exacerbated by human activities. 12. **Biomass**: Organic material derived from plants and animals, which can be used as a source of energy. 13. **Ozone Layer**: A region of Earth's stratosphere that contains a high concentration of ozone, which protects life by absorbing the majority of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation. 14. **Acid Rain**: Precipitation that has a lower pH than normal, often resulting from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides released into the atmosphere, which can harm ecosystems.

15. **Invasive Species**: Non-native species that spread rapidly in a new environment, often harming local ecosystems and biodiversity. 16. **Organic Farming**: Agricultural practices that avoid synthetic pesticides and fertilizers, focusing instead on sustainable farming techniques. 17. **Carbon Footprint**: The total amount of greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide, emitted directly and indirectly by an individual, organization, or product. 18. **Waste Management**: The collection, transport, processing, recycling, or disposal of waste materials to minimize their impact on the environment. 19. **Composting**: A natural process of recycling organic matter, such as food waste and yard debris, into a valuable fertilizer that can enrich soil. 20. **Sustainable Agriculture**: Farming practices that maintain soil health, protect water resources, and promote biodiversity while providing food. 21. **E-waste**: Discarded electronic devices and components, which can contain harmful substances and require proper recycling processes. 22. **Fossil Fuels**: Natural fuels formed from the remains of ancient organisms, primarily coal, oil, and natural gas, associated with significant greenhouse gas emissions. 23. **Natural Resources**: Materials and components found in the environment that are valuable to humans, including water, minerals, and timber. 24. **Urbanization**: The process of population movement from rural areas to cities, often leading to environmental challenges such as habitat loss and pollution. 25. **Climate Action**: Initiatives and strategies to mitigate climate change and its impacts, often involving policy changes and community engagement. 26. **Water Scarcity**: A situation where water availability is insufficient to meet the demands of a given area or population. 27. **Ecosystem Services**: The benefits that humans derive from ecosystems, including clean water, pollination, and climate regulation. 28. **Green Infrastructure**: A network of natural and semi-natural features, designed to deliver environmental, economic, and social benefits, such as parks and green roofs. 29. **Metropolitan Area**: A region consisting of a densely populated urban core and its less- populated surrounding territories, often facing unique environmental challenges.

30. **Carbon Sequestration**: The process of capturing and storing atmospheric carbon dioxide in vegetation, soils, and geological formations to mitigate climate change. 31. **Photovoltaics**: Technology that converts sunlight directly into electricity using solar cells. 32. **Sustainable Development**: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, linking economic growth with environmental stewardship. 33. **Greenwashing**: The practice of promoting an organization's products or policies as environmentally friendly while making misleading claims. 34. **Ecodesign**: A design approach that considers the environmental impacts of a product throughout its entire lifecycle, from production to disposal. 35. **Restoration Ecology**: The science and practice of renewing and restoring degraded ecosystems and habitats. 36. **Protected Areas**: Regions of land or water dedicated to the conservation of nature, often established to safeguard biodiversity and ecosystem services. 37. **Sustainable Tourism**: Tourism that respects local cultures, environments, and economies, allowing for conservation and community benefit. 38. **Land Use Planning**: The process of regulating how land is used and developed to minimize environmental impact and ensure sustainable practices. 39. **Carbon Offset**: A reduction in emissions of carbon dioxide or other greenhouse gases made in order to compensate for emissions produced elsewhere. 40. **Zero Waste**: A philosophy that encourages the redesign of resource life cycles to ensure that all products are reused and no waste is sent to landfills. 41. **Agroforestry**: A land-use management system that combines agriculture and forestry practices to create more sustainable and productive land-use systems. 42. **Climate Resilience**: The ability of a system, community, or individual to anticipate, prepare for, respond to, and recover from climate-related shocks and stresses. 43. **Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)**: A process used to assess the potential environmental effects of a proposed project or development before it is carried out. 44. **Tipping Point**: A critical threshold at which a small change can lead to significant and

often irreversible impacts on an ecosystem. 45. **Natural Capital**: The world's stocks of natural assets, including geology, soil, air, water, and all living things, which provide ecosystem services. 46. **Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK)**: Indigenous and local knowledge about the relationships between living beings and their environment, developed over time. 47. **Aquifer**: A geological formation that can store and transmit water, often tapped for groundwater supply. 48. **Soil Degradation**: The decline of soil quality due to factors such as erosion, compaction, nutrient depletion, and contamination. 49. **Pay-per-use Tiers**: Payment systems designed to incentivize energy or resource conservation by charging users based on their consumption levels. 50. **Ecotourism**: Responsible travel to natural areas that conserves the environment and improves the well-being of local people. These terms represent a broad spectrum of concepts important for understanding environmental science, policy, and conservation efforts.

title: EMPHATIC STRESS
subject: English Language
rawText: Stress in language: Stress is level of emphasis given to a word, syllable, or phrase when using language. Stress can involve changes in volume, tone, accent, or pitch. Changes in vowel sounds can also be involved in stress in language. Answer and Explanation: Emphatic stress is the placing of emphasis on a particular word of a sentence. This is typically used to connect, clarify, compare, or highlight ideas. Using emphatic stress can significantly change the meaning of a sentence. For example, if the word do is stressed in the sentence " What does she do here," it changes the meaning from a simple question asking for information to an implied questioning of the subject's efficacy or contribution. If one were to say, " Eat the red apple," while stressing the word red, it potentially adds the implication of " not one of the other colors of apple" to the intended meaning. Emphatic stress may be used in a sentence to compare, connect, or clarify things. Usually, emphatic stress singles out the word that the speaker considers the most important, and in this case, even a function word may become stressed. Emphatic stress is the placement of articulatory prominence or emphasis on a word in a sentence. In responding to questions on emphatic stress in examinations, interrogative sentences will be provided as options. The interrogative sentence that contradicts the emphasized word is the correct option.

title: NARRATIVE ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText: Narrative Essay Narrative essay is a complete account of an imaginary or true life story which one experienced or witnessed. The story must be believable. Features: a. The title should be written either in small or block letters. b. The body of the essay should be written in paragraphs starting with the introduction as the first paragraph. c. The conclusion bears the summary of the story and equally shows the state of the writer's mind whether he is happy or sad at the end. d. If it comes as an article, the writer's name and location should be written. Guidelines for a narrative essay. 1. Content: a. Events narrated must be convincing and realistic. The reader should be led to believe that what he is reading is true. b. The story should have few characters to make narration effective. c. Learn to create conflict, suspense and surprise. Make use of idiomatic and figurative expression. 2. Organizations; There should be a clear story line written in chronological order. Originality and interesting presentation are necessary. Make use of paragraphs and very good paragraph linking words e.g. previously, days earlier, etc. 3. Expression: Simple language should be used. The first or third person point of view is used and the narration should be in the past tense, past progressive and past perfect tenses. Examples of narrative essay: A] The day I will never forget B] A wedding ceremony I attended C] An accident I witnessed D] How I spent my last holiday E] An excursion to the Nigerian Television Authority
