title: MAKING A TOAST
subject: English Language
rawText: Making a Toast. Toast is an act of proposing a drink in honor of or of drinking in honor of someone or something. occasion were toast are made. 1.Weddings; To celebrate the newlyweds' love and commitment. 2. Birthdays; To wish someone a happy and successful year ahead. 3. Anniversaries; To honor the years of togetherness. 4. Graduations; To congratulate the graduates on their achievements. 5. Retirements; To bid farewell and acknowledge years of hard work. 6. Promotions; To recognize and celebrate career advancements. 7. Holidays; Such as New Year's Eve, Christmas, Sallah, for festive cheer. 8. Achievements; To acknowledge personal or professional accomplishments. 9. Memorials; To remember and pay tribute to a deceased loved one. Steps in making a toast. 1. Start by thanking your host. "First of all I’ll like to start by thanking our gracious host. " Say who you are thanking and why. Maybe thank them for having you in their home or for hosting this party. Showing your gratitude is a humble and good way to start off a toast. 2. Recognize people when appropriate: In a more informal environment, you could choose one or two people to congratulate on something big that they did that year. It could be a promotion or it could be having a baby. It’s an honor to be recognized, and so this works really well. Know your audience and who you are talking to. 3. Talk about the future: Talk about the plans for the future with your company or with the group that you are with. Look for the thing that you share with the people you are with. Again know your audience, but it’s looking towards the future in a positive way. You may share a common goal or you may just be living the future together. It gives everyone something positive and it gives you something to talk about after the toast is over. You want to close it by saying “here’s to us and to the future.”You want to close it up and then clink glasses saying Cheers!

title: FIGURES OF SPEECH
subject: English Language
rawText: Figures of Speech Figures of speech are words used in a special way quite different from the ordinary meaning for the purpose of creating a specific mental image or effect. Types of Figures of speech 1. Simile; It is a comparison drawn between two things that are basically different in nature but similar in one aspect or the other using words “like” or “as” Example; The woman charged at her tormentor like a wounded lion 2. Metaphor; It is a direct comparison drawn between two essentially different things. Examples; She has a heart of stone. 3. Personification; This is giving human attributes or qualities to an inanimate object or a non living object as though it is living. Example; The rain beats the man mercilessly. 4. Hyperbole; This is a deliberate exaggeration made for emphasis. It is at times called an overstatement. Example; He thanked me a thousand times for what I had done for me. 5. Irony; It is speaking the opposite of what it means. It is the opposite meaning of what is intended. Examples; The best way to avoid death is by jumping into fire. 6. Euphemism; It is a way of expressing an unpleasant thing in a mild or less serious matter. Examples; The man kicked the bucket. 7. Paradox; It is a statement that seems contradictory or that actually does itself but when examined closely, it had some hidden truth & wisdom. Examples; more haste, less speed. 8. Oxymoron 9. Sarcasm

title: ADJECTIVES
subject: English Language
rawText: Adjectives. Types and Order of Adjectives Adjectives are words which are used to qualify nouns and pronouns. They give fuller meanings to nouns or pronouns. Types of Adjectives 1. Descriptive Adjectives- This describes person or things. Examples * The handsome man is getting married this week. 2. Possessive Adjectives; It indicates that something or a thing belongs to a person. They show ownership of a thing. Examples * Your book has been stolen 3. Demonstrative Adjectives; They behave like demonstrative pronouns but they are used to prefix nouns or pronouns. Examples * That book is mine. The position of adjectives in English Language sentence does not always follow a definite pattern but they do have a general pattern of order. The adjective of a number or quantity like twenty, five, several etc must always come before adjectives of quality like beautiful, rough, round etc a. There are several beautiful girls in this school. b. There are many handsome boys in the town. In some cases, two or more adjectives of the same kind may qualify a noun. The general pattern could be used, The determiner, adjectives of number, quality, age, shape, color, origin (nature) and the noun they qualify in that order. a. An exciting new British television show. b. A beautiful young Nigerian girl. c. Some twenty healthy young brown Nigerian racing horses. d. Three new beautiful tough pink bags

title: VERB FORMS
subject: English Language
rawText: Active and Passive Verbs A verb is used in the active voice when the doer of an action is made to function as the subject of the sentence. Here the writer or speaker is more interested in the doer. A verb is used in the passive voice when the receiver (object) of an action is made to function as the object of the sentence. Examples; A. The teacher is teaching the students. *The students are being taught by the teacher. B. Someone saw him. * He was seen by someone. C. Our maid gave you a bowl of custard. * The custard bowl was given to you by our maid. D. John killed the snake. * The snake was killed by John. E. She was born in 2009. * 2009 was the year she was born. In the active voice, the subject is performing an action. The dog chases the ball. The subject “dog” is performing the action “chase” the target of the action “ball”. It is simple, direct active voice. In passive voice, the action’s target, ball is positioned first as the focus of the sentence. The subject is now being acted upon by the verb, the subject is passive. The ball is being chased by the dog. Passive voice is formed by using a form of the auxiliary verb “be” ( be, am, is, are, was, were, being, been) followed by the past participle of the main verb. He Loves me. I am loved by him

title: REGISTER AGRICULTURE AND HORTICULTURE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Sure! Agriculture and horticulture are two intertwined fields related to the cultivation of plants and rearing of animals for food, fiber, and other products. **Agriculture** is the broader industry that encompasses the large-scale cultivation of crops and the raising of livestock for commercial purposes. It includes various practices such as crop farming, livestock farming, aquaculture, and agroforestry. **Horticulture**, on the other hand, is a subtype of agriculture that focuses on the cultivation of plants for food, ornamental purposes, and other uses, typically on a smaller scale. It includes gardening, landscaping, and the production of fruits, vegetables, flowers, and ornamental plants. ### Key Words Associated with Agriculture and Horticulture 1. **Crop**: A plant cultivated for food, fiber, or other products. Examples include wheat, corn, and cotton. 2. **Livestock**: Domesticated animals raised for commercial purposes, such as cattle, sheep, pigs, and poultry. 3. **Irrigation**: The artificial application of water to soil to assist in the growing of crops. Methods include drip, sprinkler, and surface irrigation. 4. **Fertilizer**: Substances added to soil or plants to supply essential nutrients and promote growth. Fertilizers can be organic or synthetic. 5. **Pesticide**: Chemicals used to kill or control harmful pests, including insects, weeds, and fungi that can damage crops. 6. **Soil**: The top layer of earth where plants grow, containing organic matter, minerals, gases, liquids, and organisms. 7. **Harvest**: The process of gathering mature crops from the fields. It involves cutting, collecting, and processing the crops. 8. **Planting**: The act of placing seeds or plants into the soil for growth. Timing and technique are critical for successful cultivation. 9. **Horticulture Therapy**: The use of gardening and plant-related activities as a therapeutic process to promote physical and mental health. 10. **Ornamental Plants**: Plants cultivated for aesthetic purposes, including flowers, shrubs, and trees used in landscaping. 11. **Botany**: The scientific study of plants, including their structure, properties, and

biochemical processes. 12. **Agroecology**: A holistic approach to farming that integrates ecological principles into agricultural production to promote sustainability and biodiversity. 13. **Composting**: The process of recycling organic matter, such as kitchen scraps and yard waste, into a valuable fertilizer known as compost. 14. **Greenhouse**: A structure designed to grow plants in a controlled environment, providing optimal temperature, light, and humidity. 15. **Seedling**: A young plant that develops from a seed. Seedlings are often cultivated in nurseries before being transplanted to their final location. 16. **Crop Rotation**: The practice of growing different types of crops in the same area in sequential seasonsCertainly! Let ’ s continue with the remaining key terms: 17. **Mulching**: The practice of covering the soil with organic or inorganic materials to retain moisture, suppress weeds, and improve soil health. 18. **Pruning**: The selective removal of specific plant parts, such as branches or buds, to promote healthy growth, improve structure, and increase fruit yield. 19. **Hydroponics**: A method of growing plants without soil, using nutrient-rich water solutions. It allows for controlled environmental conditions and can increase crop yield. 20. **Aquaponics**: A sustainable farming method that combines aquaculture (raising fish) with hydroponics (growing plants in water) in a symbiotic environment. 21. **Sustainable Agriculture**: Farming practices that maintain the health of the environment, support biodiversity, and provide economic viability while meeting present and future needs. 22. **Organic Farming**: An agricultural approach that avoids synthetic chemicals and genetically modified organisms (GMOs), relying instead on organic fertilizers and non-chemical pest control. 23. **Biodiversity**: The variety of plant and animal life in a particular habitat, which is essential for ecosystem resilience and crop security. 24. **Crop Yield**: The amount of produce harvested per unit area of land, often expressed in terms of weight or volume. It is a key indicator of agricultural efficiency. 25. **Soil Fertility**: The ability of soil to provide essential nutrients to plants, which can be improved through organic practices, crop rotation, and proper fertilization.

26. **Till**: The process of preparing soil for planting by plowing, turning, and breaking up the soil. Tillage can impact soil structure and health. 27. **Farm Implements**: Tools and machinery used in farming practices, such as tractors, plows, and seeders, which increase efficiency and productivity. 28. **Genetic Modification**: The altering of the genetic makeup of plants or animals through biotechnology to enhance desired traits such as resistance to pests or improved nutritional content. 29. **Pollen**: The male gametophyte of seed plants, critical for the reproduction of flowering plants, which involves the transfer of pollen from one flower to another. 30. **Climate Resilience**: The ability of agricultural systems to withstand and adapt to climate change, including shifts in temperature, precipitation patterns, and extreme weather events. ### Summary These keywords represent fundamental concepts within the fields of agriculture and horticulture. Understanding these terms is essential for anyone involved in the cultivation of plants and the management of agricultural practices. From sustainable farming techniques to the science behind soil health, each term plays a role in the overall ecosystem of food production and plant care.

title: HUMAN INTERNAL ORGANS
subject: English Language
rawText: Human Internal body system Internal body system are the organs inside the body that work harmoniously to keep the body healthy. Words associated with internal human body system; liver, kidney, heart, intestines, stomach, brain. 1. Liver: The liver is the largest solid organ of the body. It removes toxins from the body's blood supply, maintains healthy blood sugar levels and regulates clotting. It is located beneath the rib cage in the right upper abdomen. 2. Kidney: The kidneys are a pair of bean-shaped organs on either side of the spine below the rib. The functions of the kidney include, removal of wastes, filter the blood, control the body's fluid balance and keep the right levels of electrolytes.  Heart: The heart is a muscular organ situated in the chest. The function of the heart include, pumping oxygenated blood to other body parts, maintaining blood pressure, pumping hormones and other vital substances to different parts of the body.

Earthquake: a sudden violent shaking of the earth surface 2. Volcanic eruption: it is a process when hot materials are thrown out of a volcano 3. Drought: A period of unusually low rainfall, longer and more severe than a dry spell. 4. Typhoon: A weather in the northwestern pacific that is precisely equivalent to a hurricane, which results in wind speeds of 64 knots (118 km/h) or above. Equivalent to a cyclone in the Indian Ocean and Indonesia/ Australia. 5. Hurricane: A severe tropical cyclone in the North Atlantic ocean, Caribbean, sea, Gulf of Mexico, or in the eastern North pacific off the west coast Mexico, with winds of 119km/h (74 miles per hour) or greater accompanied by rain, lightening, and thunder that sometimes moves into temperate latitudes. 6. Flood: A(usually disastrous) overflow of water from a lake or other body of water due to excessive rainfall or other input. 7.Erosion: the result of having been worn away or eroded, as by a glacier on rock or the sea on a cliff face. 8. Environmental degradation: is the deterioration of environment through depletion of resources such as air and water . 9. Ozone layer: A region of the stratosphere, between 15 and 30 kilometers in attitude, containing a relatively high concentration of ozone, which absorbs most solar ultraviolet radiation. 10. Pollution: physical contamination, now especially the contamination of the environment by harmful substances, or by disruptive levels of noise, light etc.

It's the way a verb changes to show tense, aspect, mood, voice, person, or 😊 number. *Types of Verb Forms:* 1. *Base Form* (infinitive): The basic form of the verb (e.g., go, eat, run) 2. *Past Simple* (V2): Used for completed actions in the past (e.g., went, ate, ran) 3. *Past Participle* (V3): Used with "has/had" for present/past perfect tenses (e.g., gone, eaten, run) 4. *Present Participle* (V-ing): Used for continuous tenses (e.g., going, eating, running) 5. *Third Person Singular* (V-s/es): Used for present simple tense with he/she/it (e.g., goes, eats, runs)

title: STRUCTURE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Students’ Summary Note Subject: English Language Topic: Reading for Specific Structural Patterns and Report Writing 1. Reading for Specific Structural Patterns Focus on how a passage is organized. Look for headings, subheadings, dates, steps, or numbered points in scientific or medical passages. Helps to understand the sequence of ideas and structure of the content. 2. Identifying Main and Supporting Ideas Main Idea: The most important point the writer wants to convey. Supporting Ideas: Details, examples, or explanations that explain or support the main idea. Example: Main Idea: Exercise is important for good health. Supporting Ideas: It strengthens the heart, improves mood, and prevents diseases. 3. Explaining Key Vocabulary Highlight difficult or technical words in the passage. Look for clues in the sentence to understand the meaning. Example (medical passage): Diagnosis: Identifying a disease Treatment: Care given to cure illness Patient: A person receiving medical care 4. Understanding the Format of a Report A report is a structured piece of writing that presents information clearly. Typical Structure of a Scientific/Medical Report: Title/Heading: Name of the experiment or study. Date: When the experiment or observation took place.

Introduction/Purpose: Why the experiment was conducted. Procedure/Method: Steps followed during the experiment. Results/Outcome: Findings or observations. Conclusion: Summary of findings or recommendations. 5. Writing a Simple Report Logically Use clear headings. Arrange information in chronological order or logical sequence. Write short, precise sentences. Include all main points and supporting details. Avoid unnecessary repetition. Example Structure: Title: Effect of Exercise on Heart Rate Date: 4th February 2026 Purpose: To investigate how exercise affects heart rate. Procedure: Students ran for 5 minutes; heart rates were recorded before and after. Results: Heart rate increased after exercise. Conclusion: Exercise raises heart rate, showing the heart works harder during physical activity. Importance Helps in understanding and summarizing information. Improves comprehension and analytical skills. Prepares students for structured writing tasks in exams. title: NOUN PHRASE
subject: English Language
rawText: What is a noun phrase? A noun phrase is a group of words that functions as a noun. It can consist of a single noun, or it can be more complex, with modifiers (adjectives, adverbs, etc.) and other phrases. Positions of noun phrases Noun phrases can be found in different positions in a sentence. They can be the subject of the sentence, the object of the verb, the object of a preposition, or the complement of a verb. Functions of noun phrases The function of a noun phrase depends on its position in the sentence.  Subject: The subject of a sentence is the person or thing that the sentence is about. The subject of a sentence is always a noun phrase. For example, in the sentence "The cat sat on the mat," the noun phrase "The cat" is the subject of the sentence.  Object: The object of a verb is the person or thing that the verb acts upon. The object of a verb can be a noun phrase, a pronoun, or a clause. For example, in the sentence "I saw the cat," the noun phrase "the cat" is the object of the verb "saw."  Object of a preposition: The object of a preposition is the person or thing that the preposition refers to. The object of a preposition can be a noun phrase, a pronoun, or a clause. For example, in the sentence "The cat is under the mat," the noun phrase "the mat" is the object of the preposition "under."  Complement: A complement is a word or phrase that follows a verb and completes its meaning. The complement of a verb can be a noun phrase, an adjective, or an adverb. For example, in the sentence "The cat is a furry creature," the noun phrase "a furry creature" is the complement of the verb "is." Examples of noun phrases Here are some examples of noun phrases:  The cat  The furry creature  The cat under the mat  The cat that I saw  The cat that is furry Tips for identifying noun phrases Noun phrases can be identified by their function in the sentence. If a word or phrase functions as a noun, then it is a noun phrase. Noun phrases can also be identified by their structure. They often contain a noun, but they can also contain modifiers (adjectives, adverbs, etc.) and other phrases.

title: EXPOSITORY ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText:
*1. What is an Expository Essay?* An *expository essay* is a type of writing that explains, informs, clarifies, or describes a topic in a clear, logical, and objective way. The purpose is not to persuade or entertain, but to give the reader accurate knowledge about a subject. It answers questions like _what is it? how does it work? why does it happen?_ *Example topics:* _How the National Assembly passes a bill_, _Causes of soil erosion_, _The role of IPPIS in Nigeria ’ s civil service_. --- *2. Parts of an Expository Essay* Every expository essay has 3 main parts: 1. *Introduction* - Opens with a hook or background statement. - Ends with a *thesis statement* that clearly states what the essay will explain. - Example thesis: _ “ This essay explains the process of budget preparation in Nigeria ’ s public service. ” _ 2. *Body Paragraphs* - Usually 3-5 paragraphs, each focusing on one main point or step. - Each paragraph starts with a *topic sentence*, followed by facts, examples, data, and explanations. - Logical order is key: chronological, cause-effect, problem-solution, or compare-contrast. 3. *Conclusion* - Restates the thesis in different words. - Summarizes the main points without introducing new information. - Leaves the reader with a clear understanding of the topic. --- *3. Ingredients of an Expository Essay* These are the essential elements that make an expository essay effective: - *Clear Thesis Statement*: Tells the reader the exact focus. - *Factual Evidence*: Uses facts, statistics, examples, definitions, and expert opinions. No personal opinions unless asked. - *Logical Organization*: Ideas flow in a clear order - step by step, cause to effect, general to

specific. - *Topic Sentences*: Each body paragraph has one main idea. - *Transitions*: Words like _however, therefore, moreover, in addition_ connect ideas smoothly. - *Objective Tone*: Neutral, formal, and free from emotion or bias. - *Clarity & Simplicity*: Avoids jargon unless explained. Short, precise sentences work best. - *Accurate Information*: Facts must be correct and verifiable. --- *4. Expository Essay vs Other Essay Types* **Feature** **Expository Essay** **Argumentative/Persuasive Essay** **Narrative Essay** **Descriptive Essay** **Purpose** To explain and inform To convince the reader to accept a viewpoint To tell a story or recount an experience To paint a picture with words **Tone** Objective, neutral, factual Argumentative, persuasive, opinionated Personal, emotional, engaging Vivid, sensory, detailed **Content** Facts, data, definitions, processes Arguments, evidence, counter-arguments Characters, plot, dialogue, setting Sensory details: sight, sound, smell **Thesis** States what will be explained States a claim you will defend States the purpose of the story States what will be described **Point of View** 3rd person mostly 1st or 3rd person 1st person common 1st or 3rd person **Example Topic** *How does TSA work in Nigeria?* *Why TSA should be maintained* *My first day in the civil service* *The beauty of Yankari Game Reserve* **Key Question** *How/What/Why does it work?* *Why should you agree with me?* *What happened?* *What does it look/feel/sound like?* *Simple way to remember:* - *Expository* = _Teach me_ - *Argumentative* = _Convince me_ - *Narrative* = _Tell me a story_ - *Descriptive* = _Show me a picture_

title: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH ENVIRONMENT
subject: English Language
rawText: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH ENVIRONMENT words associated with environment from the read passage and to state their meaning Atmosphere, ozone, carbon, carbon dioxide, climate, ecology, earth, global warming, pollution, gasoline, chlorine. Other words are: plants, animals, sand, house, water, rivers, cars, population, gas stations, farmlands etc. The teacher also directs the students to explain the following environmental phenomenon. 1. Earthquake: a sudden violent shaking of the earth surface 2. Volcanic eruption: it is a process when hot materials are thrown out of a volcano 3. Drought: A period of unusually low rainfall, longer and more severe than a dry spell. 4. Typhoon: A weather in the northwestern pacific that is precisely equivalent to a hurricane, which results in wind speeds of 64 knots (118 km/h) or above. Equivalent to a cyclone in the Indian Ocean and Indonesia/ Australia. 5. Hurricane: A severe tropical cyclone in the North Atlantic ocean, Caribbean, sea, Gulf of Mexico, or in the eastern North pacific off the west coast Mexico, with winds of 119km/h (74 miles per hour) or greater accompanied by rain, lightening, and thunder that sometimes moves into temperate latitudes. 6. Flood: A(usually disastrous) overflow of water from a lake or other body of water due to excessive rainfall or other input. 7.Erosion: the result of having been worn away or eroded, as by a glacier on rock or the sea on a cliff face. 8. Environmental degradation: is the deterioration of environment through depletion of resources such as air and water . 9. Ozone layer: A region of the stratosphere, between 15 and 30 kilometers in attitude, containing a relatively high concentration of ozone, which absorbs most solar ultraviolet radiation. 10. Pollution: physical contamination, now especially the contamination of the environment by harmful substances, or by disruptive levels of noise, light etc.

title: LISTENING TO POETRY FOR COMPREHENSION/ PLEASURE
subject: English Language
rawText: What is poetry? Poetry is the branch of literature that deals with poems. In other words, poetry is the art of writing poem. The effects of listening to poetry 1) It illuminates our minds. 2) It gives us insight into the world around us. 3) It helps us to understand and enjoy poems. 4) It reenergizes, enlivens make lively) and enhances the teaching of poetry at all levels. Below is a poem about two brothers. Be sure to listen for comprehension and pleasure: I have a twin Brother. His name is Jim. People think we Are alike. But I'm the Opposite of him. He likes to read Books And I like to Play ball. His favourite Season is winter And mine is fall. He's devoted to His dog And I'm crazy About my cat. He has a brain For biology. And I'm a Master of Math. He loves Anything sour. I love anything sweet. His room is nice And tidy. Mine's not always neat. We have the Same parents Though it's not Always plain to see. But I Understand Jimmy And he Understands Me.

title: ARTICLE WRITING 2
subject: English Language
rawText:
*Article Writing* is the process of writing a non-fiction piece that informs, persuades, entertains, or analyzes a topic for a specific audience. Articles are usually published in newspapers, magazines, blogs, or journals. The tone can be formal, semi-formal, or informal depending on the target reader. 1 Parts of a Good Article 1 Title A clear catchy title that shows the main idea and attracts readers 2 Introduction Opens with a hook, background, or problem. States the purpose or main idea of the article 3 Body Divided into 2 to 5 paragraphs. Each paragraph discusses one main point with facts, examples, or explanations that support the topic 4 Conclusion Summarizes key points and ends with a final thought, call to action, recommendation, or solution 5 Byline and Subheadings Byline shows the writer ’ s name. Subheadings break the body into sections for easy reading 2 Features of a Good Article 1 Clarity Uses simple direct language so readers understand easily 2 Relevance Stays focused on the topic and meets the needs of the target audience 3 Accuracy Facts, data, and names are correct and verified 4 Coherence and Cohesion Ideas flow logically with linking words like however, therefore, in addition 5 Engaging Style Uses interesting tone, examples, questions, or quotes to hold reader interest 6 Objectivity with Voice Presents balanced facts but still shows the writer ’ s perspective when needed 7 Proper Structure Follows title, introduction, body, conclusion format

8 Originality Gives fresh ideas or a new angle instead of copying others 3 Difference Between Article and Other Essay Types 1 Purpose Article: To inform, entertain, or persuade a general public audience Essay: To test knowledge, argue a thesis, or explore ideas for academic purposes 2 Audience Article: Written for newspaper or magazine readers, general public Essay: Written mainly for teachers, examiners, or academic readers 3 Tone and Style Article: Flexible tone. Can be formal, semi-formal, or conversational Essay: Usually formal and academic tone only 4 Structure Article: Title, introduction, body with subheadings, conclusion. Shorter paragraphs Essay: Introduction, body paragraphs, conclusion. No title needed and no subheadings in exams 5 Length Article: Usually 300 to 800 words depending on publication Essay: Length set by assignment. School essays 250 to 500 words, academic essays much longer 6 Publication Article: Meant for public reading in print or online Essay: Meant for assessment or academic submission, not public publication 7 Use of Personal Opinion Article: Writer ’ s opinion and voice are allowed and often expected Essay: Opinion only allowed if question asks for it and must be supported with evidence

subject: English Language
rawText: Pronouns; Other Types. 1. Possessive Pronoun; It is called so because they show or indicate possession. They include; my, mine, ours, yours, her, hers, his, their, theirs, it’s Examples; a. title: LISTENING TO POETRY FOR PLEASURE AND COMPREHENSION
subject: English Language
rawText:
### The Song of Whispering Pines In twilight ’ s cradle where shadows blend, The whispering pines weave tales of the wind, With boughs that sway, soft secrets they share, Of forgotten lovers and dreams laid bare. Underneath a blanket of star-speckled skies, The moon drapes silver on night ’ s gentle sighs, A chorus of crickets, nature ’ s sweet choir, Awakens the heart with an ember of fire. The brook sings a ballad, a crystalline flow, While memories dance on the edge of the glow, And echoes of laughter from summers gone past, Resound in the forest, a spell ever cast. Each rustle of leaves stirs the whispers of time, As echoes entwine, a rhythm, a rhyme, The tapestry woven with threads of the years, Captures both joy and the tapestry of tears. Beneath ancient boughs where the wild things rest, A solace is found, an eternal quest, For in nature ’ s embrace, where stillness entwines, We find the deep meaning in whispering pines. So let us hold close these soft murmurs of night, As shadows dissolve in the dawn ’ s tender light, For the song of the pines, in its lilted refrain, Speaks not just of loss, but of love ’ s sweet gain. --- ### Explanation of the Poem "The Song of Whispering Pines" explores the connection between nature and human emotions. The pine trees serve as a metaphor for resilience and remembrance, holding within them the stories of love, loss, and life's fleeting moments. The poem captures the transition from night to dawn, symbolizing reflection, nostalgia, and eventual hope. The various natural elements — the brook, the crickets, and the stars — intertwine with memories to evoke a sense of harmony and peace, suggesting that within every end or sorrow lies the potential for new beginnings and deeper understanding.

### Poetic Techniques Identified in the Poem 1. **Imagery**: Vivid descriptive language creates visual representations of the natural environment, such as "twilight ’ s cradle," "star-speckled skies," and "moon drapes silver." 2. **Personification**: The pines are given human-like qualities, particularly in weaving tales and sharing secrets. 3. **Metaphor**: The whispering pines symbolize resilience and the memories of love and loss intertwined with nature. 4. **Alliteration**: Repeated consonant sounds enhance the musical quality, e.g., "whispering pines," "soft secrets," and "boughs that sway." 5. **Assonance**: Use of vowel sounds for harmony, such as in "twilight ’ s cradle" and "gentle sighs." 6. **Tone**: The overall tone is reflective and serene, touching on themes of nostalgia and solace. 7. **Symbolism**: Various elements of nature (the brook, the moon, the stars) symbolize different aspects of life, love, and memory. 8. **Rhyme Scheme**: The poem follows a consistent rhyme scheme, primarily AABB, which provides rhythm and musicality. 9. **Repetition**: The continual reference to nature reinforces its importance as a backdrop for human experience. 10. **Contrast**: The juxtaposition of darkness (twilight) and light (dawn) symbolizes the shift from sorrow to hope. The careful layering of these techniques creates a rich, immersive experience that resonates with the reader on multiple emotional levels.

Words Associated with the Human Internal System and Functions The human internal system is a complex network of organs and systems that work together to maintain overall health and function. Words associated with human internal system and functions. 1. Circulatory System: The system responsible for transporting oxygen and nutrients to cells and removing waste products. 2. Respiratory System: The system responsible for bringing oxygen into the body and removing carbon dioxide. 3. Nervous System: The system that allows us to think, learn, and respond to stimuli. 4. Digestive System: The system that breaks down food into nutrients that can be absorbed by the body. 5. Excretory System: The system that removes waste products from the body. 6. Muscular System: The system that allows for movement and support of the body. 7. Skeletal System: The system that provides structure and support for the body. 8. Endocrine System: The system that produces hormones that regulate various bodily functions. 9. Neuron: A specialized cell that transmits nerve impulses. 10. Hormone: A chemical substance produced by the endocrine system that regulates various bodily functions. 11. Enzyme: A biological molecule that catalyzes chemical reactions in the body. 12. Blood Vessel: A tube that carries blood throughout the body. 5. Alveoli: Small air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange occurs. Examples of Sentences 1. The circulatory system is responsible for transporting oxygen and nutrients to cells. 2. The nervous system allows us to think, learn, and respond to stimuli. 3. The digestive system breaks down food into nutrients that can be absorbed by the body. Assignment

title: COMPREHENSION
subject: English Language
rawText:
*COMPREHENSION PASSAGE: CORRUPTION AS THE BANE OF DEVELOPMENT IN AFRICAN COUNTRIES* Corruption is the malignant cancer that has eaten deep into the marrow of many African states, crippling their quest for sustainable development. It is not merely the petty bribe demanded by a traffic officer on a dusty highway; it is the systemic looting of public treasuries, the auctioning of national assets to the highest bidder behind closed doors, and the deliberate distortion of policies to serve a privileged few. In Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Zimbabwe, and indeed across the continent, corruption has become a hydra-headed monster. When one head is cut off through a high-profile arrest, two more grow in its place through new procurement scams, ghost worker syndicates, and illicit financial flows. The cost of corruption is staggering and measurable. The African Union estimates that Africa loses $148 billion annually to corruption, a figure that exceeds the combined annual GDP of several smaller African nations. This haemorrhage drains resources that should build schools, hospitals, roads, and power plants. Instead, funds meant for primary healthcare are diverted into private offshore accounts, leaving rural clinics as mere shells without drugs or personnel. Children sit on bare floors in dilapidated classrooms while budgets for education are padded, inflated, and eventually embezzled. Infrastructure projects become white elephants: bridges to nowhere and airports without planes, commissioned with fanfare but abandoned once the kickbacks have been paid. Thus, corruption is a thief that steals not only money but also the future. Beyond economics, corruption corrodes the social fabric. It enthrones mediocrity and banishes merit. When appointments, contracts, and admissions are sold to the highest bidder, the competent are sidelined and the nation is robbed of its best minds. The civil service, which should be the engine of policy implementation, becomes a vehicle for patronage. Young Africans, seeing that hard work does not pay, either join the corrupt bandwagon or flee abroad, creating a brain drain that further impoverishes the continent. Justice itself is put on sale. The poor man ’ s cry for redress echoes unheard in courts where judgments are auctioned and the scales of justice tilt in favor of those with bulging pockets. Politically, corruption weakens institutions and fuels instability. Elections become costly bazaars where votes are bought and ballot boxes are stuffed, producing leaders whose loyalty is to their financiers rather than the electorate. Legitimacy is eroded, and citizens lose faith in the state. This vacuum of trust is quickly filled by ethnic militias, insurgents, and coup plotters who promise the change that democracy failed to deliver. From the Sahel to the Horn of Africa, the link between grand corruption and insecurity is unmistakable. Funds meant for equipping the military are siphoned off, leaving soldiers to face terrorists with obsolete weapons and unpaid allowances. Yet, to call corruption merely a challenge is to understate its venom. It is the bane of development because it attacks the four pillars upon which progress rests: accountability, transparency, rule of law, and equity. Without these, foreign investment flees like a startled bird, for no rational investor will sink capital in a swamp of uncertainty. Domestic investors, too, are strangled by multiple taxation, shakedowns, and policy summersaults designed to create rent-seeking opportunities. The

result is chronic unemployment, poverty, and the painful irony of a continent richly endowed with oil, gold, diamonds, and arable land but whose people remain desperately poor. Fighting corruption therefore demands more than rhetoric. It requires strong institutions, not strong men. It calls for an independent judiciary, a fearless press, and a citizenry that refuses to normalize wrongdoing. Digital tools like IPPIS, GIFMIS, and TSA in Nigeria have shown that technology can block leakages if the political will exists. Anti-graft agencies such as the EFCC and ICPC must be insulated from political interference. Most importantly, there must be a cultural re-orientation that redefines public office as a trust and not a ticket to wealth. Until corruption is confronted as the existential threat it is, Africa ’ s development will remain a mirage that recedes with every step forward. *Word count: 647* --- *SUMMARY OF THE PASSAGE* Corruption is a deep-rooted, systemic problem in Africa that goes beyond petty bribes to include large-scale looting and policy manipulation. It costs the continent $148 billion yearly, diverting funds from education, health, and infrastructure, and creating “ white elephant ” projects. Socially, it promotes mediocrity over merit, fuels brain drain, and puts justice up for sale. Politically, it weakens institutions, undermines elections, erodes public trust, and links to insecurity as military funds are embezzled. By attacking accountability, transparency, rule of law, and equity, corruption drives away investment and perpetuates poverty despite Africa ’ s natural wealth. Effective solutions require strong, independent institutions, technology like IPPIS and TSA, insulated anti- graft bodies, and cultural change that views public office as a trust. Until then, development will remain elusive. --- *COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS & ANSWERS* *Question 1:* _Identify and explain the metaphor used to describe corruption in the first paragraph. What effect does this figure of speech have on the reader ’ s understanding?_ *Answer:* The metaphor is “ corruption is the malignant cancer that has eaten deep into the marrow of many African states ” . It compares corruption to a deadly disease that spreads and destroys the body from within. Effect: It helps the reader understand corruption as not superficial but life-threatening, systemic, and destructive to the core of a nation, evoking a sense of urgency and severity. *Question 2:* _The passage states that “ Justice itself is put on sale ” . What figure of speech is this and what does it reveal about the judicial system described?_ *Answer:* This is personification/metaphor. Justice, an abstract concept, is described as a commodity “ on sale ” . It reveals that the judicial system is corrupt, where court judgments are

determined by bribes rather than law, and the wealthy can buy favorable verdicts while the poor are denied justice. *Question 3:* _According to the passage, how much does Africa lose annually to corruption, and what does the author compare this figure to in order to emphasize its scale?_ *Answer:* Africa loses $148 billion annually to corruption. The author compares this figure to “ the combined annual GDP of several smaller African nations ” to emphasize how massive the loss is — enough to fund entire countries. *Question 4:* _ “ Foreign investment flees like a startled bird ” is an example of what figure of speech? Explain how it illustrates the impact of corruption on investment._ *Answer:* This is a simile. It compares foreign investment to a startled bird that flies away quickly at the slightest disturbance. pages.text: *COMPREHENSION PASSAGE: CORRUPTION AS THE BANE OF DEVELOPMENT IN AFRICAN COUNTRIES* Corruption is the malignant cancer that has eaten deep into the marrow of many African states, crippling their quest for sustainable development. It is not merely the petty bribe demanded by a traffic officer on a dusty highway; it is the systemic looting of public treasuries, the auctioning of national assets to the highest bidder behind closed doors, and the deliberate distortion of policies to serve a privileged few. In Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Zimbabwe, and indeed across the continent, corruption has become a hydra-headed monster. When one head is cut off through a high-profile arrest, two more grow in its place through new procurement scams, ghost worker syndicates, and illicit financial flows. The cost of corruption is staggering and measurable. The African Union estimates that Africa loses $148 billion annually to corruption, a figure that exceeds the combined annual GDP of several smaller African nations. This haemorrhage drains resources that should build schools, hospitals, roads, and power plants. Instead, funds meant for primary healthcare are diverted into private offshore accounts, leaving rural clinics as mere shells without drugs or personnel. Children sit on bare floors in dilapidated classrooms while budgets for education are padded, inflated, and eventually embezzled. Infrastructure projects become white elephants: bridges to nowhere and airports without planes, commissioned with fanfare but abandoned once the kickbacks have been paid. Thus, corruption is a thief that steals not only money but also the future. Beyond economics, corruption corrodes the social fabric. It enthrones mediocrity and banishes merit. When appointments, contracts, and admissions are sold to the highest bidder, the competent are sidelined and the nation is robbed of its best minds. The civil service, which should be the engine of policy implementation, becomes a vehicle for patronage. Young Africans, seeing that hard work does not pay, either join the corrupt bandwagon or flee abroad, creating a brain drain that further impoverishes the continent. Justice itself is put on sale. The poor man ’ s cry for redress echoes unheard in courts where judgments are auctioned and the scales of justice tilt in favor of those with bulging pockets. Politically, corruption weakens institutions and fuels instability. Elections become costly bazaars where votes are bought and ballot boxes are stuffed, producing leaders whose loyalty is to their financiers rather than the electorate. Legitimacy is eroded, and citizens lose faith in the state. This vacuum of trust is quickly filled by ethnic militias, insurgents, and coup plotters who promise the change that democracy failed to deliver. From the Sahel to the Horn of Africa, the link between grand corruption and insecurity is unmistakable. Funds meant for equipping the military are siphoned off, leaving soldiers to face terrorists with obsolete weapons and unpaid allowances. Yet, to call corruption merely a challenge is to understate its venom. It is the bane of development because it attacks the four pillars upon which progress rests: accountability, transparency, rule of law, and equity. Without these, foreign investment flees like a startled bird, for no rational investor will sink capital in a swamp of uncertainty. Domestic investors, too, are strangled by multiple taxation, shakedowns, and policy summersaults designed to create rent-seeking opportunities. The

result is chronic unemployment, poverty, and the painful irony of a continent richly endowed with oil, gold, diamonds, and arable land but whose people remain desperately poor. Fighting corruption therefore demands more than rhetoric. It requires strong institutions, not strong men. It calls for an independent judiciary, a fearless press, and a citizenry that refuses to normalize wrongdoing. Digital tools like IPPIS, GIFMIS, and TSA in Nigeria have shown that technology can block leakages if the political will exists. Anti-graft agencies such as the EFCC and ICPC must be insulated from political interference. Most importantly, there must be a cultural re-orientation that redefines public office as a trust and not a ticket to wealth. Until corruption is confronted as the existential threat it is, Africa ’ s development will remain a mirage that recedes with every step forward. *Word count: 647* --- *SUMMARY OF THE PASSAGE* Corruption is a deep-rooted, systemic problem in Africa that goes beyond petty bribes to include large-scale looting and policy manipulation. It costs the continent $148 billion yearly, diverting funds from education, health, and infrastructure, and creating “ white elephant ” projects. Socially, it promotes mediocrity over merit, fuels brain drain, and puts justice up for sale. Politically, it weakens institutions, undermines elections, erodes public trust, and links to insecurity as military funds are embezzled. By attacking accountability, transparency, rule of law, and equity, corruption drives away investment and perpetuates poverty despite Africa ’ s natural wealth. Effective solutions require strong, independent institutions, technology like IPPIS and TSA, insulated anti- graft bodies, and cultural change that views public office as a trust. Until then, development will remain elusive. --- *COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS & ANSWERS* *Question 1:* _Identify and explain the metaphor used to describe corruption in the first paragraph. What effect does this figure of speech have on the reader ’ s understanding?_ *Answer:* The metaphor is “ corruption is the malignant cancer that has eaten deep into the marrow of many African states ” . It compares corruption to a deadly disease that spreads and destroys the body from within. Effect: It helps the reader understand corruption as not superficial but life-threatening, systemic, and destructive to the core of a nation, evoking a sense of urgency and severity. *Question 2:* _The passage states that “ Justice itself is put on sale ” . title: CONSONANTS SOUNDS- PLOSIVES
subject: English Language
rawText: A plosive consonant is an abrupt sound made by closing the mouth then releasing a burst of breath Plosive consonants are made by completely blocking the flow of air as it leaves the body, normally followed by releasing the air. English pronunciation contains 6 plosive phonemes: /p,b,t,d,k,g/: The sounds /b,d,g/ are voiced; they are pronounced with vibration in the vocal cords. /p,t,k/ are voiceless; they are produced with air only. The voiceless plosives are often aspirated (produced with a puff of air) in English pronunciation. Plosive Spellings Common spellings for each plosive are underlined below: /p/: purse /b/: bell /t/: talk, stopped /d/: done, played /k/: kite, cone, queen, chronic, excited /g/: gone, exhaust

title: PRONOUNS; OTHER TYPES
subject: English Language
rawText: Pronouns; Other Types. 1. Possessive Pronoun; It is called so because they show or indicate possession. They include; my, mine, ours, yours, her, hers, his, their, theirs, it’s Examples; a. The principal has refused to release our results. b. Her father is the new minister of Education. c. Theirs is a unique case. 2.Interrogative Pronouns; It is derived from the word interrogation. These pronouns are used to ask questions; who, what, where, when, when, who, which Examples; a. Who sent you on this dangerous journey. b. What is your Favorite food? c. Which of the building is yours? 3. Reflexive Pronouns; It makes reference to the subject in the sentence. They are; himself, herself, myself, itself, themselves, ourselves, yourselves. Examples; a. My mother washes her clothes herself. b. The president himself visited the scene of the crises. 4. Personal pronoun; I, you, he, she, it, they, him, her, we, us, them. They refer to three categories of persons (People, objects, things, animals, ideas etc) They are; 1. First Person; The person speaking or reporting an event. First person I (singular) We (plural) a. I go to school everyday. b. We go to school everyday. 2. Second Person; The person or thing or idea that is spoken to or being addressed. You singular and plural takes the plural verb. a. You have one week to read for your examination. 3. Third person; The person or thing that is being spoken about or that is being discussed. The third person plural pronoun they takes plural verb. Examples a. They have been here since yesterday. b. They attend the seminar every month.

subject: English Language
rawText: Speech writing is like crafting a message to be delivered orally, usually to an audience . It's 😊 about conveying ideas, emotions, or info in a way that resonates with listeners. Features of speech writing include: - Clear structure (intro, body, conclusion) - Engaging opening and closing - Conversational tone (even if formal) - Rhetorical devices (repetition, metaphors, etc.) - Audience awareness - Emotional appeal

Comprehension Passage After more than two decades of waiting, Arsenal finally climbed the mountain again and won the English Premier League. The season began like a quiet storm gathering over the Emirates. Fans carried the weight of past heartbreak on their shoulders, but hope was a candle that refused to go out. From the first whistle, Mikel Arteta ’ s men played like lions let out of a cage. They attacked with the fury of thunder and defended like a wall built from stone. Week after week, the Gunners marched forward. Each victory was a brick laid on the road to glory. When they beat Manchester City at home, the stadium shook so hard it felt as if the ground itself was cheering. That night the players were not just eleven men on grass, they were soldiers fighting for a city, for a badge, for every fan who had waited twenty long years. The press called them “ invincible dreamers ” and the name stuck like glue. Injuries came like winter, cold and sharp. Bukayo Saka pulled his hamstring and the crowd held its breath. But Gabriel Martinelli stepped up and became fire on the left wing, dancing past defenders as if they were cones in training. Declan Rice covered every blade of grass. He was the heartbeat of the team, the engine that never stopped running. When he scored the last minute winner against Liverpool, time itself seemed to pause before the net bulged. The title race turned into a marathon where every point was gold. Arsenal dropped points in March and doubt crept in like fog. Pundits sharpened their knives and said the same old story was repeating. Yet the team refused to drown. Arteta spoke to them in the dressing room and his words were seeds that grew into belief. The next match they played like men possessed. Passing moved like music, one touch, two touch, goal. The Emirates became a fortress where visiting teams lost their courage. On the final day, the whole of North London held its breath. Arsenal needed a win and for their rivals to slip. As the minutes ticked away, fans prayed to every star in the sky. Then the news came from another ground. The rivals had drawn. A roar went up that could be heard across the Thames. When the final whistle blew at the Emirates, grown men cried and children jumped into their fathers ’ arms. Fireworks painted the sky red and white. The wait was over. Twenty years of hurt had melted away like snow under the sun. The players lifted the trophy and it glittered like a promise kept. Arteta raised his fists and the crowd answered with a chant that rolled like ocean waves. Arsenal were champions again. Not just because of talent, but because they refused to give up when the road was steep. The league was theirs, written in sweat, belief, and the blood red of their shirshirt. Questions and Answers *Content Questions*

1 Question: How long had Arsenal waited before winning the Premier League again Answer: Arsenal had waited more than two decades before winning the Premier League again 2 Question: Which player scored a last minute winner against Liverpool according to the passage Answer: Declan Rice scored a last minute winner against Liverpool 3 Question: What happened on the final day that helped Arsenal win the title Answer: On the final day Arsenal won their match and their rivals drew, so Arsenal became champions *Figures of Speech Questions* 4 Question: Identify one metaphor used in the passage and state its meaning Answer: Metaphor is hope was a candle that refused to go out. It means the fans hope stayed alive despite many years of disappointment 5 Question: Identify one simile used in the passage and state what is being compared Answer: Simile is defended like a wall built from stone. It compares the Arsenal defence to a strong stone wall to show how solid it was 6 Question: Identify one personification used in the passage and explain it Answer: Personification is doubt crept in like fog. Doubt is given human action of creeping to show how slowly and quietly fear entered the minds of people *Grammatical Names and Functions Question* 7 Question: In the sentence The players lifted the trophy and it glittered like a promise kept, what is the grammatical name of the phrase like a promise kept and what is its function Answer: The grammatical name of like a promise kept is an adverbial phrase of manner. Its function is to show how the trophy glittered

A consonant cluster is the coming together of two or more consonant sounds within a stretch of spelling in a word with coming in-between them.[ Consonant clusters is a situation where two or more consonant sounds [not letter come together in a word witho sound and are pronounced together. Consonant clusters can occur at the initial, medial or final word positions. Two consonant clusters at word initial, medial or final position is a situation where two consonant sounds are pronounced together at the b middle, or end of a word respectively. Three consonant clusters at word initial, medial or final position is a situation where three consonant sounds occur and are pronounced tog beginning, middle or end of a word. title: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH LAW AND ORDER
subject: English Language
rawText:
What is law and order? Law and order is a situation characterized by respect for and obedience to the rules of a society. It also refers to demands for strict criminal justice system, especially in relation to violent and property crime, through stricter penalties. Examples of words associated words associated with law and order. The following are some words associated with law and order: affidavit, allegation, arrest, alimony, among others. 1 Arrest; When a person is taken into custody by a police officer and charged with a crime. The armed robber has been arrested. 2 Charge; Formal accusation of a crime. Tony was charges to court for murder. 3 Case; A lawsuit or action in a court. 4 Judge; A person who hears and decides cases for the courts. The judge dismissed the case. 5 Magistrate; A person who is not a judge but is authorized to hear and decide certain types of cases. The magistrate adjourned the case to February 10. 6 Bail (bond); Money or property given to court for the temporal release of a defendant to ensure that the defendant will return to court. The politician was bailed for N10m 7 Defendant (in civil cases) A person who is given court papers, also called respondent. The defendant pleaded not guilty. 8 Defendant (in criminal cases) A person who is arrested and charged with a crime. The defendant pleaded not guilty. 9 Plaintiff (petitioner or complainant)) A person who sues or starts a civil case. The plaintiff refused to appear in court. 10 Summons; A legal paper that is used to start a civil case and get jurisdiction over a party. The tenants were served with summons 11 Challenge Rejection of a potential juror He went to high court to challenge the outcome of the case in the lower court. 12 Juror A member of the jury. My father is a juror. 13 Conviction To be found guilty of committing crime. Hassan was convicted of the crime. 14 Affidavit A written statement made under an oath, swearing to the truth of the context of a document. I went to court to swear to affidavit for loss of my document. 15 Affirmation Declaring to be true under the perjury by a person who will not take an oath for religious or other reasons. I affirm that what I said is the truth and nothing but the truth. 16 Alimony Money a court requires one spouse to pay the other spouse for support before and/or after the divorce is granted 17 Allegation Saying that something is true It was a mere allegation 18 Dismissal A judge’s decision to end a case. The case has been dismissed. 19 Judgment (decree or order)

A court’s decision the judgment is not in their favor. 20 Felony Any criminal offense for which a person may be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of more than one year.

I affirm that what I said is the truth and nothing but the truth. 16 Alimony Money a court requires one spouse to pay the other spouse for support before and/or after the divorce is granted 17 Allegation Saying that something is true It was a mere allegation 18 Dismissal A judge’s decision to end a case. A court’s decision the judgment is not in their favor. 20 Felony Any criminal offense for which a person may be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of more than one year.

title: ADJUNCTS
subject: English Language
rawText:
1. An adjunct (an adverbial) is a word or a phrase added to a sentence to give you more information about a doing or an action. 2. Adjuncts are basically adverbials modifying verbs. They are adverbs or phrases that add meaning to the verb in sentence or parts of sentences. 3. Adjunct can also be explained as a word or group of words which tells us when, where, why, how often and how an action is or was performed. (eg) ‘She went home yesterday’ and ‘He ran away in a, panic.’ (‘yesterday’ and ‘panic’ are adjuncts.) Functions of Adjuncts Unlike adverbs, adjuncts are not just single words that belong to the class of adverbs. They can be a group of words and they can be in the form of the following: 1. The noun phrase to indicate time, as in: the previous week, last year, two hours ago etc 2. Adverbs or adverb phrases that function as adverbs to indicate manner; as in: so suddenly, quickly, very slowly. 3. The prepositional phrase to show time and place, e.g, in the backyard, after the party by the special grace of God etc Types of Adjunction (Adverbial) 1. Adjunct of time (When?) 2. Adjunct of Place (Where?) 3. Adjunct of Reason (Why?) 4. Adjunct of Purpose (Why?) 5. Adjunct of Manner (How?) 1. Adjunct of Time: is a word or group of words which tell us when an action is or was performed. (Example) a. They met last year. b. I will be there by two O’clock. 1. Adjunct of Place: is a word or group of words that tell us where an action is or was performed. (Example) a. It was found on the table. b. I met him in the university.

1. Adjunct of Reason: is a word or group of words that tell us why an action is or was performed. (Example) a. The student were making noise since they have nothing doing. b. The girls was beaten by the principals because of stealing. 1. Adjunct of Purpose: is also a word or group of words that tells us why an action is or was performed like adjunct of reason. (Example) a. She wore her best so that she would emerge as Miss World. b. He came here in order to meet with the coach. 1. Adjuncts of Manner: is a word or group of word that tells us how an action is or was performed. (Example) a. The man quickly went away. b. He caught the ball as if he were a goal keeper.

rawText:
Students’ Summary Note Subject: English Language Topic: Reading for Specific Structural Patterns and Report Writing 1. Reading for Specific Structural Patterns Focus on how a passage is organized. Look for headings, subheadings, dates, steps, or numbered points in scientific or medical passages. Helps to understand the sequence of ideas and structure of the content. 2. Identifying Main and Supporting Ideas Main Idea: The most important point the writer wants to convey. Supporting Ideas: Details, examples, or explanations that explain or support the main idea. Example: Main Idea: Exercise is important for good health. Supporting Ideas: It strengthens the heart, improves mood, and prevents diseases. 3. Explaining Key Vocabulary Highlight difficult or technical words in the passage. Look for clues in the sentence to understand the meaning. Example (medical passage): Diagnosis: Identifying a disease Treatment: Care given to cure illness Patient: A person receiving medical care 4. Understanding the Format of a Report A report is a structured piece of writing that presents information clearly. Typical Structure of a Scientific/Medical Report: Title/Heading: Name of the experiment or study. Date: When the experiment or observation took place.

Introduction/Purpose: Why the experiment was conducted. Procedure/Method: Steps followed during the experiment. Results/Outcome: Findings or observations. Conclusion: Summary of findings or recommendations. 5. Writing a Simple Report Logically Use clear headings. Arrange information in chronological order or logical sequence. Write short, precise sentences. Include all main points and supporting details. Avoid unnecessary repetition. Example Structure: Title: Effect of Exercise on Heart Rate Date: 4th February 2026 Purpose: To investigate how exercise affects heart rate. Procedure: Students ran for 5 minutes; heart rates were recorded before and after. Results: Heart rate increased after exercise. Conclusion: Exercise raises heart rate, showing the heart works harder during physical activity. Importance Helps in understanding and summarizing information. Improves comprehension and analytical skills. Prepares students for structured writing tasks in exams. title: COMPREHENSION
subject: English Language
rawText:
*COMPREHENSION PASSAGE: "The Molue to Marina"* _Word count: 548_ In 2016, Tunde Alade stepped off the night bus at Ojota Park with a tattered Ghana-Must-Go bag, a second-class upper degree in Economics from Ahmadu Bello University, and a NYSC discharge certificate folded into his breast pocket. Lagos, they said, was the city of gold, where even the mad man on the street could stumble into fortune. At 24, Tunde believed it. He had left his father ’ s two-bedroom bungalow in Ilesa with prayers, ₦ 8,000, and the phone number of his uncle who lived in a ‘ boys ’ quarters ’ somewhere in Surulere. The uncle ’ s welcome lasted three weeks. On the fourth Monday, he dropped a simple truth with the morning pap: “ Tunde, Lagos is not your father ’ s farm. Even me, I ’ m managing. ” By December, Tunde was a bona fide resident of Ikorodu, squatting in an uncompleted building with five other ‘ hustlers ’ . The room had no windows, but it had mosquitoes, heat, and the nightly chorus of generators that never let a man dream in peace. The next ten years were a brutal curriculum. He hawked La Casera in Oshodi traffic and learned to dodge LASTMA officials whose uniforms meant trouble, not order. He wrote applications on the bonnet of a danfo until his biro ran dry, and attended interviews in borrowed ties that choked his ambition. At Computer Village, he became ‘ Baba Charge ’ , repairing phone screens for ₦ 300 profit while his degree gathered dust. He sat for aptitude tests at Victoria Island towers where the security men sized him up by his worn shoes before his CV. “ We ’ ll get back to you ” became the national anthem of his despair. Lagos taught him new economics. He mastered the law of the molue: if you don ’ t shout your destination, you ’ ll miss your stop. He learned that ‘ network ’ was not MTN but the cousin of your pastor ’ s friend who knew an oga at the top. He borrowed to pay for professional exams, only to fail because he had read by candlelight after a 14-hour day. Landlords increased rent with the frequency of rainfall, and every December his Ilesa people asked, “ Tunde, when are you bringing your car home? ” In 2022, cholera from the Ikorodu water killed Ade, his roommate. That night, Tunde sat on the floor and counted his age: 30. No job, no wife, no land. He almost bought a bus ticket home. Instead, he enrolled for a free data analytics course at a Yaba tech hub, using a phone he repaired himself. He slept there three nights a week, coding while others slept. His breakthrough wore no agbada. It came via LinkedIn at 2 a.m. in 2026. A fintech in Marina needed a data analyst who understood ‘ the real Lagos ’ . His CV had ten years of unpaid internships: traffic, survival, human behavior. The HR manager, herself an Ijebu woman, read his cover letter and laughed: “ So you ’ re the famous Baba Charge? ” Today, Tunde ’ s cubicle overlooks the Third Mainland Bridge. The same bridge he once crossed hanging from the doorway of a 911, praying not to fall. His salary can pay the Ikorodu rent for a year, but he stays, because the uncompleted building now houses his foundation, ‘ Molue

Graduates ’ , where he trains other dreamers. Lagos did not give him gold. It gave him grit, and after ten years, grit became gold. When he finally drove into Ilesa last Christmas, his father touched the car and said, “ So, Lagos is truly your father ’ s farm. ” Tunde smiled. “ No, Baba. Lagos is the farm, and I am the stubborn seed. ” --- *COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS & ANSWERS* *1. Why did Tunde ’ s uncle ask him to leave after three weeks?* *Answer:* The uncle told Tunde that “ Lagos is not your father ’ s farm ” and that even he was “ managing, ” meaning he could no longer accommodate Tunde due to his own economic difficulties. *2. State three specific hardships Tunde experienced in Lagos before getting his job.* *Answer:* Any three of the following: 1. He squatted in an uncompleted building in Ikorodu with no windows, heat, and mosquitoes. 2. He hawked La Casera in Oshodi traffic and had to dodge LASTMA officials. 3. He was judged by his worn shoes at interviews and often told “ We ’ ll get back to you ” . 4. He failed professional exams because he read by candlelight after working 14-hour days. 5. His roommate Ade died of cholera from Ikorodu water. *3. What does the phrase “ the law of the molue: if you don ’ t shout your destination, you ’ ll miss your stop ” mean in the context of the passage?* *Answer:* It means that in Lagos, you must be vocal, proactive, and assertive about your goals and needs, otherwise opportunities will pass you by, just as a passenger must shout his stop or be carried past it. *4. How did Tunde eventually secure his job at the fintech company in Marina?* *Answer:* He enrolled in a free data analytics course at a Yaba tech hub, learned to code, and applied via LinkedIn at 2 a.m. The HR manager hired him because his CV reflected ten years of ‘ unpaid internships ’ in understanding ‘ the real Lagos ’ and human behavior. *5. What is ironic about Tunde ’ s father ’ s statement, “ So, Lagos is truly your father ’ s farm ” ?* *Answer:* The irony is that Tunde ’ s uncle initially used the phrase to mean Lagos was not an easy place like his father ’ s farm, implying Tunde could not rely on others. At the end, Tunde reframes it: Lagos was indeed a ‘ farm ’ where he, a ‘ stubborn seed ’ , had to toil for ten years before yielding success, contrasting the initial dismissal. *6. What does Tunde ’ s foundation ‘ Molue Graduates ’ reveal about his character and experience in Lagos?* *Answer:* It reveals that Tunde is resilient, empathetic, and community-minded. Despite his suffering, he uses his success to train other struggling graduates, showing he transformed his ten years of hardship into a means to help others navigate the same ‘ vicissitudes ’ of Lagos.

title: SPEECH
subject: English Language
rawText:
The teacher lead the students to discuss on the following: WORD STRESS AND SYLLABLES Word stress and syllables are the Syllabic stress is communicated through volume, pitch, and length. Most English words that only have two syllables will place stress on the first syllable, but where the stress belongs actually depends on the word's type: noun, adjective, or verb. Nouns will place the stress on the first syllable. things to learn about A syllable is a word, or part of a word, which contains a single vowel sound. It is a single unit of speech. Each word contains one syllable, or more. 1 SYLLABLE Here are examples of words with a single syllable: pen man pig cup hat In English, a vowel sound can be made of more the one vowel letter. So the following words have a single syllable as well: feet moon cake have break bought All of these words contain only one vowel sound, and therefore a single syllable.

2 SYLLABLES A word can have more than one syllable. THE FOLLOWING WORDS ARE EXAMPLES OF WORDS WITH TWO SYLLABLES. Here are examples of words with 2 syllables. The different syllables are shown on the right, and they are separated with a space. garden: gar den hotel: ho tel consist: con sist object: ob ject focus: fo cus 3 SYLLABLES Examples of words with three syllables: September: sep tem ber department: de part ment telephone: te le phone camera: ca mer a Saturday: sa tur day hamburger: hum bur ger vitamin: vi ta min 4 SYLLABLES Examples of words with four syllables: kindergarten: kin der gar ten information: in for ma tion January: ja nu ar y American: A mer i can discovery: di sco ver y That is not all, of course. There can be words with even more syllables. But you get the point, right?

WORD STRESS When a word has more than one syllable, not all syllables are pronounced with the same degree of force. The syllable which is pronounced with greater force is called the stressed syllable. You can also call it the accented syllable. "Accent" in this case means "emphasis".

title: SHORT STORY
subject: English Language
rawText:
### Explanation of a Short Story A short story is a brief fictional narrative typically focused on a particular theme or character. It conveys a concise plot that conveys emotional or intellectual impact while usually centering around a single incident or moment. ### Parts of a Short Story 1. **Introduction**: Sets the scene and introduces characters. 2. **Rising Action**: Presents the main conflict and builds tension. 3. **Climax**: The turning point or most intense moment of the story. 4. **Falling Action**: Actions that follow the climax and lead to resolution. 5. **Resolution**: Conclusion of the story, where conflicts are resolved. ### Characteristics of a Good Short Story 1. **Focused Theme**: A clear central message or theme that resonates. 2. **Well-developed Characters**: Characters that are relatable and evoke emotion. 3. **Compelling Plot**: An engaging and coherent storyline. 4. **Emotional Impact**: Leaves the reader with something to think about or feel. 5. **Conciseness**: Every word and scene contributes to the overall narrative. ### Short Story: "The Whispering Winds of Kanjara" In the heart of Kanjara, a small African village tucked away between lush hills and the winding river, lived a young girl named Adama. Adama was known for her bright laughter and her mom's famous groundnut stew that stirred the village ’ s senses during the market days. With hair like a midnight sky braided with beads and a spirit that danced with the wind, she was a beacon of joy for her community. As the dry season approached, the village experienced a drought. The river, once a lively ribbon of water alive with sparrows and fish, shrank into a thin trickle. The crops ceased to thrive, and worry shadowed the villagers' faces. Elders gathered under the ancient baobab tree, whispering of traditions and rituals once forgotten, pondering how to bring back the rains. Adama felt their tension and wanted to help. "We could dig deeper by the riverbank to find water," she suggested. Many villagers chuckled, dismissing her youthful optimism but one elder, Mama Nandi, nodded. “ The strength of one may not seem large, but even the tiniest seed grows into a mighty baobab, ” she said. In the following days, Adama gathered a group of children from the village, and they began their quest to dig. Day by day, they worked, the sun beating down on their backs, their hands caked with dirt. They sang songs of hope, their voices a blend of laughter and innocence. The villagers watched as the children toiled, the rhythm of their hope becoming infectious.

After weeks of digging, one fateful afternoon, they struck something solid. The children squealed with excitement as they unearthed a hidden spring, water bubbling forth like a burst of joy. It poured out, filling the dry riverbed. The villagers rushed with pots and bowls, their despair morphing into pure elation. As the water flowed, the sky darkened. Thunder rumbled, and raindrops began to fall, transforming Kanjara. Everyone joined in a joyous dance, their spirits mingled with the scent of wet earth. Adama, with tears of happiness streaming down her face, turned to Mama Nandi. "Did you see, Mama? We brought the rains!" The elder smiled. “ No, my child. You reminded us that hope, like a seed, thrives in the toughest conditions. ” From that day onwards, the village of Kanjara flourished again, but it was Adama ’ s unwavering determination and belief in each other ’ s strength that changed their fate, reminding them that even in the harshest of times, miracles were possible through unity and hope.

Theme-Structure Date: 09/06/2026 Unit Topic-Auxiliary Verb Lesson Topic-Modal and Primary Auxiliary Specific Objectives-At the end of the lesson, the students should be able to: i. give the meaning of auxiliary verb ii. list the types auxiliary verbs iii. give their functions iv. use them in sentences Instructional Resource-A chart with different auxiliary verbs Lesson Presentation Step 1 identification of prior ideas Mode-Entire class Teacher's activities-The teacher asks the students to define auxiliary verb in their own way.Thereafter, she guides them to define it appropriately. Students'activities-The students define auxiliary verbs: Auxiliary verbs are verbs that exist only in helping forms.They usually go with main or lexical verbs to which they serve as helpers hence the name helping verbs. When a verb has another verbal item after it, it is usually an auxiliary verb. Step 2-Exploration Mode-Entire class Teacher's Activities-The teacher presents the instructional resource and guides the students to list the types of auxiliary verbs. Students' activities-The students list types of auxiliary verbs: a. Primary auxiliary verbs-they include: 'be','have' and 'do'. b. Modal auxiliary verbs-they include: Can,could,may,might, must, ought to,will,would,shall,should. Step 3-Discussion Mode-Entire class

Teacher's Activities-The teacher guides the students to give the functions of the auxiliary verbs listed. Students' Activities-The students give the functions: a. Primary auxiliary verbs- these verbs can be used as main verbs, they are in passive transformations and can be used to form tenses.Examples: 'be' which are: is, am,was,were,are - She is coming with us - I am travelling - He was looking at me 'have'-has,have,had,used to form perfect tenses. - Juliet has finished eating. - I have eaten the food. - He had gone before I arrived. 'do'-do'does, did. These are used to form questions and negative statements Do you like it? - He does not know. - David did not go home b. Modal auxiliary verbs-these verbs function in the following ways: i. can-ability,possibility,permission,request. ii. Could-asking for permission, request, suggestions, future possibility,and ability in the past. iii. May-asking for permission, future possibility iv. Might-possibility or permission V. Must-necessity,obligation vi. Ought to-offer,suggestion vii. Will-promise,intention,polite request,prediction viii. Would-asking for permission,request,willingness ix.Should-saying what is right,recommendation,prediction,obligation,logical necessity Step 4-Application Mode-Entire class Teacher's activities-The teacher guides the students to use the modal auxiliary verbs in sentences.

Students' activities-The students use the verbs in sentences: i. Can-They can control their own budget. ii. Could-The road could be blocked. iii. May-Nigeria may become the world's economic giant. iv. Might-Paul might arrive from Lagos today. V. Shall-I shall attend the meeting. vi. Should-You should take care of the children. vii. Will-The moon will appear today. viii. Would-The patient would die if nobody cares for him. ix. Must-You must tell me the truth. X. Used to-He used to smoke daily. xi. Ought to-You ought to do this assignment, Step 5-Evaluation Mode-Entire class Teacher's activities-The teacher asks the following questions: 1. What is an auxiliary verb? 2. List the types of auxiliary verbs. 3. Give the functions of three modal auxiliary verbs. 4. Use them in sentences. Students'Activities-The students answer the questions. Assignment-Write five sentences using the modal auxiliary verbs. References 1. Omorodion G.N. (2007) The Basic Grammar of English Spectrum Book Limited 2. Martins I. Amaechi (2005) New Comprehensive English Language for SSS Johnson Publishers
