title: SPEECH MAKING:TOAST MAKING
subject: English Language
rawText:
Speech making: Making a toast: a. Meaning of a toast b. Occasions for a toast Define a toast, prepare a toast and deliver a toast appropriate to a given occasion. Making a Toast : a. Meaning of a Toast: A toast is a brief and celebratory public statement or gesture usually accompanied by raising a glass of drink. It's a way to express good wishes, honour someone, or commemorate a special occasion. b. Occasions for a Toast: Toasts can be appropriate for a variety of occasions, including: 1. Weddings : To celebrate the newlyweds' love and commitment. 2. Birthdays : To wish someone a happy and successful year ahead. 3. Anniversaries : To honour the years of togetherness. 4. Graduations : To congratulate the graduate on their achievements. 5. Retirements : To bid farewell and acknowledge years of hard work. 6. Promotions : To recognize and celebrate career advancements.

7. Holidays : Such as New Year's Eve, Christmas, Sallah, for festive cheer. 8. Achievements : To acknowledge personal or professional accomplishments. 9. Memorials : To remember and pay tribute to a deceased loved one. Preparing and Delivering a Toast: 1. Define Your Purpose : Understand the reason for the toast, whether it's to celebrate, honour, or remember. 2. Keep it Brief: A good toast is concise and to the point, typically lasting no more than 2-3 minutes. 3. Prepare Your Content: Craft a heartfelt message, including anecdotes, quotes, or personal experiences related to the occasion or the person you're toasting. 4. Practice : Rehearse your toast to ensure you're comfortable delivering it smoothly. 5. Use Appropriate Language: Tailor your words to the occasion, whether it's formal or casual. 6. Raise Your Glass: Lift your glass when you begin your toast, and encourage others to do the same. 7. Eye Contact: Maintain eye contact with your audience while speaking. 8. Speak Clearly and Slowly:

Ensure everyone can hear and understand you by speaking clearly and at a moderate pace. 9. Express Emotion: Show genuine emotion, whether it's joy, gratitude, or sympathy, to connect with your audience. 10. End on a Positive Note: - Conclude with a positive and memorable sentiment, such as a wish or a heartfelt "Cheers!" Remember, the key to a successful toast is sincerity and the ability to connect with your audience emotionally. Tailor your words to fit the occasion and the people you are addressing, and your toast will be both meaningful and memorable. Sample Wedding toast for my best friend: "Ladies and gentlemen, if I could kindly ask for your attention, please, could you all stand up and raise your glasses to a truly special moment in all our lives. Today, we gather not just as witnesses but as active participants in the beautiful love story of my Best Friend, Sameera and her Spouse, Musa. To say that I am honored to stand here as Sameera's best friend and toastmistress is an understatement. From the very beginning of their journey together, I've had the privilege of watching their love blossom and

grow into something truly extraordinary. Sameera and Musa, your love is an inspiration to us all. It's a testament to the power of patience, understanding, and unwavering commitment. As I look at the two of you today, I see not just a couple, but a team - a team that has navigated life's challenges together with grace and a sense of humour that's nothing short of remarkable. Your love is not only a source of joy for yourselves but for all of us who are fortunate enough to be a part of your lives. May your journey ahead be filled with laughter, adventure, and countless beautiful moments. May you continue to support and lift each other up, just as you have done from the very beginning. So, let's raise our glasses high, and let us toast to Sameera and Musa to a lifetime of happiness, love, and endless shared adventures. May your love story continue to inspire us all. Cheers!" Ask Learners to choose any occasion of their choice and craft similar toast. Created by Ewuzie Jacinta GSS Jabi.

STUDENTS’ SUMMARY NOTE Topic: Law and Order 1. Definition of Law and Order Law and Order refers to a system of rules, regulations, and institutions established by a society or government to regulate human behavior, maintain peace, protect lives and property, and ensure justice and harmony in the society. 2. Words Associated with Law and Order Law Order Justice Constitution Court Police Crime Punishment Rights Duties Authority Rules Regulations Discipline Security 3. Meaning of Some Words Associated with Law and Order Law: A set of rules made by the government to control the behavior of people in a society. Order: A state of peace, stability, and proper organization in society.

Justice: Fair treatment of all people according to the law. Constitution: The supreme law of a country that outlines the structure of government and citizens’ rights. Police: Government officers responsible for maintaining law and order and preventing crime. Crime: An act that breaks the law and is punishable by law. Punishment: A penalty given to someone who breaks the law. Rights: Legal freedoms and privileges enjoyed by citizens. Duties: Responsibilities that citizens are expected to perform. Security: Protection of lives and property from danger or crime. 4. Sentences Using Words Associated with Law and Order The law must be obeyed by all citizens. Order is necessary for peace to exist in society. The court ensures justice for everyone. The constitution protects the rights of citizens. The police arrested the criminal. Stealing is a crime punishable by law. Every offence has its punishment. Citizens have rights and responsibilities. It is our duty to obey traffic rules. The government provides security for the people.

title: REGISTER - MEDICINE
subject: English Language
rawText:
**Medicine** is a science and practice focused on the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of diseases and health conditions. It integrates various disciplines, including biology, pharmacy, surgery, public health, and mental health, aimed at improving the overall well-being of individuals and populations. Healthcare professionals, such as doctors, nurses, and pharmacists, utilize a combination of knowledge, skills, and human compassion to provide care. Here ’ s a list of 50 words associated with medicine, along with explanations for each: 1. **Diagnosis**: The determination of a disease or condition based on patient symptoms and diagnostic tests. 2. **Treatment**: The management and care of a patient to combat disease or alleviate symptoms. 3. **Prognosis**: The forecast of the likely outcome of a disease, including chances of recovery. 4. **Therapy**: A systematic treatment for a disease or condition, including medication and physical interventions. 5. **Pharmacology**: The study of drugs and their effects on living organisms, focusing on medication action, interactions, and side effects. 6. **Anatomy**: The branch of biology that studies the structure and organization of living organisms. 7. **Physiology**: The study of the functions and processes of the body's systems and organs. 8. **Surgery**: A medical discipline involving operative procedures to treat injuries, deformities, or diseases. 9. **Epidemiology**: The study of how diseases affect populations, determining the spread and control of health issues. 10. **Preventive Care**: Medical practices aimed at disease prevention rather than treatment, including screenings and vaccinations. 11. **Palliative Care**: Specialized care focused on providing relief from symptoms and improving quality of life for those with serious, chronic illness. 12. **Clinical Trials**: Research studies that test new medical approaches, drugs, or treatments on human participants for effectiveness and safety. 13. **Immunology**: The study of the immune system and its role in protecting against disease and infection.

14. **Allergy**: An immune system reaction to a foreign substance, which can cause symptoms ranging from mild to severe. 15. **Microbiology**: The study of microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites, and their roles in health and disease. 16. **Radiology**: The use of imaging technologies, such as X-rays and MRIs, to diagnose and treat diseases. 17. **Anesthesia**: A medical treatment that temporarily reduces or eliminates sensation or pain during surgical or other medical procedures. 18. **Pathology**: The study of diseases, including their causes, development, and effects on the body, often involving laboratory analysis of tissues. 19. **Nursing**: A healthcare profession focused on the care of individuals, families, and communities to maintain or improve health. 20. **Cardiology**: The branch of medicine that deals with disorders and diseases of the heart and blood vessels. 21. **Neurology**: The medical specialty that focuses on the diagnosis and treatment of disorders of the nervous system. 22. **Oncology**: The study and treatment of cancer and tumors. 23. **Psychiatry**: A branch of medicine that deals with mental health disorders and emotional disturbances. 24. **Dermatology**: The branch of medicine focused on the diagnosis and treatment of skin conditions. 25. **Gastroenterology**: The study and treatment of the digestive system and its disorders. 26. **Endocrinology**: The study of hormones and glands, and how they affect metabolism and overall health. 27. **Urology**: The medical specialty that focuses on the urinary tract and male reproductive system. 28. **Obstetrics**: The field of medicine focusing on childbirth and the care of women before, during, and after delivery. 29. **Pediatrics**: The branch of medicine that deals with the health and medical care of infants,

children, and adolescents. 30. **Geriatrics**: The branch of medicine that focuses on health care for the elderly population. 31. **Hematology**: The study and treatment of blood disorders. 32. **Virology**: The study of viruses and their impact on living organisms. 33. **Imaging**: Techniques used to visualize the internal structures of the body, including X- rays, MRIs, and CT scans. 34. **Transplantation**: The process of transferring organs or tissues from one body to another to replace damaged or lost function. 35. **Chronic Disease**: A long-lasting condition that can be controlled but not cured, such as diabetes or hypertension. 36. **Acute Care**: Immediate medical treatment for sudden and severe conditions. 37. **Telemedicine**: The use of technology to provide healthcare services remotely, allowing patients to consult healthcare providers through digital means. 38. **Health Record**: A systematic collection of patient health information that is maintained and updated by healthcare providers. 39. **Infection Control**: Practices and procedures used to prevent the spread of infections in healthcare settings. 40. **Nutritional Medicine**: The use of dietary and nutritional interventions to prevent or treat health conditions. 41. **Rehabilitation**: A process aimed at restoring function and quality of life to individuals after illness or injury. 42. **Acupuncture**: A traditional Chinese medicine practice that involves inserting thin needles into specific points on the body to alleviate pain and treat various conditions. 43. **Complementary Medicine**: Alternative therapies used alongside conventional medicine, such as acupuncture, herbal medicine, and massage therapy. 44. **Homeopathy**: A system of alternative medicine based on the principle of treating "like with like" using highly diluted substances. 45. **Holistic Medicine**: An approach to healthcare that considers the whole person — mind,

body, and spirit — in the treatment process. 46. **Biostatistics**: The application of statistics to biological and health-related processes, crucial for medical research and public health decisions. 47. **Chiropractic**: A medical practice focusing on the diagnosis and treatment of mechanical disorders of the musculoskeletal system, primarily through spinal manipulation. 48. **Patient Advocacy**: The support and actions taken to promote the rights and interests of patients in the healthcare system. 49. **Medications**: Substances used for medical treatment; these can include prescription drugs, over-the-counter pharmaceuticals, and herbal remedies. 50. **Healthcare System**: The organization of people, institutions, and resources providing healthcare services to meet the health needs of a specific population. These terms illustrate the breadth of the medical field, reflecting its complexity, interdisciplinary nature, and the comprehensive approach required to address health-related challenges.

Here ’ s a list of 50 words associated with medicine, along with explanations for each: 1. **Diagnosis**: The determination of a disease or condition based on patient symptoms and diagnostic tests. 2. **Treatment**: The management and care of a patient to combat disease or alleviate symptoms. 3. **Prognosis**: The forecast of the likely outcome of a disease, including chances of recovery. 4. **Therapy**: A systematic treatment for a disease or condition, including medication and physical interventions. 5. **Pharmacology**: The study of drugs and their effects on living organisms, focusing on medication action, interactions, and side effects. 6. **Anatomy**: The branch of biology that studies the structure and organization of living organisms. 7. **Physiology**: The study of the functions and processes of the body's systems and organs. 8. **Surgery**: A medical discipline involving operative procedures to treat injuries, deformities, or diseases. 9. **Epidemiology**: The study of how diseases affect populations, determining the spread and control of health issues. 10. **Preventive Care**: Medical practices aimed at disease prevention rather than treatment, including screenings and vaccinations. 11. **Palliative Care**: Specialized care focused on providing relief from symptoms and improving quality of life for those with serious, chronic illness. 12. **Clinical Trials**: Research studies that test new medical approaches, drugs, or treatments on human participants for effectiveness and safety. 13. **Immunology**: The study of the immune system and its role in protecting against disease and infection.

14. **Allergy**: An immune system reaction to a foreign substance, which can cause symptoms ranging from mild to severe. 15. **Microbiology**: The study of microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites, and their roles in health and disease. 16. **Radiology**: The use of imaging technologies, such as X-rays and MRIs, to diagnose and treat diseases. 17. **Anesthesia**: A medical treatment that temporarily reduces or eliminates sensation or pain during surgical or other medical procedures. 18. **Pathology**: The study of diseases, including their causes, development, and effects on the body, often involving laboratory analysis of tissues. 19. **Nursing**: A healthcare profession focused on the care of individuals, families, and communities to maintain or improve health. 20. **Cardiology**: The branch of medicine that deals with disorders and diseases of the heart and blood vessels. 21. **Neurology**: The medical specialty that focuses on the diagnosis and treatment of disorders of the nervous system. 22. **Oncology**: The study and treatment of cancer and tumors. 23. **Psychiatry**: A branch of medicine that deals with mental health disorders and emotional disturbances. 24. **Dermatology**: The branch of medicine focused on the diagnosis and treatment of skin conditions. 25. **Gastroenterology**: The study and treatment of the digestive system and its disorders. 26. **Endocrinology**: The study of hormones and glands, and how they affect metabolism and overall health. 27. **Urology**: The medical specialty that focuses on the urinary tract and male reproductive system. 28. **Obstetrics**: The field of medicine focusing on childbirth and the care of women before, during, and after delivery. 29. **Pediatrics**: The branch of medicine that deals with the health and medical care of infants,

children, and adolescents. 30. **Geriatrics**: The branch of medicine that focuses on health care for the elderly population. 31. **Hematology**: The study and treatment of blood disorders. 32. **Virology**: The study of viruses and their impact on living organisms. 33. **Imaging**: Techniques used to visualize the internal structures of the body, including X- rays, MRIs, and CT scans. 34. **Transplantation**: The process of transferring organs or tissues from one body to another to replace damaged or lost function. 35. **Chronic Disease**: A long-lasting condition that can be controlled but not cured, such as diabetes or hypertension. 36. **Acute Care**: Immediate medical treatment for sudden and severe conditions. 37. **Telemedicine**: The use of technology to provide healthcare services remotely, allowing patients to consult healthcare providers through digital means. 38. **Health Record**: A systematic collection of patient health information that is maintained and updated by healthcare providers. 39. **Infection Control**: Practices and procedures used to prevent the spread of infections in healthcare settings. 40. **Nutritional Medicine**: The use of dietary and nutritional interventions to prevent or treat health conditions. 41. **Rehabilitation**: A process aimed at restoring function and quality of life to individuals after illness or injury. 42. **Acupuncture**: A traditional Chinese medicine practice that involves inserting thin needles into specific points on the body to alleviate pain and treat various conditions. 43. **Complementary Medicine**: Alternative therapies used alongside conventional medicine, such as acupuncture, herbal medicine, and massage therapy. 44. **Homeopathy**: A system of alternative medicine based on the principle of treating "like with like" using highly diluted substances. 45. **Holistic Medicine**: An approach to healthcare that considers the whole person — mind,

body, and spirit — in the treatment process. 46. **Biostatistics**: The application of statistics to biological and health-related processes, crucial for medical research and public health decisions. 47. **Chiropractic**: A medical practice focusing on the diagnosis and treatment of mechanical disorders of the musculoskeletal system, primarily through spinal manipulation. 48. **Patient Advocacy**: The support and actions taken to promote the rights and interests of patients in the healthcare system. 49. **Medications**: Substances used for medical treatment; these can include prescription drugs, over-the-counter pharmaceuticals, and herbal remedies. 50. **Healthcare System**: The organization of people, institutions, and resources providing healthcare services to meet the health needs of a specific population. These terms illustrate the breadth of the medical field, reflecting its complexity, interdisciplinary nature, and the comprehensive approach required to address health-related challenges.

title: CONTINUOUS WRITING -FREE WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText: Free writing is basically putting pen to paper (or fingers to keyboard) and letting thoughts flow without worrying about grammar, structure, or whether it “makes sense.” It’s a way to get ideas out of your head and onto the page, kind of like a brain dump. *How students can do it effectively* - *Set a timer* – 5‑10 minutes works. Write nonstop until it rings. - *Pick a prompt* – a question, a picture, or just “What’s on my mind?” - *Ignore the rules* – no editing, no backspacing. Spelling and punctuation don’t matter. - *Keep it private* – treat it as a personal space so you feel free to be honest. - *Review later* – after the session, skim for any gems you might want to develop further. Give it a try; the more you do it, the easier the ideas start flowing.

title: SUMMARY WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText:
*SIX-HUNDRED-WORD PASSAGE: FIVE MAJOR REASONS WHY AFRICANS ARE VERY RELIGIOUS* Religion permeates virtually every aspect of life in Africa, shaping culture, politics, family, and personal identity. From the mosques of Dakar to the churches of Lagos and the shrines of rural Uganda, faith is not a weekend activity but a daily reality. Surveys by Pew Research consistently rank African nations among the most religious in the world, with over 80% of people saying religion is very important to them. This deep religiosity is not accidental. It emerges from a blend of history, worldview, social structure, and lived experience that makes spiritual belief a central pillar of African existence. Five major reasons explain why Africans hold religion in such high regard. First, the African worldview is inherently spiritual. Long before the arrival of Christianity or Islam, indigenous African societies understood the universe as one where the physical and spiritual realms are intertwined. Ancestors, deities, and unseen forces were believed to influence harvests, health, fertility, and fortune. This holistic cosmology did not disappear with new faiths; instead, it was absorbed into them. Many African Christians still pour libation for ancestors, and many Muslims consult traditional healers alongside Imams. Because life is interpreted through a spiritual lens, religion becomes the primary framework for explaining both good fortune and calamity, making it indispensable. Second, religion serves as a critical source of hope and resilience amid hardship. Many African countries wrestle with poverty, unemployment, weak healthcare, and political instability. When state institutions fail to deliver security or basic services, churches and mosques step in with food banks, school fees, hospital bills, and emotional support. The promise of divine intervention gives meaning to suffering. Phrases like “ God will provide ” or “ Insha ’ Allah ” are not clichés but survival strategies. For millions, faith is the insurance policy when no government safety net exists, and the church or mosque is the one institution that never closes its doors. Third, community and identity are built around religion. African societies place a high premium on belonging — to a clan, ethnic group, and extended family. Religious congregations extend that kinship network. Baptisms, weddings, Eid celebrations, and funeral rites are communal events that reinforce social bonds and mutual obligation. To be religious is to be part of a community that buries your dead, names your children, and defends your honor. In urban centers where traditional ties weaken, religious groups become new families. Thus, religious identity is often inseparable from social identity, and abandoning faith can mean social exile. Fourth, religion provides a moral and legal compass where state systems are distrusted. Colonialism and post-independence corruption have left many Africans skeptical of police, courts, and politicians. In contrast, religious texts and leaders are seen as custodians of unchanging moral truth. The Ten Commandments, the Qur ’ an, or the wisdom of Ifa are invoked to settle disputes, sanction behavior, and teach children. Pastors and Imams command more trust than elected officials, and their pronouncements on corruption, marriage, or honesty carry real weight. Religion therefore fills the vacuum of legitimacy left by weak governance.

Fifth, historical missionary activity and colonial legacies institutionalized religion. Both Christian missionaries and Islamic scholars established schools, hospitals, and printing presses that were the first forms of Western or Arabic literacy in many regions. To be educated was to be evangelized. Over generations, these institutions produced elites and leaders who equated religion with civilization and progress. Today, the largest universities, hospitals, and NGOs in Africa are often faith-based. This historical entrenchment means religion is not just belief but infrastructure — it owns the buildings, employs the people, and writes the curriculum that shapes the next generation. *SUMMARY OF THE PASSAGE* Africans are deeply religious due to five interlocking factors. First, a traditional spiritual worldview that sees life through supernatural causes remains influential even within Christianity and Islam. Second, religion offers hope and material support where governments fail, functioning as a safety net in times of poverty and crisis. Third, faith communities provide vital social identity and belonging, replacing or reinforcing extended family ties. Fourth, religious institutions supply moral authority and trusted guidance in societies where state systems are weak or corrupt. Fifth, colonial and missionary history embedded religion into education, health, and leadership structures, making it central to modern African life. --- *QUESTIONS: IN FIVE SENTENCES, ONE FOR EACH, STATE THE FIVE REASONS WHY AFRICANS ARE VERY RELIGIOUS.* 1. What spiritual worldview makes religion central to African life? *Answer:* The traditional African worldview that sees the physical and spiritual realms as intertwined makes religion central, as life events are interpreted through supernatural causes. 2. How does hardship in Africa contribute to high levels of religiosity? *Answer:* Religion provides hope, resilience, and material support like food and school fees when state institutions fail, acting as a survival safety net. 3. In what way does religion shape community and identity for Africans? *Answer:* Religious congregations function as extended families that provide social bonds, belonging, and communal rites, so religious identity becomes inseparable from social identity. 4. Why do Africans trust religious systems more than state systems for moral guidance? *Answer:* Due to distrust of corrupt or weak government institutions, religious texts and leaders are seen as custodians of unchanging moral truth and legitimacy. 5. What historical factor institutionalized religion in Africa ’ s education and leadership? *Answer:* Missionary and Islamic scholars established schools, hospitals, and presses during the colonial era, linking education and progress with religion and embedding faith in key institutions.

title: REGISTER - LAW AND ORDER
subject: English Language
rawText:
**Law and Order** Law and order refers to the existence of a legal system and the enforcement of laws that govern society, ensuring safety, protection of rights, and maintenance of public peace. It encompasses various structures, agencies, and processes designed to prevent crime, enforce laws, and punish offenders. Effective law and order systems are crucial for social stability and justice, and they rely on cooperation between the government, law enforcement, and the community. Here are thirty words associated with law and order, along with their explanations: 1. **Law**: A system of rules established by a governing authority to regulate behavior. 2. **Justice**: The principle of fairness and the pursuit of moral rightness in law enforcement and legal proceedings. 3. **Enforcement**: The act of ensuring compliance with laws and regulations, often carried out by law enforcement agencies. 4. **Crime**: An act or behavior that violates a law and is punishable by the government. 5. **Punishment**: A penalty imposed for committing a crime, which can include fines, imprisonment, or community service. 6. **Order**: A state of peace and conformity to laws within a society. 7. **Regulation**: Rules or directives made and maintained by an authority to control or govern conduct. 8. **Sentencing**: The judicial determination of a punishment for a convicted offender. 9. **Defendant**: A person accused of a crime in a court of law. 10. **Prosecution**: The act of bringing a legal action against someone accused of wrongdoing in the interest of justice. 11. **Trial**: A legal proceeding in which evidence is presented and a case is heard in court to determine guilt or innocence. 12. **Appeal**: A request made to a higher court to review and change the decision of a lower court. 13. **Jurisdiction**: The official power to make legal decisions and judgments; the geographic area or subject matter over which this power extends.

14. **Witness**: A person who sees an event, typically a crime or accident, and can provide a firsthand account in court. 15. **Testimony**: A formal statement or declaration made by a witness under oath during a trial. 16. **Bail**: A monetary guarantee provided by the accused to secure their release from custody, ensuring they will appear for their court date. 17. **Conviction**: The result of a trial in which the defendant is found guilty of a crime. 18. **Acquittal**: A legal judgment declaring that a defendant is not guilty of the charges against them. 19. **Civil Law**: The body of law governing disputes between private parties, distinct from criminal law. 20. **Criminal Law**: The body of law related to crimes and their punishment. 21. **Lawyer**: A professional who practices law; represents clients in legal matters and proceedings. 22. **Innocence**: The state of not being guilty of a crime or offense; often a critical aspect of defense in a trial. 23. **Due Process**: A legal requirement that the state must respect all legal rights owed to a person, ensuring fair treatment. 24. **Corruption**: The abuse of entrusted power for private gain, often undermining law and order. 25. **Deterrence**: The prevention of crime through the threat of punishment or legal consequences. 26. **Restitution**: Compensating victims for losses or harm caused by the offender, often ordered by the court. 27. **Restorative Justice**: An approach to justice focusing on repairing harm caused by criminal behavior, often involving the victim and community. 28. **Policing**: The activities carried out by law enforcement agencies to maintain public order and enforce laws. 29. **Surveillance**: Monitoring of behavior, activities, or information for the purpose of crime prevention and enforcement.

30. **Accountability**: The obligation of law enforcement and judicial authorities to answer for their actions and decisions in the administration of justice. These terms provide a foundational vocabulary for understanding the principles, processes, and entities involved in law and order.

1. Meaning of Plumbing Plumbing is the system of installing and repairing pipes, fittings, and other apparatus used for carrying water, gas, and waste in buildings. It involves the work of a plumber, who ensures that water flows properly and waste is drained efficiently. 2. Words Associated with Plumbing and Their Meanings Word Meaning Plumber A person who installs and repairs water pipes and fittings. Pipe A hollow tube used to carry water or gas from one place to another. Tap (Faucet) A device used to control the flow of water. Sink A basin used for washing dishes or hands, usually found in the kitchen or bathroom. Drain A pipe or channel that removes dirty water or liquid waste. Valve A device that controls or regulates the flow of a liquid or gas. Wrench (Spanner) A tool used to tighten or loosen nuts and bolts on pipes. Joint The point or connection between two pipes. Leak A hole or crack in a pipe that allows water or gas to escape. Plumb Line A cord with a small weight used by plumbers to find a vertical line. 3. Sentences Using Plumbing-Related Words 1. The plumber came to fix the leaking pipe. 2. The kitchen sink is blocked and needs cleaning. 3. Turn off the tap when brushing your teeth. 4. The wrench was used to tighten the loose joint. 5. Water was dripping from a leak under the pipe. 6. The valve controls the water entering the house. 4. Functions of Common Plumbing Tools and Materials

Tool/Material Function Pipe Carries water or gas from one place to another. Tap Controls water flow in bathrooms and kitchens. Wrench Used to tighten or loosen pipe connections. Valve Regulates or stops the flow of water. Plumb Line Helps in setting pipes in a straight vertical position. fix leaks and prevent property damage.

title: RHYMING WORDS

title: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE
subject: English Language
rawText:
1 . 2 . ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ 3 . ○ ○ ○ ○ ○ 1 . ○ ○ 2 . ○ ○ 3 . ○ ○ 4 . ○ ○ Adverbial Clause. What is an Adverbial Clause ? An adverbial clause is a group of words that functions as an adverb in a sentence. It modifies a verb, an adjective, or another adverb, providing additional information about the action or condition. Key Features of Adverbial Clauses: Dependent Clause: An adverbial clause cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. It needs an independent clause to form a complete thought. Introduced by Subordinating Conjunctions: Adverbial clauses begin with subordinating conjunctions. Common subordinating conjunctions include: Because Although Since If While When Until After Before Function: Adverbial clauses answer questions such as: When ? (Time) Where ? (Place) Why ? (Reason) How ? (Manner) Under what conditions ? (Condition) Examples: Time: "I will call you when I get home ." The clause "when I get home" tells us when the action will happen. Reason: "She was happy because she passed the exam ." The clause "because she passed the exam" explains why she was happy. Condition: "You can go out if you finish your homework ." The clause "if you finish your homework" sets a condition for going out. Contrast: "Although it was raining, we went for a walk." The clause "Although it was raining" shows a contrast to the action of going for a walk.

● ○ ○ ● ○ ○ 1 . ○ ○ 2 . ○ 3 . ○ ○ Structure: Placement: Adverbial clauses can appear at the beginning or end of a sentence. Beginning: "Although it was late, we decided to continue." End: "We decided to continue although it was late ." Comma Usage: Use a comma when the adverbial clause is at the beginning of the sentence. No comma is needed when the clause follows the main clause. Practice: Identify Adverbial Clauses: Read sentences and underline the adverbial clauses. Example: "She went to bed early because she was tired ." Create Your Own Sentences: Write sentences using different subordinating conjunctions to form adverbial clauses. Combine Sentences: Combine two sentences using an adverbial clause. Example: "I studied hard. I wanted to do well." → "I studied hard because I wanted to do well ."

### Comprehension Passage: Understanding Death Death is a universal experience that every living being encounters at some point in its life cycle. It is often viewed with trepidation and sadness, yet it also serves as a powerful reminder of life ’ s impermanence. Various cultures and philosophies offer differing perspectives on death, ranging from an inevitable end to a transition into another realm or existence. For some, death signifies liberation from worldly suffering, while for others, it is a profound loss, leading to grief and mourning. In many traditions, rituals surrounding death aim to honor the deceased and provide support for the bereaved. These practices can be seen in wakes, funerals, and memorial services, where friends and family gather to celebrate the life of the departed. Such gatherings provide an essential space for communal mourning, allowing individuals to express their sorrow and reflect on the impact the deceased had on their lives. Philosophically, death raises profound questions about the nature of existence. What does it mean to live a meaningful life? How should we value our time on Earth in light of its finite nature? These questions compel individuals to introspect and often inspire them to be more present in their daily lives. As people confront their own mortality, they may develop a deeper appreciation for relationships, experiences, and the beauty of the world around them. Ultimately, while death may be seen as an end, it also serves to enrich the living. It encourages love, connection, and the pursuit of purpose, reminding us to cherish every moment and to leave a legacy through our actions. In this way, the understanding of death enhances the quality and the significance of life itself. ### Questions and Answers 1. **What is the primary theme of the passage?** - The primary theme of the passage is the multifaceted nature of death, exploring its inevitability, cultural interpretations, and its impact on the living. 2. **How do different cultures perceive death according to the passage?** - Different cultures perceive death variably; some view it as an inevitable end, while others see it as a transition to another realm or as liberation from suffering. 3. **What purpose do rituals surrounding death serve as described in the passage?** - Rituals surrounding death honor the deceased and support the bereaved by providing a space for communal mourning and reflection. 4. **What philosophical questions about life does death raise?** - Death raises philosophical questions about what it means to live a meaningful life and how to value time on Earth given its finite nature.

5. **In what ways can confronting mortality influence individuals according to the passage?** - Confronting mortality can lead individuals to develop a deeper appreciation for relationships, experiences, and the beauty of life, motivating them to be more present. 6. **How does the passage suggest that death affects the living?** - The passage suggests that death enriches the living by encouraging love, connection, and the pursuit of purpose, reminding individuals to cherish every moment. 7. **What message about legacy is implicit in the passage?** - The implicit message about legacy in the passage is that individuals can leave a significant impact through their actions and relationships, making their lives meaningful even after death.

Words Associated with Law and Order 1. Law – A system of rules made by a government to regulate behaviour in society. 2. Order – A state of peace, control, and obedience to the law. 3. Justice – Fair treatment according to the law. 4. Crime – An act that breaks the law. 5. Criminal – A person who commits a crime. 6. Court – A place where legal cases are heard and judged. 7. Judge – A person who decides cases in court. 8. Magistrate – A lower court judge who handles minor cases. 9. Lawyer – A person trained to advise and represent people in court. 10. Attorney – Another word for lawyer. 11. Police – Officers who enforce the law and maintain public order. 12. Arrest – To take someone into custody for committing a crime. 13. Investigation – A careful search for facts about a crime. 14. Evidence – Facts or objects used to prove a case in court. 15. Trial – A legal process where a case is examined in court. 16. Verdict – The decision of the court or jury in a case. 17. Sentence – The punishment given to a criminal by a court. 18. Punishment – A penalty given for breaking the law. 19. Prison – A place where criminals are kept as punishment. 20. Jail – A place for keeping people who are awaiting trial or serving short sentences. 21. Bail – Money paid to release an accused person temporarily from custody. 22. Suspect – A person believed to have committed a crime. 23. Accused – A person charged with a crime. 24. Victim – A person who suffers harm because of a crime. 25. Witness – A person who sees a crime or gives evidence in court. 26. Law-abiding – Obeying the law. 27. Offence – An illegal act. 28. Prosecution – The legal process of charging someone in court. 29. Defence – The argument or lawyer that protects the accused person. 30. Appeal – A request for a higher court to review a decision. title: SEMI FORMAL LETTER
subject: English Language
rawText: Semi formal Letter A written record to another person when you have some information, a request, a demand, a question to pass on to that person. In its most basic form a letter takes the place of the spoken language. We have three types of letters and they are: 1. The formal. 2. Informal. 3. Semi-formal. Semi formal letter as: a type of letter usually written to people we do not know well or in situations which require more polite and respect e.g. 1. When you write to a pen friend whom you have never met. 2. When you write to an elderly relative who is known to you, in which case you try to show him or her respect. sample of a letter. 1.Writers address: Government secondary school, Nyanya, Abuja. 22nd May, 2024. 2. Salutation: e.g. Dear Mr. Okeke. Use the last name since you know the recipient. 3. Introduction: you may start by stating your opening remarks and clearly state the reason or purpose for writing. 4. Body of the letter: the body of the letter should be broken down in paragraphs. One paragraph should discuss a point. The points should be written sequentially and at least three well amplified points should be discussed properly to convince your examiner or reader. 5. Complimentary close: a semi formal letter closes with “yours sincerely” e.g. Yours sincerely, Lucy Paul.

### Passage on Beauty Beauty is a concept that transcends cultures and eras, often invoking a plethora of emotions and interpretations. From the delicate petals of a blooming flower to the majestic peaks of ancient mountains, beauty manifests itself in both nature and humanity. Philosophers, artists, and writers have long grappled with the essence of beauty, attempting to define and encapsulate its meaning. It intertwines the visual, emotional, and sensory experiences we encounter each day. In the realm of art, beauty can be subjective. One person may find beauty in abstract paintings, reveling in the chaotic blend of colors and forms, while another might prefer the precision of realism, where every detail is meticulously rendered. This subjectivity is reflective of individual experiences and perceptions, shaped by personal history, cultural backgrounds, and societal influences. In literature, beauty often finds expression through poetic language, where the choice of words evokes vivid images and deep feelings, transporting readers to different realms. In addition to art and literature, nature remains one of the most profound sources of beauty. The serene calm of a sunset, the vibrant hues of autumn leaves, or the gentle rustling of leaves in a breeze can evoke a sense of wonder and tranquility. Nature ’ s beauty often prompts introspection, allowing individuals to reflect on their place in the universe and the fleeting nature of existence. Moreover, the notion of beauty extends to human interactions. Kindness, compassion, and love are arguably the most profound forms of beauty one can encounter. A genuine smile, a listening ear, or the act of helping others can resonate deeply, illustrating that beauty is not confined to mere physical appearances but encompasses the very essence of humanity. In essence, beauty is a complex tapestry woven from various threads — art, nature, and human emotion. It is a fleeting, yet powerful experience, reminding us to cherish the world around us and the connections we share with one another. ### Questions 1. What are some of the sources of beauty mentioned in the passage? 2. How is beauty perceived differently in the realm of art? 3. What role does nature play in the appreciation of beauty according to the text? 4. How does the passage argue that beauty goes beyond physical appearances? 5. In what ways does the passage suggest that beauty impacts human emotions and interactions? ### Answers 1. The sources of beauty mentioned in the passage include nature, art, and human emotions such as kindness, compassion, and love. 2. Beauty in art is perceived differently because it is subjective; individuals may find beauty in different artistic styles, such as abstract or realistic expressions, shaped by their personal experiences and cultural backgrounds.

3. Nature plays a significant role in appreciating beauty as it evokes feelings of wonder and tranquility through elements like sunsets, autumn leaves, and the calming sounds of nature, prompting introspection in individuals. 4. The passage argues that beauty extends beyond physical appearances by highlighting that kindness, compassion, and emotional connections exemplify a deeper form of beauty that resonates through human interactions. 5. The passage suggests that beauty impacts human emotions and interactions by fostering feelings of connection, reflection, and appreciation for both the world around us and the shared experiences with others.

title: REGISTER COMMERCE
subject: English Language
rawText:
Commerce refers to the broader system and activities surrounding the buying and selling of goods and services. It encompasses various aspects such as trade, finance, logistics, and marketing, allowing economic transactions to take place. Below are thirty words associated with commerce, along with brief explanations for each: 1. **Trade**: The act of buying, selling, or exchanging goods and services. 2. **Marketplace**: A physical or virtual place where buyers and sellers meet to conduct transactions. 3. **E-commerce**: The buying and selling of goods and services over the internet. 4. **Retail**: The sale of goods or services directly to consumers for personal use. 5. **Wholesale**: The sale of goods in large quantities, typically to retailers or other businesses. 6. **Supply Chain**: A network of organizations and people involved in the production and distribution of goods. 7. **Logistics**: The management of the flow of goods, information, and resources from origin to consumption. 8. **Consumer**: An individual or entity that purchases goods or services for personal use. 9. **Producer**: An individual or organization that creates goods or services for sale. 10. **B2B (Business-to-Business)**: Transactions conducted between businesses, rather than between a business and individual consumers. 11. **B2C (Business-to-Consumer)**: Transactions conducted directly between a business and consumers. 12. **Inventory**: The goods and products that a business holds for sale or use. 13. **Trade Credit**: A commercial loan that is provided to a business by its suppliers. 14. **Profit**: The financial gain obtained after subtracting expenses from revenue. 15. **Revenue**: The total income generated from sales before any costs or expenses are deducted. 16. **Market Research**: The process of gathering, analyzing, and interpreting information about a market.

17. **Brand**: A name, term, design, or symbol that identifies a seller's goods or services. 18. **Marketing**: The activities that promote the buying, selling, and use of products or services. 19. **Negotiation**: Discussion aimed at reaching an agreement in business deals or transactions. 20. **Contract**: A legally binding agreement between two or more parties regarding the sale of goods or services. 21. **Customer Service**: Support offered to customers before, during, and after purchasing products or services. 22. **Commerce Law**: The body of law that governs business and commercial transactions. 23. **Import**: The act of bringing goods or services into a country from abroad for sale. 24. **Export**: The act of sending goods or services out of one country to sell in another. 25. **Trade Balance**: The difference between the value of a country's exports and imports. 26. **Merchandising**: The practice of promoting and selling products to consumers. 27. **Financial Accounting**: The field of accounting that focuses on reporting financial information to external parties. 28. **Digital Payment**: Electronic methods to transfer funds for transactions, such as credit cards and online banking. 29. **Cash Flow**: The total amount of money being transferred into and out of a business. 30. **Market Share**: The portion of a market controlled by a particular company or product. These terms collectively illustrate the various elements and processes involved in commerce, showcasing its complexity and scope in the global economy.

17. **Brand**: A name, term, design, or symbol that identifies a seller's goods or services. 18. **Marketing**: The activities that promote the buying, selling, and use of products or services. 19. **Negotiation**: Discussion aimed at reaching an agreement in business deals or transactions. 20. **Contract**: A legally binding agreement between two or more parties regarding the sale of goods or services. 21. **Customer Service**: Support offered to customers before, during, and after purchasing products or services. 22. **Commerce Law**: The body of law that governs business and commercial transactions. 23. **Import**: The act of bringing goods or services into a country from abroad for sale. 24. **Export**: The act of sending goods or services out of one country to sell in another. 25. **Trade Balance**: The difference between the value of a country's exports and imports. 26. **Merchandising**: The practice of promoting and selling products to consumers. 27. **Financial Accounting**: The field of accounting that focuses on reporting financial information to external parties. 28. **Digital Payment**: Electronic methods to transfer funds for transactions, such as credit cards and online banking. 29. **Cash Flow**: The total amount of money being transferred into and out of a business. 30. **Market Share**: The portion of a market controlled by a particular company or product. These terms collectively illustrate the various elements and processes involved in commerce, showcasing its complexity and scope in the global economy.

title: VOCABULARY DEVELOPMENT
subject: English Language
rawText: Note 1] What is a Narrative Essay all about? A narrative essay is a type of writing that tells a story or recounts an event or experience from the writer’s point of view. It aims to entertain, inform, or convey a lesson through storytelling. It usually includes characters, setting, plot, conflict, and resolution. 2] Five Types of Narrative Essays: 1. Personal Narrative – based on personal life experiences. 2. Biographical Narrative – tells the story of another person’s life. 3. Fictional Narrative – a story created from the writer’s imagination. 4. Historical Narrative – recounts past events or historical happenings. 5. Autobiographical Narrative – focuses on significant events in the writer’s own life. 3] Three Useful Hints in Writing a Narrative Essay: 1. Use first-person point of view (e.g., I, we) to make the story personal and engaging. 2. Arrange events in chronological order to maintain a clear sequence. 3. Include vivid descriptions and dialogues to make the story lively and realistic. 4] How Many Addresses are Required in a Narrative Essay? A narrative essay requires only one address — the writer’s address, because it is usually written in an informal or semi-formal style, not as a formal letter.

STUDENTS’ SUMMARY NOTE Topic: Structure – Clauses A clause is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb. Features of a Clause It has a subject (the doer of the action). It has a verb (the action or state). It forms part of a sentence. It may express a complete or incomplete meaning. Types of Clauses 1. Independent Clause (Main Clause) It can stand alone as a complete sentence. It expresses a complete thought. Examples: She is happy. The boy is playing. 2. Dependent Clause (Subordinate Clause) It cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. It depends on an independent clause to make full meaning. Examples: Because she is happy Although the boy is playing Examples in Sentences When the bell rang, the students left the class. “When the bell rang” → Dependent clause “the students left the class” → Independent clause

Conclusion Clauses are important in sentence construction. Understanding them helps in forming correct and meaningful sentences.

title: PREFIXES
subject: English Language
rawText:
**Understanding Prefixes in the English Language** A prefix is a group of letters placed before the root of a word, which alters its meaning. They are an essential part of English vocabulary, allowing speakers and writers to construct varied and complex ideas succinctly. Understanding prefixes can significantly enhance language comprehension and communication skills. ### Common Prefixes Here are some of the most frequently used prefixes along with their meanings and examples: 1. **Un-** (not): - *Example*: unhappy (not happy), unfair (not fair) - *Explanation*: This prefix negates the meaning of the base word. 2. **Re-** (again or back): - *Example*: redo (do again), rebuild (build again) - *Explanation*: It signifies repetition or returning to a previous state. 3. **Dis-** (opposite of; not): - *Example*: disagree (not agree), disconnect (to break the connection) - *Explanation*: This prefix indicates a negative or opposing concept. 4. **Pre-** (before): - *Example*: predict (say before), prehistoric (before recorded history) - *Explanation*: This prefix denotes something occurring prior to an event or time. 5. **Mis-** (wrongly): - *Example*: misunderstand (understand wrongly), misplace (place incorrectly) - *Explanation*: It suggests an error or a mistaken action. 6. **Over-** (excessive): - *Example*: overestimate (estimate too highly), overload (load too much) - *Explanation*: This prefix indicates an excess or overabundance. 7. **Sub-** (under or below): - *Example*: submarine (under the sea), substitute (to put in place of) - *Explanation*: It often refers to something that is beneath or lesser in degree. 8. **Inter-** (between or among): - *Example*: international (between nations), interact (to act between) - *Explanation*: This prefix denotes a relationship involving two or more parties. 9. **Trans-** (across or beyond): - *Example*: transport (carry across), transform (change in form or appearance) - *Explanation*: It indicates movement or change across boundaries.

10. **Anti-** (against): - *Example*: antibiotic (against bacteria), antifreeze (against freezing) - *Explanation*: This prefix signifies opposition to something. ### Importance of Prefixes 1. **Vocabulary Expansion**: Learning prefixes can help expand a speaker's vocabulary significantly. By understanding prefixes, one can derive the meanings of unfamiliar words. 2. **Word Formation**: Prefixes enable the formation of new words from existing ones. This is particularly useful in academic writing and technical fields. 3. **Enhanced Communication**: Using prefixes effectively can lead to clearer and more precise communication, allowing for nuanced expression of ideas. ### Conclusion Prefixes play a crucial role in the English language, serving as tools for modification and expansion of meaning. By familiarizing oneself with common prefixes, learners can improve their reading comprehension, vocabulary knowledge, and overall language skills. Understanding how prefixes work empowers individuals to decode unfamiliar words, recognize their meanings, and use them effectively in context.

subject: English Language
rawText: Modifiers Modifiers as words, phrases or clauses that provide description in sentences. Modifiers allow writers to take that picture that they have in their heads and transfer it accurately to the heads of their readers. Essentially modifiers breathe life into sentences. modifiers could be adjectives, adjectival clauses, adverbs, adverbial clauses and prepositional phrases. title: WRITING SPEECHES FOR SPECIFIC PURPOSES
subject: English Language
rawText: A speech is an art that has to be well planned and organized in a pattern that is acceptable and ready for oral presentation. A speech is suppose to be delivered orally to an audience. If we listen to an impromptu speech or address especially one delivered by one who speaks the language very well (fluently). We would notice that there are number of ways in which the structure of his spoken language is different from that of the written form. We can simply say that a speech is all about giving a talk to an audience. a well written speech must poses the following features. (a) The title (b) The introduction (c) The body (d) The conclusion When choosing a title, you should consider the following: decide on your audience, your purpose. Reflecting and finding answers to these questions will go a long way to making easier. Find out whether your purpose is to inform, entertain, persuade or demonstrate. Your ability to determine your purpose fully can help to improve your speech. Introduction: In the introduction, the following hints are relevant (a) identify with your audience and catch their attention (b) give your audience a preview of what you are speaking about. Examples (i) making a shocking statement. (ii) giving a starting fact or opinion. (iii) telling a short story (iv) scenario (v) quoting someone else (v) asking a question. Your target here is to arouse the interest of the audience. Make your introduction lively and friendly. Try to lead your audience towards what you are going to talk about. The body: This is the stage that carries the actual message meant for the audience. Start by giving the main points with relevant details in support of each point. The conclusion: when you round off the body of a speech, the next thing is the conclusion. The expectation is that you should summary your main points. It is important to end in a memorable way. To achieve this, you may decide to use any of the following: (a) make a shocking statement (b) refer to something you said in your introduction (c) make a forceful statement. The requirement for effective speech delivery. The teacher mentions the major things needed for effective speech delivery, all in bid to make your delivery very effective or interesting: (a) you need to have adequate knowledge of your speech (b) you need to have sufficient practice (c) to speak loudly fluently (d) to maintain good eye contact the course of delivering your speech (e) making good use of gestures (f) enthusiasm

Students’ Summary Note Subject: English Language Topic: Reading for Specific Structural Patterns and Report Writing 1. Reading for Specific Structural Patterns Focus on how a passage is organized. Look for headings, subheadings, dates, steps, or numbered points in scientific or medical passages. Helps to understand the sequence of ideas and structure of the content. 2. Identifying Main and Supporting Ideas Main Idea: The most important point the writer wants to convey. Supporting Ideas: Details, examples, or explanations that explain or support the main idea. Example: Main Idea: Exercise is important for good health. Supporting Ideas: It strengthens the heart, improves mood, and prevents diseases. 3. Explaining Key Vocabulary Highlight difficult or technical words in the passage. Look for clues in the sentence to understand the meaning. Example (medical passage): Diagnosis: Identifying a disease Treatment: Care given to cure illness Patient: A person receiving medical care 4. Understanding the Format of a Report A report is a structured piece of writing that presents information clearly. Typical Structure of a Scientific/Medical Report: Title/Heading: Name of the experiment or study. Date: When the experiment or observation took place.

Introduction/Purpose: Why the experiment was conducted. Procedure/Method: Steps followed during the experiment. Results/Outcome: Findings or observations. Conclusion: Summary of findings or recommendations. 5. Writing a Simple Report Logically Use clear headings. Arrange information in chronological order or logical sequence. Write short, precise sentences. Include all main points and supporting details. Avoid unnecessary repetition. Example Structure: Title: Effect of Exercise on Heart Rate Date: 4th February 2026 Purpose: To investigate how exercise affects heart rate. Procedure: Students ran for 5 minutes; heart rates were recorded before and after. Results: Heart rate increased after exercise. Conclusion: Exercise raises heart rate, showing the heart works harder during physical activity. Importance Helps in understanding and summarizing information. Improves comprehension and analytical skills. Prepares students for structured writing tasks in exams. The body: This is the stage that carries the actual message meant for the audience. Start by giving the main points with relevant details in support of each point. The conclusion: when you round off the body of a speech, the next thing is the conclusion. The expectation is that you should summary your main points. It is important to end in a memorable way. To achieve this, you may decide to use any of the following: (a) make a shocking statement (b) refer to something you said in your introduction (c) make a forceful statement. The requirement for effective speech delivery. The teacher mentions the major things needed for effective speech delivery, all in bid to make your delivery very effective or interesting: (a) you need to have adequate knowledge of your speech (b) you need to have sufficient practice (c) to speak loudly fluently (d) to maintain good eye contact the course of delivering your speech (e) making good use of gestures (f) enthusiasm

title: READING TO PICK OUT TOPIC AND SENTENCES.
subject: English Language
rawText: A topic sentence is a sentence that expresses the main idea of the paragraph in which it occurs. A topic sentence is the most important sentence in the paragraph. Sometimes referred to as a focus sentence; the topic sentence helps to organize the paragraph by summarizing the information in the paragraph. The topic sentence is usually but not always the first sentence of the paragraph. The purpose of a topic sentence a) Topic tells what the rest of the paragraph is all about. All sentences after it have to give more information about the sentence, prove it by offering facts about it, or describe it. b) Topic sentences also need to relate back to the main idea of the passage. c) Topic sentence reveals the direction the writer is going. d) Topic sentence tells the reader where the writer’s thoughts are leading to. e) Identifying the topic sentence helps student in summary writing. Features of a topic sentence Every topic will have a topic and a controlling idea. The controlling idea shows the direction the paragraph will take. Students read the passage title, “Animals Plan to Overthrow Man and pick out the topic sentences on pages 165-167. Some of the topic sentences from the passage include: 1) Is it not crystal clear, then Comrade, that all evils of this life of our spring from the tyranny of human beings? 2) And remember, Comrade, your resolution must never falter. 3) At this moment, there was a tremendous uproar. 4) Comrades, he said, here is a point that must be settled. 5) The vote was taken at once, and it was agreed by an overwhelming majority that rats were comrades. 6) And remember also that, in fighting against man, we must not come to resemble him. 7) And now, Comrades, I will tell you about my dream of last night Class activity: In four sentences, one for each, summarize the advice Old Major gave in the animals struggle to overthrow the human race. Answer” 1) Animals should defeat man so they could be wealthy. 2) The animals should pass on the message to future generations until man is overthrown. 3) Animals should never allow anybody to misguide them by believing that man and animals are friends. 4) Animals must not oppress other animals.

title: NOUN PHRASE
subject: English Language
rawText:
15/1/2024 PHRASES AND TYPES A phrases are group of words forming part of a larger sentence that does not make complete sense. FEATURES OF PHRASES (1) A phrase is a group of words, e.g the beautiful girl. (2)A phrase does not make sense, e.g in the room (3) A phrase may not have any verb, e.g on the table. (4) if there is a verb present in a phrase, the verb is always and must be a non-finite verb. e.g To read without light, Reading without light, The boiled yam. (5) A phrase only forms part of a sentence. TYPES OF PHRASES (1) Noun phrase.l (2) Adjectival phrase. (3) Adverbial phrase. (4) Prepositional phrase. Noun phrase:- is phrase that functions as a noun e.g (1) The youngest boy among us is very obedient. (2) l saw the village headmaster. (3)The beautiful girl comes here everyday Adjectival phrases:- are group of words that does not have verb but contain an adjective e.g (1) The man 'standing at the gate' is my father. (2) The lady was 'quite unfaithful'. The young man is 'very handsome' Adverbial phrase:- They are phrases that tells us how, when an action takes place. They are usually introduced by adverbs such as : late, later early, often. e.t.c. e.g (1) l will see you 'later in the evening.

(2)' More often than not' he misses the bus. (3) The three men arrived 'early in the evening'. Prepositional phrases:- They begin with preposition and ends with a noun (object). it shows relationship between it's objects and other words in the sentences e.g. (1) The car is 'on the bridge' (2) 'from the farm to the school' is a distance of five kilometers. (3) l saw him 'at the council hall'. (4) The man lives 'across the road'.

title: ORAL ARGUMENT AND DEBATE
subject: English Language
rawText: Debate is an argument that is orally presented. In other words, debate is an oral argument. Example of debate question includes Boarding school is better than Day School The structure of a debate The following is the structure of a debate: 1) Introduction (one paragraph): (a) Opening greetings (vocatives): study your environment to know those present and greet them appropriately: example, Mr. Chairman, Panel of Judges, the Moderator, Accurate Timekeeper, Co-debaters, My Fellow Students, Ladies and Gentlemen. (b) Introduce yourself: example, my name is Peter Bala . (c) Mention your stand in the motion you are debating on. Example, I am here to propose the motion that states, “Boarding School is Better Than Day School" with the following points backing up my argument. (d) Define key words if necessary. Example, before I proceed, permit me to define some key words, … 2) The body paragraph (three paragraphs). The body provides detail in support of your stand in the argument: (a) Give your reasons to support your stand. (b) Counter your opponent’s points. Imagine the points your opponent is like to raise. Raise each of these points and tell your audience that it is wrong, you can then go ahead and place your opinions upon the one you have disapproved. 3) The conclusion (one paragraph). This should comprise the following: (a) Call on all present by their names. Example, the Chairman, Distinguished Guests, Fellow Students, Ladies and Gentlemen (b) Conclude by saying, I believe with these points of mine, you will agree with me that Boarding school is better than day school.” Thank you. New trends (parliamentary) in debate Co-debater - Friends in argument. I am here to support the motion that states – in this house we agree that… I am here to oppose the motion that states – in this house we disagree that… You can raise point of information. You can use newspaper (or any literature) and electronic devices like projector to support your argument.

title: ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText: An argumentative essay is the type of an essay whose business is to argue. In other words, the writer here tries to prove with sound reasons, the validity of his point of view. The major issue in argumentative essay is the orderly and effective presentation of reasonable opinions in order to persuade the reader to hold the same view as the writer. Finally, in argumentative essay, there are two options. You either propose or oppose the motion. Examples of argumentative essay topics 1) Child labour should be a punishable offence. 2) Military rule is better than civilian rule. 3) Public schools are better than private schools. 4) Examinations are not the true test of knowledge. 5) Politics is a dirty game. Argumentative essay and debate all deal with argument but differ in the following; Argumentative; The mode of the question: you would be asked to argue for or against a particular topic/motion. You begin you essay with your topic boldly written out. NO VOCATIVES Debates; You would be asked, as a speaker or chief speaker, argue for or against a particular topic/motion. You begin your essay with your VOCATIVES. No need to write out the topic as heading. The structure of an argumentative essay The following is the structure of an argumentative essay: 1) The title: example. POLITICS IS A DIRTY GAME 2) Introduction (one paragraph). The following should be done in the introductory paragraph： (a) Mention your stand. Example, I write to propose the motion that states, "Politics is a dirty game" with the following points backing up my argument b) Define key words, if necessary. Example. Before I proceed, I would like to define some key words. 3) The body of the paragraph (three paragraphs). The body provides details in support of your stand in the argument. You are to do the following: (a) Give reasons to support your stand. (b) counter your opponent’s point 4. The conclusion (one paragraph) Conclude by restating your main idea.

It is written to inform, educate or entertain readers. Format of Article Writing Title or Heading Writer’s Name Introduction Body of the Article Conclusion Features of a Good Article A good title Simple and clear language Proper paragraphing Interesting introduction Logical arrangement of ideas Good conclusion Importance of Article Writing It helps to inform the public. It educates readers on important issues. It improves students’ writing skills. It develops critical thinking and creativity. Guidelines for Writing Articles Understand the topic properly. Use simple and correct English. Organize ideas into paragraphs.

Use examples where necessary. Avoid grammatical and spelling errors. Example of Article Topics The Dangers of Drug Abuse The Importance of Education Examination Malpractice in Schools The Effects of Cultism Among Students Conclusion A good article must be properly arranged, interesting and informative. The writer should use clear language and organize ideas logically to attract readers.

title: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH ENVIRONMENT
subject: English Language
rawText: Our environment can be said to be everything that makes up our surroundings, and this affects our being able to carry out our activities on the face of the earth. teacher Environment can also be defined as surrounding or conditions in which a person, animal or plant operates. It could also be said to be the natural world, as a whole or in a particular geographical area, especially as it affects human activities . Words associated with Environment; pests, environmental pollution, bush burning, sewage system, smoking, drainage, disposal of refuse 1. Environmental pollution : pollution or contamination of the environment by introduction of contaminants that can cause damage or harm or discomfort to human or other species. 2. Waste disposal: the removal and destroying or storing damaged, used or other unwanted domesticated, agricultural or industrial products and substances. Disposal methods include burning, burying, dumping at sea, recycling 3. Water contamination: this is when hazardous materials or substances of any kind are used to pollute a source of water. 4. Air pollution: when harmful or excessive quantities of substances including gases , particles are introduced to the atmosphere, which may cause diseases, allergies or even death to humans.

title: SPEECH WRITING AND A SAMPLE SPEECH
subject: English Language
rawText:
**Speech Writing: An Overview** Speech writing is the art of crafting a spoken message that is designed to inform, persuade, entertain, or motivate an audience. It requires careful consideration of the audience, purpose, context, and the message itself. A well-written speech often conveys a clear idea and captures the listeners ’ attention, encouraging engagement and reflection. ### Parts of a Speech A well-structured speech typically consists of three main parts: 1. **Introduction**: - Grabs the attention of the audience. - Introduces the speaker and establishes credibility. - States the purpose of the speech and previews the main points. 2. **Body**: - Contains the main content of the speech. - Organized into clear sections or points, each supporting the central theme. - Uses examples, anecdotes, data, or quotes to reinforce ideas. 3. **Conclusion**: - Summarizes the key points discussed. - Leaves the audience with a strong final impression or call to action. - May include reflections or a vision for the future. ### Features of a Good Speech A good speech possesses several key features: 1. **Clarity**: The message should be clear and easy to understand. 2. **Engagement**: The speech should capture and maintain the audience's attention. 3. **Relevance**: Content should resonate with the audience's experiences or interests. 4. **Structure**: A logical flow helps the audience follow the speaker's ideas. 5. **Emotion**: Effective use of emotional appeal can help create a connection with the audience. 6. **Brevity**: Concise language is often more impactful than long, convoluted sentences. 7. **Practice**: A well-rehearsed delivery enhances the effectiveness of the speech. ### Short Speech for a High School Graduation Ceremony Ceremony. **[Introduction]** Good evening, honored guests, teachers, proud parents, and, most importantly, the graduating

class of [Year]! As I stand before you today, I am filled with a sense of pride and excitement. Graduating from high school is a remarkable milestone, marking not just the culmination of years of hard work, friendships, and growth, but also the beginning of new journeys and possibilities that await you. **[Body]** Today, as you sit here donned in caps and gowns, take a moment to reflect on the memories you ’ ve created: the late-night study sessions, the laughter in the hallways, the victories and challenges that shaped you into who you are today. Each of these experiences has equipped you with unique tools to navigate the world ahead. Remember, success is not only measured by achievements and accolades. It ’ s about resilience, the courage to pursue your passions, and the heart to embrace failure as a stepping stone to growth. As you venture into the next chapter — be it college, apprenticeships, or exploring your passions — hold onto your dreams tightly. The world is vast and full of opportunities waiting for someone like you to seize them. Moreover, always strive to contribute positively to your communities. You have the power to make a difference, to inspire others, and to fuel change. So, remain curious, compassionate, and courageous. **[Conclusion]** Today marks a significant transition; remember that the end is just a new beginning. Cherish the memories of your time here, but also look forward to the adventures that lie ahead. Congratulations, Class of [Year]! Embrace the future with open arms, chase your dreams, and never stop believing in yourselves. We cannot wait to see how you will change the world! Thank you!

The major issue in argumentative essay is the orderly and effective presentation of reasonable opinions in order to persuade the reader to hold the same view as the writer. Finally, in argumentative essay, there are two options. You either propose or oppose the motion. Examples of argumentative essay topics 1) Child labour should be a punishable offence. 2) Military rule is better than civilian rule. 3) Public schools are better than private schools. 4) Examinations are not the true test of knowledge. 5) Politics is a dirty game. Argumentative essay and debate all deal with argument but differ in the following; Argumentative; The mode of the question: you would be asked to argue for or against a particular topic/motion. You begin you essay with your topic boldly written out. NO VOCATIVES Debates; You would be asked, as a speaker or chief speaker, argue for or against a particular topic/motion. You begin your essay with your VOCATIVES. No need to write out the topic as heading. The structure of an argumentative essay The following is the structure of an argumentative essay: 1) The title: example. POLITICS IS A DIRTY GAME 2) Introduction (one paragraph). The following should be done in the introductory paragraph： (a) Mention your stand. Example, I write to propose the motion that states, "Politics is a dirty game" with the following points backing up my argument b) Define key words, if necessary. Example. Before I proceed, I would like to define some key words. 3) The body of the paragraph (three paragraphs). The body provides details in support of your stand in the argument. You are to do the following: (a) Give reasons to support your stand. (b) counter your opponent’s point 4. The conclusion (one paragraph) Conclude by restating your main idea.
