title: NOUN CLAUSE
subject: English Language
rawText:
*1. What is a Clause?* A *clause* is a group of words that contains a subject and a predicate (verb). It can express a complete thought or part of a thought. *Types:* 1. *Independent/Main Clause*: Can stand alone as a sentence. _Example_: She works hard. 2. *Dependent/Subordinate Clause*: Cannot stand alone; depends on a main clause. _Example_: because she works hard --- *2. What is a Noun Clause?* A *noun clause* is a dependent clause that functions as a noun in a sentence. It usually begins with words like: _that, what, whatever, who, whom, whoever, whomever, why, how, whether, if_. You can replace a noun clause with a single noun or pronoun and the sentence still makes sense. _Example_: I know *that she passed*. → I know *the news*. --- *3. Grammatical Functions of Noun Clause* A noun clause can function in 6 main ways, just like a noun: **Function** **Explanation** 1. **Subject of a verb** The noun clause does the action 2. **Object of a verb** The noun clause receives the action 3. **Complement of a verb/subject** Renames/explains the subject after linking verbs like *is, was, seems* 4. **Object of a preposition** Comes after a preposition like *of, on, in, for* 5. **Appositive** Renames/explains a noun beside it 6. **Object complement** Completes/follows the direct object --- *4. Three Examples of Each Grammatical Function* *1. Subject of a Verb* Noun clause performs the action of the verb. 1. *What he said* shocked everyone. → _What he said_ = subject of _shocked_ 2. *That corruption is endemic* is no secret. → _That corruption is endemic_ = subject of _is_ 3. *Whoever finishes first* will get a prize. → _Whoever finishes first_ = subject of _will get_ *2. Object of a Verb* Noun clause receives the action of the verb. 1. I believe *that you are honest*. → object of _believe_

2. She asked *why I was late*. → object of _asked_ 3. Nobody knows *where he lives*. → object of _knows_ *3. Complement of a Verb / Subject Complement* Noun clause follows a linking verb and renames the subject. 1. The problem is *that we have no funds*. → complements _problem_ 2. Her belief was *that hard work pays*. → complements _belief_ 3. The truth is *that IPPIS saved billions*. → complements _truth_ *4. Object of a Preposition* Noun clause follows a preposition. 1. He is worried about *what may happen*. → object of _about_ 2. Pay attention to *how the funds are spent*. → object of _to_ 3. We argued about *whether we should proceed*. → object of _about_ *5. Appositive* Noun clause explains/renames a noun beside it. 1. The idea *that corruption kills development* is true. → explains _idea_ 2. The question *why projects fail* remains unanswered. → explains _question_ 3. Your fear *that EFCC may arrest you* is baseless. → explains _fear_ *6. Object Complement* Noun clause completes the direct object; usually after verbs like _call, name, elect, make_. 1. We named him *whatever he wanted*. → completes _him_ 2. They elected her *whoever the party nominated*. → completes _her_ 3. The board made the policy *what the staff suggested*. → completes _policy_ --- *Quick Test*: To check if it ’ s a noun clause, replace the whole clause with _it_ or _something_. _Example_: I know *that you passed* → I know *it*. ✓ It works, so it ’ s a noun clause.

title: EMPHATIC STRESS
subject: English Language
rawText:
*Stress in Spoken English* In spoken English, *stress* means making a syllable or word louder, longer, and higher in pitch than the others around it. English is a _stress-timed_ language, so the rhythm depends on stressed syllables. Stress helps listeners know what ’ s important and changes meaning. There are 2 main types: 1. *Word stress*: One syllable in a word is stressed. _Example:_ *PHO*-to-graph vs pho-*TOG*-ra-pher vs pho-to-*GRA*-phy. The meaning stays the same, but stress moves. 2. *Sentence stress*: Some words in a sentence are stressed more than others. Usually content words are stressed: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs. Function words like _a, the, is, of_ are usually unstressed. --- *Emphatic Stress* *Emphatic stress* is when you deliberately stress a word in a sentence to show contrast, emotion, correction, or strong feeling. It tells the listener: “ Pay attention to THIS word. ” You use it when: - Correcting someone: _I said *TWO*, not TOO._ - Contrasting: _I didn ’ t take *his* book, I took *hers*._ - Showing surprise, anger, emphasis: _I *am* coming!_ - Emphasizing truth or intensity: _It *was* amazing._ The stressed word is said louder, slower, and with a pitch rise/fall. --- *10 Good Examples of Emphatic Stress* The *CAPS* word is the one you stress emphatically. 1. *I* didn ’ t take your phone. → _Someone else did._ 2. I didn ’ t *TAKE* your phone. → _I didn ’ t steal it._ 3. I didn ’ t take *YOUR* phone. → _I took someone else ’ s._ 4. I didn ’ t take your *PHONE*. → _I took something else._ 5. Do you *WANT* to go? → _Emphasizing desire, not going._ 6. Do *YOU* want to go? → _Checking if it ’ s you, not someone else._

7. She *IS* my sister. → _Correcting doubt. She really is._ 8. This is *NOT* acceptable. → _Strong rejection._ 9. I *TOLD* you not to do that. → _Emphasizing that a warning was given._ 10. We *MUST* finish today. → _Showing urgency and necessity._ --- *Quick tip:* If you remove the stressed word, the sentence ’ s meaning changes or the correction becomes unclear. That ’ s how you know it ’ s emphatic stress. Want me to record how these sound with phonetic symbols and intonation marks?

**Passage: The Journey of Oliha** Oliha ’ s journey through life was one of perseverance, faith, and unwavering determination. Orphaned at a tender age, he lost both parents in a tragic accident when he was only eight years old. This sudden loss shattered his world, leaving him in the care of his distant relatives, who, despite their good intentions, struggled to provide him with the emotional and financial support he desperately needed. However, Oliha was a resilient soul. Instead of succumbing to despair, he made education his refuge, a place where he could escape the harsh realities of his childhood. With the help of scholarships and the kindness of teachers who recognized his potential, Oliha excelled in his studies. He dedicated every waking moment to his books, often studying late into the night by the dim light of a small lamp in his cramped room. His sacrifices bore fruit when he graduated high school with honors, earning a scholarship to attend a reputable university. The transition to college was challenging, but Oliha, fueled by dreams of a better life and the memory of his parents, persevered once again. After years of hard work and determination, Oliha graduated with a degree in business management. With no time to waste, he threw himself into the job market and was soon offered a position at a growing tech company. His diligence and dedication paid off; he quickly climbed the ranks, gaining respect and admiration from his colleagues and superiors alike. By the time he turned forty, Oliha had built a life he could be proud of. He had a loving wife, a beautiful home filled with laughter and love, and his own car — a symbol of his hard-earned success. Reflecting on the journey, Oliha wanted to celebrate this milestone birthday in a special way. He planned an extravagant party, inviting friends, colleagues, and family to join him in celebrating not just his birthday, but also the triumph of overcoming adversities. On the night of the celebration, the atmosphere was filled with joy and nostalgia. The room was decorated with photos chronicling Oliha's journey from a troubled child to a successful adult. Friends and loved ones shared heartfelt stories, reminding him of the obstacles he had overcome. As he stood before his guests, teary-eyed yet proud, he raised a toast to resilience, determination, and the memories of those who had helped him along the way, particularly his dear parents, who had inspired him to chase his dreams. **Questions and Answers:** 1. **What significant event in Oliha's life occurred when he was eight years old?** - Oliha lost both of his parents in a tragic accident. 2. **How did Oliha manage to excel in his studies despite his challenging circumstances?** - He received help through scholarships and the support of teachers who recognized his potential, and he dedicated himself to his education. 3. **What degree did Oliha earn, and in which field?**

- Oliha graduated with a degree in business management. 4. **At what age did Oliha celebrate his fortieth birthday, and what were some accomplishments he had achieved by then?** - Oliha celebrated his fortieth birthday; by then, he had a loving wife, his own house, and a car, along with a successful career. 5. **What was the purpose of Oliha's birthday party besides celebrating his age?** - The party was also to commemorate his journey of overcoming adversities and to honor the memory of his parents, whose inspiration guided him throughout his life.

title: ADJECTIVAL CLAUSE
subject: English Language
rawText:
*1. Adjective* An *adjective* is a word that describes or gives more information about a noun or pronoun. It tells us _what kind, which one, how many, or how much_. Examples: - _blue_ car – _blue_ describes the color of the car - _three_ students – _three_ tells how many - _honest_ man – _honest_ describes the quality --- *2. Clause* A *clause* is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb. There are 2 types: - *Independent clause*: Can stand alone as a sentence. _She passed the exam._ - *Dependent clause*: Cannot stand alone. It depends on an independent clause. _Because she studied hard._ --- *3. Adjectival Clause* An *adjectival clause*, also called a *relative clause*, is a dependent clause that functions like an adjective. It describes or gives more information about a noun or pronoun in the main clause. Think of it as an adjective, but expressed as a full clause with a subject and verb. *Example:* _The man *who lives next door* is a doctor._ “ who lives next door ” describes _the man_, so it works like the adjective “ neighboring ” . --- *4. Features of an Adjectival Clause* 1. *Functions as an adjective*: It modifies a noun or pronoun. 2. *Contains a subject and a verb*: It ’ s a full clause, not just a phrase. 3. *Starts with a relative pronoun or adverb*: _who, whom, whose, which, that, where, when, why_. 4. *Is a dependent clause*: It cannot stand alone. It must be attached to an independent clause. 5. *Can be restrictive or non-restrictive*: - Restrictive: Essential to meaning. No commas. _The book *that I borrowed* is lost._ - Non-restrictive: Extra information. Uses commas. _Lagos, *which is a port city*, is busy._

6. *Refers to an antecedent*: The noun it describes is called the antecedent. --- *5. Examples of Adjectival Clauses* 1. The girl *who won the race* is my cousin. 2. I read a book *that changed my life*. 3. The house *where I was born* was demolished. 4. Do you know the man *whose car was stolen*? 5. This is the reason *why he resigned*. 6. The teacher *whom we respect* is retiring. 7. I have a friend *who speaks five languages*. 8. The laptop *which you recommended* is fast. 9. Abuja, *where the capital is located*, is planned. 10. She bought the dress *that was on sale*.

title: PRESERVATIVE PREFIX
subject: English Language
rawText: Preservative prefixes are little word‑bits you stick on the front of a root to show that something is being kept, protected, or maintained. They signal “keep safe,” “guard,” or “hold onto.” Common ones: - *anti‑* (antioxidant, antibacterial) – works against damage - *pre‑* (pre‑treated, pre‑serve) – done before to keep something safe - *pro‑* (protect, prophylactic) – in favor of keeping something intact - *con‑* (conserve, conserve) – keep together So when you see a prefix like “anti‑” or “pre‑” attached to a word, it’s usually there to give that “preserving” meaning.

title: COMPREHENSION

rawText: ### Passage: A Glimpse of Africa Africa, the second largest continent on Earth, is renowned for its diverse cultures, languages, and landscapes. Spanning over 30 million square kilometers, Africa is home to 54 countries and an astounding array of ecosystems, from the Sahara Desert in the north to the lush rainforests of the Congo Basin in the central region. The continent boasts rich natural resources, including gold, diamonds, oil, and vast tracts of arable land. Africa is also known for its unique wildlife; the continent is home to the "Big Five" — lions, elephants, leopards, rhinoceroses, and buffaloes — making it a prime destination for tourists seeking exhilarating safaris. In addition to its natural wonders, Africa is culturally vibrant, with thousands of ethnic groups and languages, including Swahili, Arabic, Hausa, and Zulu. Traditional music, dance, and art reflect the continent ’ s rich heritage and continue to influence global culture. title: ADVERBIAL CLAUSE
subject: English Language
rawText:
*Adverbial clause* is a dependent clause that functions like an adverb. It modifies a verb, an adjective, or another adverb in the main clause, and it tells you _when, where, why, how, to what extent, under what condition, or despite what_ something happens. It usually starts with subordinating conjunctions like _when, after, before, because, although, if, unless, as, since, so that, so as to, while_. --- *15 Sentences with Adverbial Clauses* 1. I will call you *when I arrive home*. *Function*: Adverbial clause of time – tells _when_ I will call you. 2. *Because it was raining*, we stayed indoors. *Function*: Adverbial clause of reason/cause – tells _why_ we stayed indoors. 3. She sings *as if she were a professional*. *Function*: Adverbial clause of manner – tells _how_ she sings. 4. You can go out *if you finish your homework*. *Function*: Adverbial clause of condition – states the _condition_ for going out. 5. He worked hard *so that he could pass the exam*. *Function*: Adverbial clause of purpose – shows the _purpose_ of working hard. 6. *Although she was tired*, she completed the project. *Function*: Adverbial clause of concession/contrast – shows _despite what_ she still worked. 7. I recognized him *as soon as he entered the room*. *Function*: Adverbial clause of time – tells _when_ I recognized him. 8. We will leave *before the sun sets*. *Function*: Adverbial clause of time – tells _when_ we will leave. 9. He is taller *than I expected*. *Function*: Adverbial clause of comparison – shows the _extent_ of comparison. 10. *Where there is smoke*, there is fire. *Function*: Adverbial clause of place – tells _where_ the condition applies. 11. I will stay here *until you come back*. *Function*: Adverbial clause of time – tells _how long_ I will stay.

12. She left early *so as not to miss the train*. *Function*: Adverbial clause of purpose – shows the _purpose_ of leaving early. 13. *Since you asked*, I will explain it again. *Function*: Adverbial clause of reason/cause – tells _why_ I will explain it. 14. He drives *as carefully as his father does*. *Function*: Adverbial clause of manner/comparison – shows _how_ he drives in comparison. 15. They lost the match *even though they played well*. *Function*: Adverbial clause of concession – shows _despite what_ they still lost. ---

rawText:
A suffix is a letter or a group of letters added at the end of a word to modify its meaning or grammatical function. title: SAMPLE DEBATE FOR AND AGAINST THE MOTION
subject: English Language
rawText:
Debate in Support of the Motion: "School Uniform Should be Abolished in Schools" Opening Statement: School uniforms have been a long-standing tradition in many educational institutions. However, the time has come to reevaluate their purpose and relevance in a modern educational setting. We believe that school uniforms should be abolished in schools to promote individuality, creativity, and self-expression among students. Argument 1: Promotes Individuality School uniforms restrict students' ability to express their individuality and personal style. By abolishing school uniforms, students can choose their own outfits and express their unique personality, thus fostering a sense of individuality and self-confidence. Argument 2: Encourages Creativity Uniforms stifle creativity and limit students' ability to experiment with different styles and clothing choices. Allowing students to dress freely encourages creativity and fosters a sense of self-expression, which are essential skills for personal growth and development. Argument 3: Reflects Real-world Environment In the real world, individuals are judged based on their character, skills, and abilities, not by their appearance. By abolishing school uniforms, we are preparing students for the real world and teaching them that success is not determined by what they wear but by who they are and what they can achieve. Closing Statement: In conclusion, school uniforms have outlived their purpose in modern educational settings. Abolishing school uniforms will promote individuality, creativity, and self-expression among students, preparing them for success in the real world. Debate Against the Motion: "School Uniform Should be Abolished in Schools" Opening Statement: School uniforms play a crucial role in maintaining discipline, equality, and a sense of community within educational institutions. Abolishing school uniforms would have negative consequences and disrupt the learning environment for students. Argument 1: Promotes Discipline School uniforms instill a sense of discipline and professionalism among students. Uniforms create a sense of belonging and unity, encouraging students to adhere to school rules and regulations, which are essential for creating a conducive learning environment. Argument 2: Fosters Equality School uniforms eliminate social distinctions based on clothing and promote equality among students. Regardless of their background or financial status, all students are equal when wearing

the same uniform, fostering a sense of inclusivity and unity within the school community. Argument 3: Enhances School Safety School uniforms make it easier to identify students and distinguish them from outsiders, enhancing school safety and security. Uniforms also help prevent gang-related issues, peer pressure, and bullying based on clothing choices, creating a safer environment for students. Closing Statement: In summary, school uniforms serve a valuable purpose in promoting discipline, equality, and a sense of community within schools. Abolishing school uniforms would have negative consequences and disrupt the learning environment. Therefore, school uniforms should be maintained to uphold these essential values in educational institutions.

title: FREE WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText: Free writing Free writing is a useful technique of writing down your thoughts as they come to you. As its name implies it is a form of art that creates something new through thoughtful imagination . This constant writing can be whatever occurs to you, even if it seems like nonsense, doesn't have proper grammar or doesn't seem relevant to your current project or prompt. Free writing is a very flexible exercise, so you can use a pencil and paper or computer, depending on what is more comfortable for you. You can also decide whether you'd like to start from a prompt or write whatever comes to mind.

title: WORD\'S ASSOCIATED WITH BUILDING CONSTRUCTION
subject: English Language
rawText:
Building construction involves the process of erecting structures such as homes, commercial buildings, and infrastructure. It encompasses various activities, disciplines, and materials. Here is a list of fifty words commonly associated with building construction, along with brief explanations for each: 1. **Blueprint** - A detailed architectural plan used to guide construction. 2. **Foundation** - The base structure that supports a building and distributes its weight. 3. **Framing** - The skeleton of a building, usually composed of wooden or metal studs. 4. **Drywall** - A panel made from gypsum used to form interior walls and ceilings. 5. **Concrete** - A composite material made of cement, water, and aggregates used for durable structures. 6. **Rebar** - Steel bars used to reinforce concrete and improve structural strength. 7. **Insulation** - Materials used to reduce heat transfer and improve energy efficiency. 8. **Roofing** - The covering on the top of a building that protects it from weather conditions. 9. **Siding** - Exterior material applied to the walls of a building for protection and aesthetics. 10. **Masonry** - The building process using bricks, stone, or concrete blocks. 11. **Construction site** - The location where building activities take place. 12. **Load-bearing** - Refers to components that support weight or loads from above. 13. **Permit** - An official approval required to begin construction legally. 14. **Contractor** - A professional or company hired to manage and execute a construction project. 15. **Project manager** - The individual responsible for overseeing and coordinating all aspects of a construction project. 16. **Surveying** - The process of measuring land to determine boundaries and topography. 17. **2x4** - A common lumber size used for framing walls. 18. **Finishes** - The final layers or coatings applied to surfaces, such as paint or flooring.

19. **Fixtures** - Permanent or semi-permanent features such as lights and sinks. 20. **Hardscape** - Man-made features in landscaping such as walkways, patios, and walls. 21. **Softscape** - Living elements in landscaping such as plants, trees, and grass. 22. **Excavation** - The process of digging and removing soil to prepare for foundations. 23. **Scaffolding** - Temporary structures used to support work crews and materials during construction. 24. **Safety gear** - Protective equipment like helmets, gloves, and goggles worn by construction workers. 25. **Plywood** - Engineered wood made from thin layers of veneer used for sheathing and flooring. 26. **Subcontractor** - A contractor hired to perform a specific task within a larger construction project. 27. **Zoning** - Regulations governing land use, determining what types of structures can be built in specific areas. 28. **Site plan** - A detailed drawing depicting the layout of a property, including structures, landscaping, and access. 29. **HVAC** - Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems used to regulate indoor environments. 30. **Electrical** - Refers to the wiring and systems providing power and lighting in a building. 31. **Plumbing** - The system of pipes and fixtures for water supply and drainage. 32. **Building codes** - Standards and regulations governing construction practices to ensure safety and compliance. 33. **Retail** - Structures designed for commercial sales, often featuring open spaces and customer access. 34. **Residential** - Buildings primarily intended for living, such as homes and apartments. 35. **Commercial** - Structures used for business purposes, such as offices and shops. 36. **Industrial** - Buildings designed for manufacturing, warehousing, or distribution purposes.

37. **Demolition** - The process of tearing down existing structures to make way for new construction. 38. **Landscaping** - The design and arrangement of outdoor spaces, including plants, trees, and hardscape. 39. **Trowel** - A hand tool used by masons and craftsmen for shaping and applying materials. 40. **Safety inspection** - A review conducted to ensure all safety standards are met on a construction site. 41. **Contract** - A legal agreement outlining terms between the parties involved in the construction. 42. **Renovation** - The process of improving or updating an existing structure. 43. **Amendment** - A change or addition to construction plans or contracts. 44. **Tenant** - An individual or business that occupies space in a rented building. 45. **Egress** - The means of exit from a building, required for safety compliance. 46. **Tiling** - The application of tiles to floors and walls for aesthetics and durability. 47. **Carpentry** - The trade involved in working with wood to build and repair structures. 48. **Bidding** - The process of submitting proposals to undertake construction work. 49. **Inspection** - A formal examination of construction work or materials to ensure compliance with codes. 50. **Warranty** - A guarantee regarding the quality and durability of construction work or materials for a specified period. These terms represent just a fraction of the vocabulary used in building construction, highlighting the complexity and detail involved in the process.

19. **Fixtures** - Permanent or semi-permanent features such as lights and sinks. 20. **Hardscape** - Man-made features in landscaping such as walkways, patios, and walls. 21. **Softscape** - Living elements in landscaping such as plants, trees, and grass. 22. **Excavation** - The process of digging and removing soil to prepare for foundations. 23. **Scaffolding** - Temporary structures used to support work crews and materials during construction. 24. **Safety gear** - Protective equipment like helmets, gloves, and goggles worn by construction workers. 25. **Plywood** - Engineered wood made from thin layers of veneer used for sheathing and flooring. 26. **Subcontractor** - A contractor hired to perform a specific task within a larger construction project. 27. **Zoning** - Regulations governing land use, determining what types of structures can be built in specific areas. 28. **Site plan** - A detailed drawing depicting the layout of a property, including structures, landscaping, and access. 29. **HVAC** - Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems used to regulate indoor environments. 30. **Electrical** - Refers to the wiring and systems providing power and lighting in a building. 31. **Plumbing** - The system of pipes and fixtures for water supply and drainage. 32. **Building codes** - Standards and regulations governing construction practices to ensure safety and compliance. 33. **Retail** - Structures designed for commercial sales, often featuring open spaces and customer access. 34. **Residential** - Buildings primarily intended for living, such as homes and apartments. 35. **Commercial** - Structures used for business purposes, such as offices and shops. 36. **Industrial** - Buildings designed for manufacturing, warehousing, or distribution purposes.

37. **Demolition** - The process of tearing down existing structures to make way for new construction. 38. **Landscaping** - The design and arrangement of outdoor spaces, including plants, trees, and hardscape. 39. **Trowel** - A hand tool used by masons and craftsmen for shaping and applying materials. 40. **Safety inspection** - A review conducted to ensure all safety standards are met on a construction site. 41. **Contract** - A legal agreement outlining terms between the parties involved in the construction. 42. **Renovation** - The process of improving or updating an existing structure. 43. **Amendment** - A change or addition to construction plans or contracts. 44. **Tenant** - An individual or business that occupies space in a rented building. 45. **Egress** - The means of exit from a building, required for safety compliance. 46. **Tiling** - The application of tiles to floors and walls for aesthetics and durability. 47. **Carpentry** - The trade involved in working with wood to build and repair structures. 48. **Bidding** - The process of submitting proposals to undertake construction work. 49. **Inspection** - A formal examination of construction work or materials to ensure compliance with codes. 50. **Warranty** - A guarantee regarding the quality and durability of construction work or materials for a specified period. These terms represent just a fraction of the vocabulary used in building construction, highlighting the complexity and detail involved in the process.

title: ADJECTIVAL CLAUSE
subject: English Language
rawText: 1 Explanation of Adjective 1 An adjective is a word that describes or gives more information about a noun or pronoun 2 It tells us what kind, which one, or how many 3 Example The red car. Red describes the car 2 Explanation of Clause 1 A clause is a group of words that has a subject and a verb 2 It can be independent and make complete sense alone, or dependent and need another clause to complete meaning 3 Example She runs is a clause because it has subject She and verb runs 3 Explanation of Adjectival Clause 1 An adjectival clause is also called an adjective clause or relative clause 2 It is a dependent clause that works like an adjective in a sentence 3 It describes or gives more information about a noun or pronoun in the main clause 4 It usually begins with relative pronouns who, whom, whose, which, that or relative adverbs when, where, why 4 Features of Adjectival Clause 1 It must have a subject and a verb 2 It cannot stand alone as a complete sentence 3 It always modifies a noun or pronoun in the main clause 4 It usually starts with a relative pronoun or relative adverb 5 It comes directly after the noun it describes 6 It can be defining which gives essential information, or non defining which gives extra information 5 Fifteen Examples of Adjectival Clause 1 The boy who won the race is my brother 2 The house that was built last year is very big 3 The teacher whose car broke down came late 4 This is the place where we met 5 I know the reason why he left 6 The book which you borrowed is mine 7 The girl whom we saw yesterday is a doctor 8 Cars that use electric power are expensive 9 The man who called you is waiting outside 10 Lagos is a city that never sleeps 11 The day when the war ended was a holiday 12 People who work hard succeed in life 13 The phone which I bought is new 14 She is the student whose father is a judge 15 This is the road that leads to the market

title: COMPREHENSION
subject: English Language
rawText: **Passage: The Wonders of the Amazon Rainforest** The Amazon Rainforest, often referred to as the "lungs of the Earth," is one of the most biodiverse places on the planet. Spanning over five million square kilometers across nine countries, it is home to an estimated 390 billion individual trees, representing around 16,000 different species. This vibrant ecosystem supports countless species of flora and fauna, including jaguars, sloths, pink river dolphins, and over 2.5 million different insects. The rainforest plays a critical role in regulating the Earth's climate. Through photosynthesis, the trees absorb significant amounts of carbon dioxide, reducing greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. Additionally, the Amazon River, which flows through the forest, provides vital resources for the local communities and serves as a habitat for many aquatic species. However, the Amazon Rainforest faces significant threats from deforestation, illegal logging, and agriculture. Approximately 17% of the forest has been lost in the last 50 years due to human activity, leading to dire consequences for the global environment. Many organizations are working tirelessly to promote conservation efforts and raise awareness about the importance of protecting this ecological treasure. **Questions:** 1. What is the approximate area of the Amazon Rainforest? 2. How many species of trees are estimated to exist in the Amazon Rainforest? 3. List at least three species of animals found in the Amazon Rainforest. 4. What are two important ecological functions that the Amazon Rainforest performs? 5. What major threats does the Amazon Rainforest face? **Answers:** 1. The approximate area of the Amazon Rainforest is over five million square kilometers. 2. There are around 16,000 different species of trees estimated to exist in the Amazon Rainforest. 3. Three species of animals found in the Amazon Rainforest include jaguars, sloths, and pink river dolphins. 4. Two important ecological functions that the Amazon Rainforest performs are absorbing significant amounts of carbon dioxide through photosynthesis and providing vital resources for local communities via the Amazon River. 5. The major threats faced by the Amazon Rainforest include deforestation, illegal logging, and agriculture.

THE GAME OF BASKETBALL Basketball is a popular sport played around the world. It is a fast-paced team sport that involves two teams of five players each, with the objective of scoring points by putting the basketball through the opponent's hoop. The game is played on a rectangular court with a hoop at each end. The rules of basketball are fairly simple. The team that scores the most points by the end of the game wins. Points are scored by shooting the ball into the opponent's hoop, with different point values depending on the distance from which the shot is taken. Points can also be scored by making free throws, which are awarded for certain fouls committed by the other team. Basketball is a game that requires a combination of physical skills, such as speed, agility, and coordination, as well as mental skills, such as strategy, teamwork, and decision-making. Players must work together to move the ball up the court, create scoring opportunities, and defend against the other team's attacks. Good communication and understanding between teammates are essential for success in basketball. One of the most important skills in basketball is shooting, which involves throwing the ball through the hoop from various distances and angles. Shooting requires focus, accuracy, and muscle memory, as well as the ability to read the defense and adjust your shot accordingly. Other important skills in basketball include dribbling, passing, rebounding, and defending. Basketball is a highly competitive sport that requires a lot of hard work and dedication. Players must train regularly to improve their skills, conditioning, and teamwork. They must also study the game, watch film of other teams and players, and constantly work on their weaknesses to become better basketball players. In addition to physical and mental skills, basketball also teaches important life skills such as sportsmanship, discipline, perseverance, and teamwork. Players learn to work together towards a common goal, overcome challenges and setbacks, and handle successes and failures with grace and humility. Overall, basketball is a fun and exciting sport that can be enjoyed by people of all ages and abilities. Whether you are a casual player shooting hoops with friends or a professional athlete competing at the highest level, basketball offers a unique blend of athleticism, strategy, and camaraderie that makes it a truly special game. Teamwork is important in basketball because players must work together to create scoring opportunities and defend against the other team's attacks. 5. Basketball teaches important life skills such as sportsmanship, discipline, perseverance, and teamwork.

title: ENGLISH
subject: English Language
rawText: An adverb is a word that modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb by giving more information about an action. Adverbs of comparison show the degree to which an action occurs. Much – shows great extent. More – used when comparing two actions. Most – used when comparing three or more actions. Examples: He prepared much for the exam. She danced more gracefully than her friend. Janet sang most beautifully in the choir. Functions of Adverbs of Comparison: Show intensity or extent. Compare actions. Express the highest degree of performance. Modify adjectives and other adverbs.

title: PRESERVATIVE PREFIX
subject: English Language
rawText:
Explanation of Prefix A prefix is a group of letters added to the beginning of a word to modify its meaning. Often, prefixes help convey a specific meaning related to direction, negation, time, quantity, or function. For example, the prefix "un-" means "not" and changes the meaning of "happy" to "unhappy." Explanation of Preservative Prefix A **preservative prefix** typically refers to prefixes used to modify words related to preservation or conservation. These prefixes are not standardized and could be understood differently depending on the context. Common prefixes that might relate to preservation could include "bio-", "eco-", "re-", and "pre-". - **Bio-**: Relating to life or living organisms. - **Eco-**: Related to the environment or ecology. - **Re-**: To do again, often indicating repair or restoration. - **Pre-**: Before, often indicating prior existence, preparation, or readiness. ### List of Words with Preservative Prefixes Here's a table with fifty words and preservative prefixes attached to each one: | Base Word | Preservative Prefix | Resulting Word | |-------------|---------------------|---------------------| | cycle | Re- | Recycle | | conservation| Pre- | Preconservation | | process | Bio- | Bioprocess | | tour | Eco- | Ecotour | | serve | Preservative (Preserved) | Preserved | | species | Bio- | Biospecies | | material | Eco- | Ecomaterial | | farming | Eco- | Ecofarming | | system | Bio- | Biostystem | | energy | Re- | Reenergy | | habitat | Bio- | Biohabitat | | waste | Re- | Rewaste | | plant | Re- | Replant | | storage | Pre- | Prestorage | | resource | Eco- | Ecoresource | | development | Re- | Redevelopment | | management | Eco- | Ecomanagement | | solution | Pre- | Presolution | | repair | Re- | Repair | | product | Bio- | Bioproduct |

title: INTONATION; FALLING TONE
subject: English Language
rawText: A falling tone, also known as a dropping tone, is a type of intonation pattern in speech where the pitch of the voice falls or drops at the end of a sentence or phrase. It's like your voice is going down a slide. Falling tones often: 1. Indicate a statement or declaration 2. Show finality or completion 3. Can sound assertive or definitive Example: I'm going home. (voice falls on "home") 1. Statements: - I'm going to the store. - She's eating breakfast. - The meeting is at 3 PM. 2. Declarative sentences: - I love reading books. - He's a great teacher. - The weather is nice today. 3. Commands: - Close the door. - Stop talking. - Eat your dinner. 4. Exclamations: - What a beautiful day! - I'm so excited! - That's amazing! In these examples, the voice tends to fall at the end, indicating finality or assertiveness.

title: VOCABULARY DEVELOPMENT ON INTERNAL BODY SYSTEM
subject: English Language
rawText:
VOCABULARY DEVELOPMENT. NOTE ON UNDERSTANDING THE INTERNAL HUMAN BODY SYSTEM. Understanding the Internal Human Body System: The human body is an incredible and complex system made up of various interconnected parts and functions. To gain a deeper understanding of how our bodies work, it's essential to familiarize ourselves with the terminology associated with the internal human body systems. This lesson will be your guide through the rich vocabulary that describes the intricate web of systems that keep us alive and functioning. Circulatory System: Exploring how blood flows through our bodies, carrying vital nutrients and oxygen. Respiratory System: Understanding the processes that allow us to breathe and exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide. Digestive System: Delving into the journey of food from the mouth to the stomach and beyond, where nutrients are absorbed and waste is eliminated. Nervous System: Uncovering the intricacies of our body's communication network, including the brain, spinal cord, and nerves. Skeletal System: Examining the framework that supports our bodies and protects our vital organs. Muscular System: Discovering the muscles that enable movement and support our overall physical health. Endocrine System: Learning about the glands and hormones that regulate various bodily functions. By familiarizing yourself with these essential terms, you'll be better equipped to understand discussions about health, medical diagnoses, and even the way lifestyle choices impact your overall well-being. Vocabulary of the Internal Human Body System 1. Circulatory System Heart: The muscular organ that pumps blood throughout the body. Artery: Blood vessels that carry oxygenated blood away from the heart. Vein: Blood vessels that return deoxygenated blood to the heart. Capillary: Tiny blood vessels where the exchange of oxygen and nutrients occurs.

Blood: The fluid that circulates through the arteries and veins, carrying oxygen and nutrients. Circulation: The movement of blood through the body. 2. Respiratory System Lungs: The main organs of the respiratory system where oxygen is inhaled and carbon dioxide is exhaled. Bronchial Tubes: The air passages that connect the trachea to the lungs. Trachea: The windpipe, which carries air from the throat to the bronchial tubes. Diaphragm: A muscular structure that aids in breathing by expanding and contracting. Alveoli: Tiny air sacs in the lungs where gas exchange occurs. Respiration: The process of breathing, involving the intake of oxygen and the release of carbon dioxide. 3. Digestive System Stomach: An organ that breaks down food with digestive juices. Oesophagus: The tube connecting the throat to the stomach. Liver: An organ that produces bile and aids in digestion. Pancreas: An organ that produces enzymes for digestion and regulates blood sugar. Small Intestine: The part of the digestive tract where nutrients are absorbed. Large Intestine: The final part of the digestive system, where water is absorbed and waste is formed. 4. Nervous System Brain: The central control organ of the body. Spinal Cord: A bundle of nerves that transmits signals between the brain and the body. Neuron: A nerve cell that transmits electrical impulses. Synapse: The junction between two neurons where signals are transmitted. Central Nervous System (CNS): The brain and spinal cord. Peripheral Nervous System (PNS): The network of nerves outside the CNS. 5. Skeletal System Bones: Rigid structures that provide support and protection. Joints: The points where two or more bones meet. Cartilage: A connective tissue that cushions joints. Skeleton: The framework of bones in the body. Bone Marrow: The soft tissue inside bones that produces blood cells. Osteoporosis: A condition characterized by weakened bones.

6. Muscular System Muscles: Tissues that contract and enable movement. Voluntary Muscles: Muscles that are under conscious control. Involuntary Muscles: Muscles that function without conscious control. Skeletal Muscles: Muscles attached to bones that move the skeleton. Cardiac Muscle: Muscle found in the heart. Smooth Muscle: Muscle found in the walls of internal organs. 7. Endocrine System Hormones: Chemical messengers produced by glands. Glands: Organs that produce and release hormones. Pituitary Gland: The "master gland" that regulates other glands. Thyroid Gland: Regulates metabolism and energy. Adrenal Glands: Produce stress hormones like adrenaline. Pancreatic Islets: Parts of the pancreas that regulate blood sugar.

title: CLAUSES
subject: English Language
rawText:
A **clause** is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb. It can express a complete thought or a part of a thought. Clauses are the building blocks of sentences and can stand alone or be part of larger sentence structures. ### Features of a Clause 1. **Subject and Verb**: A clause contains at least a subject (the noun or pronoun that performs the action) and a predicate (the verb and any complements). 2. **Independent vs. Dependent**: Clauses can be independent (able to stand alone as a complete sentence) or dependent (cannot stand alone and requires an independent clause). 3. **Function**: Clauses can function as different parts of a sentence, including nouns, adjectives, or adverbs. 4. **Length and Complexity**: Clauses can be simple (short) or complex (long with additional phrases or clauses). ### Two Types of Clauses 1. **Independent Clauses** 2. **Dependent Clauses** #### 1. Independent Clauses An independent clause can stand alone as a complete sentence. It expresses a complete thought. **Examples:** 1. **I enjoy reading.** 2. **She loves to travel.** 3. **The sun sets in the west.** 4. **He plays the guitar.** 5. **They will go to the concert.** #### 2. Dependent Clauses A dependent clause cannot stand alone as a complete sentence because it does not express a complete thought. It usually begins with a subordinating conjunction (e.g., because, although, if) or a relative pronoun (e.g., which, that). **Examples:** 1. **Although I was tired,** 2. **Because it was raining,** 3. **If you study hard,** 4. **Which is my favorite book,** 5. **When the bell rings,** ### Combining Clauses - **Independent Clause**: "I enjoy reading." - **Dependent Clause**: "Although I was tired."

**Combined**: "Although I was tired, I enjoy reading." Understanding these clauses helps you to construct sentences correctly and improve your writing clarity.

It expresses a complete thought. **Examples:** 1. **I enjoy reading.** 2. **She loves to travel.** 3. **The sun sets in the west.** 4. **He plays the guitar.** 5. **They will go to the concert.** #### 2. Dependent Clauses A dependent clause cannot stand alone as a complete sentence because it does not express a complete thought. It usually begins with a subordinating conjunction (e.g., because, although, if) or a relative pronoun (e.g., which, that). **Examples:** 1. **Although I was tired,** 2. **Because it was raining,** 3. **If you study hard,** 4. **Which is my favorite book,** 5. **When the bell rings,** ### Combining Clauses - **Independent Clause**: "I enjoy reading." - **Dependent Clause**: "Although I was tired."
**Combined**: "Although I was tired, I enjoy reading." Understanding these clauses helps you to construct sentences correctly and improve your writing clarity.

title: VOCABULARY DEVELOPMENT: HEALTH
subject: English Language
rawText:
Subject: English Language Class: VEI 2 Topic: Vocabulary Development: Health Definition : Health refers to a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. Aspects of Health 1. Physical Health: Refers to the body's physical condition, including nutrition, fitness, and freedom from disease. 2. Mental Health: Refers to emotional, psychological, and social well-being, including the ability to cope with stress and maintain relationships. 3. Social Health: Refers to the ability to interact and function within social relationships and communities. Importance of Health 1. Quality of Life: Good health enables individuals to enjoy life, pursue their goals, and maintain relationships. 2. Productivity: Healthy individuals are more productive, contributing to economic growth and development. 3. Well-being: Health is essential for overall well-being, influencing physical, mental, and social aspects of life. Factors Influencing Health 1. Lifestyle Choices: Diet, exercise, sleep, and substance use can impact health. 2. Environmental Factors: Access to clean air, water, and living conditions can influence health. 3. Genetics: Genetic predispositions can affect health outcomes. 4. Healthcare Access: Access to quality healthcare services can impact health outcomes. Maintaining Good Health 1. Healthy Diet: Eating a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. 2. Regular Exercise: Engaging in physical activity to maintain physical fitness. 3. Stress Management: Practicing stress-reducing techniques, such as meditation or yoga.

2 4. Regular Check-ups: Scheduling regular health check-ups to monitor health and detect potential issues early.

title: READING FOR CRITICAL EVALUATION
subject: English Language
rawText:
Subject: English Language Class: VEI2/SS2 Topic: Reading for Critical Evaluation Definition: Critical evaluation in reading involves analyzing, interpreting, and assessing the content, arguments, and effectiveness of a text. Key things to note: 1. Understanding the Author's Purpose: Identify why the author wrote the text (to inform, persuade, entertain). 2. Analyzing Content: Examine the ideas, themes, and messages in the text. 3. Evaluating Arguments: Assess the logic, evidence, and reasoning used in the text. 4. Identifying Bias: Recognize any biases, prejudices, or perspectives influencing the text. 5. Assessing Credibility: Consider the author's credibility, reliability of sources. 6. Considering Context: Understand the historical, cultural, social context affecting the text. Critical Evaluation Skills 1. Inference: Drawing conclusions based on evidence in the text. 2. Analysis: Breaking down parts of the text to understand meaning. 3. Evaluation: Judging the effectiveness, validity, or quality of the text. 4. Synthesis: Combining ideas from texts or relating to broader contexts. Types of Texts for Critical Evaluation 1. Literary Texts: Novels, poems, plays involving themes, symbolism. 2. Informational Texts: Articles, reports requiring assessment of facts and arguments. 3. Persuasive Texts: Advertisements, speeches aiming to convince.

2 Tips for Critical Evaluation 1. Read Actively: Engage with the text by questioning and annotating. 2. Consider Multiple Perspectives: Look at different viewpoints related to the text. 3. Use Evidence: Support evaluations with textual evidence. 4. Be Aware of Language: Notice how language influences meaning (tone, imagery). Importance of critical analysis 1. Informed Decision-Making: Critical evaluation helps in making informed judgments about information. 2. Academic Skills: Essential for academic reading, research, and writing. 3. Real-Life Applications: Useful in evaluating media, policies, arguments in everyday life.

title: ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText:
ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY Meaning An argumentative essay is a type of essay in which the writer expresses an opinion on a controversial issue and tries to convince the reader to agree with their point of view. It involves presenting arguments for or against a given topic. In simple terms, an argumentative essay is like a debate in writing, where the writer supports one side (for or against) and provides convincing reasons, examples, and evidence. Features / Characteristics of an Argumentative Essay 1. Controversial Topic: The topic must be one that people can argue about (e.g., “School uniforms should be abolished.”). 2. Clear Standpoint: The writer must choose a side — either for or against the topic. 3. Logical Reasoning: Arguments must be based on facts, logic, and sound reasoning — not emotions. 4. Evidence and Examples: Each argument should be supported with relevant examples, facts, or statistics. 5. Formal Tone and Language: The essay should be written in a formal style, avoiding slang and contractions. 6. Connectives: Use linking words such as firstly, moreover, however, therefore, on the other hand, etc. 7. Counter-Arguments: The writer may mention and refute the opposing view to strengthen their position. Structure of an Argumentative Essay 1. Introduction - Introduce the topic. - State clearly your position (for or against). - Give a brief background or definition if necessary. Example: The issue of whether school uniforms should be abolished has generated much debate among students and teachers. While some believe that uniforms promote discipline and equality, others think they restrict freedom. I strongly believe that school uniforms should not be abolished. 2. Body Paragraphs - Each paragraph should present one strong argument supporting your position. - Begin each paragraph with a topic sentence. - Support each point with reasons, facts, and examples. - You may also include counter-arguments and refute them. Example: Firstly, school uniforms promote discipline among students. When students wear similar clothes, they concentrate more on their studies rather than on fashion or competition in dressing. Secondly, uniforms promote equality and reduce social discrimination. Students from rich and poor backgrounds all look alike, preventing class distinction. Furthermore, school uniforms help identify students easily during excursions or emergencies. 3. Conclusion - Summarize your main points. - Restate your opinion firmly. - End with a strong, convincing statement. Example: In conclusion, school uniforms play an important role in maintaining discipline and equality in schools. Therefore, they should not be abolished but rather encouraged in all learning institutions. Examples of Argumentative Essay Topics - Capital punishment should be abolished. - Women make better leaders than men. - Social media does more harm than good. - Examination malpractice is the major cause of failure in schools. - Cultism in schools should attract life imprisonment. - Science is more important than arts. - Boarding schools are better than day schools. Language Tips for Argumentative Essays Use persuasive and formal expressions such as: - I strongly believe that… - It is evident that… - There is no doubt that… - On the other hand… - Some people may argue that…, but… - Therefore, I maintain that… Sample Topic: “Social Media Does More Harm Than Good.” Introduction: Social media has become a major part of modern communication. While it helps people connect easily, I strongly believe that social media does more harm than good. Body Paragraphs: Firstly, social media wastes a lot of time. Many students spend hours chatting and scrolling through posts instead of studying. Secondly, it promotes immoral behavior. Some users post indecent pictures and videos which influence young people negatively. Furthermore,

social media spreads false information and fake news quickly, which can cause confusion and panic. Conclusion: In conclusion, although social media has some benefits, its disadvantages outweigh them. It is clear that social media does more harm than good to individuals and society.

title: MODIFIERS (ADJECTIVE OF COLOUR/SIZE)
subject: English Language
rawText:
COMPREHENSIVE NOTE ON MODIFIERS (Adjectives of Colour and Size) Prepared for SS1 Students By IJ's Exquisite Products Learning Hub

Meaning of Modifiers A modifier is a word, phrase, or clause that describes, limits, or adds meaning to another word in a sentence. Modifiers make sentences clearer and more interesting by giving additional details about nouns, pronouns, or verbs. Example: The small boy wore a red shirt. Here, small and red are modifiers. They describe boy and shirt respectively. Types of Modifiers 1. Adjectival Modifiers (Adjectives) – modify nouns or pronouns. 2. Adverbial Modifiers (Adverbs) – modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Adjectival Modifiers in Detail Adjectival modifiers give more information about nouns. They include adjectives of Quality, Quantity, Number, Colour, Size, Origin, Material, and Possession. Adjectives of Colour Adjectives of colour describe the colour or shade of a noun. Examples: • The red car is mine. • She wore a blue dress. • The green leaves fell from the tree. • The black dog barked loudly. • He painted his room white . Common colour adjectives: red, blue, yellow, green, black, white, purple, brown, grey, pink, orange, golden, silver. Adjectives of Size Adjectives of size describe how big or small a noun is. Examples: • The small child is sleeping. • She bought a large bag. • The tiny kitten looked hungry. • He lifted a huge stone. • The tall man greeted us politely.

Common size adjectives: small, big, large, huge, little, tall, short, tiny, massive, gigantic. Order of Adjectives When using more than one adjective before a noun, the order is: Opinion → Size → Age → Shape → Colour → Origin → Material → Purpose → Noun Example: A beautiful small round red Italian leather bag. Common Errors in Using Modifiers Dangling modifiers: 7 Running quickly, the gate was reached. 3 Running quickly, he reached the gate. Misplaced modifiers: 7 She almost drove her children to school every day. 3 She drove her children to school almost every day. Functions of Modifiers • Describe nouns and verbs. • Make meanings clearer and specific. • Add beauty and detail to writing. • Express opinions or attitudes. Examples in Sentences 1. The small boy carried a blue bag. 2. A large red ball rolled across the road. 3. The tiny baby smiled at her white toy. 4. I saw a tall , black man at the gate. 5. She wore a beautiful yellow gown. Summary • Modifiers describe or limit other words. • Adjectival modifiers describe nouns and pronouns. • Adjectives of colour show the colour or shade of something. • Adjectives of size show how big or small something is.

• Proper use of modifiers makes writing clear, vivid, and interesting.

title: CONSONANT CLUSTERS
subject: English Language
rawText:
Comprehensive Note on Consonant Cluster Meaning of Consonant Cluster A consonant cluster is a group of two or more consonant sounds that appear together without a vowel sound between them in a word. In simple terms, it means two or more consonants are pronounced together in a word. Examples: bl in black, str in street, mp in lamp, spl in splash. Explanation In English, consonants can combine at the beginning (initial), middle (medial), or end (final) of a word. These combinations create what we call clusters. Each consonant in a cluster retains its sound, but they are pronounced smoothly together. Examples: play (/pl/), street (/str/), asks (/sks/). Types of Consonant Clusters 1. Initial Clusters – occur at the beginning of words (e.g., bl, tr, cl, sp, str, scr, spr). 2. Medial Clusters – occur in the middle of words (e.g., extra, handbag, transport). 3. Final Clusters – occur at the end of words (e.g., mp, nd, st, nt, lpt, mps, rld). Rules/Patterns in Consonant Clusters 1. Not all consonants can appear together. 2. Clusters can have 2 to 4 consonants but never more. 3. Each consonant keeps its pronunciation; no vowel sound is inserted between them. 4. Clusters may differ in British and American English pronunciations (e.g., asked / n :skt/ vs /æst/). Importance of Consonant Clusters 1. They make speech fluent and natural. 2. They help learners understand word pronunciation better. 3. They enrich vocabulary and improve spelling skills. 4. They are useful in phonics and reading aloud exercises. Common Problems Learners Face • Adding a vowel sound between consonants (e.g., saying 'espeak' instead of 'speak'). • Dropping a consonant (e.g., saying 'pos' for 'post'). Learners must practice carefully to pronounce all consonant sounds smoothly together. Examples for Practice | Initial Cluster | Word Example | Final Cluster | Word Example | |-----------------|---------------|----------------|----------------| | bl | black | mp | lamp | | pr | pray | nd | hand | | sp | speak | st | best | | tr | tree | nt | went | | str | street | lpt | helped | | scr | scream | mps | lamps | | spl | splash | rld | world | Conclusion A consonant cluster is an important part of English pronunciation. Mastering it helps in reading, spelling, and speaking fluently. Students should practice regularly to avoid inserting unnecessary vowels or omitting consonant sounds.

Examples: • The small child is sleeping. • She bought a large bag. • The tiny kitten looked hungry. • He lifted a huge stone. • The tall man greeted us politely.

The small boy carried a blue bag. 2. A large red ball rolled across the road. 3. The tiny baby smiled at her white toy. 4. I saw a tall , black man at the gate. 5. She wore a beautiful yellow gown. • Proper use of modifiers makes writing clear, vivid, and interesting.

title: CONSONANT CLUSTERS
subject: English Language
rawText:
Comprehensive Note on Consonant Cluster Meaning of Consonant Cluster A consonant cluster is a group of two or more consonant sounds that appear together without a vowel sound between them in a word. In simple terms, it means two or more consonants are pronounced together in a word. Examples: bl in black, str in street, mp in lamp, spl in splash. Explanation In English, consonants can combine at the beginning (initial), middle (medial), or end (final) of a word. These combinations create what we call clusters. Each consonant in a cluster retains its sound, but they are pronounced smoothly together. Examples: play (/pl/), street (/str/), asks (/sks/). Types of Consonant Clusters 1. Initial Clusters – occur at the beginning of words (e.g., bl, tr, cl, sp, str, scr, spr). 2. Medial Clusters – occur in the middle of words (e.g., extra, handbag, transport). 3. Final Clusters – occur at the end of words (e.g., mp, nd, st, nt, lpt, mps, rld). Rules/Patterns in Consonant Clusters 1. Not all consonants can appear together. 2. Clusters can have 2 to 4 consonants but never more. 3. Each consonant keeps its pronunciation; no vowel sound is inserted between them. 4. Clusters may differ in British and American English pronunciations (e.g., asked / n :skt/ vs /æst/). Importance of Consonant Clusters 1. They make speech fluent and natural. 2. They help learners understand word pronunciation better. 3. They enrich vocabulary and improve spelling skills. 4. They are useful in phonics and reading aloud exercises. Common Problems Learners Face • Adding a vowel sound between consonants (e.g., saying 'espeak' instead of 'speak'). • Dropping a consonant (e.g., saying 'pos' for 'post'). Learners must practice carefully to pronounce all consonant sounds smoothly together. Examples for Practice | Initial Cluster | Word Example | Final Cluster | Word Example | |-----------------|---------------|----------------|----------------| | bl | black | mp | lamp | | pr | pray | nd | hand | | sp | speak | st | best | | tr | tree | nt | went | | str | street | lpt | helped | | scr | scream | mps | lamps | | spl | splash | rld | world | Conclusion A consonant cluster is an important part of English pronunciation. Mastering it helps in reading, spelling, and speaking fluently. Students should practice regularly to avoid inserting unnecessary vowels or omitting consonant sounds.

title: VOWEL SOUND
subject: English Language
rawText:
NOTE ON THE VOWEL SOUNDS /e/ AND / nn / 1. The Vowel Sound /e/ The /e/ sound is a short front vowel . It is produced with the tongue positioned midway between the front and the center of the mouth, and the lips are slightly spread. The sound is short and relaxed. It is often heard in words spelled with 'e' or sometimes 'ea'. Word Phonetic Transcription Meaning pen /pen/ an instrument for writing men /men/ plural of man bed /bed/ a piece of furniture for sleeping ten /ten/ the number after nine get /get/ to obtain or receive send /send/ to dispatch Features: • It is a short vowel. • It is a front vowel (produced with the front of the tongue). • It occurs in both open and closed syllables, though commonly in closed ones. 2. The Vowel Sound / nn / The / nn / sound is a long central vowel . It is produced with the tongue raised towards the center of the mouth. The lips are slightly rounded or neutral, and the sound is long and sustained. It is usually represented in spelling by 'ir', 'ur', 'er', 'ear', or 'or' when not pronounced / nn /. Word Phonetic Transcription Meaning bird /b nn d/ a creature with wings and feathers girl /g nn l/ a female child first /f nn st/ coming before others turn /t nn n/ to change direction word /w nn d/ a single unit of language learn /l nn n/ to gain knowledge Features: • It is a long vowel. • It is a central vowel (produced with the tongue in the middle of the mouth). • It does not usually occur at the end of English words. 3. Comparison Between /e/ and / nn /

Feature /e/ / nn / Length Short Long Position Front Central Lip Position Slightly spread Neutral/slightly rounded Examples pen, bed, ten bird, turn, word

title: ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY
subject: English Language
rawText:
ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY Meaning An argumentative essay is a type of essay in which the writer expresses an opinion on a controversial issue and tries to convince the reader to agree with their point of view. It involves presenting arguments for or against a given topic. In simple terms, an argumentative essay is like a debate in writing, where the writer supports one side (for or against) and provides convincing reasons, examples, and evidence. Features / Characteristics of an Argumentative Essay 1. Controversial Topic: The topic must be one that people can argue about (e.g., “School uniforms should be abolished.”). 2. Clear Standpoint: The writer must choose a side — either for or against the topic. 3. Logical Reasoning: Arguments must be based on facts, logic, and sound reasoning — not emotions. 4. Evidence and Examples: Each argument should be supported with relevant examples, facts, or statistics. 5. Formal Tone and Language: The essay should be written in a formal style, avoiding slang and contractions. 6. Connectives: Use linking words such as firstly, moreover, however, therefore, on the other hand, etc. 7. Counter-Arguments: The writer may mention and refute the opposing view to strengthen their position. Structure of an Argumentative Essay 1. Introduction - Introduce the topic. - State clearly your position (for or against). - Give a brief background or definition if necessary. Example: The issue of whether school uniforms should be abolished has generated much debate among students and teachers. While some believe that uniforms promote discipline and equality, others think they restrict freedom. I strongly believe that school uniforms should not be abolished. 2. Body Paragraphs - Each paragraph should present one strong argument supporting your position. - Begin each paragraph with a topic sentence. - Support each point with reasons, facts, and examples. - You may also include counter-arguments and refute them. Example: Firstly, school uniforms promote discipline among students. When students wear similar clothes, they concentrate more on their studies rather than on fashion or competition in dressing. Secondly, uniforms promote equality and reduce social discrimination. Students from rich and poor backgrounds all look alike, preventing class distinction. Furthermore, school uniforms help identify students easily during excursions or emergencies. 3. Conclusion - Summarize your main points. - Restate your opinion firmly. - End with a strong, convincing statement. Example: In conclusion, school uniforms play an important role in maintaining discipline and equality in schools. Therefore, they should not be abolished but rather encouraged in all learning institutions. Examples of Argumentative Essay Topics - Capital punishment should be abolished. - Women make better leaders than men. - Social media does more harm than good. - Examination malpractice is the major cause of failure in schools. - Cultism in schools should attract life imprisonment. - Science is more important than arts. - Boarding schools are better than day schools. Language Tips for Argumentative Essays Use persuasive and formal expressions such as: - I strongly believe that… - It is evident that… - There is no doubt that… - On the other hand… - Some people may argue that…, but… - Therefore, I maintain that… Sample Topic: “Social Media Does More Harm Than Good.” Introduction: Social media has become a major part of modern communication. While it helps people connect easily, I strongly believe that social media does more harm than good. Body Paragraphs: Firstly, social media wastes a lot of time. Many students spend hours chatting and scrolling through posts instead of studying. Secondly, it promotes immoral behavior. Some users post indecent pictures and videos which influence young people negatively. Furthermore,

social media spreads false information and fake news quickly, which can cause confusion and panic. Conclusion: In conclusion, although social media has some benefits, its disadvantages outweigh them. It is clear that social media does more harm than good to individuals and society.

title: CREATIVE WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText:
CREATIVE WRITING Meaning of Creative Writing Creative writing is a form of writing that expresses the writer’s thoughts, imagination, emotions, and ideas in an original and artistic way. It goes beyond simply conveying facts—it allows the writer to create something new, beautiful, or thought-provoking through imagination and creativity. Examples of Creative Writing Creative writing appears in various forms such as: 1. Poetry – expressing feelings and ideas through rhythm and imagery. 2. Short Stories – brief fictional narratives with characters, plot, and setting. 3. Novels – longer narratives with complex plots and well-developed characters. 4. Plays or Drama – written dialogue meant for performance on stage. 5. Essays – personal or reflective essays that express the writer’s views creatively. 6. Letters, speeches, and autobiographies written in an imaginative style. Features of Creative Writing 1. Imagination and Originality – ideas come from the writer’s mind, not copied. 2. Descriptive Language – uses vivid words that appeal to the senses. 3. Strong Emotions – expresses joy, anger, fear, love, or sadness clearly. 4. Character Development – in stories and plays, characters are made believable. 5. Plot and Setting – events are organized, and the scene is clearly described. 6. Figurative Language – uses figures of speech such as simile, metaphor, and personification. 7. Theme – the main message, idea, or lesson in the writing. 8. Point of View – the perspective from which the story is told. Elements of Creative Writing 1. Plot: The sequence of events in a story. 2. Character: The people or beings who take part in the story. 3. Setting: The time and place where the events happen. 4. Conflict: The struggle between opposing forces. 5. Theme: The central message or idea. 6. Style: The writer’s way of expressing ideas – word choice, tone, and sentence structure. 7. Dialogue: Conversations between characters that reveal personality and advance the plot. Types of Creative Writing 1. Fiction: Imaginary stories or events created by the writer. 2. Non-fiction: Real-life experiences told in a creative manner. 3. Poetry: Uses rhythm, rhyme, and imagery to express feelings. 4. Drama: Stories written in dialogue form for acting. 5. Scripts: Written for film, radio, or television. Purpose of Creative Writing 1. To entertain the reader or audience. 2. To express emotions and personal experiences. 3. To inspire imagination and creativity. 4. To communicate moral lessons or social messages. 5. To inform in an artistic and engaging way. 6. To preserve culture and human experiences through stories and art. Steps in Creative Writing 1. Choosing a topic or idea. 2. Planning – outline your plot, characters, and setting. 3. Writing the first draft. 4. Revising – review your work for clarity and creativity. 5. Editing – correct grammar and spelling errors. 6. Final presentation – prepare the final copy neatly. Qualities of a Good Creative Writer

1. Imaginative and observant. 2. Good command of language. 3. Emotionally expressive. 4. Patient and persistent. 5. Original thinker. Importance of Creative Writing • Develops imagination and self-expression. • Improves vocabulary and grammar. • Enhances communication skills. • Builds confidence in expressing ideas. • Can lead to careers in literature, journalism, media, or scriptwriting. Summary Creative writing is an imaginative way of expressing thoughts, ideas, and emotions through words. It uses artistic language, vivid imagery, and originality to entertain, inform, or inspire the audience. Every good creative writer must think deeply, feel strongly, and write clearly.

title: ADJECTIVAL PHRASE
subject: English Language
rawText:
ADJECTIVAL PHRASE AND ITS GRAMMATICAL FUNCTIONS Meaning of an Adjectival Phrase An adjectival phrase (also called adjective phrase) is a group of words that performs the function of an adjective in a sentence. It describes, qualifies, or gives more information about a noun or pronoun. In other words, an adjectival phrase modifies a noun just as an adjective does, but it usually contains more than one word. Examples • The girl with the long hair is my sister. • That man in the blue shirt is our teacher. • Students eager to learn often succeed. • The house at the corner belongs to my uncle. • I saw a boy full of courage . Structure of an Adjectival Phrase An adjectival phrase may have: 1. A headword (main adjective) – e.g., happy, strong, beautiful 2. Modifiers (words that give extra meaning to the adjective) – e.g., very, quite, too, really, extremely Examples: • She is very beautiful. • The child is too young to go alone. • The teacher is quite kind to everyone. Forms of Adjectival Phrases 1. Prepositional Phrases – beginning with a preposition and describing a noun. e.g., The man in the car , The food on the table . 2. Participial Phrases – starting with a present or past participle. e.g., The boy wearing a red cap , The letter written by Ada . 3. Infinitive Phrases – using the infinitive form of a verb to describe a noun. e.g., The book to read before exams , The student to watch carefully . Grammatical Functions of an Adjectival Phrase 1. As an Attribute (Pre-modifier) Appears before the noun it modifies. • The very expensive dress was stolen. • We met a kind-hearted woman. 2. As a Complement (Post-modifier) Appears after a linking verb and modifies the subject of the sentence. • The girl is full of joy. • The day seems too hot for comfort. 3. As a Post-modifier in a Noun Phrase Comes after the noun to describe it more clearly. • The man in black is a detective. • The boy with the red shoes is my friend. 4. As an Object Complement Gives more information about the object of a verb. • They found the child very tired. • She painted the room bright yellow. Differences Between an Adjective and an Adjectival Phrase Adjective: one word → The girl is beautiful. Adjectival Phrase: group of words → The girl is full of beauty. Adjective: He bought a new car.

Adjectival Phrase: He bought a car with a new engine. Summary • An adjectival phrase is a group of words that modifies a noun or pronoun. • It can come before or after the noun it describes. • It can be formed by prepositional, participial, or infinitive phrases. • It performs grammatical functions such as attribute, complement, post-modifier, and object complement.

title: UNSTRESSED SYLLABLES
subject: English Language
rawText: UNSTRESSED SYLLABLES Meaning A syllable is a single, unbroken sound of a spoken (or written) word. It is a unit of pronunciation that usually contains one vowel sound. Examples: - ta-ble (2 syllables) - beau-ti-ful (3 syllables) - in-ter-est-ing (4 syllables) In English pronunciation, not all syllables in a word are given equal importance or emphasis. Some syllables are stressed, while others are unstressed. Definition of Unstressed Syllable An unstressed syllable is a syllable that is pronounced more softly and less forcefully than the stressed one. It receives less emphasis in speech. In other words, it is the weaker syllable in a word or sentence. Example: - In ta-ble, the first syllable TA is stressed, while ble is unstressed. - In beau-ti-ful, the first syllable BEAU is stressed, while ti and ful are unstressed. Characteristics of Unstressed Syllables 1. Reduced Loudness: They are pronounced with less volume than stressed syllables. 2. Shorter Duration: They are usually shorter in length (spoken quickly). 3. Weaker Pitch: The pitch or tone of voice is lower. 4. Reduced Vowel Sound: The vowel sound in unstressed syllables is often pronounced as the / n / sound (called schwa). Example: about → / nn ba n t/, the first syllable 'a' is unstressed and pronounced / n /. Examples of Words with Unstressed Syllables Word | Stressed Syllable | Unstressed Syllable(s) ta-ble | TA | ble com-put-er | PU | com, ter a-bout | BOUT | a to-day | DAY | to de-sert (noun) | DE | sert be-come | COME | be a-lone | LONE | a en-joy | JOY | en a-round | ROUND | a pre-sent (verb) | SENT | pre Unstressed Syllables in Sentences In connected speech (normal spoken English), many small words and syllables are unstressed. Examples: - I am going to the market. → “I’m gonna the market.” (am, to, and the become weak or unstressed) - He is a teacher. → “He’s a teacher.” (a is unstressed) The Schwa Sound (/ n /) The schwa is the most common vowel sound in unstressed syllables. It is pronounced softly like “uh.” Examples: - about → / nn ba n t/ - banana → /b nn n nn n n / - problem → / n pr n bl n m/ - teacher → / n ti n t nn / Importance of Recognizing Unstressed Syllables 1. Improves Pronunciation: Helps students speak more naturally like native English speakers. 2. Improves Listening Skills: Makes it easier to understand spoken English. 3. Enhances Reading Aloud: Helps in proper rhythm and stress pattern. 4. Aids Spelling and Word Stress Learning: Helps in dividing words correctly and placing stress properly. Tips to Identify Unstressed Syllables - Say the word slowly and listen for the part that is said softer or quicker. - Check dictionary pronunciation; unstressed syllables often contain / n / or short vowels like / n /. - Remember: function words (articles, prepositions, pronouns, etc.) are often unstressed in speech. Examples in Pairs Word | Pronunciation | Unstressed Syllable about | / nn ba n t/ | a banana | /b nn n nn n n / | ba, na photograph | / n f nn t nn r nn f/ | to, graph together | /t nnnn ð n / | to, er forget | /f nnn et/ | for Summary - Every word has at least one syllable. - Some syllables are stressed; others are unstressed. - Unstressed syllables are softer, shorter, and usually have the schwa sound / n /. - Recognizing them helps improve pronunciation, reading, and listening skills.

title: TREATMENT ON COMMONLY MISSPELT WORDS IN ENGLISH LA
subject: English Language
rawText: TREATMENT OF COMMONLY MISSPELT WORDS IN THE ENGLISH LANGUAGE Meaning of Misspelt Words Misspelt words are words that are incorrectly written or wrongly spelled. They occur when a person writes a word in a way that does not follow its correct spelling form.
