title: INTONATION PATTERN
subject: English Language
rawText:
WEEK 2 TOPIC; MORE PRACTICE WITH INTONATION (LESSON 1) Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice in speech or the variation in speech while speaking. It gives special meaning and emphasis to utterances. FUNCTION OF INTONATION 1. Grammatical function: This is used to differentiate between specific sentence types:- declarative, interrogative, polar questions, etc. when a speaker wants to give information, the falling tone is used. 2. Attitudinal function: The attitude can be that of surprise, doubt, sarcasm, interest, indifference, disbelief, uncertainty. Etc. TYPES OF INTONATION. a. The falling tone b. The rising tone c. The rise and fall tone A. The falling tone: this is used to indicate a fall in the pitch of a speaker’s voice. In writing, a down ward arrow ( ) is a used to show a sentence uttered with the falling tone: USE OF FALLING TONES. 1. To make statements: these are sentences that give information. Example. a. Our teacher is teaching. ↙ b. The students are listening. ↙ 2. To give commands, Example; a. Keep the bag on the table: ↙ b. Get out of this class. ↙ 3. To give advice. Example: a. Do not steal↙ b. Do not accuse anyone falsely↙ 4. Wh – questions. These are questions that begin with adverb of question or interrogative pronouns – whose, what, who, which, when, where, how. Example. a. What is your name? ↙ b. How are you? ↙ 5. To make exclamations, Examples: a. Oh! I have lost my bag! ↙ b. Alas! He has killed my goat!. 6. Tag questions seeking confirmation. Example: a. You are a member of this class, aren’t you? ↙ b. He is lat today, isn’t he? ↙ 7. For negative statement. Example. a. I didn’t see the man: ↙ b. She is not in the class↙ B. The rising tone: this is used to indicate a rise in the pitch of a speaker’s voice. ( ↗ ). The upward arrow is used to show it in writing. THE USES.

1. It is used in polar questions (questions that demand yes or no answers). Examples. a. Is this your book? ↗ b. Have you eaten food today? ↗ 2. For polite request. Example. a. Can she go now? ↗ b. May I use your car, please? ↗ 3. For greeting. Example. a. Good morning, sir. ↗ b. Good evening, Mr. Dada↗ 4. To indicate uncertainty. Example. a. Will John come to school tomorrow? ↗ 5. For incomplete state. Example: a. When I was a student…↗ b. If Aisha had travelled to London…↗ 6. It is used for normal farewell. Example. a. Good bye. ↗ C. The rise and fall tone; THIS tone is used in making a list of items. The voice pitch begins to rise on each of the items listed while the last items receive a falling tone. Example a. One, ↗ two, ↗three, ↗four, ↗and five ↙ b. I bought fish, ↗ pepper, ↗ maggi, ↗ meat ↗ and oil↙. ASSIGNMENT: Identify the tone in the sentences below: 1. I have nothing to say 2. Who are you 3. How are you? 4. The chickens have all grown 5. You are late aren’t you 6. Go and buy bread, sugar, butter 7. Did you see them? 8. Why are they here? 9. What a terrible accident? 10. I was trying to cycle up the hill. TOPIC: INTONATION PRACTICE – USING QUESTION TAG . Tag question is a type of question often found at the end of a statement. It is used to change a statement or sentence to a question when it is added. Tag question is a common device in conversation which is aimed at making a statement and at one ask this listener to confirm it. It consist of an operator and a pronoun. Before we talk about the rules guiding the use of tag questions. We say that positive affirmative statement is a statement without ‘not’, or ‘never’ in its verb element. Example: He is early this morning. A negative statement is the one which has ‘no’, ‘not, or never in its verb element. Example: He isn’t early this morning Rules guiding the use of tag questions are: 1. Positive statement attract negative question tag. Example:

a. We are right, aren’t we? b. She is going, isn’t she? 2. Negative statement attracts positive question tag. Example: a. He is not here, is he? b. You are not hungry, are you? 3. The auxiliary or helping verbs repeat themselves in the tag. Example: a. He has finished the work, hasn’t he? b. She will sing on Sunday, won’t she? 4. Other verbs (main or lexical) use ‘do’ in the tag. Example: a. The girl cried bitterly, didn’t she? b. You don’t care about her, do you?: 5. The subject in the tag is always a pronoun. Example: a. Musa didn’t do that, did he? b. The sun is bright, isn’t it? 6. The positive forms ‘need’ and ‘dare’ are rarely used in the affirmative with question tags, but when so used, they are treated as full or main verb. Example: a. You need to come early don’t you 7. “I am” usually has the tag “aren’t I “ and “ used to” has a question tag with “did”. a. I am your friend aren’t I b. She used to take care of the poultry, didn’t she? ASSIGNMENT: Read the following statement and add the appropriate tags question. 1. He is early this morning ……………….. 2. The president has done very well,……………………….. 3. Lagos isn’t a clean city,…………………… 4. I am not so fat,…………….. 5. She drives too fast,……………………………… 6. He cannot climb the palm tree,……………………. 7. You can swim well,…………………………………….. 8. You won’t be late,………………………………………. 9. He needs to do it,……………………………………… 10. She sang well,………………………………………….. REGISTER OF MOTOR VEHICLE (LESSON 2). Road transport is a system of carrying people and loads from one place to another using vehicles. TYPES OF MOTOR VEHICLES . Cars, lorries, buses, trailers, pickup, van, station wagons, sport car, jeep, etc. EXERNAL PARTS OF MOTOR VEHICLES : Side mirror, door, boot, spare tyre, door handle, wiper, brake light, exhaust pipe, petro cap, bumper, bonnet, number plate, head light, trafficator, tyre, windscreen. Etc. INTERIOR PART.

Dashboard, horn, speedometer, ignition, fuel gauge, C.D player, airbag, heater, steering wheel, brake, clutch, gear stick, seat belt, radiator, engine, etc. WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH THE ROAD. Highway, main-road, ring-road, T-junction, cross-road, roundabout, toll-gate, sharp bend, road side narrow bridge, traffic light, etc. VERBS USED WITH MOTOR VEHICHLES. pages.text: WEEK 2 TOPIC; MORE PRACTICE WITH INTONATION (LESSON 1) Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice in speech or the variation in speech while speaking. It gives special meaning and emphasis to utterances. FUNCTION OF INTONATION 1. Grammatical function: This is used to differentiate between specific sentence types:- declarative, interrogative, polar questions, etc. when a speaker wants to give information, the falling tone is used. 2. Attitudinal function: The attitude can be that of surprise, doubt, sarcasm, interest, indifference, disbelief, uncertainty. Etc. TYPES OF INTONATION. a. The falling tone b. The rising tone c. The rise and fall tone A. The falling tone: this is used to indicate a fall in the pitch of a speaker’s voice. In writing, a down ward arrow ( ) is a used to show a sentence uttered with the falling tone: USE OF FALLING TONES. 1. To make statements: these are sentences that give information. Example. a. Our teacher is teaching. ↙ b. The students are listening. ↙ 2. To give commands, Example; a. Keep the bag on the table: ↙ b. Get out of this class. ↙ 3. To give advice. Example: a. Do not steal↙ b. Do not accuse anyone falsely↙ 4. Wh – questions. These are questions that begin with adverb of question or interrogative pronouns – whose, what, who, which, when, where, how. Example. a. What is your name? ↙ b. How are you? ↙ 5. To make exclamations, Examples: a. Oh! I have lost my bag! ↙ b. Alas! He has killed my goat!. 6. Tag questions seeking confirmation. Example: a. You are a member of this class, aren’t you? ↙ b. He is lat today, isn’t he? ↙ 7. For negative statement. Example. a. I didn’t see the man: ↙ b. She is not in the class↙ B. The rising tone: this is used to indicate a rise in the pitch of a speaker’s voice. ( ↗ ). The upward arrow is used to show it in writing. THE USES.

1. It is used in polar questions (questions that demand yes or no answers). Examples. a. Is this your book? ↗ b. Have you eaten food today? ↗ 2. For polite request. Example. a. Can she go now? ↗ b. May I use your car, please? ↗ 3. For greeting. Example. a. Good morning, sir. ↗ b. Good evening, Mr. Dada↗ 4. To indicate uncertainty. Example. a. Will John come to school tomorrow? ↗ 5. For incomplete state. Example: a. When I was a student…↗ b. If Aisha had travelled to London…↗ 6. It is used for normal farewell. Example. a. Good bye. ↗ C. The rise and fall tone; THIS tone is used in making a list of items. The voice pitch begins to rise on each of the items listed while the last items receive a falling tone. Example a. One, ↗ two, ↗three, ↗four, ↗and five ↙ b. I bought fish, ↗ pepper, ↗ maggi, ↗ meat ↗ and oil↙. ASSIGNMENT: Identify the tone in the sentences below: 1. I have nothing to say 2. Who are you 3. How are you? 4. The chickens have all grown 5. You are late aren’t you 6. Go and buy bread, sugar, butter 7. Did you see them? 8. Why are they here? 9. What a terrible accident? 10. I was trying to cycle up the hill. TOPIC: INTONATION PRACTICE – USING QUESTION TAG . Tag question is a type of question often found at the end of a statement. It is used to change a statement or sentence to a question when it is added. Tag question is a common device in conversation which is aimed at making a statement and at one ask this listener to confirm it. It consist of an operator and a pronoun. Before we talk about the rules guiding the use of tag questions. We say that positive affirmative statement is a statement without ‘not’, or ‘never’ in its verb element. Example: He is early this morning. A negative statement is the one which has ‘no’, ‘not, or never in its verb element. Example: He isn’t early this morning Rules guiding the use of tag questions are: 1. Positive statement attract negative question tag. Example:

a. We are right, aren’t we? b. She is going, isn’t she? 2. Negative statement attracts positive question tag. Example: a. He is not here, is he? b. You are not hungry, are you? 3. The auxiliary or helping verbs repeat themselves in the tag. Example: a. He has finished the work, hasn’t he? b. She will sing on Sunday, won’t she? 4. Other verbs (main or lexical) use ‘do’ in the tag. Example: a. The girl cried bitterly, didn’t she? b. You don’t care about her, do you?: 5. The subject in the tag is always a pronoun. Example: a. Musa didn’t do that, did he? b. The sun is bright, isn’t it? 6. The positive forms ‘need’ and ‘dare’ are rarely used in the affirmative with question tags, but when so used, they are treated as full or main verb. Example: a. You need to come early don’t you 7. “I am” usually has the tag “aren’t I “ and “ used to” has a question tag with “did”. a. I am your friend aren’t I b. She used to take care of the poultry, didn’t she? ASSIGNMENT: Read the following statement and add the appropriate tags question. 1. He is early this morning ……………….. 2. rawText: Types of essay are: a. Narrative essay b. Descriptive essay c. Argumentative essay d. Expository essay e. Letter writing How to approach essay wring 1. Gather ideas by writing outline 2. Organize the ideas/ outline 3. Develop the ideas (must be in paragraphs) 4. Revise the ideas (to correct errors) 5. Ideas should not be lumped into a single paragraph. Linking words like: moreover, furthermore, again, in addition, ETC should be used to start a new paragraph. Assessing an essay 1. Content : the ideas presented must be relevant to the central theme. 2. title: COMPREHENSION / SUMMARY
subject: English Language
rawText:
1. Define Descriptive Essay and Explain Its Purpose A descriptive essay is a type of writing that gives a clear, detailed, and vivid description of a person, place, object, event, or experience. It uses words to paint a picture in the reader’s mind. Purpose: To help the reader imagine and feel what the writer is describing. To make writing lively and interesting. To express emotions, impressions, and atmosphere. 2. Identify the Features of Descriptive Essays A good descriptive essay has the following features: Vivid details: precise and specific description (e.g., “a tall, dark palm tree swaying in the wind”). Sensory language: appeals to the five senses – sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Figurative expressions: similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole, etc. Coherence and unity: ideas are well-organized and flow logically. Strong impression: leaves a lasting mental image on the reader. Point of view: written in first person (“I saw...”) or third person (“He walked...”), depending on the situation. 3. Use Appropriate Vocabulary and Figures of Speech in Descriptive Writing Adjectives & Adverbs: “shiny,” “gloomy,” “softly,” “brightly.” Simile: comparing with “like” or “as” → “The sky was as red as fire.” Metaphor: direct comparison → “Her smile was sunshine.” Personification: giving human qualities to non-human things → “The wind whispered through the trees.” Onomatopoeia: words that imitate sounds → “buzz,” “clang,” “whisper.”

4. Organize and Write a Short Descriptive Essay on a Given Topic Example Topic: A Rainy Day The morning sky was covered with thick, gray clouds. The air smelled of wet earth as the first drops of rain began to fall. Soon, heavy sheets of water poured down, drumming loudly on the rooftops. Children splashed happily in puddles, while cars moved slowly on the flooded streets. The cool breeze brushed against my face, and I felt refreshed, as if nature had washed away the heat and dust of the previous days. Topic sentence: introduces the subject (The morning sky was covered with thick, gray clouds.) Supporting details: sensory descriptions (smell of wet earth, sound of rain, sight of puddles). Concluding sentence: leaves an impression (I felt refreshed, as if nature had washed away the heat and dust.)

title: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH LAW AND ORDER
subject: English Language
rawText: Words Associated With Law And Order Law: this is the whole system of rules that everyone in a country or society must obey. Words associated with law and order Accused acquit adjournment Alibi appeal arrest Bail cell evidence Gaol guilty handcuff Imprison judge judgement Jury client closing speech Contempt of court convict court-martial Courtroom criminal cross-examine Defendant lawyer magistrate Perjury plaintiff sentence Solicitor summons verdict 1. Alibi : evidence that proves that a person was in another place at the time of a crime and so could not have committed it. 2. Gaol / jailer : a person in charge of a prison. 3. Court-martial: a military court that deals with members of the armed forces who break military law. 4. Plaintiff: a person who makes who makes a formal complaint against somebody in a court of law. 5. Defendant : the person in a court of law who is accused of committing a crime. 6. Perjury : the crime of telling a lie in a court of law. 7. Solicitor : a lawyer who prepares legal documents and advises people on legal matters and can speak for them in some courts of law.

title: REPORT WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText: Report writing Report writing : this is any type of account of an event that has taken place. Types of report 1. Formal report : this is a document which can be used as a reference in future. This could be a report of an accident, burglary, armed robbery or other crimes, meeting proceedings or minutes, training session or workshop, conference or seminar or even a crusade. A formal report should contain the following details: a. The writer’s name b. The writer’s address c. Nationality or tribe d. Religion e. Age The report text should begin with a formal heading (title). example: “A Report of an Armed Robbery Incident in Hostel A on 5 th March, 2018.” Having written the title, proceed to give an account of what happened. A formal report should contain the time of the incident, place, names of actors and witnesses if possible. At the end of the report, the writer should write his name, append his signature, date of the report and address. Informal Report : this merely recounts an experience or an incident unofficially. Any report that is not for official use is informal.

title: CONTINUOUS WRITING
subject: English Language
rawText:
1. Define Descriptive Essay and Explain Its Purpose A descriptive essay is a type of writing that gives a clear, detailed, and vivid description of a person, place, object, event, or experience. It uses words to paint a picture in the reader’s mind. Purpose: To help the reader imagine and feel what the writer is describing. To make writing lively and interesting. To express emotions, impressions, and atmosphere. 2. Identify the Features of Descriptive Essays A good descriptive essay has the following features: Vivid details: precise and specific description (e.g., “a tall, dark palm tree swaying in the wind”). Sensory language: appeals to the five senses – sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Figurative expressions: similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole, etc. Coherence and unity: ideas are well-organized and flow logically. Strong impression: leaves a lasting mental image on the reader. Point of view: written in first person (“I saw...”) or third person (“He walked...”), depending on the situation. 3. Use Appropriate Vocabulary and Figures of Speech in Descriptive Writing Adjectives & Adverbs: “shiny,” “gloomy,” “softly,” “brightly.” Simile: comparing with “like” or “as” → “The sky was as red as fire.” Metaphor: direct comparison → “Her smile was sunshine.” Personification: giving human qualities to non-human things → “The wind whispered through the trees.” Onomatopoeia: words that imitate sounds → “buzz,” “clang,” “whisper.”

4. Organize and Write a Short Descriptive Essay on a Given Topic Example Topic: A Rainy Day The morning sky was covered with thick, gray clouds. The air smelled of wet earth as the first drops of rain began to fall. Soon, heavy sheets of water poured down, drumming loudly on the rooftops. Children splashed happily in puddles, while cars moved slowly on the flooded streets. The cool breeze brushed against my face, and I felt refreshed, as if nature had washed away the heat and dust of the previous days. Topic sentence: introduces the subject (The morning sky was covered with thick, gray clouds.) Supporting details: sensory descriptions (smell of wet earth, sound of rain, sight of puddles). Concluding sentence: leaves an impression (I felt refreshed, as if nature had washed away the heat and dust.)

title: TYPES OF SENTENCES
subject: English Language
rawText:
*TYPES OF SENTENCE ACCORDING TO STRUCTURE* This is the classification of sentences according to their grammatical structures. *SIMPLE SENTENCE:* This is a kind of sentence with one main verb. It consists of one subject and one predicate and makes a single thought. It may possess auxiliary verbs but has only one main verb. *Study these:* She travelled to Akure. I was left with no one at home. The captain of the team elected by the coaching crew scored a goal at the last match. The above sentences have one main verb each, which are underlined respectively. *COMPOUND SENTENCE:* This is a kind of sentence that is made up of two simple sentence joined with a coordinating conjunction – and, but, yet, or, etc. It possesses two subjects and two predicates joining the two thoughts. *Study these:* a. John likes mangoes. b. Mark likes oranges. Sentences (a) and (b) are simple sentences but can be joined with a coordinating conjunction. John likes mangoes but Mark likes oranges *More examples:* a. They told him but he did not believe. b. She saw her mother and her brother arrive. *When the subjects are the same, the second subject is usually omitted but when they differ, they are both written.* c. The boy came home. d. The boy washed his clothes Joining them to form a compound sentence, it will be written thus: *The boy came home and washed his clothes.* *3. COMPLEX SENTENCE:* lt is a kind of sentence with one simple sentence and one or more subordinate clause joined with a subordinating conjunction – when, after, while, where, immediately, because, etc.

*Study these:* a. I met the girl when she was crying b. He was dismissed because of his fraudulent acts. c. After he arrived, Bode came to see me because he needed some money. The underline words are the main or simple sentences, while the ones not underlined are the subordinate clauses. 4. *COMPOUND COMPLEX SENTENCE:* This is a kind of sentence with two or more simple sentences and one or more subordinate clauses. It has more than one simple sentence with one or more than one subordinate clause. *Study these:* a. The boy is fluent and brilliant because he attends a private school. b. The boy came to then stream and washed his clothes because it was dirty. c. The man shot at the bird, he fried it but he was unable to eat it because he felt sick after he left the farm. *Note that a simple sentence differs not from a main clause.* S

title: MORE ON CONSONANT SOUNDS
subject: English Language
rawText:
MORE ON CONSONANT SOUNDS A consonant sound is a speech sound made when the air coming from the lungs is partly or completely blocked by the lips, teeth, or tongue. Examples: /p/ as in pen, /t/ as in top, /m/ as in man. English Language has twenty- four (24) consonant sounds, divided into fifteen (15) voiced and none(9) voiceless depending on whether the vocal cords vibrate. Each sound has unique features and examples. Examples of Consonant Sounds, place and manner of articulation and words they can be found. 1. /p/ – Voiceless Bilabial Plosive Formed by closing both lips and releasing a puff of air. Examples: pen, pig, park, cap, paper, push, pick, please, apple, pepper 2. /b/ – Voiced Bilabial Plosive Same as /p/ but with vibration of the vocal cords. Examples: bat, bag, big, cab, baby, ball, boat, buy, job, table 3. /t/ – Voiceless Alveolar Plosive Tongue touches alveolar ridge, then air is released. Examples: top, tea, ten, cat, table, toy, take, time, letter, butter 4. /d/ – Voiced Alveolar Plosive Like /t/ but with vibration. Examples: dog, day, door, bed, desk, do, red, sand, hand, daddy 5. /k/ – Voiceless Velar Plosive Back of tongue touches soft palate. Examples: cat, car, key, come, cook, cake, kick, cold, king, school 6. /g/ – Voiced Velar Plosive Same as /k/ but with vibration. Examples: go, game, good, gate, gold, garden, bag, egg, green, girl 7. /f/ – Voiceless Labiodental Fricative

Lower lip touches upper teeth, air pushed out. Examples: fan, food, fish, five, face, fall, foot, fun, phone, coffee 8. /v/ – Voiced Labiodental Fricative Same as /f/ but with vibration. Examples: van, very, voice, video, vase, village, love, move, give, drive 9. /θ/ – Voiceless Dental Fricative (as in thin) Tongue between teeth, air released without vibration. Examples: think, thin, thank, three, throw, bath, both, mouth, tooth, Thursday 10. /ð/ – Voiced Dental Fricative (as in this) Same as /θ/ but with vibration. Examples: this, that, then, there, they, though, those, mother, father, brother 11. /s/ – Voiceless Alveolar Fricative Air passes between tongue and alveolar ridge. Examples: sit, sun, see, six, sing, soap, salt, sad, sister, boss 12. /z/ – Voiced Alveolar Fricative Same as /s/ but with vibration. Examples: zoo, zebra, zero, zip, busy, nose, rise, easy, music, cousin 13. / ʃ / – Voiceless Palato-Alveolar Fricative (as in she) Air passes through tongue and palate, creating “sh” sound. Examples: she, shop, shoe, fish, ship, short, show, sheep, shine, sugar 14. / ʒ / – Voiced Palato-Alveolar Fricative (as in measure) Voiced version of / ʃ /. Examples: measure, pleasure, treasure, vision, television, usual, leisure, garage, regime, beige 15. /h/ – Voiceless Glottal Fricative Air passes freely through the glottis.

Examples: hat, home, hot, head, happy, house, help, hair, hill, hope 16. /t ʃ / – Voiceless Palato-Alveolar Affricate (as in church) Combination of /t/ and / ʃ /. Examples: chair, cheese, child, church, chin, catch, watch, choose, rich, teacher 17. /d ʒ / – Voiced Palato-Alveolar Affricate (as in jam) Combination of /d/ and / ʒ /. Examples: jam, job, joy, judge, June, juice, jeep, jungle, bridge, edge 18. /m/ – Voiced Bilabial Nasal Air escapes through nose, lips closed. Examples: man, map, me, my, mother, make, moon, name, game, time 19. /n/ – Voiced Alveolar Nasal Air passes through nose, tongue touches alveolar ridge. Examples: no, net, nice, nine, nose, name, pen, run, sun, ten 20. /ŋ/ – Voiced Velar Nasal (as in sing) Back of tongue touches velum, air escapes through nose. Examples: sing, song, long, king, ring, bring, wing, hang, thing, strong 21. /l/ – Voiced Alveolar Lateral Air passes along sides of tongue. Examples: leg, look, light, love, long, little, lamp, land, leaf, ball 22. /r/ – Voiced Post-Alveolar Approximant Tongue slightly curls back, air flows freely. Examples: red, run, read, right, road, rain, ring, rose, river, rice 23. /j/ – Voiced Palatal Approximant (as in yes) Tongue raised near hard palate. Examples: yes, you, yellow, young, year, yesterday, yogurt, yard, use, yam

24. /w/ – Voiced Bilabial-Velar Approximant Lips rounded, tongue near velum. Examples: we, win, wall, water, way, woman, wood, wait, word, west

This difference is shown by keeping the tongue longer in the same position for the pronunciation of /i:/ than you will do for the pronunciation of /i/. /i/ /i:/ Sit Seat Rid Read Fit Feet bid bead did deed dip deep Lip Leap pretty people Some people tend to pronounce the long /a:/ as if it is the short /ae/ but the difference between the two vowels is clearly illustrated in the following pair of words: /ae/ /a:/ ban barn cat Cart pat Part hat heart bat bath As Ask pack park

title: SPEECH
subject: English Language
rawText: Meaning of Consonant Contrasts Consonant contrasts refer to differences between consonant sounds in words that cause a change in meaning. When one consonant sound in a word is replaced with another, the meaning of the word changes. Meaning of Minimal Pairs Minimal pairs are pairs of words that differ by only one consonant sound in the same position and have different meanings. Examples of Minimal Pairs (Consonant Contrasts) kit / kid → /t/ and /d/ leaf / leave → /f/ and /v/ feats / feeds → /s/ and /z/ ferry / very → /f/ and /v/ bat / pat → /b/ and /p/ fan / van → /f/ and /v/ sip / zip → /s/ and /z/ rice / rise → /r/ and /z/ Voiced and Voiceless Consonants Voiced consonants are produced with vibration of the vocal cords. Examples: /b/, /d/, /g/, /v/, /z/ Voiceless consonants are produced without vibration of the vocal cords. Examples: /p/, /t/, /k/, /f/, /s/ Importance of Consonant Contrasts Helps in correct pronunciation of words. Prevents misunderstanding in communication. Improves spoken English. Helps students perform better in oral English examinations (WAEC/NECO).

subject: English Language
rawText:
STUDENTS’ SUMMARY NOTE Topic: Four Consonant Words at the Final Position 1. Definition Some English words end with four consonants in a row. These are often tricky to pronounce and require careful articulation. 2. Examples of Words sixths glimpsed prompt tempts twelfths strengths glimpsed glimpsed 3. Pronunciation Tips Break the word into individual sounds: e.g., sixths → /sɪk-sθs/ Emphasize each consonant at the end. Practice slowly first, then increase speed. 4. Use in Sentences “She counted the sixths carefully.” “He glimpsed the answer in the book.” “The prompt reply impressed the teacher.” “She tempts him to join the team.” 5. Importance Correct pronunciation improves speech clarity.

Helps in reading, speaking, and effective communication.

title: INTONATION PATERN
subject: English Language
rawText:
INTONATION PATTERN (THE RISING PITCH) Intonation can be defined simply as the variation in the pitch level of the voice. That is, rising and falling of the pitch level of the voices when communication is made. Intonation gives meaning to the utterance and interpretation of the spoken sentence Types of intonation 1. Rising tune 2. Falling tune Rising tune is identified when there is rise in the level of pitch when communication is made rising tune is commonly used for; Incomplete sentence or statement or when one expresses incomplete statement. Examples  If you come (I will tell you the secret)  When I was serving (tony arrived from Lagos)  As soon as the rain stops (the visitors will leave)  Since the cost of books has risen (we buy less) 1) Yes or no question – these are questions to which the answer ‘yes’ or ‘no’ can be given. Examples  Is your name Musa?  Did the Governor visit our school?  Will you attend my birthday party?  Have you watched the latest film? 2) When making a list of items or objects. Examples  The woman went to the market and brought some food stuff, rice, beans, yam, semolina, and plantain  He needs some rice , beans , fish , and meat.  one , two , three , and four 3) To show warm personal interest Examples  You mean your sister has travelled to England.  Beautiful, you have seven distinctions in your exams. 4) To make request. Examples  Could you give me a ride to the gate? (request)  Could you tell me the time, please? (request)  Do you mind giving me a ride to the bookshop (request) 5) To ask for permission Example  Can I use your other pen (Permission)  Can I ride your bicycle (Permission)

title: GRAMMATICAL NAMES
subject: English Language

pages.text: GRAMMATICAL NAMES AND FUNCTION. Grammatical function is set as type of comprehension question where students are expected to name a structure and its function in a sentence. They are usually set on parts of speech. Example ; noun, adverb and adjectives. They are equally in form of a phrase or a clause. A phrase is a group of words forming parts of a larger sentence but without a finite verb. A phrase may also contain a non-finite verb. Example; I met him on his way to the school. Leaving the school without permission is prohibited. To succeed in our studies is our determination. A clause is a group of words forming parts of a larger sentence and having a subject and a predicate of its own. A clause also contains a finite verb. Examples; I saw him when I was going to the market yesterday. The man who came here yesterday is my brother. He left the room when he saw his mother coming. A. Grammatical names and Function a noun clause 1. As a subject of a verb - a noun clause is the subject of a verb when it proceeds (comes before) the verb in the main clause. Example: 1. How he escaped police arrest surprises everybody. (How he escaped police arrest is the subject of the verb surprise in the main clause.) 2. That death is inevitable remains an indisputable fact. (That death is inevitable is the subject of the verb remains in the main clause.) 3. When we shall meet again is known by God alone. (When we shall meet again is the subject of the verb is known.) 4. What you said led to the sudden disappearance of the girl. (What you said is the subject of the verb led in the main clause.) 5. Where the woman lives is close to her office. (Where the woman lives is the subject of the verb is in the main clause.) 2. As the object of a verb- when a noun clause comes immediately after the verb in the main clause, it is the object of that verb. Example;

GRAMMATICAL NAMES AND FUNCTION. 1. The Lady thought that the man would marry her. (That the man would marry her is the object of the verb thought in the main clause.) 2. She does what everybody likes. (What everybody likes is the object of the verb does in the main clause.) 3. The woman narrated how she escaped the assassination attempt. (How she escaped assassination attempt is the object of the verb narrated in the main clause.) 4. I do not know if he will come. (If he will come is the object of the verb do not know.) 5. We all know when the presidents will arrive. (When the president will arrive is the object of the verb ‘know’ in the main clause.) B. Adjectival/ Relative Clause 1. The man whose children were expelled came to see the principal. (Whose children were expelled qualified the noun man in the main clause.) 2. The room where we normally keep money has been broken into. (Where we normally keep our money qualifies the noun room in the main clause.) 3. The time when we go out for break is now 12:00 o'clock. (When we go out for break qualified the noun time in the main clause.) 4. The books which my father brought are for my younger brother. (Which my father brought qualifies the noun books in the main clause.) 5. The boy whom we met two days ago is very intelligent. (Whom we met two days ago qualifies the noun the boy in the main clause.) C. Adverbial clause 1. Adverbial clause of time - it answers the question ‘when’ and is often introduced by ‘while’, ‘since’, ‘after’, ‘when’, ‘as’, ‘before’, ‘until’, ‘during’, ‘whenever’, ‘till’, ‘as soon as’, ‘immediately’, etc... Example 1. She eats whenever he is hungry. (Whenever she is hungry modifies the verb eats in the main clause.) 2. The woman addressed us after we had taken our breakfast. (After we had taken our breakfast modified the verb addressed in the main clause.) 3. He takes his bath before he goes to bed. (Before he goes to bed modifies the verb takes in the main clause.) 4. The program started as soon as the chairman arrived. (As soon as the chairman arrived modifies the verb started in the main clause.) 5. The man met his wife while she was cooking. (While she was cooking modifies the verb met in the main clause.)

GRAMMATICAL NAMES AND FUNCTION. 2. Adverbial clause of place - It answers the question ‘where’ and is introduced by where, wherever, anywhere, everywhere, nowhere. Examples 1. He eats anywhere he sees food. (Anywhere he sees food modifies the verb eats in the main clause.) 2. The boy beats the girl wherever he sees her. (Wherever he sees her modifies the verb beats in the main clause.) 3. She kept the books where they could be seen. (Where they could be seen modifies the verb kept in the main clause.) 4. He plays his guitar everywhere people gather. (Everywhere people gather modifies the verb plays in the main clause.) 3. Adverbial clause of reason -It answers the question ‘why’ and it's often introduced by because, since, for, as, seeing that, in that, etc... Examples; 1. The teacher punished the students because he came late to class. (because he came late to class modifies the verb punished in the main clause.) 2. She gave him the job seeing that he was desperate. (seeing that he was desperate modifies the verb gave in the main clause.) 3. Mrs. Bisi pets Ann as she is the youngest of all her children. (as she is the youngest of all her children modifies the verb pets in the main clause.)

title: READING FOR IMPLIED MEANING
subject: English Language
rawText: READING FOR IMPLIED MEANING. Comprehension is reading and understanding a given passage. When proper understanding has been achieved, then, comprehension has taken place. It is also reading a given passage and responding to it positively by answering the questions. Reading for implied meaning means deducing from the passage we read. When information is not stated openly, we may guess, assume, conclude or infer meaning from it. We use the expressions such as those below to say that based on our observations, even when a fact has not been pronounced, we can get the underlying meaning. We use expressions such as……  It means that…  We can, then, say that …  We can deduce that…  This suggests…  It implies…  We can conclude…. Example; A bank manager asks his driver to pull up the car beside a man who was ushering passengers into a bus (a bus conductor). The conductor was this money just class meet in secondary school about 20 years ago. Question;  Why did the manager become a manager and the bus conductor a bus conductor?  The teacher allows the students to answer the questions to follow it.

title: INTONATION PATERN
subject: English Language
rawText: INTONATION PATERN (THE FALLING TUNE) Intonation can be defined simply as the variation in the pitch level of the voice. That is, rising and falling of the pitch level of the voices when communication is made. Intonation gives meaning to the utterance and interpretation of the spoken sentence Types of intonation 1) Rising tone 2) Falling tone Falling tone Falling tone is indicated when the level of pitch comes down when communication is made. It can be identified through A. Declarative statement. Examples:  We are studying English.  He has left for the month.  His parents have bought a new house.  Our friends will arrive today. B. To express command. Examples  Go to the principal’s office at once!  Stand at attention!  Sit down there!  Get out of my office! C. To express ‘wh’ questions . Examples  What is your name?  Where do your parents live?  Why did you arrive late? D. To express exclamatory expression. Examples  What a lovely picture?  What a lucky man?  This is jackpot? Identifying intonation in connected speech A rising intonation tune may be followed by a falling tune; they are used one after another e.g. 1) I will go home, after my brother has arrived. 2) I love the game, but I am very tired. 3) You may pick it up, but don’t drop it. 4) I’ve met you before, but I don’t remember your name again.
